docs.title: System Design, Step by Step
docs.text:
A free, diagram-first handbook for system design interviews and for building real systems.

Most resources show you a finished architecture and expect you to memorize it. This one shows how you get there: start with the simplest design that works, calculate where it breaks, fix only that, and repeat. Every page has hand-drawn diagrams you can open and edit in Excalidraw.

Tip

New here? Start here has a learning path for your level, from intermediate to staff, with checkpoints. Every page is marked Beginner-friendly, Intermediate or Advanced, and you can hover over technical terms for a definition, or look them up in the glossary.

docs.title: What's inside
docs.text: Section What you get Start here Learning paths for intermediate, senior and staff engineers Foundations The basics of how requests flow, the method, non-functional requirements and the numbers to know System Design 101 25 one-screen explainers: protocols, API styles, HTTPS, auth, retries, circuit breakers, deploys, SQL vs NoSQL, replication, queues vs streams, outbox Core concepts Networking, API design, data modeling, indexing, caching, sharding, consistent hashing, CAP 7 patterns Scaling reads and writes, real-time updates, contention, multi-step processes, large blobs, long-running tasks Technologies Postgres, Redis, Kafka, Cassandra, DynamoDB, Elasticsearch, Flink, ZooKeeper, API gateways: when and when not 29 problems URL shortener to payments, each from v1 to final design with an interview script DDIA, chapter by chapter All 12 chapters of Designing Data-Intensive Applications as diagrams, tied to interview problems Computer Networking All 8 chapters of Kurose & Ross's Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach as diagrams, from HTTP and DNS down to Wi-Fi, tied to system design Operating Systems The OS ideas behind real system behaviour: threads vs event loops, latency vs utilisation, page cache and GC pauses, fsync and group commit, SSDs, container limits Low-level design File system, movie booking, logger, inventory: class diagrams and tested Java Interview playbook The 45-minute framework, what senior answers sound like, quick-fire practice Staff-level answers Senior vs staff, and all 29 problems through a staff lens (interactive atlas) Sketchnotes 59 dense hand-drawn pages, one per topic, for revision and printing Slide decks Three interactive decks for review and out-loud rehearsal Glossary Plain-language definitions of 100+ terms

docs.title: Pick your path
docs.text: If you want to… Do this Learn system design Follow the intermediate path: basics, core concepts, three patterns, then eight problems in order, with checkpoints. Prepare for an interview in two weeks Read the playbook, then do two problems a day: read the page, then rehearse it with the interview deck. Know how deep to go Read What's expected at each level: the same problem answered at mid-level, senior, staff and principal. Interviewing for staff or above Read Staff-level answers, then use the staff atlas to rehearse all 29 problems at that level. Understand the theory Read the DDIA pages alongside the book; every chapter ends with how it shows up in interviews. Review the night before Flip through the sketchnotes, starting with the interview cheat sheet, then do the quick-fire questions.

docs.title: Every problem page has the same shape
docs.text:
1. TL;DR: three lines you could say out loud.
  2. Requirements: functional, then non-functional with numbers.
  3. Back-of-envelope numbers: only the ones that change the design.
  4. Core entities and API
  5. v1, and where it breaks
  6. The final design, step by step, with why each part exists
  7. Deep dives: the questions interviewers push on
  8. Interview script: what to do in each part of 45 minutes
  9. Common mistakes and related pages

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
• Website: searchable, with dark mode and mobile layout.
  • GitHub: every page is plain Markdown that renders in the repository.
  • Sketchnotes: one hand-drawn page per topic, also as a printable PDF.
  • Slides: three interactive decks that work offline.
  • PDF: the whole handbook in one file for printing or reading offline.
  • Editable diagrams: every diagram has an .excalidraw source next to its .svg.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Fixes and new pages are welcome. See CONTRIBUTING for the page template and how to edit diagrams.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: Written in our own words, with our own diagrams. The DDIA pages are study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann; please read the book. The Computer Networking pages are study notes on Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach by James Kurose and Keith Ross; please read that book too. The Operating Systems pages follow the themes of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau, free online. Diagrams use the open-source Excalifont (SIL OFL 1.1). Problem names refer to well-known products only to describe the kind of system; this project is not affiliated with any company or course.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Thanks for helping. Two rules keep this handbook useful:

  1. Every design starts simple and earns its complexity. Don't add a component without saying which number made it necessary.
  2. Your own words, your own diagrams. Don't paste text or figures from books, courses or blogs. Link to them instead.

docs.title: Run the site locally
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt
mkdocs serve          # http://127.0.0.1:8000

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
Each diagram is defined once in diagrams-src/*.js as a short list of boxes and arrows. One command generates both:

  • docs/diagrams/<name>.svg: the hand-drawn image shown on GitHub and the site.
  • docs/diagrams/<name>.excalidraw: open it at excalidraw.com (Open → choose the file) to tweak the layout by hand.

Hand-written specs live in diagrams-src/*.js; specs generated during the first conversion live in diagrams-src/generated/*.json. Edit either, then rebuild:

npm install
npm run diagrams

docs.title: The PDF
docs.text:
pip install playwright pypdf pyyaml && playwright install chromium
mkdocs build && python scripts/build_pdf.py

This writes docs/downloads/system-design-step-by-step.pdf in navigation order, with bookmarks.

docs.title: Sketchnotes
docs.text:
Each one-page sketchnote is a JSON spec in diagrams-src/sketchnotes/ (panels with text, bullets, highlighted numbers, tables and embedded diagrams). Rebuild them and their PDF with:

node tools/sketchnote.js diagrams-src/sketchnotes docs/sketchnotes
python scripts/build_sketch_pdf.py

Text in each panel shrinks automatically to fit; the tool warns if a panel still overflows.

A diagram should explain one idea. If it needs a paragraph to decode, split it in two.

docs.title: Problem page template
docs.text:
Copy this into docs/problems/<name>.md.

---
title: <Problem name>
description: <one sentence: what makes this problem interesting>
tags: [<pattern>, <difficulty>]
---

# <Problem>: <the hard part, in a few words>

**Difficulty:** · **Patterns:** · **Core concepts:** · **DDIA:**

## TL;DR
- Three bullets you could say out loud.

## 1. Requirements
**Functional:** 3 numbered items. *Out of scope:* …

**Non-functional:**
| NFR | Target | Why it matters here |
|---|---|---|

## 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
Only the numbers that change a decision.

## 3. Core entities and API

## 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
![alt text](../diagrams/<name>-v1.svg)
What v1 is and how one request flows through it.

**Where it breaks:** the specific failure, with a number from section 2.

## 5. Evolving to the final design
![alt text](../diagrams/<name>-final.svg)

### Step 1: <what you add>
**Why:** the problem with the previous step, in plain words.

**How:** how the fix works, step by step, with the key query or command if there is one.

## 6. Deep dives
### <question the interviewer will ask>
**Why it's hard:** what goes wrong with the obvious approach, as a concrete scenario.

**How:** the solution and why it works, plus the trade-off you accept.

## 7. Interview script (45 minutes)
| Time | What you do | What you say |
|---|---|---|

## 8. Common mistakes

## Self-check

<details class="question" markdown>
<summary>A question the reader should be able to answer after this page</summary>

The answer in one or two sentences.

</details>

## Related

Every section must make sense on its own to someone new to the topic: say why the problem happens (a concrete scenario beats an abstract rule) and how the fix works, step by step. Sketchnotes are for revision; they never replace the explanation on the page.

Every page ends with three self-check questions in <details> blocks like the one above. They fold open on the website and on GitHub.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Plain-language definitions of the terms used across the handbook. On the website, hovering over most of these terms on any page shows the definition.

Jump to: Numbers · Requirements · Networking · Correctness · Databases · Distribution · Caching · Messaging · Storage · Reliability · Security · Operating systems

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text: Term Meaning Back-of-envelope estimate A quick, rounded calculation (QPS, storage, bandwidth) used to decide whether a component is needed. DAU Daily active users. Multiply by actions per user and divide by 86,400 to get average requests per second. Latency How long one request takes from start to finish. p50 Median latency: half of requests are faster than this. p99 99th-percentile latency: 1 request in 100 is slower than this. Users feel the tail, so targets are set on p99. QPS Queries (requests) per second. The basic unit of load. Tail latency The slowest small share of requests (p99, p99.9). It grows when one request fans out to many services. Throughput How much work a system completes per second. TPS Transactions per second that a database commits.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Term Meaning Availability The share of time the system answers correctly. Each extra "nine" costs much more. Durability Once data is acknowledged as saved, it is not lost, even after crashes. Error budget How much failure the SLO allows (100% minus the SLO). 99.9% per month is about 43 minutes. NFR Non-functional requirement: how well the system must work (latency, availability, consistency, scale), as opposed to what it does. SLA Service level agreement: an external promise with penalties if missed. SLI Service level indicator: the thing you measure, such as the share of requests faster than 300 ms. SLO Service level objective: your internal target for an SLI, such as 99.9% of requests under 300 ms.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text: Term Meaning Anycast Announcing the same IP prefix from many locations so routing delivers each user to a nearby one. Used by DNS resolvers and CDNs. API gateway The single entry point in front of your services that handles TLS, authentication, rate limiting and routing. ARP Address Resolution Protocol: finds the MAC address for an IP address on the local network by broadcasting a question. Autonomous system A network run by one organisation (an ISP, a cloud) with its own routing policy and AS number; the Internet is tens of thousands of them. BGP Border Gateway Protocol: how autonomous systems tell each other which address blocks they can reach, and choose routes by policy. CDN Content delivery network: servers near users that cache static files and shared responses so requests never reach your origin. CIDR Classless Inter-Domain Routing: writing address blocks as prefix/length (10.0.0.0/16) so routes can cover blocks of any size. Congestion control How TCP slows down when the network is overloaded: it shrinks its sending window on loss and grows it slowly otherwise. CRC Cyclic redundancy check: an error-detecting code added to every Ethernet and Wi-Fi frame. DHCP Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: gives a device joining a network its IP address, gateway and DNS server. DNS Domain Name System: turns a name like example.com into an IP address. ECMP Equal-cost multi-path: spreading flows across several equally good paths by hashing their addresses and ports. GraphQL An API style with one endpoint where the client sends a query naming exactly the fields it wants. gRPC A fast remote-call framework using HTTP/2 and Protobuf, common between internal services. HTTP/2 Binary HTTP that multiplexes many requests as streams over one TCP connection, with header compression. HTTP/3 HTTP over QUIC instead of TCP, so a lost packet only delays its own stream and connections survive network changes. ICMP Internet Control Message Protocol: carries network errors and diagnostics; ping and traceroute use it. ISP Internet service provider: a company that connects homes, businesses or other networks to the Internet. IXP Internet exchange point: a facility where many networks connect directly to exchange traffic. L4 load balancer Spreads TCP connections across servers without reading their content. Very fast; good for long-lived connections. L7 load balancer Reads HTTP requests and routes by path, header or cookie; can terminate TLS and do sticky routing. Long polling The client sends a request that the server holds open until it has news (or a timeout), then the client asks again. Long polling The client asks for updates and the server holds the request open until something arrives. MAC address A 48-bit hardware address that identifies a network card on the local link; frames are delivered by it. NAT Network address translation: a router rewrites private addresses and ports to its public address, so many devices share one IP. OSPF Open Shortest Path First: a link-state routing protocol used inside one network; every router learns the map and runs Dijkstra. Presigned URL A temporary URL that lets a client upload or download one object directly to or from object storage. QUIC A transport protocol on top of UDP with TLS built in, faster connection setup and independent streams. HTTP/3 runs on it. REST An API style built on HTTP resources and verbs (GET, POST…). The default for public APIs. RPC Remote procedure call: calling a function on another machine over the network. RTT Round-trip time: how long a message takes to go to another machine and back. SDN Software-defined networking: a central controller computes forwarding rules and installs them on simple switches. Slow start TCP's start-up phase: the sending window doubles every round trip until loss or a threshold. SSE Server-Sent Events: one long-lived HTTP connection over which the server pushes updates to the client. Stateless service A server that keeps no user data between requests, so any instance can serve any request and you can add more freely. TCP Transmission Control Protocol: a reliable, ordered byte stream between two machines, with a handshake to open it. Used by HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and most databases. TLS The encryption behind HTTPS. UDP User Datagram Protocol: sends independent packets with no handshake, ordering or retransmission. Used for DNS, video calls, games and QUIC. VLAN Virtual LAN: tags frames so one physical switch acts as several separate local networks. Webhook An HTTP callback: when an event happens, the provider POSTs it to a URL you registered, instead of you polling. WebSocket A long-lived two-way connection between client and server, for chat, games and collaboration.

docs.title: Correctness
docs.text: Term Meaning At-least-once Every message is delivered, but some may arrive twice. Pair it with idempotent processing. Check-then-act Reading a condition and then acting on it as two steps. Two requests can both pass the check; the classic race. Cursor pagination Paging with a pointer to the last item seen instead of an offset, so new items don't shift pages. Exactly-once In practice "effectively once": at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, so duplicates have no effect. Idempotency key A unique ID the client sends with a request so the server can recognise and ignore duplicates. Idempotent Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once, so retries are safe. Race condition A bug where the result depends on the timing of concurrent operations.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text: Term Meaning ACID Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the guarantees of a database transaction. B-tree The default index structure: a shallow sorted tree of pages. Fast lookups and range scans. Column store A database that stores each column separately, so analytics read only the columns they need. Conditional update An UPDATE whose WHERE clause includes the condition (e.g. status = AVAILABLE), so the check and the write happen atomically. Denormalization Copying data into several places to make a hot read cheaper, at the cost of keeping copies in sync. fsync Forcing data from memory to disk so it survives a crash. Each commit waits for it, which limits single-row write rates. GSI Global secondary index (DynamoDB): an index partitioned separately from the table; updated asynchronously. Index A sorted lookup structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Isolation level How much concurrent transactions are shielded from each other (Read Committed, Snapshot, Serializable). Lost update Two read-modify-write cycles overlap and one overwrites the other's change. LSM-tree Log-structured merge tree: writes go to memory and are flushed to sorted files that are merged later. Very fast writes; used by Cassandra and RocksDB. MVCC Multi-version concurrency control: rows keep several versions so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers. Normalization Storing each fact once and referring to it by ID, so updates happen in one place. OLAP Online analytical processing: large scans and aggregations, as in dashboards and warehouses. OLTP Online transaction processing: many small reads and writes by key, as in an app database. Optimistic locking Allow concurrent work; at write time check a version number and retry if it changed. Good for low contention. Pessimistic locking Lock rows before changing them (SELECT … FOR UPDATE). Good for high contention on few rows. Transaction A group of reads and writes that succeed or fail together. WAL Write-ahead log: every change is appended to a log before it is applied, so a crash can be recovered by replaying the log. Write skew Two transactions each read the same condition, then write different rows; together they break a rule neither broke alone. The double-booking bug.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text: Term Meaning 2PC Two-phase commit: a coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then to commit. Blocks if the coordinator fails. CAP During a network partition, a system must choose between consistency (refuse) and availability (answer, possibly stale). Consensus Nodes agreeing on one value or order despite failures (Raft, Paxos, ZooKeeper). Consistent hashing Placing nodes and keys on a ring so adding or removing a node moves only a small share of keys. CRDT Conflict-free replicated data type: data that merges concurrent edits automatically. Eventual consistency Replicas may disagree briefly but converge if writes stop. Failover Promoting a replica to replace a failed leader. Fencing token An increasing number issued with each lock; storage rejects writes carrying an older number, so a stalled old lock-holder can't corrupt data. Hot key One key (a celebrity, a viral item) that gets so much traffic it overloads the single node holding it. Leader The one replica that accepts writes and orders them; followers copy from it. Lease A lock that expires automatically after a set time. Linearizability The system behaves as if there is one copy of the data: once anyone sees a new value, everyone does. LWW Last write wins: keep the value with the latest timestamp and silently drop the other. OT Operational transformation: a server orders concurrent edits and adjusts them so all copies converge (Google Docs). PACELC Extends CAP: even without partitions, stronger consistency costs latency. Quorum A majority (or w + r > n) of replicas that must agree, so reads overlap the latest writes. Replication Keeping copies of the same data on several machines. Replication lag How far a follower is behind the leader. Reads from a lagging follower can return old data. Saga A multi-step process across services where each step has a compensating action to undo it on failure. Shard key The field used to decide which shard a record lives on. Sharding Splitting data across machines so each holds and serves only part of it. Also called partitioning. Split brain Two nodes both believe they are the leader and accept writes.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Term Meaning Bloom filter A compact structure that answers "definitely not seen" or "probably seen", using about 10 bits per item. Cache hit ratio The share of reads answered by the cache. Cache stampede A hot key expires and many requests miss at once and overload the database. Cache-aside The app reads the cache; on a miss it reads the database and fills the cache. LRU Least recently used: evict the item that hasn't been used for the longest time. TTL Time to live: how long a cached item is kept before it expires.

docs.title: Messaging
docs.text: Term Meaning Backpressure Slowing or rejecting new work when a system is full, instead of falling over. Batch processing Processing a large, bounded dataset in one job, such as a nightly recount. CDC Change data capture: streaming every database change (from its log) to other systems. Consumer group Consumers that share a topic's partitions, each partition read by one of them. DLQ Dead-letter queue: where messages go after repeatedly failing, so they don't block others. Event sourcing Storing the sequence of events as the source of truth and deriving current state from it. Fan-out Sending one item to many recipients, such as a post to all followers. Fan-out on read Assemble each recipient's view when they read it, making writes cheap. Fan-out on write Precompute each recipient's copy when the item is created, making reads cheap. Kafka partition An ordered, append-only log that is one slice of a Kafka topic. Order is kept only within a partition. Message queue A buffer between producers and consumers so work can be done later, retried and spread over workers. Offset A consumer's position in a log such as a Kafka partition; each consumer group tracks its own. Outbox pattern Write the business change and an event row in one transaction; a relay publishes the event, so the two can't disagree. Partition key The field used to choose a partition (for example user ID); order is guaranteed only within one partition. Poison message A message that fails every time it is processed; it should be moved to a dead-letter queue. Pub/sub Publish/subscribe: senders publish to a channel and every subscriber receives the message. Stream processing Processing events continuously as they arrive. Tumbling window Fixed, non-overlapping time buckets for stream aggregation, such as one per minute. Visibility timeout How long a taken message stays hidden; if the worker doesn't finish in time, it reappears for a retry. Watermark A stream processor's estimate that all events up to a time have arrived.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Term Meaning Adaptive bitrate Video split into short segments at several qualities; the player picks quality per segment from measured bandwidth. Geohash Encoding a location as a string whose shared prefix means nearby, so ordinary indexes can do proximity search. HLS HTTP Live Streaming: a format for adaptive-bitrate video delivered as small segments. Inverted index A map from each word to the documents containing it; the basis of full-text search. Multipart upload Uploading a large file as many parts in parallel, retrying only failed parts. Object storage Storage for whole files addressed by key (S3), cheap and very durable.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text: Term Meaning Blue-green deploy Running two full environments and switching all traffic from the old (blue) to the new (green); switching back is the rollback. Bulkhead Separate pools of threads or connections per dependency, so one slow dependency can't exhaust everything. Canary deploy Releasing a new version to a small share of traffic first and comparing its errors and latency before rolling it out further. Circuit breaker Stops calling a failing dependency for a while and fails fast instead, then lets a few trial calls through to test recovery. Expand and contract Changing a schema in backward-compatible steps: add the new thing, migrate, switch over, then remove the old thing. Exponential backoff Waiting longer after each failed attempt (100 ms, 200, 400…) so a struggling service can recover. Feature flag A runtime switch that turns a feature on or off for some users without redeploying. Jitter Randomness added to retry delays so many clients don't retry at the same instant. Load shedding Rejecting some requests early (usually the least important) when a service is overloaded, so the rest stay fast. RED method Monitor every service by request Rate, Errors and Duration. Retry budget A cap on how much extra load retries may add (for example 10%), so retries can't multiply an outage. Thundering herd Many clients hitting a service at the same moment, for example all retrying together or all missing an expired cache key. Token bucket A rate-limiting algorithm: tokens refill at a steady rate, each request spends one, and bursts up to the bucket size are allowed. Trace The record of one request as it passes through several services, with the time spent in each.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Term Meaning Access token A short-lived credential an app sends with each API call (usually as a Bearer header) to prove it may act. Argon2id The recommended slow, memory-hard password hashing function. bcrypt and scrypt are acceptable alternatives. Authentication Proving who you are (password, passkey, SSO). Often shortened to authn. Authorization Deciding what an authenticated caller is allowed to do. Often shortened to authz. bcrypt A long-established slow password hashing function with a tunable cost factor. CA Certificate authority: an organisation browsers trust to sign certificates that bind a domain name to a public key. CSRF Cross-site request forgery: another site makes the user's browser send a request with their cookies. Stopped with SameSite cookies or tokens. HMAC A signature made from a message and a shared secret key; used to prove a webhook or request really came from the sender. IdP Identity provider: the service that logs users in and vouches for them to other apps (Okta, Entra ID, Google). JWT JSON Web Token: a signed, base64url-encoded set of claims (who, expiry, audience) that a server can verify without a database lookup. Readable by anyone, so it holds no secrets. MFA Multi-factor authentication: something you know plus something you have (an app code, a passkey) or are. mTLS Mutual TLS: both sides present certificates, so services authenticate each other, not just the server. OAuth OAuth 2.0: a standard for letting an app act on a user's behalf at another service, via access tokens, without ever seeing the user's password. OIDC OpenID Connect: a login layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds an ID token (a JWT) saying who the user is. PKCE Proof Key for Code Exchange: the app sends a hash of a random secret at the start of the OAuth flow and the secret itself when exchanging the code, so a stolen code is useless. Refresh token A long-lived credential used only to get new access tokens; stored carefully and revocable. Salt A random value stored with each password hash so identical passwords hash differently and precomputed tables are useless. SAML An older XML-based single sign-on standard, still common in enterprises. SSO Single sign-on: one login at an identity provider gives access to many apps.

docs.title: Operating systems
docs.text: Term Meaning cgroups Linux control groups: limit and account a group of processes' CPU, memory and I/O; the resource half of containers. Compare-and-swap An atomic operation that sets a value only if it still equals the expected old value; the basis of lock-free code and optimistic concurrency. Context switch The OS saving one thread's state and resuming another on a CPU core; costs microseconds plus cold caches. CPU throttling A container being paused for the rest of a scheduling period after using up its CPU quota, causing latency spikes. Deadlock Two or more threads each holding a lock the other needs, so none can continue; prevented by acquiring locks in a fixed order. epoll The Linux interface that tells a program which of its many sockets are ready, at a cost proportional to active ones. kqueue is the BSD/macOS equivalent. Event loop One thread that waits for any of many sockets to become ready and handles each briefly, never blocking. fsync The system call that forces a file's written data from RAM to stable storage; until it returns, a crash can lose the data. Group commit Making many transactions durable with one fsync of the log, multiplying commit throughput. IOPS Input/output operations per second: how many separate reads or writes a storage device can do. Journaling Writing an intended change to a log before applying it, so a crash can be repaired by replaying the log. Namespaces Linux features that give a process its own view of PIDs, network, file system and hostname; the isolation half of containers. OOM killer The Linux mechanism that kills a process when memory (or a container's memory limit) is exhausted. Page cache File data the OS keeps in otherwise unused RAM, so repeated reads skip the disk and writes can be flushed later. Page fault An access to a virtual memory page not currently in RAM; the kernel must load it, roughly 1,000× slower than a normal access. Thread pool A fixed set of worker threads taking tasks from a queue, so concurrency and memory stay bounded. TLB Translation lookaside buffer: a CPU cache of recent virtual-to-physical address translations. Write amplification Storage writing more data internally than the application asked for, as SSDs and LSM-trees do when rewriting data.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
This handbook covers everything from the basics to staff-level interviews. You don't need all of it. Pick the path that matches where you are.

Every page shows its level at the top:

  • Beginner-friendly assumes only that you've built a web app.
  • Intermediate assumes you know the basics and want to design systems that scale.
  • Advanced assumes the intermediate material and goes into distributed systems theory and staff-level trade-offs.

Stuck on a term? Hover over it on any page, or look it up in the glossary.

docs.title: Path 1: Intermediate engineer (about 2–3 weeks, 1 hour a day)
docs.text: You've built applications, but you haven't designed large systems or done many system design interviews.

docs.title: Stage 1: The foundations (3–4 days)
docs.text:
1. The basics: how a request travels through DNS, CDN, load balancer, app servers, cache, database and queue.
  2. How to approach any design: the loop used on every page.
  3. Non-functional requirements: just the first two sections for now.
  4. Numbers and estimation: read the conversions and the method; skim the big table.

Then skim System Design 101: 25 one-screen explainers of the protocols, security, reliability, database and messaging pieces that the rest of the handbook takes for granted. Each ends with three self-check questions.

Note

Checkpoint: you can explain why app servers should be stateless, what a cache saves you, and turn "10 million users, 5 actions a day" into requests per second.

docs.title: Stage 2: Core concepts (4–5 days)
docs.text:
1. API design
  2. Data modeling
  3. Database indexing
  4. Caching
  5. Networking essentials

Note

Checkpoint: you can design the tables and indexes for a simple app, explain cache-aside and what a stampede is, and say when you'd use SSE vs WebSockets.

docs.title: Stage 3: Your first patterns (3 days)
docs.text:
1. Scaling reads
  2. Long-running tasks
  3. Handling large blobs

Note

Checkpoint: for a read-heavy app you can say what to add first, second and third, and why uploads should never pass through your app servers.

docs.title: Stage 4: Your first problems (about a week)
docs.text:
Do these in order. For each one, cover the page and try the design yourself first, then read the v1 → final walkthrough.

  1. URL shortener
  2. News aggregator
  3. File storage and sync
  4. Local delivery
  5. Rate limiter
  6. Ticketmaster
  7. News feed
  8. Online judge

Note

Checkpoint: you can draw a working design for an unseen easy problem in 30 minutes, explain where the simple version breaks with a number, and fix it.

docs.title: Stage 5: Rounding out
docs.text:
• The remaining patterns: Scaling writes, Real-time updates, Dealing with contention.
  • The remaining concepts: Sharding, Consistent hashing, CAP theorem.
  • What's expected at each level, so you know how deep a mid-level interview goes.
  • The 45-minute delivery framework, then practise out loud with the interview deck.

You can skip the DDIA pages, the Computer Networking chapters and the staff-level material for now. Come back to them later. If networking feels shaky, read Computer Networking chapters 1–3 first; for what happens inside one server, read Operating Systems pages 1, 5 and 6.

docs.title: Path 2: Senior engineer preparing for interviews (about 2 weeks)
docs.text:
1. Skim Foundations and System Design 101, and read Numbers and estimation carefully.
  2. Read all 7 patterns and Choosing technologies.
  3. Do two problems a day, medium and hard. Try each yourself first.
  4. Read the DDIA pages behind your weakest patterns, especially Ch 5, Ch 7 and Ch 11.
  5. Rehearse with the interview deck and the quick-fire questions.

docs.title: Path 3: Staff and above
docs.text:
1. What's expected at each level and Staff-level answers.
  2. All 12 DDIA chapters, plus Operating Systems for the single-machine behaviour behind them (threads, fsync, GC pauses, container limits).
  3. Every problem's Staff-level lens section, or all 29 at once in the staff atlas.
  4. The night before: the staff cheat sheet and the interview cheat sheet.

docs.title: How to study any page
docs.text:
• Predict before you read. Cover the final design and sketch your own first. The gap is what you learn.
  • Say it out loud. Interviews test explaining, not recognising.
  • Do the numbers yourself. Redo each page's estimate without looking.
  • Revisit with sketchnotes. After a page, its one-page sketchnote is a quick way to review a few days later.

docs.title: Choosing technologies
docs.text:
Intermediate

You need fewer technologies than you think. Start with Postgres, add Redis for speed and Kafka for streams, and reach for the others only when a requirement asks for them.

Why these systems behave the way they do (Redis's single thread, Postgres's commit limits, Kafka's use of the page cache) is explained in Operating Systems for system design.

Need Default choice Source of truth with transactions Postgres Cache, counters, locks, leaderboards, geo, pub/sub Redis Durable event stream, buffering writes, change data capture Kafka Huge write volume with simple key access Cassandra (or DynamoDB on AWS) Full-text and faceted search Elasticsearch (fed from the source of truth) Windowed aggregation over streams Flink Leader election, locks with fencing, cluster metadata ZooKeeper or etcd Single entry point: auth, rate limits, routing API gateway

docs.title: Postgres
docs.text:
What it is: a relational database with ACID transactions, rich indexing (B-tree, GIN, GiST/PostGIS) and JSON support.

  • Use when: you need transactions, relations, constraints, or you're not sure yet. It is the right default.
  • Avoid when: writes exceed what one primary can take even after batching (tens of thousands per second sustained), or data is tens of TB of append-only events.
  • Numbers: ~10–50k simple transactions/s per primary; multiple TB per node; read replicas for read scaling.
  • Gotcha: the default isolation (Read Committed) does not prevent write skew. Use conditional updates or SELECT … FOR UPDATE for bookings and inventory.

Tip

"Postgres is the source of truth. I'll only move data elsewhere when a specific number says it doesn't fit."

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
What it is: an in-memory data-structure server: strings, hashes, sorted sets, streams, geo indexes, pub/sub. Commands run on a single thread, which makes each one atomic.

  • Use when: caching, rate limiting (atomic Lua scripts), counters, leaderboards (sorted sets), short-lived locks (SET NX EX), geo lookups, fan-out of messages between servers.
  • Avoid when: the data must survive anything (it's not your durable record), or it doesn't fit in memory.
  • Numbers: ~100k+ operations/s per node, sub-millisecond latency.
  • Gotcha: a lock in Redis isn't safe on its own if a process can pause and wake up after the lock expired. Use fencing tokens, or make the database enforce the rule.

docs.title: Kafka
docs.text:
What it is: a partitioned, replicated, append-only log. Consumers track their own offsets, so many independent consumers can read the same data and replay it.

  • Use when: buffering write spikes, event-driven pipelines, change data capture, stream processing, several consumers of the same events.
  • Avoid when: you need per-message work queues with individual retries and delays (use SQS/RabbitMQ), or request/response.
  • Numbers: plan ~5–10k messages/s per partition; ~1M messages/s per broker; 7-day default retention.
  • Gotcha: ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, and parallelism is capped by the number of partitions. Choose the partition key deliberately (e.g. booking_id).

docs.title: Cassandra
docs.text:
What it is: a leaderless, wide-column database built on LSM trees. Very fast writes, tunable consistency.

  • Use when: massive write volume with simple access by key: chat history, metrics, activity logs, swipes.
  • Avoid when: you need joins, ad-hoc queries or multi-row transactions.
  • Numbers: ~10k+ writes/s per node; scales linearly by adding nodes.
  • Gotcha: you model tables per query; a query without the partition key is expensive. Concurrent writes resolve by last-write-wins.

docs.title: DynamoDB
docs.text:
What it is: a managed key-value and document store on AWS with automatic scaling and single-digit-millisecond latency.

  • Use when: you're on AWS and want predictable key-based access without running a cluster.
  • Avoid when: access patterns are unknown or relational.
  • Gotcha: one hot partition key throttles; global secondary indexes are eventually consistent.

docs.title: Elasticsearch
docs.text:
What it is: a distributed search engine built on inverted indexes, with relevance ranking, fuzzy matching, facets and geo queries.

  • Use when: full-text search, faceted filtering, log search.
  • Avoid when: you'd make it the source of truth, or pg_trgm / Postgres full-text already covers the need.
  • Numbers: new documents become searchable after a refresh interval (~1 s).
  • Gotcha: feed it from the database through change data capture. Never write to both the database and the index from application code.

docs.title: Flink
docs.text:
What it is: a stateful stream processor with event-time windows, checkpoints and exactly-once state.

  • Use when: real-time aggregation (clicks per minute, top-K), alerting on streams, complex event patterns.
  • Avoid when: a simple consumer writing to a database is enough.
  • Gotcha: "exactly once" means effectively once. Sinks must be idempotent (upserts) or transactional.

docs.title: ZooKeeper / etcd
docs.text:
What it is: a small, strongly consistent key-value store built on a consensus protocol.

  • Use when: electing a leader, holding locks with fencing tokens, storing cluster membership and configuration that clients watch.
  • Avoid when: storing application data. It's built for small metadata.
  • Gotcha: every write needs a majority round trip, so keep traffic low.

docs.title: API gateway
docs.text:
What it is: the single entry point in front of your services.

  • Use when: you need authentication, rate limiting, TLS termination, routing and request logging in one place.
  • Avoid: putting business logic in it.

docs.text:

docs.title: System Design 101
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Short explainers of the building blocks that every design takes for granted. Each one fits on a screen: one diagram, a few paragraphs, when to use it, one line you can say in an interview, and three self-check questions.

Read them before Core concepts, or dip in whenever a problem page mentions something you can't explain in two sentences.

docs.title: APIs & protocols
docs.text: Topic In one line What happens when you type a URL DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP and rendering: the journey of one page load, one step at a time. TCP vs UDP Reliable and ordered, or fast and fire-and-forget: the two transport protocols under almost everything. HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 How each HTTP version fixes the waiting problem of the one before it. REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC Three API styles, what each is good at, and how to pick one in an interview. Webhooks vs polling Asking again and again versus being called when something happens, and how to receive webhooks safely. API gateway One front door for your services: what belongs in it and what doesn't.

docs.title: Security & auth
docs.text: Topic In one line How HTTPS works The TLS handshake: how a browser and server agree on secret keys over a public network. Storing passwords Salt plus a slow hash: why plain hashes are not enough, and how login checks work. Sessions vs tokens Server-side sessions or self-contained tokens: where the login state lives, and what that costs. JWT What is inside a JSON Web Token, what it proves, and the mistakes to avoid. OAuth 2.0 How an app gets permission to act for a user at another service, without seeing their password. Single sign-on (SSO) Log in once at an identity provider and get into every app that trusts it.

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text: Topic In one line Timeouts, retries and backoff How to call something that might be slow or down without making things worse. Circuit breaker Stop calling a dependency that is failing, fail fast, and test carefully before trusting it again. Rate limiting and load shedding Two ways to stay up under too much traffic: limit each caller, and drop the least important work first. Metrics, logs and traces The three signals that tell you something is wrong, where, and why, and how to alert on them. Deploying safely Canary, blue-green and feature flags: how to ship often without breaking production.

docs.title: Databases & storage
docs.text: Topic In one line SQL vs NoSQL Relational versus key-value, document, wide-column and graph databases, and how to choose. ACID and isolation levels What a transaction promises, and which concurrency bugs each isolation level still allows. Database replication Leaders, followers and replication lag: how copies of data give you read scale and failover. Block, file and object storage Three ways to store bytes, and why images and videos almost always go to object storage.

docs.title: Messaging
docs.text: Topic In one line Message queue vs event stream SQS and RabbitMQ versus Kafka: work distribution versus a replayable log many consumers share. Delivery guarantees At-most-once, at-least-once and "exactly-once", and why idempotent consumers are the real answer. Transactional outbox How to save data and publish an event without ever doing only one of the two. Dead-letter queues What to do with a message that fails every time, so it doesn't block or crash everything behind it.

docs.title: ACID and isolation levels
docs.text:
Intermediate

A transaction groups several reads and writes into one unit. ACID names what it promises:

  • Atomic: all of it happens, or none of it. No half-done transfer.
  • Consistent: your rules (constraints like "balance ≥ 0") still hold afterwards.
  • Isolated: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work.
  • Durable: once committed, it survives a crash.

Isolation comes in levels, because full isolation is expensive:

  • Read committed (Postgres default): you never read uncommitted data, but two reads in one transaction can return different values.
  • Snapshot isolation / repeatable read: the whole transaction sees one consistent snapshot. Write skew is still possible: two doctors each check "someone else is on call", then both go off call.
  • Serializable: the result is as if transactions ran one at a time. It is the safest level, with retries when conflicts happen.

For hot spots like "decrement stock", a conditional update (UPDATE … SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0) or SELECT … FOR UPDATE is often simpler than raising the level.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Any time several rows must change together: money, bookings, inventory.
  • Raise isolation, or lock explicitly, where a check-then-act race would be costly.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Reserving a seat is one transaction with a conditional update, WHERE status = 'available'. If zero rows changed, someone else got it. That avoids the check-then-act race without making everything serializable."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What does the A in ACID mean?

Atomic: all of the transaction's writes happen, or none do.

Give an example of write skew.

Two on-call doctors each check that the other is on call, then both go off call. Each transaction was valid alone, but together they break the rule. Snapshot isolation allows this; serializable doesn't.

How do you safely decrement stock without raising isolation?

A conditional update: UPDATE … SET stock = stock − 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0, then check that one row changed.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Dealing with contention
  • DDIA Ch 7: transactions
  • Ticketmaster

docs.title: API gateway
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

An API gateway sits between clients and your services. Every request passes through it, so it is the natural place for the rules that apply to all of them:

  • TLS termination: decrypt once at the edge.
  • Authentication: check the token, then pass the user ID downstream.
  • Rate limiting and quotas per user or API key.
  • Routing: /orders/* goes to the orders service, and so on.
  • Logging, metrics and request IDs, plus response caching and request size limits.

It should not contain business logic. Once the gateway knows what an order is, every team needs to change it, and it becomes the bottleneck you were trying to avoid.

Because all traffic flows through it, the gateway must be stateless and run as several instances behind a load balancer. Managed options include AWS API Gateway, Kong, Envoy and NGINX.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Several services behind one public API.
  • You need consistent auth, rate limits and logging without repeating them in every service.
  • Skip it for a single service: a load balancer is enough.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Clients hit an API gateway that terminates TLS, validates the JWT, applies per-user rate limits and routes by path. It is stateless and horizontally scaled; business rules stay in the services."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Name four things an API gateway typically does.

TLS termination, authentication, rate limiting, routing, plus logging, metrics and request IDs.

Why shouldn't business logic live in the gateway?

Every team would need to change it, it becomes a deployment bottleneck and a single point of coupling. Keep it to cross-cutting rules.

When is a gateway unnecessary?

With a single service, where a load balancer already does the job.

docs.text:

  • Choosing technologies
  • Sessions vs tokens

docs.title: Circuit breaker
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Retries help with brief failures. When a dependency is really down, every call still waits for its timeout, and your threads fill up waiting. A circuit breaker stops that.

  • Closed (normal): calls go through, and the breaker counts failures.
  • Open: once failures pass a threshold (say, half of calls in 10 seconds), the breaker fails every call immediately without touching the dependency. Your service stays responsive, and the dependency gets breathing room.
  • Half-open: after a cool-down, a few trial calls go through. If they succeed the breaker closes; if not, it opens again.

While the breaker is open, return a fallback: cached data, a sensible default ("recommendations unavailable"), or a clear error. Pair it with bulkheads, separate connection pools per dependency, so one slow dependency can't use up the threads the others need.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Calls to any dependency that can fail independently: other services, third-party APIs, a search cluster.
  • Most service meshes and libraries (Envoy, Resilience4j, Polly) have one built in.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Calls to the recommendation service go through a circuit breaker with its own connection pool. If it opens, the home page renders without recommendations rather than timing out. Checkout never depends on it."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What are the three states of a circuit breaker?

Closed (calls pass, failures counted), open (fail fast without calling), half-open (a few trial calls decide whether to close or reopen).

What do you return while the breaker is open?

A fallback: cached or default data, a degraded feature, or a clear fast error.

What is a bulkhead?

Separate resource pools (threads, connections) per dependency, so one slow dependency can't exhaust capacity needed by the others.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Timeouts, retries and backoff
  • Rate limiting and load shedding

docs.title: Dead-letter queues
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Some messages will never succeed: bad data, a bug, a deleted record. A poison message like that gets retried forever, wastes capacity, and in an ordered stream it blocks every message behind it.

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is where such messages go after a set number of attempts:

  1. The consumer fails and the message is retried with backoff.
  2. After, say, five attempts, it moves to the DLQ, keeping the original message plus the error and attempt count.
  3. The main queue keeps flowing.
  4. An alert on DLQ depth tells someone to look. They fix the bug or the data, then replay the messages from the DLQ.

Separate errors that might pass on a retry (a timeout, a 503) from errors that never will (invalid data). Send the second kind to the DLQ immediately rather than retrying.

SQS and RabbitMQ have DLQs built in. With Kafka you usually build them: a retry topic and a dead-letter topic.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Every queue or stream consumer in production.
  • Pair with alerting: a DLQ nobody watches is just a slower way to lose data.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Messages that fail five times go to a dead-letter queue with the error attached, so one bad event can't stall the partition. We alert when the DLQ is non-empty and replay after the fix."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What is a poison message?

One that fails every time it is processed, for example because of bad data or a bug, and would otherwise be retried forever or block the messages behind it.

What should be stored with a dead-lettered message?

The original message plus the error, the number of attempts and timestamps, so someone can diagnose and replay it.

Which failures should skip retries and go straight to the DLQ?

Errors that will never succeed on retry, such as validation errors or malformed data. Retry only transient ones like timeouts and 503s.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Timeouts, retries and backoff
  • Message queue vs event stream
  • Job scheduler

docs.title: Delivery guarantees
docs.text:
Intermediate

When a consumer crashes, what happens to the message it was handling? It depends on when it acknowledges.

  • At-most-once: acknowledge first, then process. A crash after the ack loses the message. That is acceptable only for data you can afford to drop, like some metrics.
  • At-least-once: process first, then acknowledge. A crash before the ack means the message is delivered again, so you get duplicates. This is the usual default.
  • Exactly-once: across a network, a message can't be guaranteed to be delivered exactly once. What you can build is effectively-once: at-least-once delivery plus a consumer that makes duplicates harmless.

Ways to make a consumer idempotent:

  • Record processed message IDs in the same transaction as the work, and skip any ID already seen.
  • Use upserts and absolute values ("set balance to 90") instead of increments ("subtract 10").
  • Use conditional writes keyed by the event, such as "insert payment where event_id is new".

Kafka's "exactly-once" feature covers reading and writing within Kafka. Side effects outside Kafka, such as sending an email, still need idempotency.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• At-least-once + idempotent consumer: almost everything, especially money, counters and notifications.
  • At-most-once: high-volume telemetry where a small loss is fine.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Delivery is at-least-once, so the consumer is idempotent: it writes the ledger entry and the event ID in one transaction with a unique constraint on the event ID. A redelivered event hits the constraint and is skipped."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why is at-least-once the usual default?

Losing messages is usually worse than duplicates, and duplicates can be neutralised with idempotent consumers.

Name two ways to make a consumer idempotent.

Store processed message IDs in the same transaction as the work (with a unique constraint), or use upserts and absolute values instead of increments.

Does Kafka exactly-once make sending an email exactly-once?

No. It covers reads and writes within Kafka. External side effects still need idempotency, for example an email-sent record keyed by event ID.

docs.text:
• Message queue vs event stream
  • Transactional outbox
  • Payment system

docs.title: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time on a connection; the next request waits for the previous response. Browsers work around this by opening about six connections per site.

HTTP/2 uses one TCP connection and splits it into many streams, so dozens of requests travel at once, interleaved. Headers are compressed. The catch: TCP delivers bytes in order, so one lost packet stalls every stream until it is resent (head-of-line blocking at the TCP level).

HTTP/3 runs on QUIC over UDP. Each stream is delivered independently, so a lost packet only delays its own stream. TLS is built in, so a new connection takes one round trip (zero on a repeat visit), and connections survive switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data.

The API you write doesn't change: methods, headers and status codes are the same in all three.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• HTTP/1.1: still fine for simple internal calls and anything behind a proxy that speaks it.
  • HTTP/2: the default for browsers and the transport under gRPC.
  • HTTP/3: mobile users and lossy networks; most CDNs turn it on for you.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Between the browser and the CDN we get HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 for free. Internally, services talk gRPC over HTTP/2, so one connection carries many calls."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What problem does HTTP/2 solve, and what problem does it leave?

It multiplexes many requests over one connection instead of one at a time. But because it runs on TCP, one lost packet still stalls every stream (TCP head-of-line blocking).

Why does HTTP/3 use UDP?

It runs on QUIC over UDP so each stream is delivered independently, connection setup is faster with TLS built in, and connections survive network changes.

Do you need to change your API to move from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2?

No. Methods, headers, status codes and URLs are the same. Only the wire format changes.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• TCP vs UDP
  • REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC

docs.title: How HTTPS works
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

HTTPS is HTTP inside a TLS connection. TLS gives you three things: encryption (no one in the middle can read it), integrity (no one can change it unnoticed) and authentication (you are really talking to that domain).

  1. The browser says hello: which ciphers it supports, plus its half of a key exchange.
  2. The server replies with its half of the key exchange, its certificate, and a signature proving it holds the certificate's private key.
  3. The browser checks the certificate: signed by a certificate authority it trusts, for this domain name, not expired.
  4. Both sides combine the two halves (ECDHE) into the same secret keys. The keys themselves never cross the network.
  5. Everything after that is encrypted with fast symmetric encryption.

With TLS 1.3 this takes one round trip. Asymmetric cryptography is only used to agree on keys, because it is slow.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Always, for anything public. Free certificates (Let's Encrypt) removed the cost excuse.
  • Terminate TLS at the load balancer or gateway; use mTLS between services when they must prove their identity to each other.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "TLS terminates at the load balancer, so the app servers don't do crypto. Service-to-service traffic uses mTLS from the service mesh, so a compromised pod can't pretend to be the payments service."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What three things does TLS provide?

Encryption (privacy), integrity (tamper detection) and authentication (you are talking to the real domain).

How does the browser know the server's certificate is genuine?

It is signed by a certificate authority the browser trusts, the name matches the domain, and it hasn't expired.

Why switch to symmetric encryption after the handshake?

Asymmetric cryptography is slow; it is used only to agree on keys. Bulk data uses fast symmetric ciphers with those keys.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• What happens when you type a URL
  • Sessions vs tokens

docs.title: JWT
docs.text:
Intermediate

A JSON Web Token is three base64url parts joined by dots: header.payload.signature.

  • The header names the signing algorithm.
  • The payload holds claims: sub (who), exp (expiry), aud (which API it's for), iss (who issued it), plus anything else such as roles.
  • The signature covers the header and payload. With RS256 or ES256 the issuer signs with a private key and anyone can verify with the public key.

Base64 is encoding, not encryption: anyone can read the payload. A JWT proves who issued it and that it wasn't changed; it does not hide anything. So never put secrets or personal data in it.

When verifying, check the signature with the algorithm you expect (never accept alg: none), then exp, aud and iss. And remember you can't take a JWT back once issued: keep them short-lived.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Access tokens and OIDC ID tokens passed between services.
  • Avoid JWTs as long-lived browser sessions: you lose instant logout.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "The access token is a JWT signed with RS256. Services verify it locally with the public key from the auth server's JWKS endpoint, check exp and aud, and read the user ID from sub. It expires in 10 minutes."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Is the payload of a JWT secret?

No. It is base64url-encoded, not encrypted; anyone can read it. The signature only proves who issued it and that it wasn't changed.

Which claims should you check when verifying a JWT?

The signature with the expected algorithm, then exp (expiry), aud (audience) and iss (issuer).

What is the "alg: none" mistake?

Accepting the algorithm named in the token header. An attacker sets it to none (or switches algorithms) and the signature check is skipped. Always enforce the algorithm you expect.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Sessions vs tokens
  • OAuth 2.0

docs.title: Rate limiting and load shedding
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Every service has a limit. Past it, latency climbs for everyone, until nothing finishes in time. Two tools keep you on the safe side of that cliff.

Rate limiting protects you from one caller sending too much. Each user or API key gets a quota, usually a token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate, each request spends one, and short bursts are allowed. Over the limit, reply 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.

Load shedding protects you when the total is too much, even if every caller is within quota. When queues are full or latency passes a threshold, reject some work early with 503, and choose what to drop: background jobs before user requests, browsing before checkout. A fast "no" is much better than a slow timeout.

Related idea: backpressure. A consumer that can't keep up signals the producer to slow down, instead of buffering until it runs out of memory.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Rate limits: every public API, login endpoints, anything a bot could hammer.
  • Load shedding: any service that can see traffic spikes (sales, launches, retry storms).

Tip

Say this in the interview: "At the gateway each API key has a token bucket of 100 requests a second. Behind it, services shed low-priority traffic when the queue is too deep, so during a spike checkout stays fast and only recommendations degrade."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What is the difference between rate limiting and load shedding?

Rate limiting caps each caller's quota. Load shedding drops work when total load is too high, even if every caller is within quota.

Which status codes do you return for each?

429 Too Many Requests (with Retry-After) for rate limits; 503 Service Unavailable when shedding.

Why is a fast rejection better than accepting everything?

Past capacity, latency climbs for all requests until none finish in time. Rejecting some early keeps the rest fast.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Rate limiter (full design)
  • API gateway
  • Circuit breaker

docs.title: OAuth 2.0
docs.text:
Intermediate

OAuth 2.0 answers: how does app X get access to my photos at service Y without my Y password? The answer is a scoped, expiring access token.

The standard flow for web and mobile apps is the authorization code flow with PKCE:

  1. The app redirects the user to the authorization server, asking for specific scopes (for example photos.read) and sending a hash of a random secret (PKCE).
  2. The user logs in there and approves the access.
  3. The authorization server redirects back with a one-time code.
  4. The app exchanges the code, plus the original secret, for an access token (and usually a refresh token).
  5. The app calls the API with Authorization: Bearer <token>.

OAuth is about authorization (what an app may do). For login (who the user is), OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top. "Sign in with Google" is OIDC.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Letting third-party apps access your API on a user's behalf.
  • "Sign in with…" buttons (OIDC).
  • Service-to-service access uses the simpler client-credentials grant.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Third-party apps use the authorization code flow with PKCE and get narrowly scoped, short-lived access tokens plus a refresh token the user can revoke from their settings page."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What problem does OAuth 2.0 solve?

Letting an app act on a user's behalf at another service with a scoped, expiring token, without the app ever seeing the user's password.

What is PKCE for?

It binds the code exchange to the app that started the flow: without the original secret (code verifier), a stolen authorization code is useless.

What is the difference between OAuth and OpenID Connect?

OAuth is about authorization (what the app may do). OIDC adds authentication: an ID token saying who the user is.

docs.title: Metrics, logs and traces
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

You can't fix what you can't see. Observability is being able to answer new questions about production without shipping new code. It rests on three signals:

  • Metrics: cheap numbers over time. For every service track rate, errors and duration (the RED method), plus saturation of CPU, memory, queues and connections. They tell you that something is wrong.
  • Traces: one request followed across every service it touches, with the time spent in each. They tell you where.
  • Logs: structured events (JSON, not free text) with the details. They tell you why.

Tie them together with a trace ID passed in every request and written into every log line.

Alert on what users feel, not on CPU. Alert on SLO burn rate, for example "at this error rate we'll use the month's error budget in two days", so you page a human for real problems only.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Every production system. In interviews, mention it in the wrap-up.
  • Common stack: Prometheus and Grafana, OpenTelemetry for traces, a log store such as Loki or Elasticsearch.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "I'd track request rate, error rate and p99 latency per endpoint, propagate a trace ID with OpenTelemetry, and alert on SLO burn rate rather than CPU. For the queue I'd also alert on consumer lag."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Metrics, traces, logs: which answers "where is it slow"?

Traces: they show one request across services and the time spent in each.

What is the RED method?

For each service track request Rate, Errors and Duration (latency).

Why alert on SLO burn rate rather than CPU?

Users feel errors and latency, not CPU. Burn-rate alerts page only when the error budget is actually being used up fast.

docs.title: Transactional outbox
docs.text:
Intermediate

A service often needs to update its database and publish an event: save the order, then tell everyone "order placed". Doing those as two separate steps is the dual-write problem:

  • If the service crashes after the database write, the event is never sent and other systems never hear about the order.
  • If you publish first and the database write then fails, others react to an order that doesn't exist.

The outbox pattern fixes it with the one thing you do have, a local transaction. In the same transaction that writes the order, insert a row into an outbox table describing the event. Either both rows commit or neither does.

A separate relay then reads the outbox and publishes each event to Kafka or a queue. It does this by polling the table, or better, by reading the database's change log (CDC, for example Debezium). It marks events as sent, and retries if publishing fails.

Publishing is at-least-once, because the relay can crash after publishing but before marking an event sent. So consumers must be idempotent.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Any service that writes to its database and must reliably emit an event about it.
  • The building block for sagas and event-driven microservices.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "The order service writes the order and an outbox row in one transaction. Debezium tails the outbox and publishes to Kafka, so an event exists if and only if the order does. Consumers dedupe by event ID."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What is the dual-write problem?

Writing to the database and publishing to a broker as two separate steps: a crash between them leaves one done without the other.

Why does the outbox pattern work?

The business row and the event row commit in one local transaction, so an event exists if and only if the data does.

Why must consumers still be idempotent?

The relay can publish an event and crash before marking it sent, so it publishes it again: delivery is at-least-once.

docs.title: Message queue vs event stream
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Both decouple the producer from the consumers, so a spike or a slow consumer doesn't break the producer. They differ in what happens to a message after it is read.

Message queue (SQS, RabbitMQ): each message is a task delivered to one worker. Once the worker acknowledges it, it is deleted. Add workers to go faster. If a worker dies mid-task, the message becomes visible again and another worker takes it.

Event stream (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar): messages are appended to an ordered log and kept for days. Each consumer group tracks its own offset, so many independent consumers (search indexing, analytics, notifications) read the same events, and any of them can rewind and replay. Order is guaranteed within a partition, so choose the partition key (for example user ID) to keep related events in order.

Rule of thumb: queue for jobs, stream for facts. "Resize this image" is a job; "order 42 was placed" is a fact that several systems care about.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Queue: background jobs, emails, image processing, anything one worker should do once.
  • Stream: event-driven systems, many consumers, replay, ordered event history, high throughput.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Order events go to Kafka, partitioned by order ID, so inventory, email and analytics each consume them at their own pace and we can replay after a bug. Thumbnail generation is a plain job, so it goes on SQS."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

A message has been processed. What happens to it in a queue vs a stream?

Queue: it is deleted once acknowledged. Stream: it stays in the log until retention expires; the consumer group just advances its offset.

How do you keep events for one user in order in Kafka?

Use the user ID as the partition key. Order is guaranteed only within a partition.

Image resizing or "order placed": which goes on a queue and which on a stream?

Resizing is a job for one worker: queue. "Order placed" is a fact several systems consume: stream.

docs.title: Database replication
docs.text:
Intermediate

Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines, for three reasons: survive a machine failing, serve more reads, and put data near users.

The common setup is leader-follower. All writes go to the leader, which streams its change log to the followers. Reads can go to any of them.

  • Synchronous followers confirm before the write commits: no data loss on failover, but slower writes. Asynchronous followers are faster but can be a little behind. Most setups use one synchronous follower and the rest asynchronous.
  • That delay is replication lag. A user who updates their profile and reads it back from a lagging follower sees the old value. Fix it with read-your-writes: send that user's reads to the leader for a short while after they write.
  • If the leader dies, a follower is promoted (failover). Watch out for two nodes both thinking they are leader (split brain). Real systems use fencing or consensus to prevent it.

Other models: multi-leader (writes in every region, conflicts to resolve) and leaderless (Cassandra, DynamoDB: write to several nodes, read from several, use quorums).

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Almost every production database: at least one follower for failover.
  • Read replicas when reads outgrow one server and can tolerate a little lag.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Postgres has one synchronous standby in another zone for failover and two async read replicas. Feed reads go to replicas; right after a user posts, their own reads go to the leader for a few seconds so they see their post."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What is replication lag and when does it hurt users?

Followers apply changes slightly after the leader. A user who writes then reads from a lagging follower sees stale data.

How do you give a user read-your-writes consistency?

Route that user's reads to the leader (or a caught-up replica) for a short time after they write.

Synchronous vs asynchronous followers: what is the trade-off?

Synchronous means no data loss on failover but slower writes and dependence on the follower; asynchronous is faster but can lose the latest writes.

docs.title: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

REST models your data as resources with URLs (/users/7/orders) and uses HTTP verbs on them. Responses have a fixed shape, so they cache well by URL and every tool understands them. The cost: a screen may need several calls, or get more fields than it uses.

GraphQL exposes one endpoint and a typed schema. The client sends a query naming exactly the fields it wants, across related objects, and gets them in one response. Great when many clients (web, iOS, Android) need different slices of the same data. The costs: HTTP caching is harder, and one innocent-looking query can be very expensive, so you need depth and cost limits.

gRPC is remote function calls with a Protobuf contract compiled into client code. Messages are small and binary, it runs on HTTP/2, and it supports streaming. Browsers can't call it directly without a proxy, so it is mostly used between services.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• REST: public APIs and the default in interviews.
  • GraphQL: a backend-for-frontend serving several apps with different data needs.
  • gRPC: internal, high-volume, latency-sensitive service-to-service calls.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "The public API is REST: simple, cacheable, and what partners expect. Internally the services talk gRPC for typed contracts and lower overhead. I'd only add GraphQL if many clients need very different views of the same data."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

When would you pick GraphQL over REST?

When several clients need different shapes of the same related data and you want to avoid many round trips or over-fetching, typically behind a backend-for-frontend.

Why is gRPC mostly used between services and not from browsers?

Browsers can't speak gRPC's HTTP/2 framing directly without a proxy. Between services its typed Protobuf contracts, small binary messages and streaming are a big win.

What is a risk of GraphQL that REST doesn't have?

One query can be very expensive (deep nesting, huge fan-out), and HTTP caching by URL is harder. You need depth and cost limits and persisted queries.

docs.title: Deploying safely
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Most outages start with a change. Safe deployment makes every change small, observable and quick to undo.

  • Rolling deploy: replace instances a few at a time. Simple, but old and new versions run side by side for a while.
  • Canary: send 1% of traffic to the new version, compare its error rate and latency with the old one, then go to 5%, 25%, 100%. Roll back automatically if the numbers get worse.
  • Blue-green: run two full environments and switch all traffic from blue (old) to green (new) at the load balancer. Rolling back is one switch, but you pay for double capacity.
  • Feature flags: deploy code switched off, then turn the feature on for staff, then 10% of users, then everyone. This separates deploy from release, and the flag is an instant kill switch.

Database changes need the same care: expand, then contract. Add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, and only then drop the old column. Every step stays compatible with the version before it.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Canary + feature flags: the default for services with real traffic.
  • Blue-green: when you need an instant, all-at-once switch and can afford two environments.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Deploys go out as canaries: 1% of traffic, automatic rollback if error rate or p99 regresses against the baseline. Risky features ship dark behind a flag, and schema changes follow expand-and-contract so old and new code both work."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

How does a canary deploy decide to roll back?

It compares the new version's error rate and latency against the old version on the same traffic, and rolls back automatically if they get worse.

What do feature flags separate?

Deploying code from releasing a feature. Code ships switched off and is turned on gradually, with an instant kill switch.

How do you rename a database column without downtime?

Expand and contract: add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old column. Each step works with the previous code version.

docs.title: Sessions vs tokens
docs.text:
Intermediate

After login, every request has to say who it comes from. There are two ways to do it.

Server-side session. The server creates a random session ID, stores session ID → user in a store such as Redis, and sends the ID in a cookie. Each request costs a lookup, but logout and revocation are instant: delete the row.

Self-contained token (usually a JWT). The server signs a token holding the user ID, roles and expiry. Any server can verify it with the public key, with no lookup, which suits many services and regions. The catch is that a valid token stays valid until it expires. So keep access tokens short-lived (5–15 minutes) and pair them with a refresh token that is checked against a store and can be revoked.

Browsers: put either in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, not in localStorage, where any injected script can read it.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• Sessions: a classic web app with one backend, or where instant logout matters (banking, admin tools).
  • Tokens: many services or regions, mobile apps and third-party APIs. Short access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "The gateway validates a short-lived JWT locally, so services don't hit a session store on every call. Refresh tokens live in a database so we can revoke them; worst case, a stolen access token works for 10 minutes."

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What is the main advantage of a server-side session?

Instant revocation: logging out or banning a user just deletes the session row.

Why keep JWT access tokens short-lived?

They can't easily be revoked; any server will accept them until they expire. Short lifetimes limit the damage of a stolen token.

Where should a browser keep its session ID or token?

In an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, not localStorage, where injected scripts can read it.
