docs.title: Chapter 7: Wireless and Mobile Networks
docs.text:
Intermediate

These pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams on Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach by James Kurose and Keith Ross, connected to system design. They don't replace the book, which is worth reading in full.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Most users reach your system over radio, which is far less reliable than a cable. Signals fade, bounce and interfere, and devices can't always hear each other. Wi-Fi shares the air with collision avoidance and link-level ACKs. Cellular networks (4G, 5G) add a core network that tracks users, authenticates them, and keeps their connections alive as they move between base stations. For system designers, the lesson is that mobile clients have variable latency, frequent short disconnects and changing addresses, so design for that.

Key ideas: fading and interference · hidden terminals · CSMA/CA · RTS/CTS · access points and association · 4G/5G architecture · handover · mobility (home and visited networks) · effects on TCP

docs.title: Why wireless links are hard
docs.text:
Why it matters: the physical link affects everything above it. A wired link loses almost nothing; a wireless link can lose frames constantly.

How radio differs from a wire:

  • Signal strength drops fast with distance, and walls and bodies absorb it (path loss).
  • Interference: other devices on the same frequency (neighbours' Wi-Fi, microwaves, Bluetooth) add noise.
  • Multipath: the signal bounces off surfaces and arrives several times, slightly out of step, smearing the bits.

The result is a higher and constantly changing bit error rate. Devices respond by switching modulation: a fast, fragile encoding when the signal is strong, and a slow, robust one when it's weak. That's why your Wi-Fi speed changes as you walk around.

docs.title: Wi-Fi: sharing the air
docs.text:
Why Ethernet's method doesn't work: wired Ethernet detected collisions by listening while transmitting. A radio can't hear a faint incoming signal while it's transmitting loudly itself. Worse, two stations may not hear each other at all.

How 802.11 handles it:

  1. Association: a device scans for access points (APs), which broadcast beacons. It picks one and joins (associates), usually with authentication (WPA2/WPA3). The AP bridges wireless traffic onto the wired network.
  2. The hidden terminal problem: stations A and C are both in range of the AP but not of each other, because of distance or a wall. Each senses the channel as free and transmits, and their frames collide at the AP. Neither knows.
  3. Collision avoidance (CSMA/CA): since collisions can't be detected reliably, Wi-Fi tries to avoid them. A station senses the channel, then waits a random backoff before sending, counting down only while the channel is idle.
  4. Link-layer ACKs: the receiver acknowledges every frame. No ACK means the sender assumes a collision or corruption, backs off longer and resends. This hides most wireless losses from TCP.
  5. RTS/CTS (optional): before a long frame, the station sends a short Request-To-Send. The AP answers Clear-To-Send, which everyone in range of the AP hears, including hidden stations, and they stay quiet for that time.

Wi-Fi throughput is shared by everyone on the same channel, and each frame carries overhead, so a busy AP (a conference, a café) feels slow even with strong signal.

docs.title: Cellular networks: 4G and 5G
docs.text:
Why they're more complex: a cellular network covers whole countries. It must authenticate millions of subscribers, track where each phone is, keep its data session alive as it moves between cells at motorway speed, and bill for it.

How the pieces fit:

  • Base stations (eNodeB in 4G, gNB in 5G) handle the radio link with phones in their cell, scheduling who transmits when, on which frequencies.
  • In the core network, the mobility management function (MME in 4G, AMF in 5G) handles signalling: attaching phones, tracking which cell they're in, and coordinating handovers. The subscriber database (HSS / UDM) holds each SIM's identity and keys, used to authenticate the phone.
  • User data flows through gateways: the serving gateway anchors the session while the phone moves between base stations, and the packet gateway connects to the Internet and gives the phone its IP address. Data is tunnelled between them, so the phone's address doesn't change as it moves.
  • 5G adds much more radio capacity (including high-frequency bands with short range), lower latency, and a core split into software services that can run in the cloud, including slices with different guarantees.

Note

Latency on mobile: a phone's radio sleeps to save battery, and waking it up to send adds tens to hundreds of milliseconds to the first request after idle. Batching requests, and avoiding constant small background calls, saves both latency and battery.

docs.title: Mobility: keeping connections while moving
docs.text:
Why it's hard: an IP address says where a device is attached. When a device moves to another network, the obvious result is a new address. Then every TCP connection breaks, because connections are identified by addresses.

How it's handled:

  1. The device has a permanent address from its home network. People send to that.
  2. When it attaches to a visited network, it gets a local care-of address and tells its home network where it is now.
  3. Packets sent to the permanent address arrive at the home network, which tunnels them to the visited network, and they're delivered to the device. Replies can go directly to the sender.

This is indirect routing. It's simple for correspondents (nothing changes for them), but traffic can take a long detour (a "triangle"). Cellular networks use exactly this idea: the packet gateway is the anchor, and data is tunnelled to whichever base station the phone is using. Moving between base stations is a handover: the network prepares the new cell, switches the tunnel, and the phone carries on, ideally losing nothing.

Moving between different networks, from Wi-Fi to mobile data, usually does change the address. That breaks TCP connections, which is one reason QUIC identifies connections by a connection ID instead of addresses, so they survive the switch.

docs.title: Effects on higher layers
docs.text:
Why designers should care: TCP assumes loss means congestion and slows down. On wireless, loss is often just a bad moment in the radio, so TCP may cut its speed for no reason. Link-layer retransmission (Wi-Fi ACKs, cellular retransmission) hides much of this, but adds variable delay.

What it means for your app:

  • Expect latency jitter and short disconnects; use timeouts, retries with backoff and idempotency.
  • Design offline-first flows where it matters: store locally, sync later (see Fitness tracking).
  • Keep payloads small, and use adaptive media (adaptive bitrate video).
  • Resume rather than restart: resumable uploads, Last-Event-ID for SSE streams, cursors for sync.

docs.title: In the system design interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "How does your app behave on a flaky mobile connection?" → Short timeouts with retries and backoff, idempotency keys on writes, resumable uploads, local queueing while offline, and adaptive bitrate for media.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Why do mobile clients reconnect so often?" → Radio sleep states, handovers, switching between Wi-Fi and cellular (which changes the IP address), and carrier NAT timeouts on idle connections. Long-lived connections need heartbeats and automatic reconnect with resume.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Why might HTTP/3 help mobile users?" → QUIC connections are identified by a connection ID, so they survive address changes. A lost packet only delays its own stream, and setup takes fewer round trips.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What is the hidden terminal problem?

Two stations can each reach the access point but can't hear each other, so carrier sensing says the channel is free, and their frames collide at the AP. RTS/CTS and random backoff reduce it.

Why does Wi-Fi acknowledge every frame at the link layer?

Radio loses and corrupts frames far more often than wires, and collisions can't be detected while transmitting. Link-level ACKs let the sender retransmit quickly, hiding most losses from TCP, which would otherwise mistake them for congestion.

How does a phone keep its IP address while moving between cell towers?

The packet gateway in the core network anchors the address, and data is tunnelled to whichever base station currently serves the phone. A handover moves the tunnel's end, not the address.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Security in Computer Networks
docs.text:
Intermediate

These pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams on Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach by James Kurose and Keith Ross, connected to system design. They don't replace the book, which is worth reading in full.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The Internet was built to connect trusting researchers, so security was added later, layer by layer. Secure communication needs confidentiality (only the intended receiver can read it), integrity (changes are detected), authentication (you know who you're talking to) and availability. Cryptography provides the first three. Symmetric keys are fast but must be shared; public-key cryptography solves sharing; hashes, MACs and signatures protect integrity; certificates bind keys to names. TLS combines all of this for the web. IPsec/VPNs, WPA, firewalls and intrusion detection protect other layers.

Key ideas: confidentiality, integrity, authentication · symmetric vs public-key · Diffie-Hellman key agreement · hashes · MACs · digital signatures · certificates and CAs · nonces and replay · TLS · IPsec and VPNs · WPA · firewalls · IDS

docs.title: What "secure" means
docs.text:
Why it needs defining: "make it secure" is too vague to design for. The book's cast is Alice and Bob, who want to talk, and Trudy, an intruder on the network who can eavesdrop, modify or inject messages, replay old ones, impersonate either side, or flood them (denial of service).

The properties we want:

  • Confidentiality: Trudy can't read the messages → encryption.
  • Integrity: Trudy can't change them unnoticed → MACs and signatures.
  • Authentication: each side knows who the other really is → certificates, signatures, challenge-response.
  • Availability: the service keeps working under attack → firewalls, rate limiting, DDoS protection.

docs.title: Symmetric and public-key cryptography
docs.text:
Why two kinds: encryption scrambles a message so that only someone with the right key can unscramble it. The question is how the two sides get the right keys.

How each works:

  • Symmetric (AES, ChaCha20): the same secret key encrypts and decrypts. It's very fast (gigabytes a second, with hardware support), so it's used for the actual data. The problem: both sides must already share the key, and you can't just send it over the network that Trudy is watching.
  • Public-key (RSA, elliptic-curve cryptography): each party has a key pair. The public key can be published to everyone; the private key never leaves its owner. What one key locks, only the other unlocks. Anyone can encrypt to Bob with his public key, and only Bob can decrypt. Bob can also sign with his private key, and anyone can verify with the public key. It's slow, around 1,000× slower than symmetric.

How they combine: use public-key methods only to agree on a fresh symmetric session key, then encrypt the data with that key. Modern protocols use Diffie-Hellman key agreement (ECDHE): each side sends a public value, and both compute the same secret without it ever crossing the network. Because the session keys are thrown away after use, recording traffic today and stealing a server's private key later still doesn't decrypt it (forward secrecy).

docs.title: Integrity: hashes, MACs and signatures
docs.text:
Why encryption alone isn't enough: encryption hides content, but Trudy might still flip bits or replay a message. Bob needs to know the message is exactly what Alice sent.

How:

  • A cryptographic hash (SHA-256) turns any message into a fixed-size fingerprint. It's practically impossible to find two messages with the same hash, or to work backwards from a hash.
  • A MAC (message authentication code, usually HMAC) hashes the message together with a shared secret key. Only someone with the key can produce the right MAC, so a valid MAC proves the message came from a key holder and wasn't changed. Webhook signatures and API request signing work like this.
  • A digital signature encrypts the message's hash with the sender's private key. Anyone can verify it with the public key, and only the private key holder could have made it. Unlike a MAC, it doesn't need a shared secret, and it proves to third parties who signed (non-repudiation).
  • A certificate solves "is this really Bob's public key?" A certificate authority (CA) that everyone trusts signs a statement: "this public key belongs to bob.com". Browsers ship with a list of trusted CAs and check the chain of signatures.

docs.title: Authentication and replay attacks
docs.text:
Why it's subtle: proving identity over a network is harder than it looks. If Alice proves who she is by sending a password, or even an encrypted password, Trudy can record that message and replay it later.

How it's done safely: challenge-response with a nonce. Bob sends a fresh random number (a nonce) used only once. Alice proves her identity by returning it encrypted or signed with her key. A recorded answer is useless next time, because the nonce will be different. The same idea protects against replays elsewhere: TLS mixes random values from both sides into its keys, and signed API requests include timestamps and nonces.

docs.title: TLS: securing TCP connections
docs.text:
Why: TLS (successor to SSL) is how nearly everything on the Internet is protected: HTTPS, secure email, database connections, gRPC.

How it works, in outline (see How HTTPS works for the step-by-step diagram):

  1. Handshake: client and server agree on algorithms and exchange Diffie-Hellman values. The server sends its certificate and signs the handshake with its private key, proving it owns the certificate.
  2. The client verifies the certificate chain up to a trusted CA, checks the name matches the site, and checks the signature.
  3. Both derive the same session keys from the shared secret and random values from both sides.
  4. Data transfer: records are encrypted and integrity-protected with the symmetric keys (authenticated encryption such as AES-GCM). Each record has a sequence number, so reordering or replaying records is detected.

TLS 1.3 completes the handshake in one round trip (zero for a resumed session) and removes old, weak options.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "All traffic uses TLS 1.3: terminated at the load balancer for public traffic, and mutual TLS between internal services, so services authenticate each other with certificates issued by our internal CA."

docs.title: IPsec, VPNs and Wi-Fi security
docs.text:
Why other layers need protection too: TLS protects one application connection. Sometimes you want to protect everything between two networks, or the wireless link itself.

How:

  • IPsec secures traffic at the network layer. In tunnel mode, whole IP packets are encrypted and wrapped inside new IP packets between two gateways. Every application benefits without changes. Site-to-site VPNs (connecting an office to a cloud VPC) commonly use it. Newer VPNs such as WireGuard follow the same idea with a much simpler design.
  • Wi-Fi security (WPA2, WPA3) authenticates devices to the access point and encrypts frames over the air, so neighbours can't read or inject traffic on the wireless link. In companies, authentication goes through a central server (802.1X with EAP), so each user has their own credentials.
  • Cellular networks authenticate each SIM against the operator's subscriber database and encrypt the radio link.

docs.title: Firewalls and intrusion detection
docs.text:
Why: even with encryption everywhere, organisations must control what traffic is allowed in and out, and spot attacks in progress.

How:

  • Packet filters (stateless firewalls) allow or block each packet by rules on addresses, protocol and ports: "allow TCP port 443 to the web servers, block everything else inbound".
  • Stateful firewalls track connections: "allow replies to connections we started, block unsolicited incoming connections". Cloud security groups work this way.
  • Application gateways and web application firewalls inspect application data, for example blocking SQL injection patterns in HTTP requests.
  • Intrusion detection and prevention systems (IDS/IPS) inspect traffic deeply, matching known attack signatures and unusual patterns, and alert on attacks or block them.
  • A DMZ is a separate network segment for public-facing servers, so a compromised web server doesn't give direct access to the internal network.

The modern trend is zero trust: don't assume anything inside the firewall is safe. Authenticate and encrypt every connection (mutual TLS), and give each service only the access it needs.

docs.title: In the system design interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "How do you secure service-to-service traffic?" → Mutual TLS with short-lived certificates from an internal CA (often via a service mesh), network policies allowing only the needed paths, and per-service authorisation.

Important

Interviewer asks: "How do you know a webhook really came from the payment provider?" → The provider signs the body with an HMAC using a shared secret. You recompute and compare in constant time, and reject old timestamps to stop replays.

Important

Interviewer asks: "How do you protect the system from DDoS?" → Absorb at the edge (CDN or anycast DDoS protection), rate limits per client at the gateway, firewall rules dropping unwanted traffic, autoscaling, and load shedding for the rest.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why does TLS use public-key cryptography only during the handshake?

Public-key operations are slow. They're used to authenticate the server and agree on a shared secret (Diffie-Hellman). Bulk data is then encrypted with fast symmetric keys derived from it.

What is the difference between a MAC and a digital signature?

A MAC uses a shared secret key, so anyone with the key could have produced it. A signature uses the signer's private key and is verified with the public key, so it proves to anyone exactly who signed, and needs no shared secret.

How does a nonce prevent replay attacks?

The verifier sends a fresh random value each time, and the prover must sign or encrypt that value. A recorded old response contains the old nonce, so it is rejected.

docs.title: API design
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Spend five minutes, get the important details right, and move on to the design.

docs.title: Why it matters, and why to keep it short
docs.text: In an interview, the API is where you show that your design actually meets the requirements: each functional requirement becomes one or two endpoints. Interviewers don't need every field. They're checking for a handful of details that separate careful engineers from the rest. Get those right in about five minutes, then move on to the architecture.

docs.title: The six details that matter
docs.text:
Rule Example Resources = core entities GET /events/{id}, POST /bookings Cursor pagination, not offset GET /feed?cursor=(ts,id)&limit=20: stable when new items arrive Idempotency on mutations Idempotency-Key header + unique index → retries are safe Auth from token, not body user_id comes from the JWT; never trust {user_id} in the request Async for long work POST returns 202 + job_id; GET /jobs/{id} Version /v1/… or header; add optional fields only

Why each one matters:

  1. Resources named after your entities. If your core entities are Event, Booking and User, your API is GET /events/{id}, POST /bookings, GET /users/{id}/bookings. It shows the API follows from the data model.
  2. Cursor pagination, not offsets. With ?page=3&size=20 (offset 40), if new items arrive while the user scrolls, everything shifts down and they see duplicates or miss items. And OFFSET 100000 makes the database read and throw away 100,000 rows. A cursor says "give me the 20 items after this one", for example after (timestamp, id) of the last item seen. That is stable and uses an index directly.
  3. Idempotency on anything that changes data. Networks lose responses, and clients retry. Without protection, a retried POST /payments charges twice. The client sends an Idempotency-Key (a unique ID per operation), and the server stores it with a unique constraint and returns the original result for repeats.
  4. Identity from the token, never the request body. If the API accepts {"user_id": 42, …} in the body, anyone can act as user 42. The server gets the user from the verified auth token (session or JWT).
  5. Long work is asynchronous. Encoding a video or generating a report can take minutes, far longer than an HTTP request should stay open. Return 202 Accepted with a job_id straight away. The client polls GET /jobs/{id} or gets notified when it finishes.
  6. Versioning. Clients (especially mobile apps) can't all update at once. Only add optional fields to existing versions; put breaking changes under /v2/.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "REST with resources from our entities: POST /bookings with an idempotency key, cursor-paginated GET /bookings. User identity comes from the auth token."

Warning

Don't over-invest: spending 15 minutes on endpoint shapes is a classic way to run out of time for the deep dives, which is where senior candidates stand out.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: API DESIGN on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Name resources after your core entities.
  2. Use cursor pagination, not offsets.
  3. Accept an Idempotency-Key on every mutating call.
  4. Take the user's identity from the auth token, never from the body.
  5. Return 202 and a job ID for long work.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"Three endpoints cover the requirements; writes take an idempotency key, lists use cursor pagination, and identity comes from the token."

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Used by: Ticketmaster · URL shortener · News feed · Local delivery · Distributed cache

Tip

One-page sketchnote: CACHING on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A cache keeps a copy of hot data in memory so you don't pay the full cost of reading it every time. A database read takes about 5–50 ms; a Redis read takes about 1 ms.
  • The default pattern is cache-aside: read from the cache, and on a miss read the database and fill the cache. On a write, update the database and delete the cached key.
  • Every cache is a trade. You get speed and less database load, and you pay with stale data, stampedes when hot keys expire, and hot keys that overload one node. Name all three before the interviewer does.

docs.title: Why cache at all?
docs.text:
Two reasons, and say which one you mean:

  1. Latency. Memory is orders of magnitude faster than a database query that touches disk or runs joins.
  2. Load. Popularity is uneven. A small share of items gets most of the traffic, so caching that share removes most of the database load. A cache hit rate of 90% means the database sees one request in ten.

Note

Rule of thumb: add a cache when a calculation shows the database can't keep up (for example, ~50k reads/sec against one Postgres primary) or when a read path misses its latency target. Don't add one "because caches are good".

docs.title: Cache-aside: the default
docs.text:
Read: GET key → hit? return it. Miss? SELECT from the database, SET key value EX 300, return it.

Write: UPDATE the database first, then DELETE key. The next read repopulates it.

Why delete instead of updating the cache? Two concurrent writers can update the cache in the wrong order and leave it permanently wrong. A delete can't be applied in the wrong order. The worst case is one extra cache miss.

docs.title: Other strategies
docs.text: Strategy How it works Choose it when Cost Cache-aside App reads cache, falls back to DB, fills cache Default for almost everything Brief staleness after writes Read-through Cache library loads from DB itself on a miss You want the logic in one place Same staleness as cache-aside Write-through Every write goes to cache and DB together Data is read right after it's written Slower writes; cache fills with data nobody reads Write-behind Write to cache now, flush to DB later Very high write rates you can afford to lose Data loss if the cache dies before flushing CDN / edge cache HTTP responses cached near users Static or identical-for-everyone responses Invalidation is slow, so use short TTLs or versioned URLs

docs.title: What to cache, and for how long
docs.text:
• Cache: things read far more often than written, such as event pages, user profiles, URL redirects and computed feeds.
  • Don't cache: data that must never be stale (a seat's booking status, an account balance at checkout), or data that's read once.
  • TTL: pick it from how stale the product can tolerate. "A price shown on a search page may be 60 seconds old" means a 60 s TTL. Always set one, so that bugs in invalidation heal themselves.
  • Eviction: when memory is full, LRU (evict least recently used) is the usual default. LFU suits stable popularity.

docs.title: The three ways caches hurt you
1. Stale data
docs.text: Readers can see an old value between the database write and the cache delete, or until the TTL expires. Decide per feature whether that's acceptable. On the booking path of Ticketmaster it isn't, so that path reads the database. On the browse path it is.

docs.title: 2. Stampede (thundering herd)
docs.text:
A very popular key expires, and thousands of requests miss at the same instant. Every one of them queries the database.

Fixes, usually combined:

  • Single-flight / request coalescing: only one request rebuilds the value, using a short lock such as SET lock:key 1 NX EX 5. The others wait briefly or get the old value.
  • Serve stale while revalidating: keep the old value a little past its TTL and refresh it in the background.
  • Jittered TTLs: add randomness so many keys don't expire together.
  • Pre-warm known hot keys before a big event.

docs.title: 3. Hot keys
docs.text:
One key gets so much traffic that the single cache node holding it saturates, for example a celebrity's profile or a viral link. Fixes:

  • Replicate the key: store copies as key#0 … key#9 on different nodes and read a random one.
  • Local in-process cache with a few seconds' TTL in front of Redis.
  • Know your hot keys: track them, because you can't fix what you can't see.

docs.title: Numbers worth knowing
docs.text: Typical Redis GET (same datacenter) ~0.5–1 ms round trip Redis throughput, one node ~100k+ simple ops/sec Postgres indexed read ~1–10 ms; complex queries 10–100 ms+ Memory per Redis node tens to a few hundred GB

docs.title: Interview phrases
docs.text:
Tip

  • "Reads outnumber writes 100 to 1 and popularity is skewed, so a cache-aside Redis layer should take 80–90% of reads off Postgres."
  • "On write I update the database, then delete the key. Deleting is safe under concurrent writers."
  • "This key is hot, so I'll guard against a stampede with single-flight and jittered TTLs."
  • "The checkout path doesn't read from cache, because it must never be stale."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Caching without a TTL, so one invalidation bug lives forever.
  • Updating the cache on write instead of deleting it.
  • Treating the cache as the source of truth. Redis can lose data, and the database must still be correct on its own.
  • Forgetting the cold start: after a deploy or failover the cache is empty and the database takes the full load.

docs.text:

  • DDIA: Ch 5 Replication. Read replicas are the other way to scale reads, with the same staleness trade-off.
  • Patterns: Scaling reads

docs.title: CAP theorem and PACELC
docs.text:
Intermediate

When the network splits, choose between refusing requests and answering with possibly stale data, separately for each feature.

docs.title: The situation CAP is about
docs.text:
Your data is copied on two servers, maybe in two data centres. Normally every write reaches both. Now the network link between them breaks: a network partition. Both servers are still running, and users can still reach each of them, but the servers can't talk to each other. A write lands on one; the other never hears about it. Then a user asks the other server for that data. What should it do?

  1. The link between Node 1 and Node 2 breaks. Partitions will happen in any distributed system (a switch fails, a cable is cut, a cloud zone has problems), so you can't choose to avoid them. That's why "P" isn't really optional.
  2. A user writes x = 2 to Node 1. Node 2 still has the old value, x = 1, and can't find out about the change.
  3. Another user reads x from Node 2. There are only two choices:
  4. Refuse to answer (return an error or wait) because it can't confirm it has the latest value. You stay consistent, but that part of the system is unavailable. This is CP.
  5. Answer with x = 1, which may be stale. You stay available, but the answer may be inconsistent. This is AP.

That's the whole theorem: during a partition, choose between consistency and availability. When there's no partition, you can have both.

docs.title: Choose per feature, not per system
docs.text:
The common mistake is calling a whole system "CP" or "AP". In practice you choose per feature, based on what a wrong answer costs:

Feature Choice Booking, payments, inventory CP: never oversell or double-charge Search, feeds, reviews, likes AP: stale for seconds is fine Usernames / unique constraints CP (linearizable)

The question to ask for each feature: is a stale or conflicting answer worse than no answer? Selling the same seat twice is worse than a "please try again" error, so booking is CP. A like count that's a few seconds old is far better than an error page, so likes are AP.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "CAP is a per-feature choice: the booking path is CP, browsing is AP."

Note

PACELC, the everyday version: even with no partition, strong consistency costs latency, because each write must wait for other replicas to confirm. So the extended rule is: during a Partition choose A or C; Else choose Latency or Consistency. More in DDIA Chapter 9.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: CAP THEOREM AND PACELC on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Partitions will happen, so the real choice is C or A during one.
  2. Choose per feature, not per system.
  3. Money, inventory and uniqueness: consistency (CP).
  4. Feeds, search, reviews, counters: availability (AP).
  5. PACELC: even without partitions, stronger consistency costs latency.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"Booking is CP: I'd rather reject than double-sell. Browsing is AP: a few seconds stale is fine."

docs.title: Consistent hashing
docs.text:
Intermediate

Add or remove a node and move only a small share of the keys.

docs.title: The problem it solves
docs.text:
You have a cache spread over 4 servers. To decide which server holds a key, the obvious rule is server = hash(key) % 4. It works, until you add a fifth server. Now the rule is hash(key) % 5, and for about 80% of keys the answer changes. Those keys are looked up on the wrong server, every lookup misses, and all that traffic falls through to the database at once. Adding capacity has just caused an outage.

Consistent hashing is a placement rule where adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys, about 1/N of them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Make a ring. Imagine the full range of hash values bent into a circle, so the largest value wraps round to 0.
  2. Place the servers. Hash each server's name, and put the server at that point on the ring (nodes A, B, C, D).
  3. Place the keys. Hash each key to a point on the same ring. A key belongs to the first server you meet going clockwise from it.
  4. Add a server. New node E lands somewhere on the ring, between B and C, say. It takes over only the keys between B and itself, keys that used to belong to C. Every other key stays exactly where it was. With N servers, about 1/N of the keys move. Removing a server works the same way in reverse: only its keys move, to the next server clockwise.

Virtual nodes. With only a few servers, their random positions can leave one server with a huge arc (lots of keys) and another with a tiny one. The fix is to place each server at many points, say 100 or 200, by hashing A#1, A#2 and so on. The arcs then average out, so load is even. A more powerful server can be given more virtual nodes so it takes a bigger share.

Note

Used by: distributed caches (Memcached clients, Redis client-side sharding), Cassandra and DynamoDB for placing data, and load balancers that send the same video or document ID to the same server so its cache stays warm.

What it doesn't fix: a single hot key still lives on one server, however you place keys. That needs replication or key splitting (see Sharding).

Tip

One-page sketchnote: CONSISTENT HASHING on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Place nodes and keys on the same hash ring.
  2. A key belongs to the first node clockwise from it.
  3. Use virtual nodes (many points per server) to even out load.
  4. Adding a node moves roughly 1/N of keys; hash % N moves almost all of them.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"Cache nodes sit on a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes, so adding a node remaps about 1/N of keys instead of emptying the whole cache."

docs.title: Data modeling
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Start from the queries the product runs, then choose keys and indexes that make each one cheap.

docs.title: Start from the queries, not the nouns
docs.text:
The usual beginner approach is to list the nouns (User, Post, Comment), give each a table, and add columns. That produces a valid schema that may be slow for exactly the things your product does most. In system design, the data model exists to make the hot queries fast, so work backwards from them.

  1. List the queries the product actually runs, and how often. For a social app: "show a user's posts, newest first" (constantly), "show one post by ID" (constantly), "create a post" (much less often).
  2. Design keys and indexes so each hot query is one index lookup or one range scan. "Posts by author, newest first" becomes a posts table with an index on (author_id, created_at DESC). The database jumps to that author's entries, already in order, and reads the first 20. "Post by ID" is the primary key. If a hot query needs several lookups or a large sort, the model isn't finished.
  3. Pick the database last. Default to a relational database such as Postgres: it handles these patterns well, gives you transactions, and lets you run queries you didn't plan for. Move away from it only with a concrete reason:
  4. very high write volume with simple key access: Cassandra;
  5. flexible documents read by key: DynamoDB or MongoDB;
  6. full-text search: Elasticsearch, as a second store fed from the main one.

Note

Normalize vs denormalize: normalizing means storing each fact once (a user's name lives only in users, and posts reference user_id). One place to update, so no inconsistencies. That's the default. Denormalizing means deliberately copying data to make a hot read faster, for example storing the author's name and avatar on each post, so the feed doesn't need a join. When you do, say how the copy stays in sync (an async job, CDC), and accept that it can briefly be stale.

What interviewers look for: the core tables with their primary keys, the one or two indexes that make the hot queries fast, and a sentence on why this database. You don't need every column.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DATA MODELING on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. List the two or three hottest queries first.
  2. Make each one a key lookup or a single index range scan.
  3. Default to Postgres; switch only with a reason you can state.
  4. Normalize by default; denormalize deliberately for a hot read and say how the copy stays in sync.
  5. Choose the partition key from the hottest query if you will shard.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"The hot query is a user's posts, newest first, so the posts table gets an index on (author_id, created_at DESC)."

docs.title: Database indexing
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

An index turns a scan of every row into a short walk down a tree. Pick the right kind for the query.

docs.title: What an index is
docs.text:
Without an index, finding "all orders for user 42" means reading every row in the orders table and checking each one: a full table scan. With 100 million rows, that takes seconds or minutes. An index is a separate, sorted structure that maps values to row locations, like the index at the back of a book. The database jumps straight to user 42's entries, typically in 3–4 disk reads, whatever the table size.

The default index is a B-tree: a shallow, sorted tree. It answers equality (= 42), ranges (created_at > '2026-01-01') and sorting (ORDER BY created_at). See DDIA Chapter 3 for how it works inside.

docs.title: Pick the right kind
docs.text:
Index Use for Example B-tree Equality + range + ORDER BY created_at > X; composite (user_id, ts) Hash Equality only session lookup Geospatial (R-tree, geohash) Nearby queries Yelp, Uber, Gopuff Inverted Full-text search Post search, Elasticsearch Composite Multi-column filters (leftmost prefix rule) WHERE user_id=? ORDER BY ts Covering Index-only scans INCLUDE (title)

Three that come up constantly in interviews:

  • Composite index. An index on (user_id, created_at) is sorted by user first, then by time within each user. The query WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 jumps to user 42 and reads 20 entries already in order, with no sorting needed. The leftmost-prefix rule: the index helps queries that filter on user_id, or on user_id and created_at, but not queries on created_at alone, just as a phone book sorted by surname then first name doesn't help you find everyone called "Asha".
  • Geospatial index. "Restaurants within 2 km" filters on two dimensions at once. Two separate B-tree indexes on latitude and longitude each narrow only one dimension, leaving a long strip to scan. A geospatial index (PostGIS R-tree, geohash, quadtree) narrows both at once.
  • Inverted index. For text search, map each word to the list of documents containing it: "pizza" → [doc 3, doc 17, …]. A search for "cheap pizza" intersects two lists. This is what Elasticsearch is built on.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "A composite index on (user_id, created_at DESC) makes the feed query a single range scan."

Warning

Indexes cost writes. Every insert or update has to update every index on the table, and each index uses disk and memory. Add indexes for the hot queries you identified, not for every column.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DATABASE INDEXING on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Equality and ranges: B-tree (the default).
  2. Several filters: a composite index, ordered by the leftmost-prefix rule.
  3. Distance queries: a geospatial index (R-tree, geohash).
  4. Full-text search: an inverted index.
  5. Every index slows writes, so index only the queries you need.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"A composite index on (user_id, created_at DESC) turns the feed query into one index range scan."

docs.title: Networking essentials
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

How a request travels from a user to your service, and which protocol to pick for which job.

docs.title: What you need to know
docs.text: You don't need to be a network engineer for system design interviews. You need to know the path a request takes, what a load balancer does at each "layer", and which protocol to pick for which kind of communication. (For the full step-by-step of a page load, see What happens when you type a URL.)

docs.title: The request path, and two kinds of load balancer
docs.text:
1. The client looks up your domain name in DNS and gets back the IP address of your load balancer, not of an individual server. The load balancer spreads requests across many servers, and lets you add, remove or replace servers without clients noticing.
  2. An L4 load balancer works at the transport layer (TCP/UDP). It sees IP addresses and ports, but not the content of the request. It just forwards each connection to a server. That makes it very fast and cheap, and good for long-lived connections such as WebSockets, or for non-HTTP protocols.
  3. An L7 load balancer works at the application layer (HTTP). It reads each request, so it can route by path (/api/* to service A, /ws/* to service B), by header or by cookie. It can also decrypt HTTPS (TLS termination), add headers, retry failed requests, and keep a user on the same server (sticky sessions). It's more flexible, but does more work per request.

Most systems use both: an L4 balancer at the very edge for raw throughput, and L7 (often an API gateway) in front of the services.

docs.title: Which protocol for what
docs.text:
The key question is who needs to send data to whom, and how often:

Protocol Use REST over HTTP Default public API gRPC (HTTP/2 + Protobuf) Internal service-to-service, high QPS SSE Server→client stream (feeds, tokens, comments) WebSocket Bidirectional real-time (chat, docs, games) Long polling Fallback push when nothing else works
  • The client asks, the server answers (most APIs): plain HTTP with REST, or gRPC between internal services.
  • The server needs to push updates to the client (live comments, a stock ticker, an AI reply streaming in word by word): Server-Sent Events (SSE). It's one long HTTP response that the server keeps writing to. It's simple, works through proxies, and reconnects automatically.
  • Both sides send often (chat, collaborative editing, multiplayer games): WebSockets, a persistent two-way connection. These connections are long-lived and stateful, so you need to track which server holds which user's connection.
  • Long polling (the client asks, and the server holds the request open until there is news) is a fallback for environments where neither of the above works.

See REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC and HTTP versions for more detail.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: NETWORKING ESSENTIALS on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Public API used by browsers and partners: REST over HTTPS.
  2. High-volume calls between internal services: gRPC.
  3. Server pushes a stream to the client: SSE.
  4. Two-way, low-latency messages: WebSocket.
  5. Routing by URL path, header or cookie: L7 load balancer. Raw TCP or very high throughput: L4.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"Clients talk REST through an L7 load balancer; internal services use gRPC. Live updates go over SSE, which reconnects automatically."

docs.title: Sharding
docs.text:
Intermediate

Split data across machines when one can't hold it or keep up with the writes, but only then.

docs.title: What it is, and when you need it
docs.text:
Sharding (also called partitioning) splits one big dataset across several database servers, so each shard holds part of the data. Shard 1 has some users, shard 2 others, and so on. It is different from replication, where every server holds a copy of all the data.

You need it when one primary database can't keep up: the data is too big for one machine, or there are more writes than one machine can handle. Read load alone is usually solved more cheaply with caches and read replicas. Sharding comes after those, because it makes everything else harder: queries across shards, transactions across shards, schema changes, and rebalancing.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a shard key. This is the field that decides which shard a row lives on, for example user_id. Pick it from your hottest queries: if nearly every request is "do something for this user", sharding by user means each request touches exactly one shard.
  2. Choose how to map keys to shards.
  3. Hash the key (hash(user_id)): spreads data evenly and avoids hot spots, but neighbouring keys end up on different shards.
  4. Ranges (users 0–1M on shard A, 1M–2M on shard B): keeps neighbouring keys together for range scans, but sequential keys such as timestamps all land on the newest shard.
  5. A router (in the application, a proxy, or the database driver) computes the shard for each request and sends it there.
  6. The cost: a query that doesn't include the shard key, such as "all orders over $1,000 across all users", has to ask every shard and merge the answers (scatter-gather). That's slow, and it gets slower as you add shards. Accept it for rare queries, or answer them from a separate store such as a data warehouse or search index.

Warning

The biggest mistake is sharding too early. One Postgres server handles roughly 10–50k transactions a second and several TB of data. Shard only when your numbers show one primary can't take the write load, even after caching and read replicas.

Note

Hot spots: even with hashing, one very popular key (a celebrity, a flash-sale item) puts all its load on one shard. Fixes: split the key across several shards, cache it, or buffer its writes and apply them in batches.

Plan for growth: don't map keys with hash % number_of_shards, because adding a shard then moves almost every row. Create many logical partitions up front (say 1,024) and assign several to each physical server, or use consistent hashing. Then adding a server means moving a few whole partitions.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: SHARDING on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Has the calculation shown one primary isn't enough after caching and replicas?
  2. Pick the shard key from the hottest query, so most requests hit one shard.
  3. Hash for even spread; ranges only if you need range scans on the key.
  4. Plan for hot keys and for rebalancing (many logical partitions, or consistent hashing).
  5. Accept that queries without the shard key fan out to every shard.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"Writes outgrow one primary, so I'll shard by hash of user_id: every hot query includes it. Cross-user analytics can scatter-gather or run on a warehouse."

docs.text:
These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

  1. Part I is about one database on one machine: what "good" means, how data is shaped, stored, and encoded.
  2. Part II spreads data across machines. Replication copies it, partitioning splits it. Ch 8 lists everything that breaks and Ch 9 shows how nodes still agree.
  3. Part III connects many systems: the source of truth plus derived data (caches, search indexes, analytics) kept in sync with batch and stream processing.

docs.title: DDIA Chapter 1: Reliable, Scalable, Maintainable
docs.text:
Intermediate

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 1 · RELIABLE, SCALABLE, MAINTAINABLE on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The three words every NFR discussion comes back to. This chapter gives them precise meaning: reliability means tolerating faults, scalability means describing load and performance with numbers, and maintainability means keeping the system easy to run and change.

Key ideas: faults vs failures · load parameters · p99 latency · tail amplification · scale up vs out

docs.title: Fault ≠ failure
docs.text:
Reliability

"Reliable" doesn't mean nothing ever goes wrong. In any system bigger than one machine, something is always going wrong: a disk dies, a server reboots, a network cable gets unplugged, someone deploys a bug. The book separates two words to make this precise.

  • A fault is one part misbehaving: one disk, one server, one bad config value.
  • A failure is the system as a whole stopping working for users: the site is down, or orders are lost.

You can't prevent faults, so a reliable system is one that keeps working despite them:

  1. A fault happens, for example one of three database replicas dies.
  2. Mechanisms built in advance absorb it. The load balancer stops sending traffic to the dead node, a replica takes over, and clients retry the requests that were in flight.
  3. Users notice nothing, or maybe one slow request. The fault never became a failure.

That is the mindset for every design: for each component, ask "what happens when this breaks?" and make sure the answer isn't "the whole system stops".

Note

Scale makes faults routine: a disk fails at roughly 2–5% per year. That sounds rare, but with 10,000 disks you should expect about one disk to die every day. At scale, failure handling is everyday work, not a rare emergency.

Warning

The most dangerous faults are in software. Hardware faults are mostly independent: two disks rarely die in the same minute. A software bug is correlated: the same bug runs on every server, so it hits them all at once. Examples are a bad deploy, a leap-second bug, or a dependency that every service calls. Adding replicas doesn't help, because every replica runs the same bug. Defences: staged rollouts (canaries), fast rollback, and limits on how much a single change can affect.

docs.title: Describing load: the Twitter timeline
docs.text:
Scalability · load parameters

"Will it scale?" can't be answered until you say what is growing. "Lots of users" isn't specific enough. You need load parameters: the few numbers that actually stress your system, such as requests per second, the read-to-write ratio, or how many followers a post goes out to.

The book's example is Twitter around 2012. Users posted about 4.6k tweets a second on average (12k at peak), but home timelines were read about 300k times a second. Reads outnumbered writes by about 65 to 1, and that ratio shaped the whole design.

There are two ways to build a home timeline:

  1. Compute it when someone reads it (fan-out on read). Posting a tweet is cheap: insert one row. But every time a user opens the app, the database must find everyone they follow, fetch their recent tweets and merge them by time.
  2. At 300k timeline reads a second, each one a big join across follows and tweets, the database can't keep up.
  3. Compute it when someone writes (fan-out on write). When a user tweets, a background worker inserts the tweet ID into a cached timeline for each of their followers.
  4. Now reading a timeline is a single cache lookup, which is very cheap. The cost has moved to write time: a user with 200 followers causes 200 cache writes per tweet. That's fine, because reads are far more common than writes.

But one load parameter breaks approach 2: the number of followers per user. A celebrity with 30 million followers would trigger 30 million cache writes per tweet. So Twitter uses a hybrid: normal users' tweets are fanned out on write, and celebrities' tweets are fetched at read time and merged in.

The lesson isn't really about Twitter. Find the number that decides the design (here, the read:write ratio and the fan-out per post) and design around it.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "The load parameter that matters here is fan-out per post, not total users. That number decides push vs pull."

docs.title: Describing performance: percentiles and tail latency
docs.text:
Scalability · performance

Once you know the load, you need to say how fast is fast enough. The natural instinct is to use the average response time. That's a mistake, because averages hide the users having a bad time.

  1. Response times aren't all similar. Most requests are fast, but there is a long tail of slow ones: a cache miss, a GC pause, a retransmitted packet. A 50 ms average can hide 1 in 100 requests taking 2 seconds.
  2. So use percentiles. Sort all response times. The p50 (median) is what a typical request sees. The p99 is the time that 99% of requests beat, so 1 in 100 is slower. The slowest requests often belong to your most valuable users, the ones with the most data, the biggest carts and the most history.
  3. Tail latency amplification makes the tail matter even more. Loading one page often calls many backend services in parallel: profile, recommendations, cart, ads, and so on.
  4. The page can't render until the slowest of those calls returns. Even if each backend is slow only 1% of the time, a page that calls 100 of them is slow most of the time.

Note

The math: the chance that all 100 calls are fast is 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.37. So 63% of page loads hit at least one slow call. This is why each service's p99 matters more than its average.

Two common defences: give each backend call a tight timeout and show the page without that piece if it is late, and use hedged requests: if a call hasn't returned by the p95 time, send the same request to a second replica and use whichever answer comes first.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "I'll set the SLO on p99, not average. Because the page fans out to several services, the tail compounds, so I'll add timeouts and hedged requests."

docs.title: Scaling up vs scaling out, and maintainability
docs.text:
Scalability · maintainability

When load grows past what one machine can handle, there are two basic moves. Scaling up means buying a bigger machine. Scaling out means spreading the work across many machines. The second sounds more impressive, but it brings all the hard problems in this book: replication lag, partial failure, distributed transactions. So start simple, and scale out only the parts that need it.

The chapter's third word, maintainability, is a reminder that most of a system's cost comes after launch: running it, debugging it and changing it for years. The book splits it into three parts, at the bottom of this table.

Choice What it means When it wins Scale up (vertical) Bigger machine: more cores, RAM, NVMe Simple, no distribution bugs. A single Postgres box handles 10–50k TPS. Start here. Scale out (horizontal) More machines, shared-nothing When one box is not enough or you need fault tolerance. Stateless services scale out easily; stateful ones (databases) are hard. Elastic Add or remove capacity automatically Unpredictable load. Manual scaling is simpler and has fewer surprises. Operability Easy for ops to keep running Monitoring, good defaults, predictable behaviour, runbooks. Simplicity Remove accidental complexity Good abstractions, for example SQL hiding storage and concurrency. Evolvability Easy to change later Loose coupling, schema evolution (Ch 4), tests.

Warning

Over-scaling: there is no general-purpose "scalable architecture". A system for 100k requests a second of 1 KB reads looks nothing like one for 3 uploads a minute of 2 GB files, even though both are "large scale". Design for the load parameters you calculated, not for a generic idea of scale.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "How will this scale?" → Name the load parameter (reads/sec, fan-out, data size), calculate it, then say which component breaks first.

Important

Interviewer asks: "What's your latency target?" → p99 < 200ms for reads, not averages. Mention tail amplification if requests fan out.

Important

Interviewer asks: "What if a node dies?" → Separate fault from failure: "A node dying is a fault. Replicas plus health checks mean it never becomes a failure."

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Before choosing components, let me pin down the load parameters: DAU, read:write ratio, and peak QPS, because they decide whether we need any distribution at all."

Ch 2: Data models →

docs.title: DDIA Chapter 2: Data Models & Query Languages
docs.text:
Intermediate

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 2 · DATA MODELS & QUERY LANGUAGES on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The shape of your data decides which database fits. Trees of data that are read together (one-to-many) suit documents. Data full of references (many-to-many) suits relational. Data where relationships are the point suits graphs.

Key ideas: relational · document · graph · normalization · schema-on-read · locality

docs.title: One LinkedIn profile, two models
docs.text:
Relational vs document

Take one LinkedIn-style profile: a name, a headline, several past jobs, a few schools and some contact details. How should it be stored?

  1. Relational: split the profile into tables, with users holding one row per person, positions one row per job, education one row per school, each pointing back with user_id. To show the page, you join them back together. In your code, though, a profile is one object with nested lists. Translating between that object and the tables is boilerplate (it's why ORMs exist), and the book calls the mismatch impedance mismatch.
  2. Document: store the whole profile as one JSON document, with the jobs and schools nested inside it. One read returns everything the page needs, because all of it is stored together on disk. This is called locality. The structure in the database matches the object in your code.

The document model fits well here because of the data's shape: a profile is a tree. One person has many jobs (one-to-many), each job belongs to exactly one profile, and you usually load the whole profile at once.

Note

When the document model wins: the data forms a tree, you nearly always load the whole tree together, and there are few references from one document to another. Examples: a resume, a product page, an order with its line items.

docs.title: Where documents break: many-to-one and many-to-many
docs.text:
Normalization

Look at the profile again. "Worked at Acme Corp". Is the company name just text in the profile, or a link to a company that exists on its own?

  1. If you store "company": "Acme Corp" as text in every profile, the same company is copied into thousands of documents.
  2. Copies drift apart. One says "Acme Corp", another "ACME Corporation", a third has a typo. If Acme renames itself or changes its logo, you must find and update every document that mentions it, and you'll miss some.
  3. The fix is to normalize: store the company once, with an ID, and put only company_id: 42 in each profile. Many profiles now point to one company. That is a many-to-one relationship. Add "people can endorse each other's skills" and you have many-to-many.
  4. Now, to display a profile, you need the company names, which means a join. Document databases traditionally have weak join support, so your application code ends up doing it: fetch the profile, collect the company IDs, fetch the companies, stitch them together.

That is the real trade-off. Documents are great while the data is a self-contained tree. As soon as the data is full of references between records, you are doing joins anyway, and the relational model, which was built for joins, wins again. Most real applications start as trees and grow references over time.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Bookings reference hotels, users and rooms, which is many-to-many, so I'll use Postgres. Each hotel's static content is one tree read as a whole, so it can live in a document store or as cached JSON."

docs.title: Schema-on-write vs schema-on-read
docs.text:
Schema flexibility

Document databases are often called "schemaless", but that isn't quite true. The real question is when the structure of your data is checked.

  • Schema-on-write (relational): the database enforces the structure when you write. Every row in users has the same columns, and inserting a row that doesn't fit fails immediately.
  • Schema-on-read (document): the database accepts any shape, and your reading code interprets it. If old documents have name and new ones have first_name and last_name, the code that reads them must handle both.

It is like static versus dynamic typing in programming languages: neither is always better, and the table shows where each fits.

Schema-on-write (relational) Schema-on-read (document) Analogy Static typing: checked at compile time Dynamic typing: checked at run time Change a field ALTER TABLE + migration (fast in Postgres; MySQL used to copy the whole table) Just write new docs; code handles both old and new shapes Good for Uniform records with stable structure Heterogeneous items: different shapes per type, or external data you don't control Locality Rows are spread across tables (but see Postgres JSONB, Spanner interleaving) Whole doc stored together; rewrites the whole doc on update, so keep docs small Joins Native, optimized by query planner Weak or none; done in application

Warning

"NoSQL is schemaless" is misleading. There is always a schema; with documents it is implicit, spread through every piece of code that reads the data. You still pay for changing it, just later and in more places, often as if field missing then … branches that stay forever.

docs.title: Graph model: when relationships are the data
docs.text:
Property graphs

Some data is mostly connections: who knows whom, which account sent money to which, which place is inside which region. You can store connections in tables, but the questions you ask, like "friends of friends of friends" or "everything inside Europe, however deeply nested", need a variable number of joins. A graph model makes the connections themselves the main thing.

  1. A graph has vertices (things: people, places, accounts) and edges (relationships: LIVES_IN, KNOWS, WITHIN). Both can carry properties, such as a name or a date.
  2. Real-world structure is irregular. Boise is WITHIN Idaho, which is WITHIN the USA. A French city is WITHIN a département, WITHIN a region, WITHIN France. The depth differs from place to place.
  3. Anything can connect to anything. A new kind of relationship is just a new edge label; no schema change is needed.
  4. That makes recursive questions easy. "Find people born in the USA and now living in Europe" follows WITHIN edges any number of hops up from each city. In a graph query language like Cypher that's one short pattern. In SQL it needs a recursive common table expression, which is long and hard to get right.

Note

In interviews: graph databases come up for fraud rings, "people you may know" and knowledge graphs. Most interview problems don't need one: a follows table in Postgres, or adjacency lists in Redis, handle one or two hops perfectly well.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Data shape Pick Interview example Lots of cross-references, need transactions Relational (Postgres) Bookings, payments, inventory, users Self-contained tree, read whole Document (Mongo, DynamoDB item, JSONB) Hotel content, product catalog page, chat message Relationships are the query Graph (Neo4j) or adjacency list Social graph, recommendations, fraud Huge write volume, simple key access Wide-column (Cassandra) Chat history, metrics, activity logs

docs.title: DDIA Chapter 3: Storage & Retrieval
docs.text:
Intermediate

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 3 · STORAGE & RETRIEVAL on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
How a database actually stores bytes. Two families power almost everything: log-structured engines (LSM trees in Cassandra, RocksDB, Kafka) that append, and page-oriented engines (B-trees in Postgres, MySQL) that update in place. Plus why analytics needs column storage.

Key ideas: append-only log · hash index · SSTable · LSM-tree · B-tree · WAL · column store · star schema

docs.title: The simplest database: append-only log + hash index
docs.text:
Log-structured storage (Bitcask)

To understand real storage engines, start by building the simplest possible database: a key-value store backed by one file.

  1. Writing: every set(key, value) is appended to the end of the file. Nothing is ever changed in place. Appending is the fastest thing a disk can do, because it writes sequentially instead of jumping around the disk.
  2. Finding things: scanning the whole file on every read would be hopeless, so keep an index in memory: a hash map from each key to the byte position (offset) where its latest value starts in the file.
  3. Reading: look the key up in the hash map, jump straight to that offset, and read the value. That's one memory lookup and one disk read.
  4. Cleaning up: if a key is updated a million times, the file holds a million old values. So the file is split into segments, and a background process called compaction rewrites old segments keeping only the newest value for each key, then deletes the old files.

This is a real design: Bitcask, the storage engine of the Riak database, works exactly like this, and it is very fast.

Warning

Two limits: every key must fit in the in-memory hash map, so you can't have billions of keys. And a hash map has no order, so range queries ("all keys between user:100 and user:200") are impossible. Sorting the data, next, fixes both.

docs.title: LSM-tree: how Cassandra and RocksDB write so fast
docs.text:
SSTables + LSM

Keep the "only append, never overwrite" idea, but store the keys sorted. A sorted file of key-value pairs is called an SSTable (Sorted String Table). Because it is sorted, you no longer need every key in memory: a sparse index of every few-thousandth key is enough to find the right region of the file. Range scans become easy too. The challenge is keeping things sorted while writes arrive in random order. An LSM-tree (log-structured merge-tree) does it like this:

  1. Write: each write is appended to a write-ahead log on disk (so it survives a crash) and inserted into a memtable, a sorted structure in memory such as a balanced tree. Sorting in memory is cheap, and no random disk writes happen.
  2. Flush: when the memtable reaches a few megabytes, it is written to disk in one go as a new SSTable. That's one big sequential write. The file is never modified again.
  3. Compact: over time there are many SSTables, and a key may appear in several of them. Background compaction merges files (like the merge step of merge sort), keeps only the newest value for each key, and drops deleted keys. Deletes are recorded as special markers called tombstones.
  4. Read: check the memtable first, then the SSTables from newest to oldest, stopping at the first match. Checking many files would be slow, so each SSTable has a Bloom filter, a small structure that can say "this key is definitely not in this file" and skip it.

The result: writes are very cheap, always sequential and batched. Reads do a bit more work. That's the right trade for workloads that write far more than they read.

Note

Why it matters: sequential writes give very high write throughput. Cassandra handles 10k+ writes a second per node comfortably. That makes LSM-trees the default for metrics, logs, chat messages and event data.

docs.title: B-tree: how Postgres and MySQL store data
docs.text:
Page-oriented storage

The B-tree is the other big family, and it is the default in almost every relational database. Instead of appending files, it divides the disk into fixed-size pages (usually 4–16 KB) and updates them in place.

  1. Pages form a tree. The root page holds a few keys that split the key space into ranges, and each range points to a child page: keys under 100 go left, 100 to 300 go to the middle, and so on.
  2. Each level narrows the range further. A page holds hundreds of references (the branching factor, often about 500), so the tree is very shallow: 4 levels can address about 256 TB.
  3. At the bottom, the leaf page contains the row itself, or a pointer to it. Finding any key takes one page read per level, usually 3–4 reads, and the top levels are almost always in memory.
  4. Updating a value means overwriting the leaf page where the key lives. Overwriting is dangerous: if the machine crashes halfway through writing a page, the page is corrupted. So every change is first written to a write-ahead log (WAL), and after a crash the database replays the log to repair the pages. When a page fills up, it splits into two half-full pages, and the parent gets a new pointer.

Note

Why it matters: reads are fast and predictable, and each key lives in exactly one place. That makes locking a row or a range of rows simple, which is why transactional (OLTP) databases are built on B-trees.

docs.title: LSM vs B-tree: the trade-off you will be asked about
docs.text:
Comparison

Neither engine is better overall. An LSM-tree turns random writes into sequential ones, at the cost of reads that may look in several files and background compaction work. A B-tree gives fast, predictable reads and simple locking, at the cost of random writes and writing everything twice (WAL plus page). Choose by the workload:

LSM-tree (Cassandra, RocksDB, HBase) B-tree (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB) Writes Faster: sequential appends, less write amplification Slower: random page writes + WAL (each write ≥ 2 writes) Reads Slower: may check several SSTables (Bloom filters help) Faster, predictable: one path root → leaf Space Compresses well, little fragmentation Pages partly empty after splits Weak spot Compaction competes with live traffic, so p99 spikes Write-heavy workloads hit I/O limits Transactions Key may exist in many files, so locking is harder Key in one place: easy range locks Pick when Write-heavy: metrics, logs, chat, IoT, events Read-heavy, transactional: bookings, payments, users

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Ad clicks are write-heavy and append-only, around 10k/sec, so an LSM-based store like Cassandra fits. Bookings need transactions and point reads, so a B-tree store like Postgres fits."

docs.title: Index types you should name in interviews
docs.text:
Secondary indexes

The primary index finds a row by its key. Real queries also filter by other columns, such as "this user's orders, newest first" or "hotels near me". Each of those needs a secondary index of the right type. Naming the exact index is one of the clearest signs of experience in an interview.

Index How Use for B-tree (default) Sorted tree on column(s) Equality + range: WHERE created_at > X, ORDER BY Composite Sorted by (a, b): leftmost prefix rule WHERE user_id=? ORDER BY ts DESC: one index scan Covering / INCLUDE Index stores extra columns Index-only scans: no heap lookup Clustered Rows stored in index order InnoDB primary key; range scans on PK are cheap Hash Hash map Equality only; no ranges Geospatial R-tree, geohash, quadtree (PostGIS) "Hotels within 5km": Yelp, Uber, Gopuff Inverted term → list of doc IDs Full-text search: Elasticsearch, Postgres GIN Bloom filter Probabilistic set membership "Seen this URL?" in a web crawler, LSM reads

Warning

Indexes are not free: every index must be updated on every write, and each one uses disk and memory. Index the hot read queries you identified, not every column "just in case".

docs.title: OLTP vs OLAP, and the star schema
docs.text:
Analytics

So far we've looked at databases serving an application: look up a user, insert a booking, a few rows at a time. That is OLTP (online transaction processing). Analysts ask a different kind of question, such as "total revenue per city per weekday last quarter". That means scanning millions of rows and aggregating them. This is OLAP (online analytical processing), and it is usually run on a separate system, a data warehouse, so heavy reports don't slow down the live application.

Warehouse data is usually organized as a star schema:

  1. In the middle, the fact table has one row per event, for example each booking: date, hotel ID, customer ID, price. It can have billions of rows. It is very long, and each row is fairly narrow.
  2. Around it, dimension tables describe the who, what, where and when: hotel (city, star rating), customer (country, tier), date (weekday, holiday). A typical query filters and groups by dimensions and sums the facts: "revenue by city by weekday".
OLTP OLAP Pattern Few rows by key Scan millions, aggregate Users App / customers Analysts, dashboards Size GB – TB TB – PB Engine Postgres, MySQL Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse, Druid

docs.title: Column-oriented storage: why analytics is fast
docs.text:
Column stores

A fact table might have 100 columns, but a typical analytics query uses only three or four of them. How the data is laid out on disk makes a huge difference.

  1. A normal database is a row store: each row's values sit together on disk. To sum price by hotel, it must read every column of every row from disk and throw most of it away.
  2. A column store keeps each column in its own file. The same query reads only the hotel file and the price file, touching a small fraction of the data.
  3. All the values in one column are similar (the same few hotel IDs repeated millions of times), so they compress extremely well, often 10× or more. And the CPU can process a tight array of one column very efficiently (vectorized processing). Together these make analytics scans 10–100× faster.

The catch: writing one new row means touching every column file. So column stores load data in large batches, and they don't replace your OLTP database.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "The ad-click dashboard is an OLAP query, so I won't run it on the OLTP Postgres. Clicks flow through Kafka into a column store like ClickHouse or Druid for aggregation."

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "Why Cassandra for this?" → "LSM-tree storage: writes are sequential appends to memtable + commit log, so write throughput is very high. Reads are slower, which is fine for this append-heavy workload."

Important

Interviewer asks: "How do you make this query fast?" → Name the exact index: "a composite index on (user_id, created_at DESC) turns it into a single index range scan."

Important

Interviewer asks: "Where do analytics queries run?" → Never on the OLTP primary. Use CDC or Kafka into a column store (ClickHouse, BigQuery, Druid).

Important

Interviewer asks: "What does a WAL do?" → Log the change before applying it. After a crash, replay the log. The same idea powers replication (Ch 5) and CDC (Ch 11).

Note

Underneath: why sequential writes win and what fsync costs are explained in OS 6: Files and durability and OS 7: Storage devices.
