docs.title: DDIA Chapter 4: Encoding & Evolution
docs.text:
Intermediate

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 4 · ENCODING & EVOLUTION on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Data outlives code. During a rolling deploy, old and new versions of your service run at the same time, reading each other's data. Encoding formats such as Protobuf, Avro, and JSON decide whether that works or silently corrupts data.

Key ideas: backward compat · forward compat · Protobuf field tags · Avro schemas · schema registry · REST / RPC / messages

docs.title: Rolling upgrade: old and new code at the same time
docs.text:
Why compatibility matters

You almost never upgrade every server at the same instant. A rolling deploy replaces servers a few at a time, and mobile apps stay on old versions for months. So at any moment, old code and new code are running side by side, reading and writing the same database and the same messages. Each version must cope with data written by the other.

There are two directions to think about:

  • Backward compatibility: new code can read data written by old code. This is usually easy: you know the old format, so you handle it.
  • Forward compatibility: old code can read data written by new code. This is harder, because the old code was written before the new format existed.

Here is the classic way forward compatibility goes wrong:

  1. You deploy v2 of the user service, which adds a new field, phone. A user updates their profile through a v2 server, and the record now includes a phone number.
  2. The same user, a minute later, hits a server still running v1. It reads the record.
  3. v1 decodes the record into its User class, which has no phone field, so the phone number is silently dropped in memory.
  4. The user changes their name. v1 writes the whole object back, without phone. The phone number is now deleted from the database, and no error was raised anywhere.

The rule that prevents this: old code must keep fields it doesn't understand and write them back unchanged. Good encoding libraries (Protobuf, Avro) do this for you. Hand-written mapping code often doesn't.

Note

Summary of the two directions: backward compatible means new code reads old data (easy). Forward compatible means old code reads new data (hard, and the example above).

docs.title: Protobuf / Thrift: field tags make evolution safe
docs.text:
Binary encoding

When data leaves a process, to disk or across the network, it must be turned into bytes (encoding or serialization). The format you choose decides how big the data is, how fast it is to process, and above all how safely it can evolve.

  1. JSON is readable and everywhere, but it repeats every field name in every record, has no schema to check against, and is vague about numbers. JavaScript, for example, loses precision on integers above 2⁵³, which breaks large IDs.
  2. Protocol Buffers (and Thrift) use a schema file in which every field gets a tag number: string name = 1; string phone = 2;. The encoded bytes contain only the tag numbers and values, not the names, so records are typically 2–3× smaller than JSON and faster to parse. Code for reading and writing is generated from the schema.
  3. Tags are what make evolution safe. A reader that meets a tag it doesn't know just skips it (or keeps it, to write back). So the rules are: add new fields with new tag numbers, make them optional, and never reuse a tag number that was once used for something else.
  4. Breaking changes are anything that makes old and new code read the same bytes differently: making a field required, changing a field's tag number, or changing its type to something incompatible (such as a string to a number).

Note

Avro does it differently: Avro has no tag numbers. The reader is given two schemas, the one the data was written with (writer's schema) and the one it expects (reader's schema), and matches fields by name. That means every schema version must be stored somewhere, usually a schema registry, with each message carrying a schema ID. This setup is very common with Kafka.

docs.title: Three ways data flows between processes
docs.text:
Modes of dataflow

Encoded data travels in three main ways. Each has its own compatibility concerns.

  1. Through a database. Writing to a database is like sending a message to your future self, or to a newer version of your code. A row written five years ago must still be readable today. Data outlives code, so you can't just rename a column and forget the old rows.
  2. Through service calls (REST, gRPC). This looks like calling a function, but it isn't one. The call can time out, the network can lose the reply, and a retry can run it twice (see Chapter 8). And because client and server deploy separately, the API must stay compatible: add optional fields, never change the meaning of existing ones, and use a new version (/v2/) for breaking changes.
  3. Through messages (Kafka, RabbitMQ). The sender doesn't wait for the receiver. A broker in between stores the message, retries delivery and can deliver to several consumers. Producers and consumers are deployed by different teams at different times, so a schema registry that rejects incompatible schema changes keeps them from breaking each other.

Warning

The RPC illusion: frameworks that make a remote call look exactly like a local function call hide the important parts: timeouts, retries and partial failure. Design every remote call with a timeout, and make it idempotent so a retry is harmless.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "How do you deploy schema changes with zero downtime?" → Expand → migrate → contract: add the nullable column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, and only then drop the old column.

Important

Interviewer asks: "How do Kafka producers and consumers evolve?" → Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry enforcing backward-compatible changes. Consumers upgrade on their own schedule.

Important

Interviewer asks: "REST or gRPC between services?" → gRPC (Protobuf, HTTP/2) for internal high-QPS calls; REST/JSON for public APIs and browsers.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Every message carries a schema version, and we only add optional fields. That lets the booking service deploy without coordinating with its consumers."

docs.title: DDIA Chapter 5: Replication
docs.text:
Advanced

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 5 · REPLICATION on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Replication means keeping copies of the same data on several machines: to survive failures, to serve more reads, and to be closer to users.
  • Copying data is easy. The hard part is changes: who accepts writes, how changes reach the copies, and what readers see while the copies disagree.
  • Three designs: single leader (the default), multi-leader (writes in several regions), and leaderless (any replica accepts writes, using quorums).
  • Most interview bugs here are replication lag bugs: a user writes something, reads it back from a replica, and it isn't there yet.

docs.title: 1. Leader–follower (single-leader) replication
docs.text:
• All writes go to one leader, which decides their order.
  • The leader sends a stream of changes (its replication log) to every follower, and each follower applies them in the same order.
  • Reads can go to followers. That spreads the load, but followers may be slightly behind.

Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis and Kafka (per partition) all work this way.

docs.title: Synchronous or asynchronous?
docs.text:
Synchronous follower Asynchronous follower Leader waits for it before confirming a write Yes No Write latency Higher; a slow follower slows every write Unaffected If the leader dies right after confirming The write survives on the follower Recent writes may be lost

The common setup is semi-synchronous: one synchronous follower and the rest asynchronous. Every confirmed write then exists on at least two machines, without one slow follower blocking everything.

docs.title: When the leader dies (failover)
docs.text:
1. Detect it, usually because it stops answering for N seconds. Too short a timeout causes needless failovers; too long means more downtime.
  2. Promote the most up-to-date follower.
  3. Reconfigure clients and the remaining followers to use the new leader.

What goes wrong:

  • Lost writes: with asynchronous replication, writes the old leader confirmed but never sent are gone.
  • Split brain: the old leader comes back and still believes it's the leader, so two nodes accept writes. You need fencing: shut it out, or reject anything stamped with its old term number.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Failover is automatic, but with async replication we can lose the last moment of writes. For payments I'd require a synchronous replica before confirming."

docs.title: 2. Replication lag: the bugs users actually see
docs.text:
Followers are usually milliseconds behind, but under load it can be seconds or more. Three guarantees you may need:

Guarantee The bug without it Common fix Read-your-writes "I posted a comment, refreshed, and it's gone." Read the user's own data from the leader for a short window after they write, or until a replica has caught up to their last write. Monotonic reads "I saw 3 comments, refreshed, and now there are 2." Pin each user to one replica, for example by a hash of their user id. Consistent prefix "I saw the reply before the question." Keep related writes in the same partition, for example chat messages by conversation id.

docs.title: 3. Multi-leader replication
docs.text:
Each region has its own leader that accepts local writes and syncs with the other regions asynchronously. Writes are fast everywhere and survive a region outage, but two regions can change the same record at the same time, and that conflict must be resolved somehow:

  • Last write wins: simple, but it silently throws one write away.
  • Merge the values, or keep both and ask the user, as file-sync tools do with "conflicted copy".
  • Conflict-free data types (CRDTs): counters, sets and text editing that merge automatically.

The best strategy is usually to avoid conflicts: give each user or record a home region, so all its writes go to one leader.

docs.title: 4. Leaderless replication and quorums
docs.text:
There's no leader. The client (or a coordinator) sends each write to all n replicas and waits for w acknowledgements, and reads from r replicas.

  • If w + r > n, the set of replicas you read from overlaps the set that took the latest write, so at least one reply is up to date. Pick the newest version.
  • Read repair writes the newest value back to stale replicas you happened to read. A background anti-entropy process fixes the rest.
  • Common setting: n = 3, w = 2, r = 2, which tolerates one replica down for both reads and writes.

Cassandra and DynamoDB-style systems use this. The catch: concurrent writes to the same key still need conflict handling, and "last write wins" by timestamp can drop data when clocks disagree.

docs.title: 5. How this shows up in interviews
docs.text: Interviewer asks Answer from this chapter "Your primary database dies. What happens?" Automatic failover to a replica in tens of seconds. With async replication the last writes can be lost, so use a synchronous replica where that's unacceptable. "A user updates a price, refreshes, and sees the old one." Replication lag. Read-your-writes: route that user to the primary briefly. "Active-active across regions?" Multi-leader with conflicts. Prefer a home region per user or entity, and CRDTs for counters. "Why Cassandra rather than Postgres replicas?" Leaderless: no failover pause and writes keep working with a node down. The price is conflict handling and weaker consistency.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Problems: Ticketmaster: the seat map can come from a lagging replica; the booking must not.
  • Core concepts: Caching has the same staleness trade-off as reading from replicas.
  • Pattern: Scaling reads

docs.title: DDIA Chapter 6: Partitioning (Sharding)
docs.text:
Advanced

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 6 · PARTITIONING (SHARDING) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
When data or write load is too big for one machine, split it. Each record belongs to exactly one partition. The goals are to spread data and load evenly, avoid hot spots, and move as little data as possible when nodes are added.

Key ideas: key-range · hash partitioning · hot spots · secondary indexes · rebalancing · consistent hashing · request routing

docs.title: Key-range vs hash partitioning
docs.text:
How to split

Replication (Chapter 5) puts copies of the same data on several machines. Partitioning, also called sharding, is different: it splits the data so each machine holds a different part. You need it when the data is too big for one machine, or there are too many writes for one machine. Every record lives in exactly one partition, and the first decision is how to choose the partition for a key.

  1. By key range. Like volumes of an encyclopedia: A–F on partition 1, G–M on partition 2, and so on. Keys stay sorted, so a range query such as "all orders from 1 to 7 March" reads one or two neighbouring partitions. The danger is keys that arrive in order. If the key is a timestamp or an auto-increment ID, every new write lands at the end, in the same partition. That partition gets all the write load while the others sit idle. This is a hot spot.
  2. By hash of the key. Run the key through a hash function and use the result to pick the partition. Similar keys get completely different hashes, so data and load spread evenly. The cost: neighbouring keys are now scattered, so a range query over the key has to ask every partition.

A common way to get both is a compound key. Hash the first part, for example user_id, to pick the partition, and keep rows sorted by the second part, for example a timestamp, inside it. "User 42's messages from last week" then lives in one partition, already in order. This is how Cassandra's partition key plus clustering key works.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "I'll partition messages by hash(conversation_id) and cluster by message timestamp, so one conversation's history is a single-partition range scan."

docs.title: Skew and hot spots: the celebrity problem
docs.text:
Hot keys

Hashing spreads different keys evenly, but it can't help when one key gets a huge share of the traffic. Every write for that key goes to the same partition, whatever the hash function.

  1. A celebrity posts, and millions of likes and comments for that one post ID hit one partition. The rest of the cluster is fine; that one node is overloaded.
  2. The fix is to split the key. Append a random number from 00 to 99 to it (post123_07, post123_42…), so the writes spread across up to 100 partitions.
  3. The cost moves to reads: to get the full count or all the comments, you now read all 100 sub-keys and combine them. So only split keys you know are hot, and keep a list of which ones they are so readers know to combine.

Note

Interview examples: live comments on a celebrity post, a Taylor Swift on-sale on Ticketmaster, YouTube view counters, an ad campaign's click counter. All use key splitting or write buffering: absorb the writes in Redis or Kafka and apply them in batches.

docs.title: Secondary indexes: local vs global
docs.text:
Partitioning + indexes

Partitioning by the primary key makes "get item 123" easy: hash the key, go to that partition. But what about "find all red cars"? Colour is not the partition key, so red cars are spread over every partition. A secondary index is needed, and there are two ways to partition it.

  1. Local index (one index per partition): each partition indexes only its own records. Writing a car touches one partition, simple and fast. But a query for red cars must ask every partition and merge the answers (scatter-gather). The query is as slow as the slowest partition, and that gets worse as partitions are added (tail latency amplification, Chapter 1). MongoDB, Cassandra and Elasticsearch work this way.
  2. Global index (the index is partitioned by the indexed value): all the "red" entries live on one index partition, so a query reads one place. But writing one car may now update index partitions on other machines. That is usually done asynchronously, so the index lags behind for a moment. DynamoDB's global secondary indexes work this way.

Warning

DynamoDB GSI: global secondary indexes are eventually consistent. A read through the GSI right after a write may not see it yet.

docs.title: Rebalancing: never use hash mod N
docs.text:
Adding nodes

Sooner or later you add machines, and some data must move to them. Moving data is expensive (network, disk, slower queries while it happens), so a good scheme moves as little as possible.

  1. The tempting approach is partition = hash(key) mod N, where N is the number of nodes. Going from 3 to 4 nodes changes the result of mod N for about 75% of keys, so nearly all the data has to move at once.
  2. Better: create many more partitions than nodes from the start, for example 1,000 partitions on 10 nodes (100 each). The key-to-partition mapping is fixed forever. Only the partition-to-node assignment changes.
  3. When an 11th node joins, it takes a few whole partitions from each existing node until all are even. Only those partitions move. Elasticsearch, Kafka, Riak and Couchbase work this way. Consistent hashing, next, is the same idea arranged as a ring.

Note

Other strategies: dynamic partitioning splits a partition when it grows past a size, such as about 10 GB, and merges small ones (HBase, MongoDB). Per-node partitioning gives each node a fixed number of partitions (Cassandra's virtual nodes).

docs.title: Consistent hashing: the ring
docs.text:
Consistent hashing

Consistent hashing is a way to assign keys to nodes so that adding or removing a node moves only a small share of keys. It is used by caches, Cassandra and DynamoDB.

  1. Picture a circle of hash values. Hash each node to a point on the circle, and hash each key to a point too.
  2. A key belongs to the first node clockwise from it.
  3. Add a new node E. It lands somewhere on the circle and takes over only the keys between its position and the previous node, keys that used to belong to the next node clockwise. Everything else stays put. On average about 1/N of the keys move, not 75%.
  4. With only a few nodes, their points can land unevenly, leaving one node a huge arc. Virtual nodes fix this: each server is placed at many points (say 100) around the circle, so arcs average out. A bigger server can be given more points so it takes more load.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Cache keys are placed on a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes, so adding a cache node remaps only about 1/N of keys and avoids a cold-cache stampede on the database."

docs.title: Request routing: who knows where key K lives?
docs.text:
Service discovery

Once data is split across machines, every request needs to reach the right one. And because partitions move during rebalancing, the answer changes over time. There are three common designs:

  1. ① Ask any node. The client connects to any node. If that node doesn't hold the key, it forwards the request to the one that does. Nodes share the partition map with each other by gossip. Used by Cassandra and Riak.
  2. ② A routing tier. Clients talk to a separate layer of routers that know the map and forward each request. Used by MongoDB (mongos) and Vitess (VTGate).
  3. ③ A smart client. The client library itself knows the map and connects directly to the right node, with no extra hop. Used by Kafka clients, Redis Cluster clients and Cassandra drivers.
  4. Whoever does the routing needs an up-to-date map. It is usually stored in a coordination service such as ZooKeeper or etcd (or Kafka's KRaft). Routers and clients watch it, so they hear about every change immediately.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "How would you shard this?" → Name the shard key from the hottest query: "hash(user_id), because every hot query filters by user". Then name the cost: cross-user queries scatter.

Important

Interviewer asks: "What about the celebrity or hot hotel?" → Key splitting with a suffix, write buffering in Redis or Kafka, and a cache in front for reads.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Adding shards later?" → Pre-split into many logical partitions (e.g., 1024) mapped to few physical nodes, or consistent hashing. Never mod N.

Warning

Sharding too early: A single Postgres handles ~10–50k TPS and multiple TB. Shard only when the calculation says one primary can't take the write load.

docs.title: DDIA Chapter 7: Transactions
docs.text:
Advanced

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 7 · TRANSACTIONS on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
A transaction groups reads and writes into one unit: all of it happens or none of it does, and concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work. Most interview "contention" questions, such as seat booking, inventory, payments, and auctions, come down to which isolation anomaly you are defending against.

Key ideas: ACID · dirty reads · read skew · MVCC · lost update · write skew · phantoms · 2PL · SSI

docs.title: What ACID really means
docs.text:
ACID

A transaction wraps several reads and writes into one unit: BEGIN … COMMIT. The point is to let you write code as if nothing else were happening, and as if nothing could fail halfway through. The database handles the messy cases. Databases describe this promise with the letters ACID, but each letter means something more specific (and sometimes weaker) than people assume:

Letter Common belief What it actually guarantees A · Atomicity "Atomic like threads" Abortability: on any error mid-transaction, all writes are rolled back. Safe to retry. C · Consistency "DB keeps data consistent" Your application's invariants (debits = credits). This one is mostly the app's job, not the DB's. I · Isolation "Transactions are serial" Concurrent transactions don't interfere. The strength depends on the isolation level, and most DBs default to weaker than serializable. D · Durability "Never lost" Committed data survives crashes (WAL + fsync, or replication). Nothing is 100%.

The letter that causes nearly all interview bugs is I. Perfect isolation would mean concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one after another. That is expensive, so databases offer weaker isolation levels, each allowing certain kinds of interference, called anomalies. The rest of this chapter goes through them from weakest to strongest, with the bug each one lets through.

Warning

The default is not serializable: Postgres defaults to Read Committed, and MySQL InnoDB to Repeatable Read. Neither prevents write skew, so booking code can double-book unless you add locks or constraints.

docs.title: Read committed: no dirty reads, no dirty writes
docs.text:
Weakest useful level

The most basic promise: you never see another transaction's unfinished work.

  1. Transaction 1 sets an account balance to 0 but hasn't committed yet. It might still roll back.
  2. Without isolation, Transaction 2 reads the balance and sees 0. That is a dirty read: reading data that isn't committed.
  3. Transaction 1 hits an error and rolls back. The balance was never really 0, but Transaction 2 has already acted on it, perhaps declining a payment or sending a "you're overdrawn" email.
  4. Read committed prevents this. Readers always see the last committed value; Transaction 2 sees the old balance until Transaction 1 commits. It also prevents dirty writes (overwriting someone else's uncommitted change) by locking a row from the moment it is written until commit. This is Postgres's default level.

docs.title: Read skew → snapshot isolation (MVCC)
docs.text:
Repeatable read

Read committed still has a gap: if your transaction reads several things, other transactions can commit in between your reads, and you see a mix of before and after.

  1. Alice has $500 in each of two accounts, $1,000 in total. She opens her banking app, which reads account 1: $500.
  2. At that moment, a transfer of $100 from account 2 to account 1 runs and commits.
  3. The app then reads account 2: $400, the value after the transfer. Alice sees a total of $900, and $100 seems to have vanished. This is read skew: each read was of committed data, but they came from different moments. For Alice a refresh fixes it, but for a backup, an analytics query or an integrity check ("do all balances add up?"), it produces wrong results.
  4. Snapshot isolation fixes it: each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of the database as it was when the transaction started. Changes committed later are invisible to it, so Alice sees $500 + $500.

How can the database show each transaction a different point in time? With MVCC (multi-version concurrency control). It keeps several versions of each row, each tagged with the ID of the transaction that created it, and of the one that deleted it, if any. A transaction simply ignores versions created after it started. A nice consequence: readers never block writers, and writers never block readers.

Note

MVCC in one line: an UPDATE doesn't overwrite. It marks the old version "deleted by transaction 13" and inserts a new version "created by transaction 13". Your snapshot ignores versions from transactions that started after you. Old versions are cleaned up later (Postgres calls this VACUUM).

docs.title: Lost update: read-modify-write races
docs.text:
Concurrent writes

A very common pattern in application code: read a value, change it in code, write it back. Run it twice at the same time and one change disappears.

  1. A post has 42 likes. Users A and B both click "like" at the same moment, and both requests read likes = 42.
  2. Both compute 42 + 1 and write 43. The second write overwrites the first. There should be 44 likes, and one is lost. No error was raised.

Three ways to fix it, from simplest to most general:

  1. Atomic operation: let the database do the read and write as one step: UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 WHERE id = ?. There's no gap to race in. Redis INCR works the same way. Use this whenever the change can be expressed this way.
  2. Pessimistic lock: SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the row when you read it, so the second request waits until the first commits, then reads 43. Good when many requests fight over the same rows.
  3. Optimistic check (compare-and-set): keep a version column. Write with UPDATE … SET likes = 43, version = 8 WHERE id = ? AND version = 7. If another write got there first, the version is no longer 7, zero rows are updated, and you re-read and retry. Good when conflicts are rare. (Postgres at Repeatable Read also detects lost updates itself and aborts one of the transactions.)

Tip

Say this in the interview: "For the auction, bids use a conditional write, UPDATE … SET max_bid=? WHERE max_bid < ?, so concurrent bids can't overwrite each other."

docs.title: Write skew: the double-booking bug
docs.text:
The anomaly that bites interviews

This is the hardest anomaly to spot, because the two transactions don't write the same row, so nothing looks like a conflict.

  1. A hospital rule: at least one doctor must be on call. Alice and Bob are both on call, and both feel unwell. At the same moment, each asks the app to go off call. Each transaction checks: "how many doctors are on call?" Both see 2, so it's safe for one to leave.
  2. Alice's transaction sets Alice off call. Bob's sets Bob off call. They update different rows, so there's no write conflict, and even snapshot isolation lets both commit. Now zero doctors are on call. Each decision was correct on its own snapshot; together they broke the rule. This is write skew.
  3. It's the shape of nearly every booking bug: "check that the room is free (no booking row exists), then insert a booking". Two requests both see no booking and both insert one. Here there isn't even an existing row to lock, because the conflict is about a row that doesn't exist yet, a phantom.
  4. The fixes:
  5. Lock the rows you checked with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, so the second transaction waits and then sees the first one's change.
  6. Use the SERIALIZABLE isolation level and retry on abort.
  7. Add a unique constraint such as UNIQUE (room_id, date), so the database rejects the second booking.
  8. Materialize the conflict: create a row in advance for every seat, or every room-night, so there's always a real row to lock or conditionally update.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Each seat is a row with status AVAILABLE/HELD/SOLD. A hold is UPDATE seats SET status=HELD WHERE id=? AND status=AVAILABLE. If one row was updated I won it, if zero someone else did. No write skew possible."

docs.title: Isolation levels: what each prevents
docs.text:
Cheat sheet

Putting it together: each level closes more gaps and costs more. Know your database's default, and know which anomaly your feature is exposed to.

Anomaly Read Committed Snapshot / Repeatable Read Serializable Dirty read / write ✓ prevented ✓ ✓ Read skew (non-repeatable read) ✗ ✓ prevented ✓ Lost update ✗ (use atomic op / lock) ✓ Postgres detects; MySQL ✗ ✓ Write skew ✗ ✗ ✓ prevented Phantoms ✗ ✗ (mostly) ✓ prevented Default in Postgres, Oracle, SQL Server MySQL InnoDB CockroachDB, FoundationDB

Note

Serializable, three ways: actual serial execution runs transactions one at a time on a single thread, which is fast if each is tiny (VoltDB, Redis Lua scripts). Two-phase locking (2PL) makes readers and writers block each other. Serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) lets everyone run, then aborts transactions whose reads went stale. The last two are compared next.

docs.title: Two-phase locking vs serializable snapshot isolation
docs.text:
Serializability

There are two main ways a database provides full serializability while running transactions in parallel: wait when there might be a conflict (pessimistic), or carry on and check at the end (optimistic).

  1. Two-phase locking (2PL), pessimistic: reading a row takes a shared lock, and writing needs an exclusive lock. Locks are held until the transaction ends. If Transaction 1 has read a row, Transaction 2 must wait to write it. It is correct, but under contention transactions queue behind each other, throughput drops, latency becomes unpredictable, and deadlocks happen (the database kills one transaction to break them).
  2. Serializable snapshot isolation (SSI), optimistic: everyone runs on their own snapshot with no blocking. At commit, the database checks: "has anything this transaction read been changed by a transaction that committed since?" If so, the decision might have been based on stale data, so this transaction is aborted and the application retries it. This is fast when conflicts are rare. When many transactions fight over the same rows, it causes lots of aborts and retries. Postgres's SERIALIZABLE level uses SSI.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "Two users book the last room at the same time." → Write skew. Use a row per room-night + conditional UPDATE, or SELECT FOR UPDATE, or a unique constraint on (room, date).

Important

Interviewer asks: "Like counter at 50k/sec?" → Not row locks. Use atomic INCR in Redis, sharded counters, or batch into the DB asynchronously. The lost update is avoided because the increment is atomic.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Optimistic or pessimistic?" → Low contention: optimistic version check. High contention on few rows (hot seat map): pessimistic lock or a queue to serialize.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Transaction across 2 services?" → No distributed ACID. Use a saga with compensations plus the outbox pattern (Ch 9 and 12).

docs.title: DDIA Chapter 8: The Trouble with Distributed Systems
docs.text:
Advanced

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 8 · THE TROUBLE WITH DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
On one machine, things either work or crash. Across machines you get partial failure: some parts work, some don't, and you often can't tell which. The three villains are unreliable networks, unreliable clocks, and process pauses.

Key ideas: partial failure · timeouts · clock skew · LWW danger · GC pauses · leases · fencing tokens · majority quorum

docs.title: The network: you cannot tell why there was no reply
docs.text:
Unreliable networks

Imagine your order service calls the payment service: "charge this card $50". You wait, and nothing comes back. What happened? On one computer a function call either returns or throws an error. Across a network there is a third outcome, silence, and silence can mean very different things.

There are three common reasons you got no reply:

  1. ① The request never arrived. It was dropped by a switch, or it is still sitting in a queue somewhere. The card was not charged.
  2. ② The request arrived, but the server is stuck. It crashed, or it is frozen in a long garbage-collection pause. The card may or may not be charged later.
  3. ③ The server did the work, but the reply got lost. The card was charged. If you retry now, you charge it twice.

From the caller's side, all three look exactly the same: no answer before the timeout. You can't find out which one happened by waiting longer. So the system has to be safe whichever one it was.

The standard answer is to make the operation idempotent: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. The caller generates an ID for the operation (an idempotency key) and sends the same ID on every retry. The server remembers which IDs it has already processed and, for a repeat, returns the stored result instead of charging again.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Payment calls to the provider can time out after the charge succeeded. Every request carries an idempotency key, so a retry is safe."

Note

Choosing a timeout: a timeout is the only way to detect a problem, and it is always a guess. If it is too short, healthy but slow nodes are declared dead, work moves to other nodes, those get slower, and failures cascade. If it is too long, users wait. Start from the real p99.9 latency plus a margin, or use an adaptive detector (such as phi-accrual) that learns normal response times.

docs.title: Clocks: last-write-wins can drop the newer write
docs.text:
Unreliable clocks

Every machine has its own clock, and no two clocks agree exactly. NTP keeps them close, but "close" usually means a few milliseconds apart, sometimes much more. That sounds harmless until you use timestamps to decide which write happened last.

Many databases (Cassandra by default, and many caches) resolve conflicting writes with last-write-wins (LWW): each write is stamped with the clock time of the node that received it, and the highest timestamp is kept.

Here is how that silently loses data:

  1. Node 1's clock runs 3 ms fast. Client A writes x = 1 through Node 1, and it is stamped 42.004.
  2. A moment later in real time, Client B writes x = 2 through Node 2, whose clock is accurate. It is stamped 42.003.
  3. The two writes meet. Last-write-wins keeps the higher timestamp, so x = 1 wins, even though x = 2 really happened later.

Nobody gets an error. Client B was told its write succeeded, and it simply disappears. The clocks weren't broken; a 3 ms difference is normal.

So: don't use wall-clock time to order events across machines. Use something that can't disagree: a sequence number from a single leader, a Kafka partition offset, a version number checked with a conditional write, or logical clocks (see Chapter 9).

Note

Two kinds of clock on every machine: the time-of-day clock (System.currentTimeMillis(), Date.now()) tells the date and time, but it can jump backwards when NTP corrects it, so never use it to measure how long something took. The monotonic clock (System.nanoTime(), performance.now()) only moves forward. Use it for durations and timeouts, but its value means nothing on another machine.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Can't you just use better clocks?" Google Spanner does: its TrueTime API returns an interval [earliest, latest] instead of one value, using GPS and atomic clocks to keep it about 7 ms wide. Before committing, a transaction waits out that uncertainty, so timestamps are guaranteed to respect real order. Without that hardware, you can't rely on timestamps for ordering.

docs.title: Process pauses: the expired-lease bug
docs.text:
GC pauses

A common way to make sure only one worker does something, such as writing a file or processing a job, is a lease: a lock that expires automatically after, say, 10 seconds. The expiry is there so that if the lock holder crashes, the lock frees itself and someone else can take over.

The trouble is that a program can stop running for a while without knowing it. Common causes:

  • a "stop-the-world" garbage-collection pause, which can last seconds in Java or Go under memory pressure;
  • the virtual machine being paused and moved to another host;
  • the operating system swapping memory to disk;
  • a laptop lid closing.

When the program resumes, it carries on from the exact line it was on, as if no time had passed.

Follow the diagram:

  1. Client 1 gets a 10-second lease from the lock service.
  2. Client 1 freezes in a 15-second GC pause. From its own point of view, nothing happens.
  3. After 10 seconds the lease expires. As far as the lock service knows, Client 1 has crashed.
  4. Client 2 asks for the lease, gets it, and writes the file. So far everything is correct.
  5. Client 1 wakes up. It still believes it holds the lock, because nothing told it otherwise, and it writes the file too. Two writers have now overwritten each other: the file is corrupted.

Warning

"Just check the lease before writing" does not fix it. The pause can happen after the check and before the write: check (still valid) → pause 15 s → write (lease long gone). No check inside the client can close that gap, because the client can't know it paused.

docs.title: Fencing tokens: the fix
docs.text:
Fencing

The problem above is that the storage believes whoever writes to it. A paused client with an out-of-date lease looks exactly like a legitimate one. The fix is to give the storage a way to tell them apart, and that way is a number.

The idea: every time the lock service hands out the lock, it also hands out a fencing token: a number that goes up by one with every grant (33, then 34, then 35…). Every write to the storage must include the token. The storage remembers the highest token it has accepted and refuses any write with a lower one. A lower token means "you were the lock holder before someone else", so your lock is out of date.

Replay the same story with tokens:

  1. Client 1 gets the lease with token 33, then freezes in a GC pause.
  2. The lease expires. Client 2 gets the lease with token 34.
  3. Client 2 writes with token 34. The storage accepts it and records "highest token seen = 34".
  4. Client 1 wakes up and writes with token 33. The storage compares: 33 < 34, so the write is rejected. Client 1 learns it has lost the lock, and the file stays correct.

The crucial point is who does the check. The client can't reliably know it is stale, so the resource being protected (the database, the file store) enforces it. The safety no longer depends on clients behaving well.

Where the numbers come from: ZooKeeper's transaction ID (zxid) or an etcd revision both increase on every change, so they make good fencing tokens. A plain Redis lock has no such number, which is why a Redis lock alone isn't enough when correctness matters.

In a SQL database, a version column does the same job:

-- token 34 was given with the lock; only apply if no newer holder has written
UPDATE files
SET    content = :new_content, lock_token = :token
WHERE  id = :file_id
  AND  lock_token < :token;
-- 0 rows updated  →  a newer lock holder exists; stop and give up the work

Tip

Say this in the interview: "A Redis lock alone isn't safe under GC pauses: the lock can expire while the holder is paused, and it will still write when it wakes up. I'd pair the lock with a fencing token, for example a version column the database checks with UPDATE … WHERE lock_token < :token, so a stale holder's write is rejected."

Note

Truth is decided by the majority. The deeper lesson: a node can't trust its own view of the world ("am I still the leader?", "do I still hold the lock?"), because it might have been paused or cut off. Important decisions are made by a quorum, a majority of nodes, and enforced where the data lives. That idea is the foundation of Chapter 9.

docs.title: System models and Byzantine faults
docs.text:
Assumptions

To reason about whether an algorithm (such as a leader election) is correct, you first have to state what can go wrong. A system model is that list of assumptions: how late messages can be, whether crashed nodes come back, whether nodes can lie. The more realistic the model, the harder the algorithm, but the more you can trust it in production.

Model Assumes Reality Timing: synchronous Bounded network delay, pauses, clock drift Not realistic Timing: partially synchronous Usually bounded, sometimes not The realistic model; algorithms must stay safe when bounds break Timing: asynchronous No timing assumptions at all Very restrictive; no timeouts Node: crash-stop Crashed nodes never return Simplifies proofs Node: crash-recovery Nodes crash and return; disk survives, RAM doesn't Realistic for datacenters Node: Byzantine Nodes may lie or act maliciously Blockchains, aerospace. Rarely needed inside one company.

Note

Safety vs liveness: Safety: nothing bad ever happens (no two leaders). This must always hold. Liveness: something good eventually happens (a leader gets elected). This may wait for the network to heal.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "What if the payment provider times out?" → Outcome unknown. Retry with the same idempotency key, or reconcile with a status query. Never blindly charge again.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Distributed lock with Redis?" → Fine for efficiency (avoid duplicate work). For correctness add fencing tokens, or use the DB's own conditional writes.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Order events by timestamp?" → Wall clocks skew. Use a sequence from one leader, a Kafka partition offset, or logical clocks (Ch 9).

Important

Interviewer asks: "How do you detect a dead node?" → Heartbeats + timeouts tuned to p99.9, and accept false positives. Leader election by majority, with epochs to fence the old leader.

Note

Underneath: where process pauses come from (GC, swapping, CPU throttling) is explained in OS 3: Memory and GC pauses and OS 8: Containers.

← Ch 7: Transactions · Ch 9: Consistency and consensus →

docs.title: DDIA Chapter 9: Consistency & Consensus
docs.text:
Advanced

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 9 · CONSISTENCY & CONSENSUS on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Given everything in Ch 8, how do nodes agree? This chapter covers linearizability (behave like one copy), ordering and causality, distributed transactions (2PC), and consensus (Raft, Paxos, ZooKeeper), the tools behind leader election, locks, and uniqueness.

Key ideas: linearizability · CAP · causality · Lamport clocks · total order broadcast · 2PC · Raft · ZooKeeper

docs.title: Linearizability: behave as if there is one copy
docs.text:
Strongest single-object guarantee

Chapter 8 showed how networks, clocks and pauses make distributed systems unreliable. This chapter asks: given all that, how can several machines agree on anything? It starts with the strongest promise a replicated system can make: that it behaves as if there were only one copy of the data.

  1. The referee records the final score of a match, 2–1, on the leader database.
  2. Alice refreshes her phone. Her read goes to the leader, she sees FINAL 2–1, and she shouts "it's over!"
  3. Bob, sitting next to her, hears her and refreshes after she did. His read goes to a follower that is a few seconds behind, and he sees 1–1, still playing. Bob read later in real time but got an older answer.
  4. Linearizability forbids exactly this. Once any reader has seen the new value, every later read, by anyone, must see it too (or something newer). The system must look like a single copy where each operation takes effect at one instant. Both readers did nothing wrong; the system broke the promise.

Warning

Not the same as serializability, despite the similar name. Serializable (Chapter 7) is about transactions touching many objects: they behave as if run one at a time. Linearizable is about one object: reads always reflect the latest write in real time. A database can be one without the other; "strict serializability" means both.

docs.title: When you actually need linearizability
docs.text:
Use cases

Linearizability is expensive: every read and write has to coordinate with other nodes. Most features don't need it. Here's where you do:

  1. Locks and leader election: if two nodes can both believe they hold the lock, it isn't a lock. Every node must see the same, latest answer to "who holds it?".
  2. Uniqueness and limits: "this username is taken", "seat 42 is sold", "the balance can't go below zero". When two people race for the last one, everyone must agree on who got there first.
  3. Two channels racing each other: a web server saves an uploaded image to storage (1), then puts "resize image 7" on a queue (2). The queue message can arrive faster than the storage replication. The resizer fetches image 7 from a lagging storage replica and resizes the old version (3). Fixes: make that storage read linearizable (read from the leader), or put the version number in the message so the resizer can tell it got the wrong one and retry.

Note

Everything else: feeds, likes, view counts and search results are fine with eventual consistency: slightly stale for a few seconds. Saying explicitly which parts of your design need linearizability and which don't is a strong staff-level signal.

docs.title: Which systems are linearizable, and CAP done right
docs.text:
CAP · PACELC

Whether a replicated database can be linearizable depends on how it replicates (see Chapter 5):

Replication Linearizable? Why Single-leader (reads from leader) Potentially yes If reads hit the leader and the leader is really the leader (fencing) Consensus (Raft / ZooKeeper / etcd) Yes Designed for it Multi-leader No Concurrent writes on different leaders Leaderless (Dynamo / Cassandra) Probably not LWW + clock skew, sloppy quorums, timing edge cases

This is also where the famous CAP theorem fits. It is often stated as "pick 2 of 3", which is misleading. The accurate version is narrower:

Note

CAP, correctly stated: network partitions will happen; you don't get to opt out of them. While one is happening, a node cut off from the others has two choices: refuse requests it can't safely answer, staying consistent (CP), or answer from data that might be stale, staying available (AP). It's a decision per feature, not per database.

Note

PACELC adds the everyday case: Else, when there's no partition, you still trade Latency against Consistency. Linearizability is slow even when nothing is failing, because each operation waits for other nodes (a quorum round trip, possibly across regions).

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Inventory and payments are CP: I'd rather reject than oversell. Hotel search and reviews are AP: stale by a few seconds is fine."

docs.title: Ordering: Lamport timestamps
docs.text:
Causality without clocks

Chapter 8 showed that wall clocks can't order events across machines. But we often need to know that one thing caused another: a reply must come after the message it answers. Lamport timestamps give an ordering that respects cause and effect, using only counters.

  1. Every node keeps a simple counter, starting at 0. Each time it does something, it increments the counter and stamps the operation with (counter, node ID). Node A writes something and stamps it (1, A).
  2. Every message carries the sender's counter. When a node receives one, it sets its counter to max(its own, the received one) + 1. Node B receives A's message (counter 1), so its next write is (2, B). Node C hears from B and stamps (3, C). The counter travels along the chain of cause and effect.
  3. The result: if event X could have influenced event Y, X's timestamp is always smaller. To get one complete order, compare counters and break ties by node ID.
  4. The limitation: you only know the order after the fact, once you've collected everyone's timestamps. Suppose two users register the same username at the same moment on different nodes. To answer "is it taken?" right now, a node needs to know nobody else is claiming it concurrently. Lamport timestamps can't tell you that. You need every node to process requests in the same order as they happen, and that requires total order broadcast, which turns out to be equivalent to consensus.

Note

Total order broadcast: deliver every message to every node, reliably, in the same order. That is exactly a replicated log: Kafka partitions (within one partition), Raft's log, ZooKeeper's Zab protocol. If every node applies the same log in the same order, they all end up in the same state.

docs.title: Two-phase commit (2PC)
docs.text:
Distributed atomic commit

Sometimes one transaction has to change data in two different databases, say the payments database and the bookings database, and both changes must happen or neither. Each database can only promise atomicity for itself, so a coordinator runs a protocol across them: two-phase commit.

  1. Phase 1, prepare: the coordinator asks every participant, "can you commit this?"
  2. Each participant checks it can (constraints pass, data written durably to disk) and replies YES. A YES is a binding promise: the participant must be able to commit later, even if it crashes and restarts in between. So it keeps the affected rows locked while it waits.
  3. Phase 2, commit: once all participants have said YES, the coordinator writes its decision, "COMMIT", to its own log. That is the point of no return. Then it tells every participant to commit. If anyone said NO, it tells everyone to abort.
  4. The weakness: if the coordinator dies after the prepare phase, the participants are stuck "in doubt". They promised to commit, so they can't abort on their own, and they don't know the decision, so they can't commit. They wait, holding their locks, until the coordinator recovers. Other transactions touching those rows stall too. That blocking, plus tight coupling between services, is why microservice architectures use sagas instead: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo it if a later step fails.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "I won't use 2PC across the payment and booking services. I'll use a saga: reserve room → charge → confirm, with compensations (release room, refund), driven by events with the outbox pattern."

docs.title: Consensus: Raft in one picture
docs.text:
Raft / Paxos / Zab

Consensus means getting several nodes to agree on a value, such as "who is the leader" or "what is the next entry in the log", in a way that survives crashes and network problems. Raft is the most widely taught algorithm. The idea:

  1. A cluster of 5 nodes elects one leader for each term (a numbered epoch: term 5, term 6…). The others are followers. Five nodes can tolerate 2 failures.
  2. Every change goes to the leader, which appends it to its log and sends it to the followers.
  3. An entry is committed as soon as a majority (3 of 5) have stored it. Why does that make it safe? Any future majority of 3 must include at least one node from this majority, because two groups of 3 out of 5 always overlap. So a committed entry can never be forgotten, whoever becomes leader next.
  4. If the leader dies or goes silent, a follower's timer runs out. It becomes a candidate, increments the term to 6, and asks for votes. With votes from a majority it becomes the new leader. If the old leader comes back, it sees the higher term and steps down, and any message it sends with the old term is rejected. That is the same fencing idea as in Chapter 8.

Note

Sizing: 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures: 3 nodes survive 1 failure, 5 nodes survive 2. Every write waits for a majority round trip, so consensus is used for small, critical metadata (who's leader, which node owns which shard), not for bulk data.

docs.title: ZooKeeper / etcd: consensus as a service
docs.text:
Coordination services

Consensus algorithms are hard to implement correctly, so in practice you don't. You run a small cluster of ZooKeeper or etcd, which implements it for you and exposes a simple, strongly consistent key-value store. Your services use it for a handful of coordination jobs:

  1. It's a small store (keys with small values, a few nodes), where every read and write is linearizable.
  2. Leader election: many scheduler instances try to create the same key, and exactly one succeeds. That one is active; the rest wait as standbys. Distributed locks work the same way, and the store's ever-increasing revision number is a ready-made fencing token (Chapter 8).
  3. Membership: each live server registers an ephemeral key that disappears automatically when its session dies, so "which servers are alive?" is just a list. Configuration and shard maps live here too, and clients watch keys to be notified the moment they change (the routing in Chapter 6).

Tip

Say this in the interview: "The job scheduler runs active-passive. Leader election goes through etcd with a lease, and the lease revision is the fencing token on job-claim writes."

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "Is this CP or AP?" → Answer per feature: booking and payment are CP, search and feeds are AP. Mention PACELC latency cost.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Transaction spanning booking + payment services?" → Not 2PC (blocking, coupling). Use a saga + outbox + idempotent consumers.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Exactly one scheduler must run." → Leader election via ZooKeeper or etcd (consensus), lease + fencing token.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Unique usernames across regions?" → Needs linearizable compare-and-set: one strongly consistent store (Spanner, CockroachDB, or a single-leader region for usernames).

docs.title: DDIA Chapter 10: Batch Processing
docs.text:
Advanced

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 10 · BATCH PROCESSING on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Take a big, bounded, immutable input, run a pure function over it, and produce a derived output. Because inputs are never modified, a buggy job is fixed by re-running it. That property, being able to recompute from source, runs through all of Part III.

Key ideas: Unix philosophy · MapReduce · HDFS · shuffle · sort-merge join · broadcast join · Spark DAG

docs.title: The Unix philosophy: small tools, one interface
docs.text:
Where batch comes from

Part III of the book is about derived data: indexes, caches, reports and recommendations computed from a source of truth. The simplest way to compute derived data is a batch job. Take a large, fixed input (yesterday's logs, say), run it through a program, and write a new output. The ideas behind modern batch systems were already in Unix decades ago.

Say you want the five most-visited pages from a web server log. In a Unix shell, this is one line:

cat access.log | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

  1. awk reads each line of the log and prints only the 7th field, the URL.
  2. sort puts identical URLs next to each other, and uniq -c collapses each run into a count. If the log is bigger than memory, sort spills to disk and merges, so this works on files far larger than RAM.
  3. sort -rn orders by count, highest first, and head -5 keeps the top five. That's six tiny programs, none of which knows about the others, combined into a useful analysis.

Why does this work so well? Three properties, which carry straight over to big-data systems:

  • The input is never modified. You can run the command a hundred times while experimenting, and the log is untouched. A mistake costs nothing.
  • One uniform interface: every tool reads lines of text and writes lines of text, so any tool can feed any other.
  • Logic is separate from wiring: sort doesn't know or care where its input comes from or where its output goes.

MapReduce is this same idea spread over thousands of machines, with a distributed filesystem (HDFS) playing the role of the file.

docs.title: MapReduce: map, shuffle, reduce
docs.text:
Distributed batch

Now the log is 10 TB, spread over hundreds of machines. MapReduce runs the same "extract, group, count" logic in parallel:

  1. The input is stored in HDFS, split into blocks of about 128 MB, with each block copied to three machines.
  2. The scheduler starts a mapper on a machine that already holds each block. Moving the code to the data is far cheaper than moving terabytes over the network. Each mapper reads its records and emits key-value pairs, for example (url, 1) for every log line. This is the awk step.
  3. The shuffle then routes every pair to a reducer chosen by hashing its key, so all pairs for the same URL end up at the same reducer, sorted by key. This is the sort step. It is the expensive part, because most of the data crosses the network here.
  4. Each reducer receives, for each key, all its values together (url → 1, 1, 1, …), combines them (adds them up), and writes its output files back to HDFS. This is the uniq -c step.

Fault tolerance comes almost for free. Because inputs are immutable and tasks have no side effects, if a machine dies mid-task the scheduler simply re-runs that one task somewhere else.

Note

Scale: mapper output is written to local disk, and reducers pull it over the network. Google and Yahoo ran MapReduce over petabytes a day, and the same map-shuffle-reduce shape still runs inside Spark, BigQuery and Snowflake today.

docs.title: Joins in batch: bring related records together
docs.text:
Sort-merge · broadcast · partitioned

Batch jobs often need to combine two datasets. Question: "which URLs are popular with which age group?" Clicks come from the event log (user_id, url). Ages come from the user database (user_id, birth_year).

  1. The naive way is to look up each user in the live database for each click. With billions of clicks, that's billions of random network requests: far too slow, and it would hammer the production database. Instead, take a snapshot (a dump) of the user table into HDFS, so both datasets are plain files.
  2. Sort-merge join: one mapper reads clicks and another reads users, and both emit user_id as the key. The shuffle delivers everything for user 104, the profile and all of their clicks, to the same reducer, next to each other, with the profile first. The reducer reads the birth year, then streams through the clicks emitting (url, age) pairs. It is one linear pass, with no random lookups.
  3. Broadcast hash join: if one side is small, such as a table of 5,000 hotels, skip the shuffle entirely. Load the small table into memory in every mapper, and each mapper joins its share of the big dataset by looking up the in-memory table. Partitioned hash join: if both datasets are already partitioned the same way (by the same key, into the same number of parts), each partition of one can be joined with the matching partition of the other independently.

Warning

Skew: if one key is extremely common, such as a celebrity with millions of clicks, all of its records go to one reducer, and the whole job waits for it. The fix is the same as hot keys in Chapter 6: detect the hot keys (for example by sampling) and spread their records across several reducers.

docs.title: Beyond MapReduce: dataflow engines and batch outputs
docs.text:
Spark · Flink · outputs

Real pipelines aren't one MapReduce job; they're chains of ten or twenty. MapReduce handles chains badly:

  1. In MapReduce, every job writes its full output to HDFS, replicated three times, before the next job can start reading it. Most of those intermediate files are thrown away straight after. Each job also waits for the entire previous job to finish, even if the first results were ready long before.
  2. Dataflow engines like Spark and Flink treat the whole pipeline as one graph of operators (a DAG). Data streams from one stage to the next in memory or on local disk, without the replicated writes. If a machine fails, lost pieces are recomputed from the steps that produced them (the lineage) instead of being stored three times just in case. The result is often 10–100× faster.

Note

What batch jobs produce: search indexes (built offline, then swapped in atomically), precomputed recommendations, machine-learning features, and read-only key-value stores bulk-loaded into serving systems. Because outputs are new files rather than in-place changes, rolling back a bad run just means pointing back at yesterday's output.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "Web crawler for 10B pages?" → The frontier queue feeds fetchers. Text extraction and dedup run as batch (Spark) over S3. Re-runnable because raw pages are stored immutably.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Daily top-K or reconciliation reports?" → Nightly batch over the event log in S3 or the warehouse. The streaming path gives fast approximate results and batch gives exact ones (Ch 12, Lambda).

Important

Interviewer asks: "How do you rebuild the search index?" → Batch-build a new index from the source of truth, then atomically switch the alias. Old index kept for rollback.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Raw events land immutably in S3, partitioned by date. Any derived table can be recomputed from them, which is our safety net for bugs."

docs.title: DDIA Chapter 11: Stream Processing
docs.text:
Advanced

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 11 · STREAM PROCESSING on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Batch with the input never ending. Events are processed shortly after they happen. This is Kafka, CDC, the outbox pattern, event sourcing, windowed aggregation, and exactly-once semantics: the backbone of most modern interview designs.

Key ideas: message brokers · Kafka partitions · consumer groups · CDC · outbox · event sourcing · windows · watermarks · exactly-once

docs.title: Two kinds of message broker
docs.text:
Queue vs log

A batch job processes yesterday's data. A stream processor handles each event moments after it happens: a click, a booking, a payment. The events travel through a message broker, a service that sits between the producers sending events and the consumers handling them. It holds events until consumers are ready, so neither side has to wait for the other.

There are two very different kinds of broker, and choosing the wrong one is a common interview mistake:

  • A queue (RabbitMQ, SQS) works like a to-do list shared by a team. Each message is a task. One worker takes it, does it, acknowledges it, and the message is deleted. Add workers to get through the list faster.
  • A log (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar) works like an append-only journal. Messages are written in order and kept for days. Each consumer remembers how far it has read (its offset), so many independent consumers can read the same messages, and any of them can go back and re-read history.
Queue (RabbitMQ, SQS, JMS) Log (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar) After consume Message deleted once acked Message stays; consumer just advances an offset Ordering Lost under parallel consumers + redelivery Strict order within a partition Parallelism Any consumer takes any message (load balancing) One consumer per partition per group Replay No: gone after ack Yes: reset offset, re-read days of history Slow message Others continue (per-message ack) Blocks its partition (head-of-line) Best for Task queues: send email, resize image, each job independent Event streams: ordering matters, multiple consumers, replay, CDC

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Image resize jobs go on SQS, since they are independent with per-message retry. Booking events go on Kafka, since order per booking matters and several services consume them."

docs.title: Kafka: partitions, offsets, consumer groups
docs.text:
Log-based broker

One log on one machine can't handle millions of events a second, so Kafka splits each topic (a named stream, such as bookings) into partitions.

  1. Each partition is its own append-only log, with messages numbered 0, 1, 2… (the offset). The producer chooses the partition by hashing the message key. With key = booking_id, every event for booking 123 lands in the same partition, in the order it was sent. Kafka guarantees order only within a partition, so the key is how you say what must stay in order.
  2. Consumers join a consumer group. Kafka gives each partition to exactly one consumer in the group, so the partitions are shared out like work. The group can never have more active consumers than there are partitions, so the partition count caps your parallelism. Each consumer periodically saves (commits) its offset, and after a crash, it or its replacement resumes from the last committed offset.
  3. A different group, say analytics, reads the very same partitions with its own offsets, at its own speed. Adding a new consumer group costs the producers nothing; they don't even know it exists.

Note

Numbers: about 5–10k messages a second per partition is a comfortable planning figure, and one broker handles around a million messages a second. Default retention is 7 days. Size the partition count as target throughput ÷ what one consumer can handle, with room to grow.

docs.title: The dual-write problem
docs.text:
Why not just write to both?

A very common situation: your data lives in Postgres, but you also need it in a search index (Elasticsearch) and a cache (Redis). The obvious approach is for the application to write to all of them. That approach is broken in two ways:

  1. Two clients change the same product's price at almost the same time: client 1 sets 100, client 2 sets 120. The database applies them in one order and ends at 120.
  2. Each client then writes to the search index too, but those requests travel separately, and the network delivers them in the other order. The index ends at 100.
  3. Now the database says 120 and search says 100, and nothing will ever fix it. There's no error, and no later process notices.
  4. Even without a race, if the application crashes (or the second write fails) after writing to the database but before writing to the index, one system has the change and the other never will. Writing to two systems is never atomic.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "I won't dual-write to Postgres and Elasticsearch. I'll write only to Postgres and stream changes to Elasticsearch with CDC, so one order, defined by the DB log, reaches every consumer."

docs.title: Change data capture (CDC) and the outbox pattern
docs.text:
One source of truth → many views

The fix is to write to one place, the database, and let everything else follow the database's own record of changes, in the database's order.

  1. Outbox: when the app saves an order, it also inserts a row describing the event ("order 42 placed") into an outbox table, in the same transaction. Either both rows commit or neither does, so an event exists if and only if the change does.
  2. Change data capture (CDC): every database already keeps a log of all changes for its own replicas, Postgres's WAL or MySQL's binlog (Chapter 5). A CDC tool such as Debezium reads that log like a replica would and publishes each change, outbox rows included, to Kafka, in commit order.
  3. Every other system consumes from Kafka and updates itself: the search index, the cache, the data warehouse. They all see changes in the same order as the database, so they converge on the same state. And if one gets corrupted, or you add a new one, you rebuild it by replaying the log, or from a snapshot plus the log since then.

Note

Consumers must be idempotent: the relay can publish an event twice (for example if it crashes after publishing but before recording that it did). Consumers should dedupe by event ID, or use upserts so applying the same change twice is harmless.

docs.title: Event sourcing: store what happened, derive the state
docs.text:
Events as the source of truth

Normally a database stores the current state: the booking's status is CANCELLED. Event sourcing flips that around and stores what happened, as a list of events that is never changed, and works out the current state from it.

  1. Each user action is appended as an immutable event describing it: RoomHeld (seat 12A), PaymentTaken ($120), HoldExtended (+5 min), BookingConfirmed.
  2. When the customer cancels, nothing is deleted or overwritten. A new BookingCancelled event is appended, and the full history stays.
  3. The current state ("status = CANCELLED") is a view computed by replaying the events in order (a fold). You can build other views from the same events later, such as an audit trail or an analytics table, even ones you didn't think of at the start. To debug, you can replay up to any moment and see exactly what the state was then.

Warning

Costs: replaying a long history gets slow, so you store periodic snapshots. Changing the format of old events is hard (Chapter 4). And "delete my data" requests (GDPR) clash with "never delete anything". Use event sourcing where the history really matters, such as payments, ledgers and orders, not everywhere.

Note

CDC vs event sourcing: CDC turns low-level row changes into events after the fact ("row 42's status column changed"). Event sourcing records high-level business events as the source of truth ("customer cancelled"), so the intent is preserved.

docs.title: Time and windows
docs.text:
Event time vs processing time

Many stream questions are about counting over time: clicks per minute, failed logins in the last 5 minutes, sessions per user. Since a stream never ends, you count within windows, and there are four common kinds:

  1. Tumbling: fixed, back-to-back windows, like 10:00–10:01, then 10:01–10:02. Each event falls in exactly one. Use for "clicks per minute".
  2. Hopping: fixed-length windows that overlap, such as a 5-minute window starting every minute. Each event falls in several. Use for "5-minute moving average, updated every minute".
  3. Sliding: defined by the events themselves, as in "any two failed logins within 5 minutes of each other". Use for fraud and abuse rules.
  4. Session: groups one user's events until they go quiet for some time, say 30 minutes. Use for web analytics sessions or a workout recording.

Warning

When it happened is not when it arrived. A phone in a tunnel queues events and sends them 10 minutes late. If you count by arrival time, those clicks land in the wrong minute. Count by event time, the timestamp from when it happened. But then, when can you close the 10:00 window and publish its count? A watermark is the processor's estimate that "all events up to 10:00 have probably arrived". Events arriving after it are either dropped or used to correct the published result.

docs.title: Stream joins
docs.text:
Three kinds

Just like batch jobs, stream processors often need to combine data. Because both sides can keep changing, there are three different situations:

Join Example How Stream–stream (window join) Search event + click event within 1 hour → click-through rate Buffer both streams in state, indexed by session ID, for the window length Stream–table (enrichment) Click event + user profile → add country and age Keep a local copy of the table in the processor, updated by CDC. No remote DB call per event. Table–table (materialized view) Tweets ⋈ follows → each user's timeline cache Both are changelogs; maintain the joined view incrementally (fan-out on write from Ch 1)

Note

Joins depend on time: if you join a sale with a tax-rate table, do you want the rate when the sale happened or today's rate? Replaying later could give a different answer. To keep results reproducible, give each version of the record its own ID and join on that version.

docs.title: Exactly-once really means effectively-once
docs.text:
Fault tolerance

A stream processor runs forever, so it will crash at some point. When it restarts, how do you avoid losing events, or counting them twice?

  1. The danger: a crash in the middle leaves things half-done. The processor may have read some events and updated its counts in memory, but not saved them, or saved the output but not the position it had read up to.
  2. Checkpointing (as Flink does it): special barrier markers flow through the data with the events. When an operator sees barrier #42, it saves its state (the counts so far) to durable storage such as S3, together with the source offsets it had reached. After a crash, everything restores from the last complete checkpoint and re-reads the source from those offsets, so nothing is lost. Spark Streaming gets the same effect by processing small micro-batches.
  3. But replaying from the checkpoint means some events are processed again, and their output may be written twice. So the destination must handle duplicates. Either make writes idempotent (upsert by key, so writing "ad 7, 10:00 → 523 clicks" twice gives the same result), or transactional (Kafka transactions commit the output and the new offsets together, atomically). Duplicates still occur inside the system; they just have no effect on the result. That's what "exactly-once" really means.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Flink checkpoints every 10s. The sink upserts (ad_id, minute) → count, so replays after a failure overwrite instead of double-counting."

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "Ad click aggregation at 10k/sec?" → Kafka partitioned by ad_id → Flink 1-min tumbling windows on event time → OLAP store. Raw clicks to S3 for batch reconciliation.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Keep search, cache, and DB in sync?" → CDC (Debezium) or outbox → Kafka → idempotent consumers. Never dual-write.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Kafka or SQS?" → Ordering, replay, or many consumers → Kafka. Independent tasks with per-message retry and DLQ → SQS.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Exactly-once?" → "At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing equals effectively-once. I make the consumer idempotent with an event ID."
