docs.title: DDIA Chapter 12: The Future of Data Systems
docs.text:
Advanced

These DDIA pages are study notes in our own words and diagrams, connecting the book to interview problems. They don't replace the book; Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann is worth reading in full.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DDIA 12 · THE FUTURE OF DATA SYSTEMS on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The book's conclusion: there is no one database that does everything. Build systems as a source of truth plus derived views connected by logs. Push correctness to the ends with idempotency, and separate "eventually up to date" (timeliness) from "never wrong" (integrity).

Key ideas: derived data · unbundling the DB · Lambda vs Kappa · end-to-end argument · idempotency keys · timeliness vs integrity · audit

docs.title: Unbundling the database
docs.text:
Data integration

By the last chapter, the book's big lesson is that no single database does everything well. Postgres is great for transactions, Elasticsearch for text search, Redis for fast lookups, a column store for analytics. Real systems use several. The question is how to keep them all consistent without the dual-write mess from Chapter 11.

  1. Pick one system of record, such as Postgres. It is the only place the application writes to, and the source of truth. Its change log, read via CDC into Kafka, is the single ordered history of everything that happened.
  2. Every other store is a derived view of that history: the Redis cache, the Elasticsearch index, the analytics warehouse, the ML features. Each one consumes the log and keeps itself up to date. If one is wrong, or you need a new one, you drop it and rebuild it by replaying the log.

Why "unbundling"? Inside a single database, an index is exactly this: a derived copy of the data, organized differently, kept up to date automatically. The book's point is that at company scale you do the same thing with the database's parts taken apart: the log in Kafka, and each index in its own specialized system.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Postgres is the source of truth for bookings. Search, the cache, and analytics are derived views fed from CDC, so they are eventually consistent and rebuildable."

docs.title: Lambda vs Kappa architecture
docs.text:
Batch + stream

You often want results that are both fast (a live dashboard) and exact (billing). Two architectures combine batch (Chapter 10) and stream (Chapter 11) processing to get there.

  1. Lambda architecture: run two paths side by side over the same events. A speed layer (stream processing) gives approximate answers within seconds. A batch layer recomputes exact answers from all the raw data every few hours. Queries merge the two: the batch result for older periods, the stream result for the last few hours. It is correct and robust, but you write the same logic twice in two different frameworks, and keeping them in agreement is painful.
  2. Kappa architecture: use only the stream path. To fix a bug or change the logic, you don't patch old results. You start version 2 of the stream job reading the log from the beginning into a new output table, let it catch up to the present, compare, then switch reads to the new table and stop version 1. This needs the log to keep all history, for example with Kafka's long retention or tiered storage.

Note

In interviews: top-K and ad-click problems often still use a Lambda-like design: Flink for real-time dashboards, plus a nightly batch job that reconciles the exact counts for billing. Say why: money needs exact numbers, and a batch recount from immutable raw data is the simplest way to get them.

docs.title: The end-to-end argument: idempotency keys
docs.text:
Correctness at the edges

Where should duplicate protection live? You might think the lower layers handle it: TCP drops duplicate packets, and the database deduplicates its own retries. But duplicates that start at the user's end slip past all of them. The book's answer, the end-to-end argument, is that only a check spanning the whole path, from where the operation starts to where its effect is stored, can catch every case.

  1. Before the first attempt, the mobile app generates a unique ID for this payment, for example 7f3. It generates this once per payment, not once per attempt.
  2. It sends POST /pay with the header Idempotency-Key: 7f3. The server stores the key in a column with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the payment itself, and saves the result.
  3. The server's 200 OK is lost on the way back, so the app doesn't know the payment worked and retries with the same key. To TCP, the load balancer and the database, this is a brand-new connection and a brand-new request. None of them can tell it's a repeat.
  4. The insert hits the unique constraint on 7f3. The server recognises the duplicate and returns the original stored result instead of charging again. Only an ID created at the origin of the operation, and carried end to end, catches every duplicate.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Every mutating API takes an Idempotency-Key from the client. It is stored with a unique index, results are cached for 24h, and retries are always safe."

docs.title: Timeliness vs integrity
docs.text:
Two kinds of "consistency"

"Consistency" mixes up two very different requirements, and separating them is one of the most useful habits in system design:

  • Timeliness: is the user seeing the latest state? If not, it's annoying but temporary. Wait a moment and refresh, and it's fixed.
  • Integrity: is the data correct, with no money lost or created, nothing sold twice, nothing contradicting itself? If not, the damage is permanent until someone repairs it by hand.

Most systems can relax timeliness, which is what makes eventual consistency, caches and derived views acceptable. Almost none can relax integrity.

Timeliness Integrity Means Users see an up-to-date state No corruption: no lost or double money, no contradictions If violated Temporary and self-healing: "wait and refresh" Permanent: needs manual repair Example Booking shows in "My trips" 2s late Room sold twice; card charged twice Mechanism Read-your-writes, sync replication Idempotency, unique constraints, atomic log append, reconciliation Can relax? Often yes (eventual consistency) Almost never

Note

Prevent or apologise: some rules don't have to be enforced up front. Airlines overbook on purpose, then compensate the few passengers who don't get a seat. Checking a constraint after the fact, with a compensating action, can be cheaper than strict coordination. For each rule, ask what a violation costs, and how often it would happen.

Note

Trust, but verify: run regular reconciliation and audit jobs that recompute derived data from the source and compare: do ledger entries sum to zero, do inventory counts match? Bugs, bad deploys and disk corruption happen in real systems, so plan to detect them.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "How do you guarantee no double charge?" → Client idempotency key + unique constraint + the payment provider's idempotency + a daily reconciliation job against provider settlement files.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Search shows a stale price." → "Search is a derived view. Timeliness can lag seconds; the checkout price is read from the source of truth (integrity)."

Important

Interviewer asks: "How would you change the aggregation logic?" → Kappa: deploy v2 consumer from offset 0 to a new table, compare, switch.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "I separate integrity from timeliness: money and inventory are strongly consistent and audited; everything the user browses is a derived, eventually consistent view."

docs.title: Foundations
docs.text:
Read these first. They give you the method that every other page uses.

  1. The basics: how a request travels through DNS, CDN, load balancer, app servers, cache, database and queue. Start here if any of those are new.
  2. How to approach any design: the loop of simple design → find the break → fix only that.
  3. Non-functional requirements: the qualities that drive architecture, with SLOs and error budgets.
  4. Numbers and estimation: what hardware can do, and how to estimate quickly.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Every system design builds on the same handful of parts. This page walks one request through them, in plain language. If these feel familiar, skip to How to approach any design.

docs.title: 1. DNS: finding the server
docs.text:
Your browser knows a name (api.example.com), but the network needs an IP address. DNS is the internet's phone book: the browser asks a resolver, which finds the address and caches it for a while (the record's TTL).

Why it matters in design: DNS can send users in different countries to different data centers, and it is one of the first things involved in failover between regions.

docs.title: 2. CDN: serving files close to the user
docs.text:
Images, JavaScript, videos and pages that look the same for everyone don't need to come from your servers. A CDN keeps copies on servers in hundreds of cities, so a user in Dhaka gets the file from nearby instead of from a data center on another continent.

Why it matters: a CDN removes most of the traffic before it reaches you, and makes pages load faster. If 90% of requests hit the CDN, your servers only see the other 10%.

docs.title: 3. Load balancer: spreading the work
docs.text:
You run several copies of your application so that one machine isn't a bottleneck or a single point of failure. A load balancer sits in front of them, sends each request to a healthy server, and stops sending traffic to servers that fail health checks.

  • An L4 load balancer forwards network connections without looking inside them. It's very fast.
  • An L7 load balancer reads the HTTP request and can route by URL path or header, for example /api/* to one group of servers and /ws/* to another.

docs.title: 4. Stateless app servers: easy to add more
docs.text:
An app server is stateless when it keeps nothing about a user between requests: no sessions in memory, no files on local disk. Everything it needs comes with the request (such as a login token) or from shared storage (a database or cache).

Why it matters: if servers are stateless, any server can handle any request. Scaling becomes adding servers behind the load balancer, and a crashed server loses nothing. Keeping state outside your servers is the single most important habit in system design.

docs.title: 5. Cache: answering from memory
docs.text:
Reading from a database takes a few to tens of milliseconds. Reading from memory takes about one. A cache such as Redis keeps copies of frequently read data in memory.

The usual pattern (cache-aside): check the cache; if the data is there, use it; if not, read the database and store a copy in the cache with an expiry time (TTL).

Why it matters: most apps read far more than they write, and a small share of items gets most of the reads. A cache can absorb the large majority of reads. See Caching.

docs.title: 6. Database and indexes: the source of truth
docs.text:
The database holds the real, durable copy of the data. When the cache and the database disagree, the database is right.

An index is what makes a database fast. Without one, finding a user by email means checking every row. With an index on email, the database looks it up in a sorted tree in a few steps, like using the index at the back of a book instead of reading every page.

Why it matters: choosing the right index is often the cheapest performance fix there is. But every index also slows down writes slightly, so index the queries you actually run. See Database indexing.

docs.title: 7. Queue and workers: doing slow work later
docs.text:
Some work is too slow to do while the user waits: sending email, resizing an image, generating a report. The app puts a message on a queue and responds immediately. Separate worker processes take messages from the queue and do the work.

Why it matters: users get fast responses, spikes of work are smoothed out, failed jobs can be retried, and workers can be scaled separately from the app. See Long-running tasks.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text:
Piece Solves Typical tool DNS Finding the server by name Route 53, Cloudflare DNS CDN Slow, repeated downloads of the same content CloudFront, Cloudflare, Akamai Load balancer Spreading traffic; surviving a dead server nginx, Envoy, cloud load balancers Stateless app servers Handling more requests by adding machines Your application Cache Repeated reads hitting the database Redis, Memcached Database + indexes Storing data safely and finding it fast Postgres, MySQL Queue + workers Slow or bursty work SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka

Almost every design in this handbook is this picture, plus one or two extra pieces added because a specific number required them.

docs.title: How to approach any design
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Good designs aren't memorized. They are derived: you start from what the system must do, put numbers on how well it must do it, and add complexity only when a number forces you to.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
1. Requirements. Write down what users can do (functional) and how well it must work (non-functional: latency, availability, consistency, scale, durability). See NFRs.
  2. Estimate. Turn the NFRs into a few numbers: requests per second, storage, fan-out, bandwidth. See Numbers and estimation.
  3. Simple design. Client → service → one database. It is almost always the right starting point, and often more capable than people assume.
  4. Find the break. Compare your numbers with what each component can handle. The first limit you exceed is the bottleneck.
  5. Fix only that. Apply the pattern that removes that specific bottleneck: a cache for reads, a queue for spiky writes, a conditional update for contention.
  6. Repeat until every NFR is met. Then stop.

docs.title: Why this works in interviews
docs.text:
• It shows reasoning, which is what interviewers grade, rather than a recited architecture.
  • It keeps you out of trouble: you never add Kafka, sharding or microservices without a reason you can state.
  • It gives you natural deep dives: each "break" is a place the interviewer can push, and you've already thought about it.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Let me start with the simplest design that meets the functional requirements, then use the numbers to find where it breaks and fix those points one at a time."

docs.title: A worked mini-example
docs.text:
"Design a URL shortener for 100M daily users."

Step What you say Requirements Create short links; redirect fast (p99 < 100 ms); links never collide. Estimate 1B redirects/day ≈ 12k/s average, ~100k/s peak. Writes ≈ 12/s. 1B links × 500 B = 500 GB. Simple design API service + Postgres. 500 GB and 12 writes/s fit one database easily. Find the break 100k reads/s on one Postgres is too much. Fix only that Redis cache in front; popular links dominate traffic, so most reads never reach Postgres. Repeat Codes must be unique: counter + base62. Done. No sharding needed.

The full version is the URL shortener page.

docs.title: Non-functional requirements
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Functional requirements say what the system does. Non-functional requirements (NFRs) say how well, and they decide the architecture. Two systems with identical features but different NFRs look nothing alike.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Before designing, let me pin down the NFRs with numbers, because they drive every decision that follows."

docs.title: The NFRs that matter, and how to quantify them
docs.text:
NFR Question to ask Say it as a number What it changes in the design Scale How many users? Peak vs average? "100M DAU, 50k reads/s at peak" Caching, replicas, sharding Latency Which path must be fast? "Feed p99 < 200 ms" Caches, precomputation, CDN Availability What can be down, and for how long? "99.99% for reads (≈ 4 min/month)" Redundancy, failover, multi-AZ Consistency Where is stale data unacceptable? "Booking: never oversell; browse: ≤ 5 s stale" Transactions, read-from-primary, CP vs AP Durability Can we ever lose data? "Payments: zero loss after ack" Sync replication, write-ahead logs, backups Throughput Sustained work per second? "10k events/s ingest" Queues, batching, partitions Read:write ratio Which dominates? "100:1" Read path vs write path optimizations Data size / growth How much, how fast? "500 GB now, +1 TB/year" Storage engine, partitioning, tiering Freshness How quickly must changes appear? "New posts visible within 1 min" Sync vs async pipelines Security / privacy Who can see what? PII? "Card data never leaves the vault" Tokenization, isolation, encryption Cost Any hard constraints? "GPU capacity is fixed" Queues, priorities, admission control

You rarely need all of them. Pick the three to five that matter for this problem and quantify those.

docs.title: Latency: use percentiles, not averages
docs.text:
An average hides the slow requests users actually notice. Use p50 (typical user), p99 (one request in a hundred) and sometimes p99.9.

Tail latency compounds: if one page calls 10 services in parallel and each is slow 1% of the time, about 10% of page loads hit at least one slow call (1 − 0.99¹⁰ ≈ 0.096). Set targets on p99 and use timeouts.

docs.title: SLIs, SLOs, SLAs and error budgets
docs.text:
Term Meaning Example SLI (indicator) What you measure Share of requests served in < 300 ms SLO (objective) Your internal target for the SLI 99.9% of requests < 300 ms over 30 days SLA (agreement) External promise, with penalties 99.5%, or customers get credits Error budget 100% − SLO: how much failure you can "spend" 0.1% of a month ≈ 43 minutes

The error budget turns reliability into a decision rule: while budget remains, ship features; when it's spent, focus on reliability.

docs.title: Availability in minutes
docs.text:
Availability Downtime per month Per year 99% ~7.3 hours ~3.65 days 99.9% ~43 minutes ~8.8 hours 99.99% ~4.3 minutes ~53 minutes 99.999% ~26 seconds ~5 minutes

Two components in series multiply: 99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%. Redundant components in parallel help: two independent 99% replicas give ≈ 99.99%.

docs.title: Consistency is a per-feature choice
docs.text:
Don't declare a whole system "strongly consistent" or "eventually consistent". Decide feature by feature:

  • Strong (CP): money, inventory, seat holds, unique usernames.
  • Eventual (AP): feeds, search results, like counts, reviews, recommendations.

See CAP theorem and PACELC.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Listing NFRs without numbers ("it should be fast and scalable").
  • Using averages instead of percentiles for latency.
  • Asking for "five nines" everywhere. Each extra nine costs a lot; choose it where it matters.
  • Forgetting that consistency can differ between the read path and the write path.

docs.title: Numbers and estimation
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Estimates exist for one reason: to decide whether you need a given component. Calculate only what changes a decision, round aggressively, and say the number out loud.

docs.title: Conversions you'll use every time
docs.text: Fact Use it as 1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10⁵ s 1M requests/day ≈ 12/s; 1B/day ≈ 12k/s Peak ≈ 2–5 × average Design for peak, quote both 1 KB × 1M = 1 GB; 1 KB × 1B = 1 TB Storage per year: daily items × size × 365 1 Gbps ≈ 125 MB/s Bandwidth: requests/s × response size

docs.title: What one machine or service can handle
docs.text:
These are planning numbers for well-configured systems on modern hardware. Real numbers depend on payload size, query shape and configuration, so use them to find orders of magnitude, not exact limits. Managed-service quotas change over time; check the provider's documentation before relying on one.

How to read the table: Limited by is the resource that runs out first, which tells you what to scale. Reach for it when is the problem it solves. Seen in links to problems that use it.

docs.title: Compute and the edge

docs.text: Component Rough capacity Limited by Reach for it when Seen in Redis (one node) ~100k+ simple ops/s, sub-millisecond; much more with pipelining; tens to hundreds of GB RAM; a single thread executes commands, so one hot key can saturate a node Cache, counters, rate limits, locks, leaderboards, geo, pub/sub Rate limiter, News feed, Ride sharing Memcached Several hundred thousand ops/s per node (multi-threaded) RAM; no persistence or data structures A plain, very fast key-value cache Distributed cache ZooKeeper / etcd Thousands of writes/s; reads scale with members; keep data small (MBs to a few GB) Every write needs a majority round trip Leader election, locks with fencing tokens, cluster config Job scheduler, Collaborative editor Bloom filter ~10 bits (1.2 bytes) per item for a ~1% false-positive rate Memory; items can't be removed (use a counting filter) "Have I seen this before?" checks without storing every item Web crawler, Dating app

docs.title: Messaging and processing
docs.text: Component Rough capacity Limited by Reach for it when Seen in Kafka ~5–10k messages/s per partition is a comfortable plan (tens of MB/s); ~1M messages/s per broker; 7-day default retention Partition count caps consumer parallelism; ordering only within a partition Buffering write spikes, event streams, CDC, replay, several consumers Ad click aggregator, Top-K videos, News feed SQS Standard queues: nearly unlimited throughput; FIFO queues: about 300 messages/s per API action (higher with batching); delays up to 15 minutes FIFO ordering limits throughput Independent jobs with per-message retries and dead-letter queues Online judge, Job scheduler, Web crawler RabbitMQ Tens of thousands of messages/s per node Memory when queues back up Task queues with routing rules, acknowledgements, priorities LLM chat Flink (stream processor) Hundreds of thousands of events/s per task slot for simple jobs; scales with parallelism State size; checkpoint duration Windowed counts, joins and alerts on live streams Ad click aggregator, Metrics monitoring Spark (batch) Terabytes per hour across a cluster Shuffle (network) and cluster size Large batch jobs: recounts, rebuilding indexes, reconciliation Web crawler, Ad click aggregator

docs.title: Storage and network
docs.text: Component Rough capacity Limited by Reach for it when Seen in Object storage (S3) 3,500 writes/s and 5,500 reads/s per key prefix (spread prefixes to go higher); objects up to 5 TB; multipart upload up to 10,000 parts; 11 nines of durability Request rate per prefix; per-request latency (tens of ms) Files, images, video, backups, raw logs Video platform, File sync, Photo sharing NVMe SSD Hundreds of thousands to 1M+ random reads/s; several GB/s sequential Random write endurance Databases and anything latency-sensitive on disk — Hard disk (HDD) ~100–200 random reads/s; ~100–250 MB/s sequential Seek time Cheap bulk storage read sequentially — Network link 1 Gbps ≈ 125 MB/s; 10 Gbps ≈ 1.25 GB/s Bandwidth, especially for media Size fleets that move bytes (crawlers, video) by bandwidth, not CPU Web crawler, Video platform

docs.title: Rules of thumb from this table
docs.text:
• Fits on one machine? Keep it there. 10 GB of data, or a few thousand writes per second, does not need sharding.
  • Reads too high → cache, replicas, CDN, in that order. Each removes most of the load before the next is needed.
  • Writes too high → buffer, batch, pre-aggregate, then shard. Sharding is the last step, not the first.
  • Find the scarce resource. It is usually the database primary, RAM for caches, the network for media, or GPUs for models. Design around that one.
  • Watch for single hot things. One hot row, Redis key, Kafka partition or DynamoDB partition caps you no matter how many machines you add.

docs.title: Latency ladder
docs.text: Operation Time Read from RAM ~100 ns Read from SSD ~100 µs Round trip within a datacenter ~0.5 ms Redis GET (same datacenter) ~0.5–1 ms Indexed database read ~1–10 ms Round trip across a continent ~50–100 ms Round trip across the world ~150–250 ms

docs.title: The method
docs.text:
1. Users → requests: DAU × actions per user per day ÷ 86,400 = average QPS. Multiply by 3 for peak.
  2. Split reads and writes: apply the read:write ratio.
  3. Storage: new items per day × size × retention.
  4. Compare each number with the table above. If it fits one component with headroom, you don't need to scale that part yet.

docs.title: Example: photo-sharing app
docs.text:
• 500M DAU × 20 feed views = 10B reads/day ≈ 115k reads/s → needs caching (one Postgres can't serve this).
  • 100M uploads/day ≈ 1.2k writes/s → one primary could take the metadata, but…
  • 100M × 2 MB = 200 TB of media per day → object storage plus a CDN, never the database.

Three numbers, three decisions.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "1B requests a day is about 12k per second on average, maybe 40k at peak. A single Redis handles that; Postgres needs a cache in front."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Spending ten minutes on arithmetic that doesn't change any decision.
  • Using outdated limits and sharding systems that fit on one modern machine.
  • Forgetting peak traffic, or forgetting bandwidth for large responses.

docs.title: Low-level design
docs.text:
Intermediate

Low-level design (LLD) interviews ask you to model one component in code: its classes, their responsibilities, and how they behave when many threads use them at once.

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
1. Clarify requirements. List the operations (mkdir, book, log, transfer) and the rules (no double booking, levels filter logs).
  2. Find the entities. Nouns in the requirements become candidate classes. Keep only the ones with behavior or state.
  3. Assign responsibilities. Each class should have one reason to change. Put a method on the class that owns the data it needs.
  4. Choose relationships. Prefer composition ("has a") to inheritance; use interfaces where behavior varies (sinks, strategies).
  5. Handle concurrency. Ask "what if two threads do this at once?" for every operation that reads then writes. Lock at the right granularity.
  6. Plan for change. Show where a new requirement plugs in: a new sink, a new seat type, a new storage backend.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "I'll start with the entities and their responsibilities, then walk through each operation, and then check every read-then-write for race conditions."

docs.title: Patterns that come up again and again
docs.text: Pattern Use it for Example here Composite Trees where leaves and containers share an interface File system Strategy Interchangeable behavior Log formatters in the logger Observer Notify others when something happens Low-stock alerts in inventory Producer–consumer Decouple callers from slow work Async log dispatch Fine-grained locking Concurrency without one global lock Per-show locks in movie booking Lock ordering Avoid deadlocks when taking two locks Warehouse transfers in inventory

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Problem Main idea In-memory file system Composite tree, path resolution, read/write locking Movie ticket booking Atomic all-or-nothing seat holds with expiry, locked per show Logging library Levels, pluggable sinks and formatters, async dispatch Inventory management Per-warehouse locks, deadlock-free transfers, low-stock observers

docs.title: LLD: In-memory file system
docs.text: Intermediate

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• mkdir(path) creates directories, including missing parents.
  • write(path, text) creates or appends to a file; read(path) returns its content.
  • ls(path) lists a directory's children in sorted order (or returns the file name).
  • rm(path) deletes a file or directory; mv(src, dst) moves one.
  • Paths are absolute, like /a/b/c.txt. Many threads may call these at once.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Composite pattern: File and Directory both extend Entry, so code that walks the tree treats them the same way. size() is a leaf value for a file and the sum of children for a directory.
  • Directory children are a map from name to entry, giving O(1) lookup per path segment. ls sorts the keys, or uses a TreeMap if listing is frequent.
  • Parent pointers let any entry compute its full path and let mv detach an entry from its old parent cheaply.
  • Concurrency: reads (ls, read) far outnumber structural changes, so one ReentrantReadWriteLock lets reads run in parallel while writes are exclusive. Finer locks (per directory) are possible but make mv across directories much harder to get right; mention it as a later step.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock;

abstract class Entry {
    String name;
    Directory parent;
    Entry(String name, Directory parent) { this.name = name; this.parent = parent; }
    abstract long size();
    String path() { return parent == null ? "/" : (parent.parent == null ? "" : parent.path()) + "/" + name; }
}

class File extends Entry {
    private final StringBuilder content = new StringBuilder();
    File(String name, Directory parent) { super(name, parent); }
    long size() { return content.length(); }
    void append(String text) { content.append(text); }
    String read() { return content.toString(); }
}

class Directory extends Entry {
    final Map<String, Entry> children = new HashMap<>();
    Directory(String name, Directory parent) { super(name, parent); }
    long size() { return children.values().stream().mapToLong(Entry::size).sum(); }
}

public class FileSystem {
    private final Directory root = new Directory("", null);
    private final ReentrantReadWriteLock lock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

    private static List<String> parts(String path) {
        if (!path.startsWith("/")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("absolute path required: " + path);
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String p : path.split("/")) if (!p.isEmpty()) out.add(p);
        return out;
    }

    /** Walks to the entry at path; returns null if any segment is missing. */
    private Entry find(String path) {
        Entry cur = root;
        for (String p : parts(path)) {
            if (!(cur instanceof Directory d)) return null;
            cur = d.children.get(p);
            if (cur == null) return null;
        }
        return cur;
    }

    /** Walks to the directory at path, creating missing directories. */
    private Directory mkdirs(List<String> segments) {
        Directory cur = root;
        for (String p : segments) {
            Entry next = cur.children.computeIfAbsent(p, n -> new Directory(n, null));
            if (!(next instanceof Directory d)) throw new IllegalStateException(p + " is a file");
            d.parent = cur;
            cur = d;
        }
        return cur;
    }

    public void mkdir(String path) {
        lock.writeLock().lock();
        try { mkdirs(parts(path)); } finally { lock.writeLock().unlock(); }
    }

    public void write(String path, String text) {
        lock.writeLock().lock();
        try {
            List<String> ps = parts(path);
            Directory dir = mkdirs(ps.subList(0, ps.size() - 1));
            String name = ps.get(ps.size() - 1);
            Entry e = dir.children.computeIfAbsent(name, n -> new File(n, dir));
            if (!(e instanceof File f)) throw new IllegalStateException(path + " is a directory");
            f.append(text);
        } finally { lock.writeLock().unlock(); }
    }

    public String read(String path) {
        lock.readLock().lock();
        try {
            if (!(find(path) instanceof File f)) throw new NoSuchElementException(path);
            return f.read();
        } finally { lock.readLock().unlock(); }
    }

    public List<String> ls(String path) {
        lock.readLock().lock();
        try {
            Entry e = find(path);
            if (e == null) throw new NoSuchElementException(path);
            if (e instanceof File) return List.of(e.name);
            List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(((Directory) e).children.keySet());
            Collections.sort(names);
            return names;
        } finally { lock.readLock().unlock(); }
    }

    public void rm(String path) {
        lock.writeLock().lock();
        try {
            Entry e = find(path);
            if (e == null || e == root) throw new NoSuchElementException(path);
            e.parent.children.remove(e.name);
        } finally { lock.writeLock().unlock(); }
    }

    public void mv(String src, String dst) {
        lock.writeLock().lock();
        try {
            Entry e = find(src);
            if (e == null || e == root) throw new NoSuchElementException(src);
            List<String> ps = parts(dst);
            Directory target = mkdirs(ps.subList(0, ps.size() - 1));
            for (Directory d = target; d != null; d = d.parent)
                if (d == e) throw new IllegalArgumentException("cannot move a directory into itself");
            String newName = ps.get(ps.size() - 1);
            if (target.children.containsKey(newName)) throw new IllegalStateException(dst + " exists");
            e.parent.children.remove(e.name);
            e.name = newName;
            e.parent = target;
            target.children.put(newName, e);
        } finally { lock.writeLock().unlock(); }
    }
}

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text: Question Answer How would you support permissions? Add owner and mode to Entry; check them during path resolution. Very large directories? TreeMap for sorted listing, or paginate ls with a cursor. More write concurrency? Lock per directory, taking locks top-down in path order; mv locks the common ancestor. Persist to disk? Separate the tree from storage behind an interface; write an append-only journal of operations.

docs.title: LLD: Inventory management
docs.text: Intermediate

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Track stock of each product in each warehouse.
  • add stock (deliveries) and remove stock (orders); never let stock go negative.
  • transfer stock between two warehouses atomically: it leaves one and arrives in the other, or nothing happens.
  • Notify interested parties when a product's stock in a warehouse falls below its reorder level.
  • Many threads operate at once.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• One lock per warehouse. Operations on different warehouses run in parallel; only operations on the same warehouse wait for each other.
  • Remove is check-then-act, so it happens under the warehouse lock: check stock ≥ quantity, then subtract.
  • Transfer needs two locks. If one thread transfers A→B while another transfers B→A, each could hold one lock and wait forever for the other. Fix: always lock the warehouse with the smaller id first. With one global order, a cycle of waiting is impossible.
  • Observer for low stock. The service doesn't know who cares (purchasing, alerting). Listeners register themselves; notifications are sent after releasing locks, so a slow listener can't block inventory operations.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

record Product(String id, String name, int reorderLevel) {}

interface StockListener { void onLowStock(String warehouseId, Product product, int remaining); }

final class Warehouse {
    final String id;
    final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>();   // guarded by lock
    Warehouse(String id) { this.id = id; }
    int get(String productId) { return stock.getOrDefault(productId, 0); }
    void set(String productId, int qty) { stock.put(productId, qty); }
}

public class InventoryService {
    private final Map<String, Warehouse> warehouses = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Product> products = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final List<StockListener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    public void addWarehouse(String id) { warehouses.putIfAbsent(id, new Warehouse(id)); }
    public void addProduct(Product p) { products.put(p.id(), p); }
    public void subscribe(StockListener l) { listeners.add(l); }

    public void add(String warehouseId, String productId, int qty) {
        if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive");
        Warehouse w = warehouses.get(warehouseId);
        w.lock.lock();
        try { w.set(productId, w.get(productId) + qty); } finally { w.lock.unlock(); }
    }

    /** Returns false (and changes nothing) if there isn't enough stock. */
    public boolean remove(String warehouseId, String productId, int qty) {
        if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive");
        Warehouse w = warehouses.get(warehouseId);
        int remaining;
        w.lock.lock();
        try {
            int have = w.get(productId);
            if (have < qty) return false;
            remaining = have - qty;
            w.set(productId, remaining);
        } finally { w.lock.unlock(); }
        notifyIfLow(warehouseId, productId, remaining);    // outside the lock
        return true;
    }

    /** Moves stock atomically. Locks are always taken in warehouse-id order to prevent deadlock. */
    public boolean transfer(String fromId, String toId, String productId, int qty) {
        if (fromId.equals(toId)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("same warehouse");
        if (qty <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be positive");
        Warehouse from = warehouses.get(fromId), to = warehouses.get(toId);
        Warehouse first = fromId.compareTo(toId) < 0 ? from : to;
        Warehouse second = first == from ? to : from;
        int remaining;
        first.lock.lock();
        try {
            second.lock.lock();
            try {
                int have = from.get(productId);
                if (have < qty) return false;
                remaining = have - qty;
                from.set(productId, remaining);
                to.set(productId, to.get(productId) + qty);
            } finally { second.lock.unlock(); }
        } finally { first.lock.unlock(); }
        notifyIfLow(fromId, productId, remaining);
        return true;
    }

    public int stock(String warehouseId, String productId) {
        Warehouse w = warehouses.get(warehouseId);
        w.lock.lock();
        try { return w.get(productId); } finally { w.lock.unlock(); }
    }

    private void notifyIfLow(String warehouseId, String productId, int remaining) {
        Product p = products.get(productId);
        if (p != null && remaining < p.reorderLevel())
            for (StockListener l : listeners) l.onLowStock(warehouseId, p, remaining);
    }
}

docs.title: Why lock ordering works
docs.text: Deadlock needs a cycle: thread 1 holds A and waits for B, while thread 2 holds B and waits for A. If every thread takes locks in the same global order (here, by warehouse id), thread 2 must also take A first, so it waits before holding B. No cycle can form.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text: Question Answer Reserve stock for an order before payment? Add a reserved count per product: available = stock − reserved; a reservation expires like a seat hold. One very hot product? Split its stock into several buckets, each with its own lock, and take from any bucket that has enough. Distributed across services? Conditional database updates: UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - :n WHERE … AND qty >= :n. A transfer becomes one transaction, or a saga across databases. Audit trail? Append every change to a movements table (who, what, when, why) and derive totals from it.

docs.title: LLD: Logging library
docs.text: Intermediate

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Log messages at levels DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR; each logger has a minimum level.
  • Send records to one or more destinations (sinks): console, file, later a network service.
  • Format records differently per sink (plain text, JSON).
  • Logging must not slow the application down, must be safe from many threads, and must flush on shutdown.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Sink is an interface, so a new destination is a new class, not an edit to the logger (open/closed principle). Composition, not inheritance: the logger has sinks.
  • Formatter is a strategy each sink is given, so the same record can be plain text on the console and JSON in a file.
  • Level filtering happens first, in the caller's thread, before any work like string formatting is done.
  • Asynchronous dispatch: the caller puts the record on a bounded queue and returns immediately; one background thread writes to the sinks. Sinks then see one thread and need no locks of their own.
  • Backpressure policy: when the queue is full, drop DEBUG/INFO but block briefly for WARN/ERROR. Losing an error log is worse than a short pause.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
import java.io.*;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

enum Level { DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR }

record LogRecord(Instant time, Level level, String logger, String message, Throwable error) {}

interface Formatter { String format(LogRecord r); }

class PlainFormatter implements Formatter {
    public String format(LogRecord r) {
        String base = r.time() + " " + r.level() + " [" + r.logger() + "] " + r.message();
        return r.error() == null ? base : base + " | " + r.error();
    }
}

class JsonFormatter implements Formatter {
    private static String q(String s) { return "\"" + s.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace("\"", "\\\"") + "\""; }
    public String format(LogRecord r) {
        return "{\"time\":" + q(r.time().toString()) + ",\"level\":" + q(r.level().name())
             + ",\"logger\":" + q(r.logger()) + ",\"message\":" + q(r.message()) + "}";
    }
}

interface Sink extends Closeable { void write(LogRecord r) throws IOException; }

class ConsoleSink implements Sink {
    private final Formatter fmt;
    ConsoleSink(Formatter fmt) { this.fmt = fmt; }
    public void write(LogRecord r) { System.out.println(fmt.format(r)); }
    public void close() { System.out.flush(); }
}

class FileSink implements Sink {
    private final Formatter fmt;
    private final Writer out;
    FileSink(String path, Formatter fmt) throws IOException {
        this.fmt = fmt;
        this.out = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(path, true));
    }
    public void write(LogRecord r) throws IOException { out.write(fmt.format(r)); out.write('\n'); }
    public void close() throws IOException { out.close(); }
}

/** One background thread drains a bounded queue into the sinks. */
class AsyncDispatcher implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final LogRecord STOP = new LogRecord(Instant.EPOCH, Level.ERROR, "", "", null);
    private final BlockingQueue<LogRecord> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10_000);
    private final List<Sink> sinks;
    private final Thread worker;

    AsyncDispatcher(List<Sink> sinks) {
        this.sinks = List.copyOf(sinks);
        this.worker = new Thread(this::run, "log-dispatcher");
        this.worker.setDaemon(true);
        this.worker.start();
    }

    void submit(LogRecord r) {
        if (r.level().compareTo(Level.WARN) < 0) {
            queue.offer(r);                                    // drop low-priority records if full
        } else {
            try { queue.offer(r, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }  // wait briefly for important ones
            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        }
    }

    private void run() {
        try {
            for (LogRecord r = queue.take(); r != STOP; r = queue.take())
                for (Sink s : sinks) {
                    try { s.write(r); } catch (IOException e) { System.err.println("sink failed: " + e); }
                }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    }

    public void close() throws Exception {
        queue.put(STOP);           // records already queued are written first
        worker.join(5_000);
        for (Sink s : sinks) s.close();
    }
}

public class Logger {
    private final String name;
    private final Level minLevel;
    private final AsyncDispatcher dispatcher;

    public Logger(String name, Level minLevel, AsyncDispatcher dispatcher) {
        this.name = name; this.minLevel = minLevel; this.dispatcher = dispatcher;
    }

    public boolean isEnabled(Level level) { return level.compareTo(minLevel) >= 0; }

    public void log(Level level, String message, Throwable error) {
        if (!isEnabled(level)) return;                      // cheap filter in the caller's thread
        dispatcher.submit(new LogRecord(Instant.now(), level, name, message, error));
    }
    public void debug(String m) { log(Level.DEBUG, m, null); }
    public void info(String m)  { log(Level.INFO, m, null); }
    public void warn(String m)  { log(Level.WARN, m, null); }
    public void error(String m, Throwable t) { log(Level.ERROR, m, t); }
}

Usage:

var dispatcher = new AsyncDispatcher(List.of(
        new ConsoleSink(new PlainFormatter()),
        new FileSink("app.log", new JsonFormatter())));
var log = new Logger("checkout", Level.INFO, dispatcher);
log.info("order placed");
log.debug("ignored: below INFO");
dispatcher.close();   // flush on shutdown

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text: Question Answer A sink is slow (network) Give it its own queue and thread so it can't delay the others. Expensive messages at DEBUG Check isEnabled(DEBUG) first, or accept a Supplier<String> so the message is built only when needed. File grows forever A rolling FileSink: rotate when size or date crosses a limit. Per-package levels A LoggerFactory holding a level per name prefix, returning cached loggers.

docs.title: LLD: Movie ticket booking
docs.text: Intermediate

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Browse shows (a movie on a screen at a time) and see which seats are free.
  • Hold several seats at once for a few minutes while the user pays: all of them or none.
  • Confirm a hold after payment; release it if the user cancels. Expired holds free their seats automatically.
  • A seat is never sold twice, even when many users click the same seats at the same moment.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• ShowSeat carries the state for one seat in one show: AVAILABLE, HELD (with holder and expiry) or BOOKED. The physical Seat stays immutable and is shared by all shows on that screen.
  • One lock per show. Holding seats is a check-then-act over several seats, so it must be atomic. Locking the whole service would serialize every booking in the city; locking one show only serializes users fighting over the same screening, which is exactly where contention is.
  • All-or-nothing holds: check every requested seat first, and only then mark them all held. If any seat is unavailable, change nothing.
  • Lazy expiry: a held seat whose expiry has passed counts as available. No background thread is needed for correctness; an optional sweeper just tidies up.
  • Injected clock, so expiry is testable.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
import java.time.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

enum SeatStatus { AVAILABLE, HELD, BOOKED }

final class ShowSeat {
    final String seatId;
    SeatStatus status = SeatStatus.AVAILABLE;
    String heldBy;
    Instant holdExpiresAt;
    ShowSeat(String seatId) { this.seatId = seatId; }

    boolean isFree(Instant now) {
        return status == SeatStatus.AVAILABLE
            || (status == SeatStatus.HELD && holdExpiresAt.isBefore(now));
    }
}

final class Show {
    final String id;
    final Map<String, ShowSeat> seats = new HashMap<>();
    Show(String id, Collection<String> seatIds) {
        this.id = id;
        seatIds.forEach(s -> seats.put(s, new ShowSeat(s)));
    }
}

record Booking(String id, String userId, String showId, List<String> seatIds, Instant expiresAt) {}

public class BookingService {
    private final Map<String, Show> shows = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, ReentrantLock> locks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Booking> holds = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Clock clock;
    private final Duration holdTime;

    public BookingService(Clock clock, Duration holdTime) { this.clock = clock; this.holdTime = holdTime; }

    public void addShow(Show show) { shows.put(show.id, show); locks.put(show.id, new ReentrantLock()); }

    /** Holds all requested seats or none. Returns the hold, or empty if any seat is taken. */
    public Optional<Booking> hold(String showId, String userId, List<String> seatIds) {
        Show show = shows.get(showId);
        ReentrantLock lock = locks.get(showId);
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Instant now = clock.instant();
            for (String id : seatIds) {
                ShowSeat s = show.seats.get(id);
                if (s == null || !s.isFree(now)) return Optional.empty();   // nothing changed yet
            }
            Instant expires = now.plus(holdTime);
            for (String id : seatIds) {
                ShowSeat s = show.seats.get(id);
                s.status = SeatStatus.HELD; s.heldBy = userId; s.holdExpiresAt = expires;
            }
            Booking b = new Booking(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), userId, showId, List.copyOf(seatIds), expires);
            holds.put(b.id(), b);
            return Optional.of(b);
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    /** Called after payment succeeds. Fails if the hold expired and someone else took a seat. */
    public boolean confirm(String bookingId) {
        Booking b = holds.get(bookingId);
        if (b == null) return false;
        Show show = shows.get(b.showId());
        ReentrantLock lock = locks.get(b.showId());
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Instant now = clock.instant();
            for (String id : b.seatIds()) {
                ShowSeat s = show.seats.get(id);
                boolean stillMine = s.status == SeatStatus.HELD && b.userId().equals(s.heldBy) && !s.holdExpiresAt.isBefore(now);
                if (!stillMine) return false;          // caller refunds the payment
            }
            for (String id : b.seatIds()) show.seats.get(id).status = SeatStatus.BOOKED;
            holds.remove(bookingId);
            return true;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public void release(String bookingId) {
        Booking b = holds.remove(bookingId);
        if (b == null) return;
        Show show = shows.get(b.showId());
        ReentrantLock lock = locks.get(b.showId());
        lock.lock();
        try {
            for (String id : b.seatIds()) {
                ShowSeat s = show.seats.get(id);
                if (s.status == SeatStatus.HELD && b.userId().equals(s.heldBy)) {
                    s.status = SeatStatus.AVAILABLE; s.heldBy = null; s.holdExpiresAt = null;
                }
            }
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public List<String> freeSeats(String showId) {
        Show show = shows.get(showId);
        ReentrantLock lock = locks.get(showId);
        lock.lock();
        try {
            Instant now = clock.instant();
            return show.seats.values().stream().filter(s -> s.isFree(now)).map(s -> s.seatId).sorted().toList();
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

docs.title: Why the details matter
docs.text: Detail What goes wrong without it Check all seats before changing any A user gets seats 1–2 of 3 they asked for, and the others are left half-held. Lock per show, not global Every booking in every cinema waits on one lock. confirm re-checks ownership A hold expires during a slow payment, another user takes the seat, and the first user's confirm overwrites it. Lazy expiry inside isFree A crashed sweeper thread would leave seats stuck as held forever.

docs.title: Taking it to a real system
docs.text:
In a distributed service the in-memory lock becomes a conditional update in the database, so the database enforces the rule for all servers:

UPDATE show_seats SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :user, hold_until = now() + interval '10 minutes'
WHERE show_id = :show AND seat_id = ANY(:seats)
  AND (status = 'AVAILABLE' OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_until < now()));
-- success only if the number of updated rows equals the number of seats requested; otherwise roll back

See the system design version in Ticketmaster.

docs.title: Operating Systems for system design
docs.text:
Notes in our own words, following the three themes of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (OSTEP) by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau: virtualisation, concurrency and persistence. The book is excellent and free to read at ostep.org.

This isn't a full operating systems course. It covers only the parts that keep showing up when you design, scale and debug real systems: why a service's latency explodes at 90% CPU, how one server holds a million WebSockets, why Postgres single-row commits are limited, why Kafka is fast on plain disks, why a Java process can wake up after a pause and corrupt data, and why containers get throttled or OOM-killed.

Each page explains why the problem exists and how the mechanism works, then shows how it appears in system design interviews, with self-check questions at the end.

docs.title: Processes, threads and context switches
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Part of Operating Systems for system design: notes in our own words, following the themes of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau (free at ostep.org).

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
A process is a running program with its own private memory. A thread is a path of execution inside a process; threads share the process's memory. The OS gives each the illusion of having the CPU to itself by switching between them very quickly, and each context switch costs a few microseconds plus colder caches. That's why "one thread per request" works for hundreds of concurrent requests but not for tens of thousands, and why servers use thread pools and event loops.

Key ideas: process · address space · thread · shared memory · context switch · system call · thread pool · process vs thread trade-offs

docs.title: Processes and threads
docs.text:
Why the OS has them: a machine runs hundreds of programs at once on a handful of CPU cores, and a bug in one program mustn't crash or read another. The OS virtualises the CPU and memory, so each program behaves as if it had the machine to itself.

How they differ:

  • A process has its own address space: its own view of memory, containing its code, its heap (data allocated while running) and a stack (function calls and local variables), plus open files and sockets. One process cannot read another's memory. They communicate only through the OS: pipes, sockets, files or explicitly shared memory. If one crashes, the others carry on.
  • A thread runs inside a process. All threads of a process share its code, heap and open files, and each has its own stack and registers (its current position in the code). Sharing makes threads cheap to create and makes passing data between them trivial. But a bug in one thread, such as writing to the wrong memory, can corrupt them all, and shared data needs careful locking (see Concurrency).

System calls are how programs ask the OS to do something privileged: read a file, send on a socket, start a process. The CPU switches into kernel mode, the OS does the work, and control returns. Each crossing costs time, which is why batching I/O (one large write instead of thousands of small ones) is faster.

Note

Processes vs threads in practice: Postgres runs one process per connection: isolated and robust, but heavy, which is why it needs a connection pooler such as PgBouncer. MySQL uses threads, which are lighter. Python often uses several processes to get around its global interpreter lock. Chrome runs each tab as a process so one bad page can't crash the browser.

docs.title: Context switches
docs.text:
Why they happen: there are more threads that want to run than there are CPU cores. The OS time-slices: it runs a thread for a short while, then switches to another. It also switches whenever a thread blocks, for example waiting for disk or network, so the core isn't left idle.

How a switch works:

  1. Thread A is running. A timer interrupt fires (its time slice is up), or A makes a blocking system call (it waits for data).
  2. The CPU traps into the kernel, which saves A's registers (where it was, what it was holding).
  3. The scheduler picks the next thread to run (see CPU scheduling).
  4. The kernel restores B's registers, and B continues exactly where it last stopped.

What it costs: the direct cost is a few microseconds. The hidden cost is larger: B's data isn't in the CPU caches (A's was), so B runs slowly for a while as caches refill. Switching to a different process also changes the memory mapping, which flushes the address-translation cache (TLB). A few thousand switches a second is nothing. Hundreds of thousands a second spend a real share of the CPU on switching instead of work.

docs.title: Why thread-per-request stops scaling
docs.text:
Why it's tempting: the simplest server design gives each connection its own thread. The code reads top to bottom: read the request, query the database (the thread just waits), write the response. It's easy to write and debug.

How it breaks:

  • Memory: each thread reserves a stack, often about 1 MB by default. 10,000 connections means roughly 10 GB of stacks before doing any work.
  • Switching: thousands of threads waking and sleeping means constant context switches, and caches that never stay warm.
  • Contention: more threads fighting over the same locks and connection pools makes everything slower.
  • No backpressure: if every incoming request gets a new thread, a traffic spike creates thousands of threads, and the server falls over instead of saying "busy".

The fixes:

  1. A bounded thread pool: a fixed number of worker threads take work from a queue. For CPU-bound work, about one thread per core. For work that blocks on I/O, more, sized to keep the cores busy. When the queue is full, reject quickly (HTTP 503) instead of accepting work you can't finish.
  2. Event-driven I/O: a few threads each handle thousands of connections by only touching the ones with data ready. This is how Nginx, Node.js and Redis work (see I/O models).
  3. Lightweight threads: language runtimes with very cheap user-space threads, like Go's goroutines or Java's virtual threads, keep the simple "one per request" code but map millions of them onto a few OS threads, with an event loop underneath.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Each service instance runs a bounded worker pool sized to its cores, with a short queue in front. When the queue is full we return 503 so the load balancer tries another instance, instead of piling up thousands of threads."

docs.title: In the system design interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "Why does Postgres need a connection pooler?" → Each connection is a separate OS process with its own memory. Thousands of them waste memory and cause heavy context switching. PgBouncer multiplexes many client connections onto a few dozen server connections.

Important

Interviewer asks: "How many threads should this service have?" → CPU-bound work: about the number of cores. Blocking I/O: more, roughly cores × (1 + wait time ÷ compute time). Always bounded, with a queue and rejection when full.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Why is Redis single-threaded and still fast?" → Its operations are in-memory and tiny, so one thread with an event loop avoids locks and context switches entirely. The bottleneck is the network, not the CPU. (Recent versions add I/O threads for network reads and writes.)

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What do threads of the same process share, and what does each have of its own?

They share the code, heap and open files. Each has its own stack and registers.

What is the hidden cost of a context switch?

Besides saving and restoring registers (microseconds), the new thread starts with cold CPU caches (and, between processes, a flushed TLB), so it runs slower until they refill.

Give two reasons thread-per-connection fails at 50,000 connections.

Memory: each thread's stack (~1 MB) adds up to tens of GB. CPU: constant context switching and lock contention. Also, there's no natural backpressure.

OS 2: CPU scheduling →

docs.title: CPU scheduling and utilisation
docs.text:
Intermediate

Part of Operating Systems for system design: notes in our own words, following the themes of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau (free at ostep.org).

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
When more threads want to run than there are cores, they wait in a run queue, and the scheduler decides who runs next and for how long. The details of scheduling algorithms rarely matter in system design. One consequence matters a lot: waiting time grows explosively as utilisation approaches 100%. A service at 95% CPU isn't "using its hardware efficiently"; it's queueing every request. Plan for headroom, and watch out for noisy neighbours sharing the same machine.

Key ideas: run queue · time slice · preemption · fairness (CFS) · priorities · load average · utilisation vs latency · noisy neighbours

docs.title: How the scheduler shares the CPU
docs.text:
Why it's needed: a server might have 16 cores and 500 threads. Most threads are blocked (waiting for network, disk or a lock) and don't need a core. The ones that are runnable compete for the cores.

How it works:

  1. Runnable threads wait in a run queue (in Linux, one per core, with balancing between them).
  2. The scheduler picks one, runs it for a time slice (a few milliseconds), then preempts it: interrupts it and puts it back in the queue, so others get a turn.
  3. A thread that blocks leaves the queue entirely, and returns to it when its I/O completes or its lock is free.
  4. Linux's default scheduler (CFS, and its successor EEVDF) tries to give every runnable thread a fair share: it picks the thread that has had the least CPU time so far, adjusted by priority (nice values).

Two classic goals pull in opposite directions. Throughput favours long time slices (fewer switches). Responsiveness favours short slices (nobody waits long). Interactive and latency-sensitive work wants the second.

Note

Load average (shown by uptime and top) is the average number of threads running or waiting to run (on Linux, also those waiting on disk). On a 16-core machine, a load of 16 means all cores are busy. 48 means each runnable thread waits for two others ahead of it.

docs.title: Why latency explodes near 100% utilisation
docs.text:
Why it surprises people: if a request takes 10 ms of CPU, it seems it should take 10 ms whether the server is 50% or 95% busy. It doesn't, because requests don't arrive evenly. They arrive in random bursts, and during a burst they queue.

How it grows: in the simplest queueing model, the average wait is about ρ / (1 − ρ) service times, where ρ is the utilisation:

Utilisation Average wait (in service times) A 10 ms request takes about 50% 1 20 ms 80% 4 50 ms 90% 9 100 ms 95% 19 200 ms 99% 99 1 second

Real systems differ in the exact numbers, but the shape always holds: flat for a long time, then a cliff. And tail latency (p99) hits the cliff earlier than the average does.

What to do:

  • Keep headroom. Run latency-sensitive services at around 50–70% CPU at peak, and autoscale on that target.
  • Shed load before the cliff: reject excess requests quickly rather than letting queues grow (see Rate limiting and load shedding).
  • Separate batch work from latency-sensitive work: different machines, or a lower priority, so a big background job can't push interactive requests to the back of the queue.

docs.title: Noisy neighbours
docs.text:
Why it happens: your service often shares a physical machine with others: other containers on the same host, other VMs on the same hypervisor. They share CPU cores, CPU caches, memory bandwidth, disk and network. When a neighbour suddenly gets busy, your latency rises even though your load didn't change.

How to handle it:

  • Set CPU and memory limits on everything, so no one can take the whole machine (see Containers).
  • For very latency-sensitive services, use dedicated cores or instances, or pin threads to specific cores.
  • Watch for CPU steal time (in VMs, the share of time your virtual CPU wanted to run but the hypervisor ran someone else). High steal means a noisy neighbour.
  • Spread replicas across hosts, so one bad neighbour affects only one replica.

docs.title: In the system design interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "What CPU utilisation would you target?" → For latency-sensitive services, about 60–70% at peak, because queueing delay grows sharply near 100%. Batch jobs can run close to 100%.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Latency doubled but traffic only rose 10%. Why?" → The service crossed into the steep part of the utilisation curve: from 80% to 88% busy roughly doubles the queueing delay. Scale out, or shed load.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Should the nightly batch job run on the API servers?" → No, or only at a lower priority and with limits. It competes for the same cores and pushes interactive requests into longer queues.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Which threads are in the run queue: blocked ones or runnable ones?

Runnable ones. Blocked threads (waiting for I/O or a lock) leave the queue and return when they can run again.

Why does p99 latency rise long before average CPU reaches 100%?

Requests arrive in bursts. As utilisation rises, bursts create queues more often and longer, and the unlucky requests at the back of those queues are the tail. Waiting time grows like ρ / (1 − ρ).

What is a noisy neighbour, and one way to detect it in a VM?

Another workload on the same physical machine competing for CPU, cache, memory bandwidth or I/O. In a VM, high CPU steal time shows the hypervisor is running someone else when you wanted to run.

docs.title: Memory, the page cache and GC pauses
docs.text:
Intermediate

Part of Operating Systems for system design: notes in our own words, following the themes of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau (free at ostep.org).

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Every process sees a private virtual address space; the OS maps it onto physical RAM page by page, and can push rarely used pages to disk. Touching a page that isn't in RAM causes a page fault, which costs about 1,000× a normal memory access. The OS uses all spare RAM as a page cache for files, so low "free" memory on a server is normal and good. When memory really runs out, the system either swaps (and gets very slow) or the OOM killer ends a process. In garbage-collected languages, the runtime's own GC pauses can freeze a process for long enough to cause tail latency and even correctness bugs.

Key ideas: virtual memory · pages and page tables · TLB · page faults · swapping · page cache · mmap · OOM killer · GC pauses

docs.title: Virtual memory
docs.text:
Why it exists: if programs used physical memory addresses directly, any program could overwrite another's memory, and every program would need to know where in RAM it had been loaded. Virtual memory gives each process its own private, simple view of memory, and lets the OS move things around underneath.

How it works:

  1. Memory is divided into pages, usually 4 KB. Each process has a page table that maps its virtual pages to physical frames in RAM.
  2. On every memory access, the CPU translates the virtual address through the page table. That would be slow, so recent translations are cached in the TLB (translation lookaside buffer).
  3. A page table entry can say "not present": the page was never loaded, or it was moved out to disk. Touching it causes a page fault. The CPU traps into the kernel, which finds a free frame, loads the page from disk, updates the table, and lets the program continue.
  4. A RAM access takes about 100 ns. A page fault that reads from an SSD takes about 100 µs, 1,000× slower, and on a spinning disk about 10 ms.

Virtual memory also enables tricks that systems rely on: memory-mapped files (mmap), where file contents appear directly in memory and are loaded page by page on demand (used by databases such as LMDB and by Kafka's index files), and copy-on-write after fork(), which Redis uses to snapshot its data while still serving requests.

docs.title: The page cache
docs.text:
Why it exists: disk is thousands of times slower than RAM, and programs often read the same file data repeatedly. So the OS keeps recently used file data in RAM.

How it works:

  • Reads go through the page cache. If the data is there (a hit), it returns at memory speed with no disk I/O. If not, the kernel reads it from disk and keeps a copy.
  • Writes usually just update the page in the cache and mark it dirty. The kernel writes dirty pages to disk later, in the background. write() returning doesn't mean the data is on disk; that's what fsync() is for (see Files and durability).
  • The kernel uses all otherwise unused RAM as page cache, and gives it back instantly when programs need memory.

So a database server showing "1 GB free" out of 64 GB is usually healthy: most of the rest is cached file data. Look at "available" memory, not "free". This is also why Kafka is fast without its own cache: it writes to the page cache and lets the OS serve recent messages straight from RAM. And it's why Postgres sizes its own buffer cache at only about a quarter of RAM, leaving the rest for the OS page cache.

docs.title: Swapping and the OOM killer
docs.text:
Why it goes wrong: when programs need more memory than physically exists, the OS has two choices, and both hurt.

How each plays out:

  • Swapping: move rarely used pages of process memory to a swap area on disk, freeing RAM. Fine for idle pages. But if the working set doesn't fit, the system starts thrashing: constantly faulting pages in and out, with latency rising from microseconds to milliseconds or seconds. A swapping server is often worse than a dead one, because it's too slow to be useful but still passes health checks. Many production servers run with little or no swap for this reason.
  • The OOM killer: when memory is exhausted, Linux picks a process (usually the biggest) and kills it to free memory. Containers have their own memory limit (see Containers), and exceeding it gets the container killed, often appearing as a mysterious restart with exit code 137.

What to do: size memory for the real working set plus headroom, set memory limits deliberately, alert on memory pressure (not on low "free" memory), and make services restart cleanly when killed.

docs.title: Garbage-collection pauses
docs.text:
Why they happen: in Java, Go, C#, JavaScript and Python, memory is freed automatically by a garbage collector that finds objects no longer in use. Some collection work requires stopping all application threads briefly, a stop-the-world pause, so the heap doesn't change while it's examined. With large heaps or heavy allocation, pauses can last hundreds of milliseconds, sometimes seconds.

How a pause becomes a production problem:

  1. Tail latency: every request in flight during the pause waits. A 300 ms pause every few minutes shows up as a p99.9 spike.
  2. Missed heartbeats: the process doesn't answer health checks, so the load balancer or cluster manager may mark it dead and fail over.
  3. Expired leases (correctness bug): a process holding a lock or lease pauses, the lease expires, another process takes over, and then the first process wakes up and acts as if it still holds it. This is the scenario in DDIA Ch 8, and the reason fencing tokens exist.

Swapping, VM migration and CPU throttling (see Containers) cause exactly the same kind of freeze.

What to do:

  • Use a low-pause collector (Java's G1 or ZGC, and Go's concurrent collector), keep heaps reasonably sized, and reduce allocation in hot paths.
  • Set timeouts and heartbeat intervals comfortably longer than the worst pauses you observe.
  • Never rely on "I checked my lease a moment ago" for correctness. Use fencing tokens enforced by the storage.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "A Java service can freeze for a GC pause longer than its lock's TTL, wake up and still think it holds the lock. So the lock comes with a fencing token, and the database rejects writes with a stale token."

docs.title: In the system design interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "The database server shows almost no free memory. Is that a problem?" → Usually not. Linux uses spare RAM as page cache. Check "available" memory, swap activity and page-fault rates instead.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Why do Kafka and other log systems rely on the OS page cache?" → Recent messages stay in RAM through the page cache, so consumers reading near the end of the log are served from memory, and the broker doesn't need its own cache or the GC pressure that comes with one.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Where do random p99.9 latency spikes come from?" → Often GC pauses, swapping, CPU throttling or noisy neighbours, not the code path itself. Correlate spikes with GC logs, page faults and throttling metrics.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What is a page fault, and roughly how much slower is it than a normal memory access?

An access to a virtual page that isn't in RAM. The kernel must load it from disk: about 100 µs from SSD versus about 100 ns from RAM, roughly 1,000× slower.

Does write() returning mean the data is on disk?

No. It usually means the data was copied into the page cache and marked dirty. It reaches disk later, or when fsync is called.

How can a GC pause cause a correctness bug, not just latency?

A process paused longer than its lease's TTL loses the lease to another process, then wakes up still believing it holds it, and writes. Without fencing tokens, two writers corrupt data.
