docs.title: Concurrency: races, locks and deadlock
docs.text:
Intermediate

Part of Operating Systems for system design: notes in our own words, following the themes of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau (free at ostep.org).

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
When threads share memory, operations that look like one step (counter++) are really several, and the scheduler can interleave threads between them. That's a race condition, and it loses updates silently. Locks make a section of code run one thread at a time; atomic instructions do small updates indivisibly; condition variables let threads wait for something to happen. Locks bring their own problems: contention (threads queueing) and deadlock (threads waiting for each other forever). Every one of these ideas reappears in distributed systems, with databases and lock services in place of memory.

Key ideas: race condition · critical section · mutex · atomic operations (compare-and-swap) · condition variables · contention · deadlock and lock ordering · lock-free structures

docs.title: Race conditions
docs.text:
Why they happen: counter++ compiles to three steps: load the value from memory, add one in a register, store it back. The scheduler can switch threads, or two cores can run truly in parallel, between any of those steps.

How an update gets lost:

  1. The counter is 41. Thread 1 loads 41.
  2. Before it stores, thread 2 also loads 41.
  3. Thread 1 adds one and stores 42. Thread 2 adds one and stores 42.
  4. Two increments happened; the counter went up by one. No error, no crash, just a wrong number, and only sometimes, depending on timing. That makes races notoriously hard to reproduce and debug.

The code that touches shared data and must not be interleaved is a critical section. The goal is mutual exclusion: only one thread inside it at a time.

This is exactly the lost update from databases (DDIA Ch 7), with threads in place of transactions and memory in place of rows.

docs.title: Locks, atomics and condition variables
docs.text:
Why several tools: different situations need different strengths and costs.

How each works:

  • Mutex (lock): lock(); counter++; unlock();. Only one thread can hold the lock. Others trying to take it wait, either by spinning (looping, good for very short waits) or by sleeping until woken (the OS parks them). Correct, and easy to reason about, as long as every access to the shared data takes the lock.
  • Atomic operations: the CPU provides instructions that do a read-modify-write indivisibly, such as fetch-and-add and compare-and-swap (CAS). CAS means "set this to the new value only if it still equals the old value I saw", and it reports whether it worked. No lock needed. That's ideal for counters, flags and building lock-free data structures.
  • Condition variables: let a thread sleep until a condition becomes true, such as "the queue is not empty", without wasting CPU checking. A producer adds an item and signals, and a waiting consumer wakes. This is how bounded queues between threads work: producers wait when full, consumers wait when empty.
  • Read-write locks: many readers at once, or one writer alone. Useful when reads vastly outnumber writes.

Note

CAS is everywhere in system design: a database conditional update (UPDATE … WHERE version = 7), Redis SET key value NX, and DynamoDB conditional writes are all compare-and-swap across a network. When the condition fails, you re-read and retry, exactly as with the CPU instruction.

docs.title: Contention
docs.text:
Why locks get slow: a lock is free to take when nobody else wants it. When many threads want the same lock, they queue: only one makes progress, and the rest wait, sleep and wake (with context switches). Adding threads makes it worse, not better.

How to reduce it:

  • Hold locks briefly: never do I/O (database calls, network) while holding a lock.
  • Split the lock: instead of one lock for a whole hash map, use one per bucket or shard (lock striping). Different keys no longer block each other.
  • Avoid sharing: give each thread its own counter and add them up on read (like sharded counters).
  • Use atomics or lock-free structures for simple updates.

These are the same moves used for hot rows and hot keys in databases: hold briefly, split the key, aggregate locally.

docs.title: Deadlock
docs.text:
Why it happens: with more than one lock, threads can end up waiting for each other in a circle.

How it happens: a transfer between accounts locks both accounts. Thread 1 transfers A → B: it locks A, then tries to lock B. At the same moment, thread 2 transfers B → A: it locks B, then tries to lock A. Each holds what the other needs, and neither can ever continue.

Deadlock needs four conditions at once: locks are exclusive; threads hold one lock while waiting for another; locks can't be taken away; and there's a cycle of waiting. Break any one and deadlock is impossible. The practical fixes:

  1. Global lock ordering: always acquire locks in the same order, for example by account ID, lowest first. Then a cycle can't form. This is the standard fix.
  2. Try-lock with timeout: if the second lock isn't available within a short time, release the first, back off and retry.
  3. Take all locks at once, or redesign to need only one.

Databases detect deadlocks between transactions automatically and abort one of them, which is why applications must be ready to retry a transaction that failed with a deadlock error.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "When a booking touches several seats, I lock them in a fixed order, sorted by seat ID, so two overlapping bookings can't deadlock. The database would detect a deadlock anyway, but ordering avoids the abort and retry."

docs.title: In the system design interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "How is a distributed lock different from a mutex?" → A mutex lives in one process's memory, and the holder can't vanish without the OS noticing. A distributed lock lives in another system (Redis, etcd), so the holder can crash or pause, which means it needs a TTL, and correctness needs fencing tokens.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Your in-memory counter is wrong under load. Why?" → A race: count++ isn't atomic. Use an atomic increment, or a lock, or per-thread counters summed on read.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Transactions occasionally fail with a deadlock error. What do you do?" → Acquire rows in a consistent order (sort the IDs), keep transactions short, and retry the failed transaction.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why can two threads doing counter++ lose an update?

counter++ is load, add, store. If both threads load the same value before either stores, both store the same result, and one increment is lost.

What does compare-and-swap do, and where does the same idea appear in databases?

It sets a value only if it still equals the value you read, atomically, and tells you whether it succeeded. Databases use the same idea in conditional updates (WHERE version = ?) and optimistic concurrency control.

What is the standard way to prevent deadlock with several locks?

Always acquire locks in one global order (for example, sorted by ID), so no cycle of waiting can form.

docs.title: I/O models: blocking, event loops and epoll
docs.text:
Intermediate

Part of Operating Systems for system design: notes in our own words, following the themes of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau (free at ostep.org).

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Most server time is spent waiting: for the client to send, for the database to answer, for the disk. How a program waits decides how many connections one machine can handle. Blocking I/O parks a thread per waiting operation, which is simple but limited by threads. Non-blocking I/O with an event loop lets one thread watch thousands of sockets and handle whichever are ready, using the kernel's epoll (Linux) or kqueue (BSD/macOS). That's how Nginx, Node.js, Redis and Netty serve huge numbers of connections, and how a well-built server holds a million mostly idle WebSockets.

Key ideas: blocking vs non-blocking · file descriptors · select/poll/epoll · event loop · async/await · io_uring · C10K → C10M · per-connection cost

docs.title: Blocking I/O and its limits
docs.text:
Why it's the default: a blocking read() on a socket puts the calling thread to sleep until data arrives, then returns it. The code reads naturally, step by step. With one thread per connection, it works well for hundreds of connections.

How it breaks at scale: each waiting connection holds a whole thread: its stack memory, its scheduler entry, a context switch every time it wakes. Most of those threads are just sleeping. At tens of thousands of connections, memory and switching costs dominate (see Processes and threads). In the early 2000s this was known as the C10K problem: how to handle 10,000 concurrent connections on one server.

docs.title: Non-blocking I/O and the event loop
docs.text:
Why it scales: instead of one thread waiting on each socket, one thread asks the kernel which sockets are ready and only touches those. Waiting costs almost nothing, because a waiting connection is just an entry in a kernel table.

How it works:

  1. Sockets are set to non-blocking: read() returns immediately with whatever is available, or "would block" if nothing is.
  2. The program registers all its sockets (as file descriptors) with epoll: "tell me when any of these can be read or written".
  3. The event loop calls epoll_wait(), which sleeps until at least one socket is ready, then returns only the ready ones.
  4. For each ready socket, the loop runs a short handler: read what's there, parse, maybe start a database query (also non-blocking), write a response. Then it goes back to waiting.

The crucial property: epoll's cost is proportional to the number of active sockets, not the total. The older select and poll scanned the whole list on every call. That's what makes tens of thousands, and then millions, of connections practical.

The catch: a handler must never block. One slow computation, or one accidental blocking call, inside the loop stalls every connection on that thread. Heavy CPU work goes to a separate worker pool. Servers run one event loop per core to use all CPUs.

Note

async/await is syntax that lets you write event-loop code as if it were blocking. await db.query() pauses that function and returns control to the loop, which resumes it when the result is ready. Python asyncio, JavaScript, C# and Rust work this way. Go and Java virtual threads hide the loop entirely: you write blocking code, and the runtime turns it into non-blocking I/O underneath.

Note

Disk I/O is different. epoll works for sockets, but regular files always count as "ready", so traditional event loops send disk reads to a thread pool (as Node.js's libuv does). Linux's newer io_uring interface makes both network and disk I/O truly asynchronous, with fewer system calls.

docs.title: Holding a million connections
docs.text:
Why it comes up: chat apps, live comments, notifications and multiplayer games keep a long-lived connection (WebSocket or SSE) open for every online user. Most of those connections are idle most of the time.

How one server holds a million:

  • A file descriptor per connection: raise the per-process limit (ulimit -n) and the system-wide limit from the defaults (often 1,024) to over a million.
  • Memory per connection: kernel socket buffers plus your own per-connection state. At a few KB each, a million connections need a few GB, which is fine. At 100 KB each it's 100 GB, which isn't. Keep per-connection state small, and tune socket buffer sizes.
  • An event loop (epoll): only active connections cost CPU.
  • Heartbeats: idle connections are silently dropped by NATs and load balancers after a timeout, so send small pings every 30–60 seconds, and let clients reconnect automatically.
  • Ports: each connection is identified by the four-tuple, so a server can hold millions on one listening port. The client-side ephemeral port limit only matters for proxies making many outbound connections to the same backend.

In practice you'd run many such servers for redundancy, with a load balancer that supports long-lived connections, and accept that a deploy or crash disconnects that server's users, who then reconnect elsewhere.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Connection servers use an event loop, epoll-based through Netty or Go, so a server holds a few hundred thousand idle WebSockets with a few KB of state each. We size by memory per connection, not threads, and clients reconnect with backoff when a server is drained for deploy."

docs.title: In the system design interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "How many WebSocket connections can one server handle?" → Hundreds of thousands to a million mostly idle connections with an event-loop server, limited mainly by memory per connection and file descriptor limits, not CPU. Plan for far fewer if each connection is busy.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Why is Node.js fast for I/O but bad for CPU-heavy work?" → One event loop thread serves all connections. Waiting is cheap, but any long computation blocks every connection on that loop. Move CPU work to worker threads or another service.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Why do idle connections drop after a few minutes?" → NATs, firewalls and load balancers forget idle connections after a timeout. Send application-level heartbeats more often than the shortest timeout on the path.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why does epoll scale better than select or poll?

It returns only the ready file descriptors, so its cost grows with active connections, not total connections. select and poll scan the whole list on every call.

What is the one rule an event-loop handler must never break?

It must never block (no blocking I/O, no long computation), because the loop thread serves every connection, and blocking it stalls them all.

What limits a server holding a million idle WebSockets?

Mainly memory per connection (kernel buffers plus app state) and file descriptor limits. Not threads or CPU, as long as an event loop is used and few connections are active at once.

docs.title: Files and durability: the write path and fsync
docs.text:
Advanced

Part of Operating Systems for system design: notes in our own words, following the themes of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau (free at ostep.org).

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
When write() returns, your data is usually only in RAM. A crash or power cut can still lose it. fsync() forces it all the way to stable storage, and it's slow: from well under a millisecond on a good SSD to many milliseconds on spinning disks or network storage. Databases make commits durable by appending to a write-ahead log and fsyncing it before saying "committed". They make that fast with group commit: one fsync covers many transactions. This is why a database's single-row commit rate is limited, while batched writes go much faster.

Key ideas: files and inodes · the write path · page cache · fsync and fdatasync · disk write caches · journaling file systems · write-ahead logs · group commit · crash consistency

docs.title: Files in one paragraph
docs.text: A file is a named sequence of bytes. Behind the name, the file system keeps an inode with the file's metadata (size, owner, permissions) and pointers to the blocks on disk that hold its data. A directory is a file that maps names to inodes. Opening a file gives the program a file descriptor, and reads and writes go through it. Renaming a file within a directory is atomic, which gives a simple way to replace a file safely: write a new copy under a temporary name, fsync it, then rename it over the old one.

docs.title: The write path
docs.text:
Why write() isn't enough: disks are slow, so the OS doesn't make programs wait for them. write() copies your data into the page cache and returns. The data reaches the disk later, typically within seconds, in the background.

How data travels, and where it can be lost:

  1. write() copies the data into the page cache and marks those pages dirty. A crash or power loss now loses it, even though the program was told the write succeeded.
  2. The kernel flushes dirty pages to the disk in the background, or immediately when you call fsync(fd).
  3. Many disks have their own small volatile write cache. Data there can also be lost on power failure. fsync asks the disk to flush that cache too. Enterprise SSDs with power-loss protection can treat their cache as durable, which makes fsync much faster.
  4. Only after fsync returns successfully is the data on stable storage and guaranteed to survive a crash.

fsync can take anywhere from tens of microseconds (NVMe with power-loss protection) to 10+ ms (spinning disks, some cloud network volumes). That number directly limits how many commits per second a system can make one at a time.

Warning

fsync errors matter. If fsync reports an error, the dirty data may already have been discarded by the kernel, and retrying fsync can falsely report success. Postgres learned this the hard way in 2018 and now crashes and recovers from its log on fsync failure rather than continuing.

docs.title: Crash consistency and journaling
docs.text:
Why it's a problem: a single logical change, like appending to a file, touches several places on disk: the data block, the inode (new size), and the bitmap of free blocks. A crash halfway through can leave them inconsistent: an inode pointing at garbage, or a block marked used but belonging to nothing.

How file systems handle it: journaling (ext4, XFS, NTFS). Before changing the real structures, the file system writes a description of the change to a journal and makes it durable. Then it applies the change. After a crash, it replays the journal: completed entries are reapplied, incomplete ones discarded. The structures always end up consistent. Most file systems journal only metadata by default, so the file system's own structure survives, but your application data is only safe if you fsync it.

Databases use exactly the same idea for user data: the write-ahead log.

docs.title: Write-ahead logs and group commit
docs.text:
Why databases need a log: a transaction may change many pages scattered across the data files. Writing and fsyncing all of them on every commit would be slow (many random writes), and a crash in the middle would leave the data half-updated.

How the WAL works:

  1. The transaction's changes are described as records appended to the WAL, a single sequential file. Appends are the fastest kind of disk write.
  2. On COMMIT, the database fsyncs the WAL and only then tells the client "committed". From that moment the commit survives any crash.
  3. The changed data pages are written to the data files later, in the background (at checkpoints), with no fsync on the critical path.
  4. After a crash, the database replays the WAL from the last checkpoint, redoing committed changes. The data files are brought back up to date.

The same log is reused for replication: replicas just apply the leader's WAL (DDIA Ch 5), and change data capture reads it (DDIA Ch 11).

Group commit makes it fast. If each commit needed its own fsync, a disk with 1 ms fsyncs would cap the database at about 1,000 commits a second, however fast the CPU. But one fsync costs about the same whether it flushes one transaction's records or a hundred. So while one fsync is in progress, the database collects the commits arriving behind it and makes them durable together with the next fsync. Under load, hundreds of commits share each fsync. That's why:

  • many concurrent clients get far higher total commit throughput than one client committing in a loop;
  • batching writes (multi-row inserts, several statements per transaction) is so much faster than one row per transaction;
  • some systems offer a "relaxed durability" option (Postgres synchronous_commit = off) that acknowledges before the fsync, trading the last few milliseconds of commits on a crash for speed.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Single-row commits on Postgres are bounded by WAL fsync latency, a few thousand to around ten thousand per second depending on the disk. For the click firehose I'd batch: buffer in Kafka and insert thousands of rows per transaction, so one fsync covers them all."

docs.title: In the system design interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "Why is Postgres's write throughput lower for single-row inserts than batched ones?" → Every commit waits for a WAL fsync. Batching (and group commit across concurrent clients) shares one fsync among many rows.

Important

Interviewer asks: "When is data actually durable in Kafka?" → Kafka writes to the page cache and relies on replication (acks=all to in-sync replicas) rather than fsyncing every message. Durability comes from copies on several machines that are unlikely to all lose power at once.

Important

Interviewer asks: "How do you replace a config file safely?" → Write a temporary file, fsync it, rename it over the old file (atomic), then fsync the directory. Readers always see either the old or the new file, never a half-written one.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

A program calls write() and the machine loses power a second later. Is the data safe?

Not necessarily. write() usually only puts data in the page cache. It's only guaranteed durable after a successful fsync (and the disk honouring cache flushes).

Why does a database fsync the WAL on commit but not the data files?

The WAL is one sequential append, which is fast to flush. Data pages are scattered random writes. Once the WAL is durable, the data pages can be written later, and replayed from the WAL after a crash.

What does group commit do?

It makes many transactions durable with a single fsync, by collecting the commits that arrive while a flush is in progress, which multiplies commit throughput.

docs.title: Storage devices: HDDs, SSDs and access patterns
docs.text:
Intermediate

Part of Operating Systems for system design: notes in our own words, following the themes of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau (free at ostep.org).

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Storage performance has two numbers: IOPS (how many separate operations per second) and throughput (how many bytes per second). On a hard disk, every random access means physically moving an arm and waiting for the platter to spin round, so random I/O is about 1,000× slower than sequential. SSDs have no moving parts and handle random reads well, but they write in pages and erase in large blocks, which brings write amplification and wear. Many database and log designs, LSM-trees and append-only logs above all, exist to turn random writes into sequential ones.

Key ideas: IOPS vs throughput vs latency · seek and rotation · sequential vs random · flash pages and erase blocks · flash translation layer · write amplification · wear · NVMe · network block storage · RAID

docs.title: Hard disks
docs.text:
Why random access is slow: a hard disk stores data on spinning magnetic platters. To read a particular block, the arm must move to the right track (seek, a few milliseconds), then wait for the right part of the track to rotate under the head (rotational delay, ~4 ms at 7,200 rpm). Only then does the transfer start.

How that plays out:

  • Random small reads: about 5–10 ms each, so only 100–200 IOPS. Reading 1 GB as random 4 KB blocks would take over 20 minutes.
  • Sequential reads: once the head is in place, data streams off the platter at 100–250 MB/s. The same 1 GB takes about 5 seconds.

Hard disks are still used where capacity per pound matters and access is mostly sequential: backups, archives, big object stores and data lakes.

docs.title: SSDs
docs.text:
Why they're different: SSDs store data in flash memory chips, with no moving parts. A random read takes about 0.1 ms or less, and a modern NVMe SSD handles hundreds of thousands of IOPS and several GB/s.

How flash complicates writes:

  1. Flash is written in pages (a few KB), but can only be erased in much larger blocks (hundreds of KB to MB). You can't overwrite a page in place; it must be erased first, and erasing hits the whole block.
  2. So the SSD's controller, the flash translation layer, writes updates to fresh pages, marks the old ones invalid, and later garbage-collects blocks: it copies the still-valid pages elsewhere, then erases the block.
  3. That copying means the drive writes more data internally than you asked for: write amplification. It also uses up the drive, since each cell survives only a limited number of erase cycles (wear).
  4. Sustained heavy random writes can make an SSD slow down noticeably once its spare space is used up and garbage collection runs constantly.

Sequential writes and large writes are still friendlier to SSDs than small random overwrites: they fill whole blocks, which can later be erased with little copying.

docs.title: Why sequential access shapes system design
docs.text:
Why it matters: many famous designs exist to avoid random writes:

  • Append-only logs (Kafka, write-ahead logs): every write goes to the end of a file, purely sequential.
  • LSM-trees (Cassandra, RocksDB): buffer writes in memory, then write sorted files sequentially, and merge them in the background (see DDIA Ch 3). Random writes become sequential ones.
  • Column stores read long contiguous runs of one column (sequential), rather than hopping between rows.
  • B-trees do random page writes. That's fine on SSDs, but it's why write-heavy workloads often prefer LSM engines.

The rule of thumb survives even on SSDs: batch small writes into large sequential ones whenever you can.

docs.title: Cloud and network storage
docs.text:
Why it's different again: cloud block volumes (AWS EBS, GCP persistent disks) are network storage. Every I/O crosses the data centre network to a storage service that keeps several copies.

What that means:

  • Latency is higher than a local SSD, roughly 0.5–2 ms instead of ~0.1 ms, and fsync costs more.
  • Performance is often provisioned: you pay for a number of IOPS and an amount of throughput, and exceeding them throttles you. Check them when a database is slow.
  • Local NVMe instance storage is much faster but disappears if the instance stops or fails. It's fine for caches, or for databases that replicate to other machines, but never the only copy.
  • RAID combines disks, either for speed (striping) or safety (mirroring, parity). In the cloud, replication inside the storage service, and between your own database replicas, plays that role.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "The metrics store is write-heavy, about 5M points a second, so I want an LSM-style engine that turns writes into sequential appends, on local NVMe with replication across nodes, rather than a B-tree database on network volumes."

docs.title: In the system design interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "Why is Kafka fast on ordinary disks?" → It only appends to log files and consumers read them sequentially, which disks (even HDDs) handle at high throughput. Recent data is served from the page cache.

Important

Interviewer asks: "The database got slow but CPU is low. What do you check?" → Disk: IOPS and throughput against the volume's provisioned limits, I/O wait, queue depth and fsync latency. Then cache hit rate: is the working set still fitting in memory?

Important

Interviewer asks: "Local SSD or network volume for the database?" → Network volumes survive instance failure and are easy to snapshot, at higher latency. Local NVMe is much faster but ephemeral, so it's only safe with replication to other machines.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why are random reads so slow on a hard disk compared with sequential ones?

Each random access needs a mechanical seek plus waiting for the platter to rotate (several ms), while sequential reads stream continuously once the head is in place.

What is write amplification on an SSD?

The drive writes more data internally than the host asked for, because it can only erase large blocks and must copy still-valid pages out before erasing. It costs performance and wears the flash.

How do LSM-trees use the sequential-is-faster rule?

They buffer writes in memory and flush them as sorted files with large sequential writes, merging files in the background, instead of updating pages in place randomly.

docs.title: Containers: namespaces, cgroups and limits
docs.text:
Intermediate

Part of Operating Systems for system design: notes in our own words, following the themes of Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau (free at ostep.org).

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
A container isn't a small virtual machine. It's an ordinary process on a shared Linux kernel, given its own view of the system by namespaces (its own process list, network, file system) and kept within resource limits by cgroups (CPU, memory, I/O). That makes containers fast to start and cheap to run, but the limits behave in ways that surprise people: a CPU limit can throttle a busy container into latency spikes while average usage looks low, and a memory limit kills the container when exceeded. Understanding both prevents a whole class of production mysteries.

Key ideas: containers vs VMs · namespaces · cgroups · images and layers · CPU requests and limits · CFS throttling · memory limits and OOM kills · sizing thread pools and heaps to limits

docs.title: Containers vs virtual machines
docs.text:
Why containers took over: a VM emulates a whole machine and runs a full guest operating system, which means seconds to minutes to boot and hundreds of MB of overhead each. Most of the time we only want to isolate applications from each other on the same OS.

How each isolates:

  • Virtual machines: a hypervisor runs several guest kernels, each believing it owns the hardware. Isolation is strong (separate kernels), at the cost of overhead and slow start-up. Cloud instances are VMs.
  • Containers: all containers share one host kernel. Each container's processes are ordinary Linux processes, isolated by two kernel features:
  • Namespaces control what a process can see: its own process IDs (it sees itself as PID 1), its own network interfaces and ports, its own file system root, hostname and users.
  • cgroups control how much a process can use: CPU time, memory, disk I/O and number of processes.
  • A container image is a stack of read-only file system layers (base OS files, runtime, your app) plus a thin writable layer on top. Layers are shared between containers and cached, so starting a container takes about a second.

Sharing a kernel means weaker isolation than VMs: a kernel bug can let one container affect others. For untrusted code (an online judge, multi-tenant platforms), add a sandbox such as gVisor, or use lightweight VMs (Firecracker), as described in the Online judge problem.

docs.title: CPU requests, limits and throttling
docs.text:
Why it matters: in Kubernetes, each container has a CPU request (what it's guaranteed, used for scheduling it onto a node) and optionally a limit (the most it may use). The limit is enforced in a way that often surprises people.

How the limit is enforced: the kernel gives the container a quota of CPU time per period, usually 100 ms. A limit of 2 CPUs means 200 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period, which can be spent on any number of cores.

  1. A request arrives and the service runs 8 threads in parallel (say the JVM or Go runtime saw the host's 64 cores and sized its pools for them).
  2. 8 threads × 25 ms = 200 ms: the whole quota is used in the first 25 ms of the period.
  3. For the remaining 75 ms, the container is throttled: none of its threads may run at all.
  4. Requests caught in that window wait up to 75 ms extra. The p99 latency spikes, while the dashboard shows average CPU at a comfortable 40%.

What to do:

  • Size thread pools and runtimes to the container's limit, not the host's core count. Modern JVMs and Go (with GOMAXPROCS set, or automatic in newer versions) can read cgroup limits.
  • Monitor throttling metrics (nr_throttled, throttled time), not only CPU usage.
  • For latency-sensitive services, many teams set CPU requests but no CPU limits, or generous ones, and rely on requests for fair sharing.

docs.title: Memory limits and OOM kills
docs.text:
Why it's different from CPU: CPU over the limit is slowed; memory over the limit is killed. Memory can't be throttled: if a process needs a page and none is allowed, something has to give.

How it plays out:

  • When the container's total memory (application heap, native memory, thread stacks and, depending on settings, page cache it dirtied) hits the limit, the kernel's OOM killer kills a process in the container. The orchestrator restarts it, and you see restarts with exit code 137 (killed by signal 9) and reason OOMKilled.
  • Garbage-collected runtimes make this easy to hit. If the JVM's maximum heap is set from the host's RAM, it happily grows past the container's limit. Set the heap as a fraction of the container limit (for example 70–75%), leaving room for off-heap memory and stacks.
  • Memory requests affect scheduling. If many pods use more than they requested, the node runs short, and the kernel and kubelet evict or kill pods, starting with those furthest over their requests.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Each service has CPU and memory requests based on load tests, a memory limit with the heap set to about 75% of it, and thread pools sized to the CPU request. We alert on CPU throttling and OOM kills, because both show up as latency spikes and restarts rather than obvious errors."

docs.title: In the system design interview
docs.text:
Important

Interviewer asks: "Pods restart randomly with exit code 137. What's happening?" → They're being OOM-killed for exceeding their memory limit. Check heap sizing relative to the limit, off-heap usage and leaks, then raise the limit or fix the usage.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Latency spikes, but CPU usage is only 40%. Why?" → Likely CFS throttling. A bursty multi-threaded service uses its CPU quota early in each 100 ms period and is frozen for the rest. Check throttling metrics, size thread pools to the limit, or raise or remove the CPU limit.

Important

Interviewer asks: "Containers or VMs for running customer code?" → Containers alone share the host kernel, which isn't enough isolation for untrusted code. Use microVMs (Firecracker) or a sandboxed runtime (gVisor), plus no network and strict limits.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What do namespaces control, and what do cgroups control?

Namespaces control what a process can see (PIDs, network, file system, hostname). cgroups control how much it can use (CPU, memory, I/O).

Why can a container be throttled when its average CPU usage is well under its limit?

The limit is a quota per short period (e.g. 200 ms per 100 ms). A burst on many threads spends the quota early in the period, and the container is frozen until the period ends, even though the average is low.

What happens when a container exceeds its memory limit, and how do you avoid it for a JVM?

The kernel OOM-kills a process in it (exit code 137) and it restarts. Set the JVM heap as a fraction of the container limit (about 70–75%), leaving room for off-heap memory and thread stacks.

docs.title: The 7 patterns
docs.text:
Almost every system design problem combines two or three of these. Learn each as a picture: what breaks, and what fixes it.

Pattern In one line Problems Scaling reads Most systems read far more than they write. Make the common read cheap, and the database only sees what the cache can't answer. 13 Scaling writes When writes outgrow one machine, absorb the spikes, write in batches, split the data, and write less. 7 Real-time updates Push changes to clients the moment they happen, even when the sender and receiver are connected to different servers. 7 Dealing with contention Many users want the same thing at the same moment. Exactly one should win, every time. 3 Multi-step processes A business action spans several services and any step can fail halfway. Make progress durable and failures reversible. 3 Handling large blobs Files, photos and videos belong in object storage, and their bytes should never pass through your application servers. 3 Long-running tasks If work takes longer than a request should, accept it, queue it, and let the client check back. 3

docs.title: Dealing with contention
docs.text:
Intermediate

Many users want the same thing at the same moment. Exactly one should win, every time.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DEALING WITH CONTENTION on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: When to reach for it
docs.text:
• Limited resources: seats, stock, a username, a driver, the highest bid.
  • Any "check, then act" sequence that two requests can run at the same time.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Contention is many users competing for the same limited thing at the same moment: the last seat, the last item in stock, the highest bid, the nearest driver. The natural way to write it is check, then act: read whether the seat is free, and if so, book it. Under concurrency, that has a gap between the check and the act, and two users can both pass the check.

docs.title: The idea, step by step
docs.text:
1. The bug. Users A and B both load seat 12A at the same moment. Both read status = AVAILABLE. Both send "book". Both bookings succeed, and the seat is sold twice. No error was raised; each request was correct on its own. In database terms this is a race condition (write skew, see DDIA Ch 7).

  2. The fix: make the check and the write a single atomic step, so there's no gap. Put the condition inside the update:

    UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :user
WHERE id = '12A' AND status = 'AVAILABLE';

    The database applies updates to one row one at a time. The first request finds the seat AVAILABLE, changes it, and reports 1 row updated: you won. The second finds it already HELD, matches nothing, and reports 0 rows updated: tell that user "sorry, just taken". No locks to manage, no window for a race. 3. Other tools, for situations the single statement doesn't cover:

Tool Use when Atomic conditional UPDATE Single row, single DB: the default SELECT … FOR UPDATE Multi-step logic on few rows, high contention Optimistic (version column) Low contention; retry on conflict Redis lock SET NX PX Temporary holds across services (seat hold, driver lock) Queue per resource Extreme hot spots (auction last seconds)
  • SELECT … FOR UPDATE (pessimistic lock): lock the rows when you read them, so other transactions wait until you commit. Use it when you must read, run some logic, then write, and conflicts are frequent.
  • Version column (optimistic): read the row with its version, then UPDATE … WHERE version = 7. If someone else changed it first, 0 rows update and you retry. It's cheap when conflicts are rare.
  • Redis lock with an expiry (SET key value NX PX 600000): a temporary hold that spans services or minutes, such as "this seat is held for you for 10 minutes while you pay" or "this driver is being offered a ride". The expiry frees it automatically if the user walks away. For correctness, back it with the database check (see fencing tokens).
  • A queue per item: for extreme hot spots, such as the last seconds of a popular auction, send every request for that item through one queue and process them one at a time. No contention is possible, at the cost of throughput on that one item.

docs.title: Decision checklist
docs.text:
1. Can the check and the write be one statement? Use a conditional UPDATE (… WHERE status = AVAILABLE). This is the default.
  2. Multi-step logic on a few rows with high contention? SELECT … FOR UPDATE, locking rows in a fixed order.
  3. Low contention? Optimistic concurrency with a version column; retry on conflict.
  4. A temporary hold that spans services? A lock with a TTL (Redis SET NX EX), plus a fencing token if correctness depends on it.
  5. Extremely hot single item? Serialize requests through a queue partitioned by item.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"The check and the write must be atomic, so the hold is a single conditional UPDATE. One row updated means you got the seat; zero means someone else did."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Check-then-act in application code.
  • Holding database locks while waiting on a human (payment, form).
  • Trusting a distributed lock without fencing when a paused process could wake up later.

docs.title: Problems that use it
docs.text:
• Rate limiter: Every public API needs one, and the obvious implementation has a race condition.
  • Online auction: Many people bid on one row at the same time, and exactly one of them must win each race.
  • Ticketmaster: Millions of people arrive for one on-sale, and no seat may ever be sold twice.

docs.title: Handling large blobs
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Files, photos and videos belong in object storage, and their bytes should never pass through your application servers.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: HANDLING LARGE BLOBS on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: When to reach for it
docs.text:
• Users upload or download files larger than a few megabytes.
  • Media needs processing after upload (thumbnails, transcoding).

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Some data is big: videos, photos, PDFs, backups, from megabytes to many gigabytes per file. Your app servers are built for small, quick requests. If a 2 GB upload flows through them:

  • it ties up a server's connection, memory and bandwidth for minutes;
  • a dropped connection at 95% means starting again from zero;
  • a few hundred simultaneous uploads can starve every other request.

Databases are the wrong place for the bytes too: big rows bloat backups and replication.

The idea is that the bytes and the information about the bytes take different paths. The bytes go straight between the client and object storage (S3, Google Cloud Storage), which is built for exactly this. Your servers only handle the small metadata.

docs.title: The idea, step by step
docs.text:
1. The client asks your API for permission to upload ("I want to upload video.mp4, 2 GB"). The API checks the user is allowed, creates a metadata row in the database (owner, size, status = PENDING, the storage key), and…
  2. …returns a presigned URL. This is a URL to the storage bucket with a signature built in, granting permission to upload that one object, for a short time (say 15 minutes), without giving the client any storage credentials.
  3. The client uploads directly to object storage using that URL. For big files it uses multipart upload: the file is split into parts (say 10 MB each) that upload in parallel, and if one fails, only that part is retried. If the connection drops, the upload resumes where it left off. Your servers handle none of these bytes.
  4. Object storage tells you when it's done. When the upload completes, the storage service emits an event notification, which triggers your processing: thumbnails, virus scanning, video transcoding. When processing finishes, the metadata row is set to READY. Don't rely on the client saying "I'm done", because clients crash or lie. Trust the storage event, or check the object exists.
  5. Downloads come from a CDN in front of the storage (or via presigned download URLs for private files). Users get the bytes from a server near them, and again your app servers never touch them.

What to mention: set an expiry on unfinished multipart uploads so abandoned parts don't cost money forever, store a checksum to detect corruption, and keep the bucket private, with access only through presigned URLs or the CDN.

docs.title: Decision checklist
docs.text:
1. Upload with presigned URLs directly to object storage.
  2. Use multipart upload for anything big: parallel, resumable chunks.
  3. Store metadata (owner, status, size, checksum) in a database, separate from the bytes.
  4. React to storage events to start processing; mark the item ready only when done.
  5. Serve downloads through a CDN or presigned GET URLs.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"The API only hands out a presigned multipart URL; the client uploads straight to S3. An S3 event triggers processing, and the file shows as ready when processing finishes."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Streaming file bytes through API servers.
  • Storing blobs in the database.
  • Trusting the client to report that an upload completed.

docs.title: Problems that use it
docs.text:
• Video platform (YouTube): Two hard problems: getting gigabyte uploads in reliably, and streaming smoothly on any connection.
  • File storage and sync (Dropbox): Syncing a 50 GB file after a one-byte edit should not mean uploading 50 GB again.
  • Photo sharing (Instagram): A news feed plus a media pipeline: two well-known problems combined.

docs.title: Long-running tasks
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

If work takes longer than a request should, accept it, queue it, and let the client check back.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: LONG-RUNNING TASKS on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: When to reach for it
docs.text:
• Work takes more than a second or two: transcoding, report generation, code execution, model inference.
  • Work is bursty and expensive, so it needs backpressure.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Some work takes far longer than a web request should: transcoding a video (minutes), generating a large report, running code submitted to an online judge, sending 100,000 emails. If you do it inside the HTTP request:

  • Timeouts: load balancers and browsers give up after 30–60 seconds, so the user gets an error even if the work later succeeds.
  • Duplicates: the client, seeing a timeout, retries, and now the work runs twice.
  • No control over load: a burst of requests starts a burst of heavy jobs at once, all on your web servers, slowing every other request.
  • Lost work: a deploy or crash mid-job loses it with no record.

The fix is to separate accepting the work from doing the work.

docs.title: The idea, step by step
docs.text:
1. Accept fast. The API validates the request, writes a row in a jobs table (status = QUEUED), puts a message on a queue, and immediately returns 202 Accepted with a job_id. This takes milliseconds.
  2. Do the work elsewhere. A separate pool of workers takes jobs off the queue and does the heavy lifting. Because workers are separate from the web servers, each side scales on its own. Workers autoscale on queue depth: when 10,000 jobs are waiting, add workers; when the queue is empty, scale down. A burst just makes the queue longer for a while; nothing falls over.
  3. Report progress. Workers update the job's status (RUNNING, then DONE with a link to the result, or FAILED with a reason). The client either polls GET /jobs/{id} every few seconds, or subscribes with SSE or a WebSocket for live progress. For very long jobs, send an email or push notification.
  4. Handle failure. If a worker crashes mid-job, it never acknowledges the message, so after a visibility timeout the queue hands the job to another worker. Failed jobs are retried with backoff. A job that keeps failing (a poison job, for example a corrupt input file) goes to a dead-letter queue after a few attempts, so it doesn't block the others, and someone gets alerted.

Because a job may be retried, it might run more than once, so every job must be idempotent. Writing the result to a path named by job_id (so a rerun overwrites the same file), or checking "already done?" first, makes a second run harmless.

Note

Queue choice: a simple task queue (SQS, RabbitMQ, or a Postgres table with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) is enough for most job systems. Use Kafka when you also need ordering per key, replay, or several consumers of the same events (see Message queue vs event stream).

docs.title: Decision checklist
docs.text:
1. Return a job ID immediately (HTTP 202) and enqueue the work.
  2. Workers scale on queue depth, independently of the API.
  3. Store status (queued, running, done, failed); clients poll or subscribe.
  4. Retry with backoff using a visibility timeout; send poison jobs to a dead-letter queue.
  5. Make jobs idempotent: a retried job must not duplicate side effects.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"Submission returns a job ID right away. The job goes on a queue; autoscaled workers run it and update its status, and the client polls every second."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Doing heavy work inside the HTTP request.
  • No dead-letter queue, so one bad job blocks or loops forever.
  • Non-idempotent jobs combined with at-least-once delivery.

docs.title: Problems that use it
docs.text:
• Distributed cache: Design Redis itself: data structures inside one node, then distribution across many.
  • Online judge (LeetCode): You are running strangers' code on your servers, so isolation comes first.
  • Job scheduler: Ten thousand jobs per second, each within two seconds of its scheduled time.

docs.title: Multi-step processes
docs.text:
Advanced

A business action spans several services and any step can fail halfway. Make progress durable and failures reversible.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: MULTI-STEP PROCESSES on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: When to reach for it
docs.text:
• One user action touches several services or external APIs: booking + payment + confirmation, ride lifecycle, order fulfilment.
  • Steps can take seconds to days, or depend on outside callbacks.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Booking a hotel room isn't one action. It's three, in three different services: reserve the room, charge the card, confirm the booking (and send the email). Inside a single database you'd wrap them in one transaction, so all of it happens or none of it does. But these steps live in different services, each with its own database, and some talk to outside companies like the payment provider. There is no transaction that spans all of them (and the protocol that tries, two-phase commit, blocks and couples services too tightly, see DDIA Ch 9).

So you need another way to guarantee that the process either finishes or is cleanly undone, even if a step fails or a server crashes in the middle.

docs.title: The idea, step by step
docs.text:
1. The setup. An orchestrator runs the steps in order: 1. reserve the room, 2. charge the card, 3. confirm the booking.
  2. The failure. The room is reserved, then the card charge fails: declined, or the provider is down. Step 1 has already happened in another service, and you can't roll it back with a database rollback.
  3. The saga: undo with compensating actions. For every step, define an action that semantically reverses it: release the room for "reserve", refund for "charge", cancel for "confirm". When a step fails, run the compensations for the steps that already succeeded, in reverse order. Here: release the room. The overall result is as if the booking never happened. This sequence of local steps, each with its compensation, is called a saga.
  4. Make it crash-proof. The orchestrator itself can crash halfway. So it records progress durably after every step ("room reserved", "card charged"). When it restarts, it reads that record and carries on from where it stopped, instead of starting again (double-charging) or forgetting (leaving the room reserved forever). Workflow engines such as Temporal, AWS Step Functions or Cadence do this bookkeeping for you. You write the steps as ordinary code, and they persist and replay it.

Note

Building blocks that make sagas safe:

  • Idempotent steps: after a crash, a step may run twice, so "charge the card" must carry an idempotency key.
  • The outbox pattern: reliably emit "step done" events from a service's database (see Transactional outbox).
  • Timeouts with unknown outcomes: if the payment call times out, you don't know whether it charged. Query its status by your key before deciding to retry or compensate.

Orchestration vs choreography: a central orchestrator, as above, is easiest to follow and debug. The alternative, choreography, has each service react to the previous service's events with no central coordinator. It's more decoupled, but the overall flow is hard to see. Prefer orchestration for anything involving money.

docs.title: Decision checklist
docs.text:
1. Is there a cross-service transaction? Replace it with a saga: a compensating action for each step.
  2. Who drives the steps? An orchestrator (Temporal, Step Functions) is easier to reason about than event choreography for complex flows.
  3. Are all steps idempotent so retries are safe?
  4. Do events leave the database reliably? Use the outbox pattern.
  5. What happens on timeouts with unknown outcomes? Query status; don't blindly retry side effects.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"There is no distributed transaction across booking and payment, so I'll run a saga: hold the room, charge, confirm, and if the charge fails, release the hold. A workflow engine persists progress so a crash resumes instead of restarting."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Proposing two-phase commit across microservices.
  • Non-idempotent steps that double-charge on retry.
  • Dual writes to a database and a queue without an outbox.

docs.title: Problems that use it
docs.text:
• Payment system (Stripe): Throughput is moderate. The hard part is staying correct when a call to the bank has an unknown outcome.
  • Online judge (LeetCode): You are running strangers' code on your servers, so isolation comes first.
  • Job scheduler: Ten thousand jobs per second, each within two seconds of its scheduled time.

docs.title: Real-time updates
docs.text:
Intermediate

Push changes to clients the moment they happen, even when the sender and receiver are connected to different servers.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: REAL-TIME UPDATES on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: When to reach for it
docs.text:
• Users expect to see changes within about a second: chat, live comments, prices, collaboration, ride tracking.
  • Polling would be mostly empty responses or far too frequent.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: The web was built for the client to ask and the server to answer. But many features need the server to tell the client something the moment it happens: a new chat message, a comment on a live stream, a driver's position, a price change. The server can't start a conversation with a browser on its own. So you need a way to push updates, and once you have many servers, a way to get each update to the right server.

docs.title: The idea, step by step
docs.text:
1. Polling. The client asks "anything new?" every few seconds. It's simple and works everywhere. But updates arrive up to one interval late, and most requests return nothing. A million viewers polling every 2 seconds is 500,000 mostly-empty requests a second. Polling is fine when updates are slow and few people are watching, such as a dashboard refreshed every 30 seconds.
  2. Push over a held-open connection. The client opens a connection and keeps it open, and the server writes to it whenever something happens:
  3. Server-Sent Events (SSE): one-way, server to client, over ordinary HTTP. It's simple, goes through proxies, and the browser reconnects automatically. Ideal for feeds, live comments, notifications and streaming AI responses.
  4. WebSocket: two-way. Both sides can send at any time. Needed for chat, multiplayer games and collaborative editing.
  5. Long polling: the client asks, and the server holds the request until there's news, then the client immediately asks again. It's a fallback when the others are blocked.
  6. The multi-server problem. You have many servers, each holding thousands of open connections. Client A is connected to Server 1. Client B, watching the same live stream, is connected to Server 2. A new comment arrives at Server 1. How does it reach Client B, whose connection lives on a different server?
  7. Pub/sub between servers. Add a publish/subscribe layer such as Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka. Each server subscribes to the channels its connected clients care about: "video 123", "user 42", "symbol AAPL". When an event happens, it is published once to its channel, and every server subscribed to that channel receives it and forwards it to its own connected clients. The event source doesn't need to know where anyone is connected.

Note

Choosing: updates rare, or a few seconds' delay is fine → poll. Server-to-client stream → SSE. Both directions, high frequency (chat, games, collaboration) → WebSocket. Getting events between your servers → pub/sub.

Things to mention: held-open connections are stateful, so a deploy or crash drops them, and clients must reconnect and catch up (send "last event ID seen"). And routing viewers of the same stream to the same few servers reduces how many channels each server must subscribe to.

docs.title: Decision checklist
docs.text:
1. How fresh must it be? Every 30 s or slower: just poll.
  2. Server-to-client only? Use Server-Sent Events (plain HTTP, auto-reconnect).
  3. Both directions, low latency? Use WebSockets.
  4. Many servers? Route events with pub/sub (Redis, Kafka) to whichever server holds the connection.
  5. Can events be lost? If not, persist first and let clients resume from an offset after reconnecting.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"Viewers only receive, so SSE is enough. Each comment is published once to a channel per video; every server holding viewers of that video is subscribed and pushes it to them."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Polling at large scale.
  • Assuming sender and receiver share a server.
  • No plan for reconnects and missed messages.

docs.title: Problems that use it
docs.text:
• Ride sharing (Uber): Four problems in one: a flood of location updates, matching, locking drivers, and a multi-step trip lifecycle.
  • Live comments (Facebook Live): One popular stream can mean a million viewers each expecting new comments within a fraction of a second.
  • Collaborative editor (Google Docs): The challenge is correctness, not scale: everyone must end up with the same document.
  • Stock trading (Robinhood): Two separate problems: pushing live prices to millions, and never losing or duplicating an order.
  • Online auction: Many people bid on one row at the same time, and exactly one of them must win each race.
  • LLM chat (ChatGPT): GPUs are the scarce resource, so every queueing decision is really a cost decision.
  • Chat app (WhatsApp): Chat looks like CRUD until you notice the two users are on different servers and one of them is offline.

docs.text: • DDIA Ch 11: Stream processing

docs.title: Scaling reads
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Most systems read far more than they write. Make the common read cheap, and the database only sees what the cache can't answer.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: SCALING READS on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: When to reach for it
docs.text:
• Read:write ratio is 10:1 or higher.
  • The same items are read over and over (popularity is skewed).
  • A read path misses its latency target, or the calculated read QPS exceeds what one database serves (~10–50k/s).

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Most products are read-heavy. People view a post far more often than anyone writes one, and a typical ratio is 10 to 100 reads per write. Early on, one database answers everything. As traffic grows, that database spends all its time answering the same popular questions again and again, until it hits its limit (roughly 10k+ reads a second for typical queries). Then latency climbs for everyone, writes included, because they share the same machine.

The fix comes in layers, cheapest first. Each layer stops a share of reads from ever reaching the database.

docs.title: The idea, step by step
docs.text:
1. Start: one database serves every read. This is fine until the numbers say otherwise. Calculate peak reads per second before adding anything.
  2. Add a cache (cache-aside). Put Redis or Memcached in front of the database. On each read, the app checks the cache first. On a hit, it returns the value in under a millisecond, and the database isn't touched. On a miss, it reads the database (5–50 ms), stores the result in the cache with an expiry time (TTL), and returns it. Popular data is requested most, so it is usually in the cache: hit rates of 80–99% are common, which cuts database reads by 5 to 100 times.
  3. Add read replicas for the reads that still miss. Replicas are copies of the database that receive every write from the primary and serve reads. Three replicas roughly triple read capacity. The catch is replication lag: a replica can be a little behind, so a user who just changed something might not see it yet. Send those reads to the primary (see DDIA Ch 5).
  4. Add a CDN for content that's the same for many users: images, scripts, and even API responses like "today's top stories". CDN servers near the user answer directly, so those requests never reach your servers at all.

Warning

Three cache problems to name in an interview:

  • Stampede: a very popular key expires, and in that instant 10,000 requests all miss and hit the database together. Fixes: let only one request reload the key while the others wait (single-flight, or a short lock), and add random jitter to TTLs so keys don't all expire at once.
  • Invalidation: when data changes, the cached copy is wrong. Delete the cache key on every write, and keep a TTL as a safety net.
  • Hot key: one key gets so much traffic that the single cache server holding it is overwhelmed. Fixes: keep copies of it on several cache servers, or cache it in each app server's memory for a second or two.

More detail on caching strategies in Caching.

docs.title: Decision checklist
docs.text:
1. Is the response the same for many users? Put a CDN in front.
  2. Is it per-user but read often? Cache-aside in Redis with a TTL.
  3. Still too much load on the primary? Add read replicas and accept replication lag.
  4. Is one key extremely hot? Replicate the key or add a short-lived local cache.
  5. Which reads must never be stale? Send those to the primary.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"Reads outnumber writes about 100 to 1 and popularity is skewed, so a cache-aside Redis layer should absorb most reads. The rest go to replicas; only checkout reads the primary."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sharding the database before trying a cache and replicas.
  • Caching data that must be exact (stock at checkout, balances).
  • Forgetting cache stampedes on hot keys.

docs.title: Problems that use it
docs.text:
• URL shortener (Bitly): It sounds like a toy, but it is the cleanest example of a read-heavy system: almost every request is a redirect.
  • Rate limiter: Every public API needs one, and the obvious implementation has a race condition.
  • Business discovery (Yelp): The trap is over-engineering: the whole dataset fits on one database server.
  • News feed (Facebook): The canonical fan-out problem: build a personalised feed for billions of users in a few hundred milliseconds.
  • News aggregator (Google News): A feed problem where the feed is the same for everyone in a region, which changes everything.
  • Local delivery (Gopuff): It looks like an ordering system, but most of the load is people checking what is available near them.
  • Dating app (Tinder): Swipes are a firehose of writes, and two people swiping right at the same moment must never miss their match.
  • Distributed cache: Design Redis itself: data structures inside one node, then distribution across many.
  • Post search (Facebook): Search over billions of posts, where like counts change constantly.
  • Price tracker (CamelCamelCamel): Five hundred million products can't all be crawled often, so decide what is worth checking.
  • Ticketmaster: Millions of people arrive for one on-sale, and no seat may ever be sold twice.
  • Video platform (YouTube): Two hard problems: getting gigabyte uploads in reliably, and streaming smoothly on any connection.
  • Photo sharing (Instagram): A news feed plus a media pipeline: two well-known problems combined.

docs.title: Scaling writes
docs.text:
Intermediate

When writes outgrow one machine, absorb the spikes, write in batches, split the data, and write less.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: SCALING WRITES on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: When to reach for it
docs.text:
• Sustained writes exceed what one primary handles (roughly 10k+ per second for simple rows).
  • Write traffic is spiky: events, clicks, telemetry.
  • Data is append-mostly and read in aggregate (counts, time series).

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Reads can be scaled with copies, as caches and replicas. Writes can't: every write must eventually land in the one place that owns that data. With one primary database, every write in the system goes through one machine. For simple rows, that machine tops out around 10k+ writes a second, and far less for complex transactions. Some systems blow straight past that: ad clicks, video views, sensor readings, metrics. They often arrive in spikes, when a big event starts or a campaign launches.

There are four moves, best applied in this order: absorb the spikes, batch the writes, write less, and only then split the data across machines.

docs.title: The idea, step by step
docs.text:
1. Start: every event is one synchronous database write. The user's request waits for the database. A spike to 50k events a second means 50k individual inserts, the database falls behind, requests time out, and the retries make it worse.
  2. Absorb with a log, then batch. The ingest service appends each event to Kafka and replies immediately. Appending to Kafka is very fast, and Kafka stores events durably, so nothing is lost even if the database is slow. Consumers read events at the pace the database can handle, and write them in batches: one insert of 1,000 rows is far cheaper than 1,000 inserts of one row. A spike now just makes the queue a bit longer for a few minutes, instead of an outage.
  3. Shard. If the sustained rate is still more than one database can take, split the data across several databases by a key that spreads load evenly, such as hash(ad_id). Each shard takes a fraction of the writes, and each Kafka partition can feed its own shard.
  4. Write less, and use storage built for writes.
  5. Pre-aggregate: if the product only ever needs "clicks per ad per minute", count them in the stream processor and write one row per ad per minute instead of one row per click. 10,000 clicks become 1 write.
  6. Choose a write-optimized store (an LSM-tree database such as Cassandra), which turns random writes into sequential appends (see DDIA Ch 3).

Warning

Hot partition: sharding spreads different keys. One very hot key, such as a viral ad or a celebrity's post, still lands on one shard and can overload it. Fixes: split that key across several sub-keys with a suffix (ad42_0 … ad42_9) and add them up on read, or aggregate its events in memory before writing.

docs.title: Decision checklist
docs.text:
1. Can the client get a quick ack while the work happens later? Put a durable log (Kafka) in front.
  2. Can writes be grouped? Batch inserts in consumers.
  3. Can you store less? Pre-aggregate (one row per key per minute instead of one per event).
  4. Still too much for one node? Shard by a key that spreads load evenly.
  5. Write-heavy and simple key access? Use an LSM-based store such as Cassandra.

docs.title: In the interview
docs.text:
Tip

"Clicks arrive at 10k/s with spikes, so they go to Kafka first. A stream job aggregates per ad per minute, which cuts the database writes by orders of magnitude."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A hot partition: one key still lands on one shard.
  • Losing data by acknowledging before anything is durable.
  • Using a B-tree OLTP database for a firehose of append-only events.

docs.title: Problems that use it
docs.text:
• Top-K videos (YouTube): The design falls straight out of one number: hundreds of thousands of views per second.
  • Ad click aggregator: Clicks are money, so the numbers must be fast for dashboards and exact for billing.
  • Web crawler: Ten billion pages in five days is a pipeline problem, constrained by politeness and network bandwidth.
  • Metrics monitoring (Datadog): Millions of data points per second arrive, and alerts must fire within a minute.
  • Fitness tracking (Strava): The key insight is where the work happens: on the phone, not the server.
  • Post search (Facebook): Search over billions of posts, where like counts change constantly.
  • Price tracker (CamelCamelCamel): Five hundred million products can't all be crawled often, so decide what is worth checking.

docs.title: Interview playbook
docs.text:
• The 45-minute delivery framework: what to do in each phase.
  • Phrases, signals and traps: what senior answers sound like.
  • Quick-fire practice: 18 short questions to answer out loud.
  • What's expected at each level: mid-level to principal, with the same problem answered at each.
  • Staff-level answers: what changes from senior to staff, applied to all 29 problems. Also as an interactive atlas.

Each problem page also has its own interview script in section 7.

docs.title: The 45-minute delivery framework
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Time Phase Do Avoid 0–5 Functional requirements 3 "users can…" statements. Say what's out of scope. Listing ten features. 5–8 Non-functional requirements 3–5 NFRs with numbers. Say where you need consistency vs availability. "It should be fast and scalable." 8–10 Estimates Only the numbers that change a decision: QPS, storage, fan-out. Ten minutes of arithmetic. 10–13 Entities and API Core entities; 3–5 endpoints; idempotency keys; cursor pagination. Perfecting every field. 13–25 High-level design Satisfy each functional requirement with the simplest components. Walk one request end to end. Adding Kafka or sharding nobody asked for. 25–40 Deep dives Take each NFR, show where the simple design breaks with a number, fix it. Follow the interviewer's lead. Defending a choice instead of discussing trade-offs. 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you'd monitor, what you'd do next. Silence.

docs.title: Requirements (0–8 minutes)
docs.text:
Ask, then write down. Good questions: Who are the users? What's the most important action? How many users, and how spiky? What must never go wrong?

Tip

"Let me confirm scope: users can A, B and C. I'll leave D out unless you want it. For NFRs, the key ones are…"

docs.title: Estimates (8–10 minutes)
docs.text: Use the method in Numbers and estimation. Finish each number with a conclusion: "…so one Postgres is enough for writes, but reads need a cache."

docs.title: High-level design (13–25 minutes)
docs.text: Start from the simplest design. Draw the client, the service and the database, then trace one request through it for each functional requirement. Add components only when a requirement needs them.

docs.title: Deep dives (25–40 minutes)
docs.text:
This is where senior candidates separate themselves. For each NFR:

  1. Point to where the current design fails it, with a number.
  2. Propose the fix (usually one of the 7 patterns).
  3. Name the trade-off you're accepting.
  4. Mention a failure mode and how you'd handle it.

If the interviewer steers you somewhere else, follow them. They're telling you what they want to grade.

docs.title: Wrap-up (40–45 minutes)
docs.text:
Tip

"The biggest remaining risk is X. I'd monitor p99 latency, error rate and queue depth, and I'd alert on Y. With more time I'd look at Z."

docs.title: What's expected at each level
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

The same question, "design a URL shortener", is asked at every level. What changes is how much of the answer you're expected to drive, and how deep you go without being asked. Knowing your target level tells you where to stop and where to keep going.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Mid-level Senior Staff Principal Who drives The interviewer guides; you follow hints well You drive; the interviewer steers deep dives You drive and set the agenda; you check in You reframe the problem; it becomes a discussion between peers Requirements Lists the main features Adds NFRs with numbers Picks the 2–3 NFRs that actually decide the design Questions the requirements against the business goal Design A working design with sensible parts A design that meets the NFRs, with justified choices The simplest design that meets them, and why nothing more Designs across team and system boundaries Trade-offs Knows pros and cons when asked Chooses and explains why States what is given up and when the choice would change Weighs organisational and long-term costs too Failure Handles failures when asked Covers the main failures Raises failure modes before being asked Plans for failure across systems and teams Operations Rarely discussed Mentions monitoring SLOs, alerts, rollout and rollback Cost, ownership, on-call load, migrations Depth One or two areas, with help Two or three deep dives Deep dives chosen by risk Depth where it changes the decision

docs.title: Mid-level
docs.text:
The bar: a correct, working design for a well-scoped problem, built with reasonable components, with some guidance.

  • Clarify the main features; don't get lost in edge cases.
  • Draw a clear design: client, API, service, database, and probably a cache.
  • Design sensible tables and APIs.
  • Know the common building blocks (cache, queue, load balancer, replicas) and roughly when each helps.
  • Respond well to hints. If the interviewer asks "what if this table gets huge?", work it through.

Common reasons for a no: a design that doesn't work end to end; vague components with no reason ("we'll add Kafka"); getting stuck without asking questions.

Focus on: The basics, the core concepts, and the easy and medium problems.

docs.title: Senior
docs.text:
The bar: you lead the interview, the design meets clear non-functional requirements, and you can go deep where the interviewer pushes.

  • Set NFRs with numbers and use estimates to justify choices.
  • Explain trade-offs between real options (SQL vs NoSQL, push vs pull, sync vs async).
  • Handle concurrency and consistency correctly (double booking, lost updates, replication lag).
  • Cover the main failure cases: retries, timeouts, idempotency.
  • Manage your time so you reach the deep dives.

Common reasons for a no: needing to be led; trade-offs listed but no decision made; missing a race condition or data-loss scenario.

Focus on: all 7 patterns, Numbers and estimation, medium and hard problems, and DDIA Ch 5–7.

docs.title: Staff
docs.text:
The bar: a design that is simple on purpose, where every choice is tied to a number, failures are raised before anyone asks, and you show how it would be run and changed. See Staff-level answers.

  • Frame the core tension in one sentence.
  • Use one decisive number to rule options in or out.
  • Decide, and say what you accept in exchange.
  • Raise failure modes unprompted, with how you'd detect and recover from them.
  • Talk about SLOs, metrics, rollout, cost, and what changes at 10× scale.

Common reasons for a no: a correct senior answer with no sense of operations or cost; over-engineering; trade-offs never tied to the business.

docs.title: Principal
docs.text:
The bar: everything at staff, plus judgement at the level of the organisation. Principal interviews are often less about one system and more about how you'd shape many.

  • Challenge the problem itself: should this be built, bought, or not done at all?
  • Think across systems: shared platforms, data ownership, migration paths from the current system.
  • Weigh team structure, ownership and on-call load as design inputs.
  • Plan multi-year evolution, including how to migrate safely without downtime.

docs.title: The same problem at each level: URL shortener
docs.text: Level What a strong answer sounds like Mid-level "An API stores short code → long URL in Postgres and redirects. Codes are random strings with a uniqueness check. I'd add a cache because reads are frequent." Senior "Redirects are about 100 times more common than writes, about 100k/s at peak, so a Redis cache takes most reads and replicas take the rest. Codes come from a counter in base62, so there are no collisions to check. 302 rather than 301, so every click is counted." Staff Everything senior said, plus: "500 GB fits one primary, so no sharding. The risk is a viral link expiring from cache all at once, so I'd use single-flight rebuilds. SLO is p99 redirect under 100 ms; I'd watch hit ratio and database miss rate. Phishing links need scanning. At 10×, redirects move to the CDN edge." Principal Everything staff said, plus: "Is this a product or internal infrastructure? If several teams need short links, it should be a shared platform with per-team quotas and abuse handling owned in one place. Migrating existing links means dual-writing during the switch-over, and links must never break."
