docs.title: Phrases, signals and traps
docs.text: Intermediate

docs.title: What a senior answer sounds like
docs.text: Signal Example Quantify the break "At 100k reads per second a single Postgres falls over, so the first thing I'd add is a cache. Traffic is skewed, so I expect an 80%+ hit rate." Name the trade-off "Fan-out on write makes reads one lookup but costs one write per follower, so I'll switch to pull above ~100k followers." Choose consistency per feature "The stock decrement is strongly consistent through a conditional update; the product page is cached and can be a few seconds stale." Raise failure modes unprompted "If the payment call times out we don't know whether it charged, so the order stays pending and we reconcile by our idempotency key." Start simple, on purpose "One Postgres handles this write rate, so I won't shard. If writes grow 10×, I'd shard by user ID." Tie choices to requirements "We need replay and several consumers, so Kafka rather than a queue."

docs.title: Habits that give away a junior answer
docs.text:
• Listing technologies without saying what problem each solves.
  • "We'll use microservices and Kafka" before any numbers.
  • Ignoring retries, timeouts and partial failure.
  • Sharding at a few hundred requests per second.
  • Treating the whole system as either "strongly" or "eventually" consistent.
  • Designing in silence, then presenting.

docs.title: Phrases to avoid, and what to say instead
docs.text: Instead of Say "It's eventually consistent" (about money) "Payments are strongly consistent; only the dashboard is eventually consistent." "Just add more servers" (for a hot key) "More servers don't help one hot key. I'll split the key or cache it locally." "We'll use a distributed transaction across services" "I'll use a saga with compensating steps and idempotent handlers." "Redis lock, done" "A Redis lock with a TTL plus a fencing check in the database, so a paused process can't write late." "NoSQL scales better" "This access pattern is key-based at 50k writes/s, which suits Cassandra. Postgres would need sharding to match." "We'll cache everything" "We'll cache the read-heavy, tolerant-of-staleness paths; checkout reads the database."

docs.title: NFR checklist for the first five minutes
docs.text:
• [ ] Scale: DAU, peak QPS, read:write ratio
  • [ ] Latency: which path, which percentile
  • [ ] Availability target, and what can degrade
  • [ ] Consistency: where stale or duplicate data is unacceptable
  • [ ] Durability: can anything ever be lost?
  • [ ] Data size and growth
  • [ ] Anything special: security, privacy, cost, regions

docs.title: Quick-fire practice
docs.text:
Intermediate

Answer each question out loud in under 30 seconds, then open it to compare.

1. Cache-aside vs write-through? Cache-aside: app reads cache, on miss reads DB and fills cache; writes update DB then delete key. Write-through writes both synchronously: fresher, slower writes. 2. How do you stop a cache stampede? Single-flight lock per key (only one request recomputes), jittered TTLs, serve stale while revalidating, pre-warm hot keys. 3. SSE vs WebSocket vs long polling? SSE: server→client over HTTP with auto-reconnect. WebSocket: bidirectional, stateful. Long polling: fallback. Pick the simplest that fits the traffic direction. 4. Two users book the last seat. What exactly goes wrong and how do you fix it? Check-then-act race (write skew). An atomic conditional UPDATE … WHERE status=AVAILABLE, or a lock with TTL; exactly one row update succeeds. 5. Why not 2PC across microservices? It blocks on coordinator failure and couples availability. Use a saga with compensations, outbox, and idempotent consumers. 6. What is the outbox pattern? Write the business row and an event row in one local transaction; a relay/CDC publishes the event. No dual-write inconsistency. 7. At-least-once vs exactly-once? Delivery is at-least-once in practice; make processing idempotent (dedupe by ID, upserts) to get an effectively-once result. 8. When do you shard? When the calculated write load or data size exceeds one primary (~10–50k TPS, multiple TB) after caching and replicas. Pick the key from the hottest query. 9. Consistent hashing in one sentence? Nodes and keys on a ring, key → next node clockwise; adding a node moves ~1/N of keys; virtual nodes balance load. 10. Hot key, e.g., a celebrity or viral item? Split the key with suffixes, cache with local L1, buffer writes and aggregate, or special-case it (hybrid fan-out). 11. Presigned URLs: why? Clients upload and download directly to object storage; app servers never carry the bytes; multipart allows resumable parallel chunks. 12. Kafka vs SQS? Kafka: ordered partitions, replay, multiple consumer groups, stream processing. SQS: simple task queue with per-message retry, visibility timeout, DLQ. 13. How do you make an API retry-safe? Client-generated Idempotency-Key stored with a unique constraint; return the stored result on duplicates. 14. Replication lag bites how? Read-your-writes failures, non-monotonic reads, causally reordered reads. Fixes: read-from-leader after write, sticky replicas, partition by causal key. 15. Redis lock is enough for correctness? No. GC pauses or clock issues can leave two holders. Add a fencing token checked by the resource, or use DB conditional writes. 16. CAP in an interview? Per feature: during a partition choose to reject (CP) or serve stale (AP). Booking and payments CP; feeds and search AP. 17. p99 vs average? Users feel the tail; with fan-out, tail latency compounds. Set SLOs on p99; use timeouts and hedged requests. 18. LSM vs B-tree? LSM: sequential writes, compaction, great for write-heavy (Cassandra). B-tree: in-place pages, predictable reads, transactions (Postgres).

docs.title: Staff-level answers
docs.text:
Advanced

A senior answer produces a working design. A staff answer also says which number decided it, what trade-off it accepts, what will break before anyone asks, and how it will be run and changed. Interviewers for staff roles grade those four things more than the boxes on the whiteboard.

Tip

See all 29 at once: the interactive staff atlas has cards, a compact view and a full table, with filters. For printing, use the staff cheat sheet and the 29-problem staff table.

docs.title: The staff lens
docs.text: Move What it means Sounds like Frame Name the one tension the problem is really about. "This is really a fan-out problem: the cost moves between write time and read time." Quantify Find the number that forces the design and say it out loud. "115k feed reads a second, so computing feeds on read is off the table." Decide Pick one option and state the trade-off you accept. "Hybrid fan-out; I accept a merge step at read and feeds up to a minute stale." Anticipate Raise failure modes before the interviewer does. "The risk is a celebrity post creating a fan-out backlog, so…" Operate SLOs, the metrics you would watch, how you would roll it out. "I'd alert on fan-out lag and roll out the threshold change behind a flag." Evolve What changes at 10× and when you would make that change. "At 10× I'd split ranking into its own service; not before."

docs.title: Senior vs staff, in general
docs.text: Area Senior answer Staff answer Scope Designs what was asked. Clarifies the business goal, cuts scope deliberately, says what is out and why. Numbers Estimates QPS and storage. Uses one decisive number to rule options in or out. Trade-offs Lists pros and cons. Chooses, states what is given up, and when the choice would change. Failure Handles failures when asked. Raises failure modes, retries, idempotency and recovery unprompted. Consistency Picks a database. Chooses consistency per feature (CP checkout, AP browse) and explains the cost. Operations Mentions monitoring. Names SLOs, the metrics and alerts, rollout and rollback, on-call load. Cost Rarely mentioned. Estimates the expensive part (GPUs, storage, egress) and designs around it. Evolution Designs for the stated scale. Says what breaks at 10×, and keeps today's design simple on purpose. Conversation Follows the interviewer. Drives the agenda, checks in, and lets the interviewer steer the deep dives.

Accept rare skipped profiles from Bloom false positives. Distributed cache 1 TB ÷ ~32 GB per node ≈ 32+ nodes; each node ≫ 100k ops/s, so memory sets the count. Kafka partitioned by video; in-memory counts and local heaps; merge. Accept ~1 min freshness, with a batch recount for exact totals. Ad click aggregator 10k clicks/s at peak, 100M/day, ~10 GB/day raw. Kafka → Flink (dedupe by signed impression ID) → OLAP store, plus a nightly batch recount. Accept running two paths to get money right. Web crawler ~23k pages/s; ~46 GB/s of bandwidth; ~20 PB raw. Separate fetch and parse stages with queues and raw pages in S3. Accept storage cost to make each stage independently retryable. Metrics monitoring (Datadog) 5M points/s; ~600 GB/day compressed. Kafka → time-series DB with compression and downsampling; alerts evaluated on the stream. Accept lower resolution for old data. Fitness tracking (Strava) 10M activities/day; ~1 TB/day of tracks. Inverted index built from the stream, sharded by term; like-based ranking updated in batches or at thresholds. Accept slightly stale like ranking. Price tracker (CamelCamelCamel) 500M products; ~6k pages/s to crawl each one daily. Crawl by priority (trackers, volatility) + validated crowd-sourced prices + event-driven alerts. Accept staler prices on the long tail. Ride sharing (Uber) 250k location writes/s; ~100 ride requests/s on average. Redis GEO for locations; offer to one driver at a time with a driver lock and conditional assignment; durable per-region queue. Accept slightly slower matching. Live comments (Facebook Live) 1M viewers × 1k comments/s ≈ 1B deliveries/s for one stream. SSE + pub/sub per video, viewers of a video routed to the same servers; sample comments on mega-streams. Accept that not every viewer sees every comment. Collaborative editor (Google Docs) ~500 ops/s on a hot document; correctness, not scale. One owner server per document running OT, with an op log and snapshots. Accept a short pause when the owner fails over. Stock trading (Robinhood) Thousands of updates/s across ~10k symbols; 20M users, so push not poll. Persist the order as pending before calling the exchange, reconcile on timeout; throttle prices per symbol. Accept coarser price updates in the app. Online auction ~1k bids/s on one auction in its final seconds. Conditional update on the auction row; a Kafka partition per auction for the hottest ones. Accept serialized throughput per auction. LLM chat (ChatGPT) ~12k generations/s, each holding a GPU for seconds. Priority queue with admission control in front of the GPU pool, streamed tokens. Accept 429s or waiting for the free tier. Chat app (WhatsApp) ~600k messages/s; hundreds of millions of open connections. WebSockets + user→server registry + per-user pub/sub; persist before ack; an inbox per device. Accept at-least-once delivery with client dedupe. Ticketmaster ~100k seats vs 10M users: bookings are capped, reads are not. Conditional-update holds; virtual waiting room; browse is AP, booking is CP. Accept fans waiting in a queue. Payment system (Stripe) ~10k TPS: moderate. Correctness is the problem. Pending record first, idempotency keys, outbox, double-entry ledger, daily reconciliation. Accept extra writes for auditability. Online judge (LeetCode) ~100 submissions/s at peak; ~500 sandboxes running at once. Queue + microVM sandboxes + autoscaling workers. Accept a few seconds of latency. Job scheduler 864M executions/day. Time-bucketed store + poller + delay queue + leases. Accept at-least-once execution, so jobs must be idempotent. Video platform (YouTube) ~1 PB/day raw uploads. Presigned multipart uploads, a segment-parallel transcoding DAG, CDN delivery. Accept encoding long-tail formats lazily. File storage and sync (Dropbox) A 50 GB file is ~10k chunks; a 1-byte edit changes one chunk. Content-defined chunking with dedupe, a change log with cursors. Accept "conflicted copy" files for offline edits. Photo sharing (Instagram) ~115k feed reads/s; ~200 TB/day of media. Presigned uploads, async processing, CDN; hybrid fan-out. Accept a post appearing only after processing.

docs.title: URL shortener (Bitly)
docs.text:
Serve redirects fast at 100:1 read-heavy, and make codes unique without coordination.

  • Deciding number: ~100k redirects/s peak vs ~12 writes/s; 1B links × 500 B ≈ 500 GB, one Postgres.
  • Staff call: Cache-aside Redis plus replicas; counter + base62 with servers leasing ID ranges. Accept guessable codes, or add a reversible shuffle.
  • Raise before you're asked: A viral link expiring from cache (stampede); losing the counter node (leased ranges make gaps harmless); phishing links.
  • Senior stops at: Cache in front of the DB. Staff goes on to: Treats 301 vs 302 as a product decision (analytics vs load), adds abuse scanning, serves redirects from the edge for global latency.
  • Run it: SLO: p99 redirect < 100 ms. Watch hit ratio and DB miss QPS. Next step at 10×: edge key-value store at the CDN.

docs.title: Rate limiter
docs.text:
Count requests atomically across many gateways while adding under 10 ms.

  • Deciding number: 1M checks/s ≈ 10–20 Redis shards; ~1 GB of bucket state.
  • Staff call: Token bucket in a Redis Lua script. Accept approximate limits for very hot tenants (local allowances synced periodically).
  • Raise before you're asked: Redis outage: fail-open or fail-closed, decided per endpoint; clock skew in refill (use Redis time); one tenant overloading a shard.
  • Senior stops at: Algorithm + Redis. Staff goes on to: Plan tiers, global vs regional limits, rules as versioned config with shadow mode, and protecting the limiter itself.
  • Run it: Watch rejection rate per rule, limiter p99, Redis CPU. Roll out new rules in shadow (log-only) first.

docs.title: Business discovery (Yelp)
docs.text:
2-D "near me" search and correct ratings, without over-engineering.

  • Deciding number: 10M businesses × 1 KB ≈ 10 GB; ~20k searches/s at peak.
  • Staff call: One Postgres + PostGIS + replicas + page cache. Accept simpler ranking for far less to operate; add Elasticsearch only when relevance needs it.
  • Raise before you're asked: Replica lag hiding a new review; hot cities skewing load; review spam.
  • Senior stops at: Adds a geo index. Staff goes on to: Uses the 10 GB number to argue against a search cluster, and defines the trigger and CDC migration path for adding one later.
  • Run it: Watch search p99, replica lag, cache hit. Trigger for Elasticsearch: fuzzy relevance or QPS beyond replicas.

docs.title: News feed (Facebook)
docs.text:
Fan-out cost at write time vs latency at read time.

  • Deciding number: 115k feed reads/s; ~1.2M feed inserts/s with fan-out on write; celebrities with 100M followers.
  • Staff call: Hybrid: push to followers below a threshold (~100k), pull celebrity posts at read. Accept a merge step at read and feeds up to a minute stale.
  • Raise before you're asked: Fan-out backlog after a celebrity post; Redis memory (only active users, capped lists); deletes and unfollows propagating.
  • Senior stops at: Fan-out on write. Staff goes on to: Picks the threshold from numbers, rebuilds feeds for inactive users on demand, separates ranking into its own service, counts memory cost.
  • Run it: Watch feed p99, fan-out lag, worker queue depth, Redis memory. Next: candidate generation + ranking model.

docs.title: News aggregator (Google News)
docs.text:
The feed is the same for everyone in a region, so the edge can serve it.

  • Deciding number: ~12k reads/s, 50k+/s on breaking news; ~1 new article/s.
  • Staff call: Precompute per region and category, cache at the CDN for ~60 s. Accept a minute of staleness.
  • Raise before you're asked: Many CDN entries expiring at once (serve stale, stagger TTLs); publisher outages; duplicate stories.
  • Senior stops at: Adds a cache. Staff goes on to: Spots that the response is not personalised, calculates origin load after the CDN, sets an adaptive crawl budget.
  • Run it: Watch CDN hit ratio, origin QPS, ingest-to-visible lag.

docs.title: Local delivery (Gopuff)
docs.text:
Huge browse traffic on availability; strict stock at checkout.

  • Deciding number: ~10k browse/s at peak vs ~12 orders/s; the 10k-row warehouse list fits in memory.
  • Staff call: Browse is AP (cache + replicas); checkout is CP (conditional decrements in one transaction). Accept occasional "sold out at checkout".
  • Raise before you're asked: Flash-sale hot rows; cache showing stock that is gone; travel-time API outage (fall back to distance).
  • Senior stops at: A transaction on order. Staff goes on to: States consistency per path, partitions stock by region so no transaction crosses shards, plans for the third-party API failing.
  • Run it: Watch checkout failures due to stock, availability p99, external API spend.

docs.title: Dating app (Tinder)
docs.text:
Write-heavy swipes, and a mutual match must never be missed.

  • Deciding number: ~100k swipes/s at peak; precomputed stacks ≈ 32 GB.
  • Staff call: Precomputed stacks + Bloom filter of swiped profiles; one atomic operation per pair of users for matches. Accept rare skipped profiles from Bloom false positives.
  • Raise before you're asked: Two right-swipes at the same instant (write skew); stacks stale after the user moves; bots.
  • Senior stops at: Stores swipes. Staff goes on to: Names the race precisely, uses a pair-keyed atomic op, sizes precomputation, weighs recommendation quality against cost.
  • Run it: Watch match detection latency, stack freshness, swipe write lag.

docs.title: Distributed cache
docs.text:
Build the cache itself: eviction, distribution, failover.

  • Deciding number: 1 TB ÷ ~32 GB per node ≈ 32+ nodes; each node ≫ 100k ops/s, so memory sets the count.
  • Staff call: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes, async replica per primary. Accept losing a few writes on failover.
  • Raise before you're asked: Hot key overloading one node; scale-out causing cold misses and a DB stampede; split brain on promotion.
  • Senior stops at: LRU + consistent hashing. Staff goes on to: Membership via a config service, gradual warm-up on scale-out, client routing vs proxy trade-off.
  • Run it: Watch hit ratio, evictions, per-node p99 and memory, rebalance traffic.

docs.title: Top-K videos (YouTube)
docs.text:
Count ~800k events/s and rank across hour, day, month and all time.

  • Deciding number: 70B views/day ≈ 800k/s; 4B videos × 8 B ≈ 32 GB of counters.
  • Staff call: Kafka partitioned by video; in-memory counts and local heaps; merge. Accept ~1 min freshness, with a batch recount for exact totals.
  • Raise before you're asked: One viral video skewing a partition (pre-aggregate at producers); counts lost on restart (checkpoint); late events.
  • Senior stops at: Streaming counts. Staff goes on to: Proves the merge is exact, chooses exact vs Count-Min per window, adds a reconciliation path.
  • Run it: Watch consumer lag, window freshness, stream vs batch difference.

docs.title: Ad click aggregator
docs.text:
Counts that are fast for dashboards and exact for billing.

  • Deciding number: 10k clicks/s at peak, 100M/day, ~10 GB/day raw.
  • Staff call: Kafka → Flink (dedupe by signed impression ID) → OLAP store, plus a nightly batch recount. Accept running two paths to get money right.
  • Raise before you're asked: Click fraud; double counting on replay (idempotent upserts); events arriving after the window closed.
  • Senior stops at: Stream aggregation. Staff goes on to: Adds batch reconciliation because it is money, signed impression IDs, and an audit trail for advertiser disputes.
  • Run it: Watch stream vs batch difference, consumer lag, dedupe rate.

docs.title: Web crawler
docs.text:
A politeness-limited pipeline that must finish 10B pages in 5 days.

  • Deciding number: ~23k pages/s; ~46 GB/s of bandwidth; ~20 PB raw.
  • Staff call: Separate fetch and parse stages with queues and raw pages in S3. Accept storage cost to make each stage independently retryable.
  • Raise before you're asked: Crawler traps; breaking per-domain rate limits; DNS as a bottleneck; duplicate content.
  • Senior stops at: Queue + workers. Staff goes on to: Sizes the fleet by bandwidth not CPU, prices the storage, prioritises the frontier, treats robots.txt as a hard rule.
  • Run it: Watch pages/s, per-domain errors, frontier size, dedupe ratio.

docs.title: Metrics monitoring (Datadog)
docs.text:
A write firehose plus alerts within a minute.

  • Deciding number: 5M points/s; ~600 GB/day compressed.
  • Staff call: Kafka → time-series DB with compression and downsampling; alerts evaluated on the stream. Accept lower resolution for old data.
  • Raise before you're asked: Cardinality explosion from user-ID tags; who monitors the monitoring; alert storms.
  • Senior stops at: A TSDB. Staff goes on to: Cardinality limits as policy, alert path separate from query path, retention tiers priced out.
  • Run it: Watch ingest lag, dropped points, alert evaluation latency, active series count.

docs.title: Fitness tracking (Strava)
docs.text:
Do the work on the phone; make uploads reliable.

  • Deciding number: 10M activities/day; ~1 TB/day of tracks.
  • Staff call: Record on device; idempotent, resumable upload; process asynchronously. Accept no live server view by default.
  • Raise before you're asked: Duplicate uploads; device clock and timezone errors; leaking home locations (privacy zones).
  • Senior stops at: Upload then process. Staff goes on to: Rejects streaming every GPS point with numbers, adds privacy zones, considers leaderboard cheating.
  • Run it: Watch upload success, processing lag, leaderboard freshness.

docs.title: Post search (Facebook)
docs.text:
Index a firehose whose ranking signals change constantly.

  • Deciding number: ~12k posts/s and ~10× that in likes.
  • Staff call: Inverted index built from the stream, sharded by term; like-based ranking updated in batches or at thresholds. Accept slightly stale like ranking.
  • Raise before you're asked: Hot terms overloading one shard; privacy (who may see a post) enforced at query time; reindexing.
  • Senior stops at: "use Elasticsearch". Staff goes on to: Explains the inverted index, term vs document partitioning, and privacy-aware retrieval.
  • Run it: Watch index lag, query p99, shard skew.

docs.title: Price tracker (CamelCamelCamel)
docs.text:
Too many products to crawl often, so spend the crawl budget where it matters.

  • Deciding number: 500M products; ~6k pages/s to crawl each one daily.
  • Staff call: Crawl by priority (trackers, volatility) + validated crowd-sourced prices + event-driven alerts. Accept staler prices on the long tail.
  • Raise before you're asked: Being blocked by the site; poisoned extension data; alert spam.
  • Senior stops at: A cron crawl and a scan of subscriptions. Staff goes on to: Prioritises by value, validates crowd data, reacts to price events instead of scanning.
  • Run it: Watch freshness of tracked products, alert latency, crawl budget used.

docs.title: Ride sharing (Uber)
docs.text:
A flood of location updates and exclusive driver assignment.

  • Deciding number: 250k location writes/s; ~100 ride requests/s on average.
  • Staff call: Redis GEO for locations; offer to one driver at a time with a driver lock and conditional assignment; durable per-region queue. Accept slightly slower matching.
  • Raise before you're asked: A driver assigned twice; matcher crashing mid-match; city hot spots and surge.
  • Senior stops at: Geo index + matching. Staff goes on to: Cells per city to isolate failures, surge as a feedback loop, regional failover.
  • Run it: Watch time-to-match p95, offer acceptance, location update lag.

docs.title: Live comments (Facebook Live)
docs.text:
Fan-out to a million viewers in under 200 ms.

  • Deciding number: 1M viewers × 1k comments/s ≈ 1B deliveries/s for one stream.
  • Staff call: SSE + pub/sub per video, viewers of a video routed to the same servers; sample comments on mega-streams. Accept that not every viewer sees every comment.
  • Raise before you're asked: Reconnection storms after a deploy; slow consumers; moderation.
  • Senior stops at: WebSocket + pub/sub. Staff goes on to: Points out nobody can read 1k comments/s and samples, plans for reconnect storms, sizes connections per server.
  • Run it: Watch delivery p99, connections per server, dropped messages.

docs.title: Collaborative editor (Google Docs)
docs.text:
Every client must converge to the same document.

  • Deciding number: ~500 ops/s on a hot document; correctness, not scale.
  • Staff call: One owner server per document running OT, with an op log and snapshots. Accept a short pause when the owner fails over.
  • Raise before you're asked: Owner failover; merging offline edits; very large documents.
  • Senior stops at: Names OT or CRDT. Staff goes on to: Chooses between them from requirements (offline, server cost), assigns ownership via a coordination service, plans version history.
  • Run it: Watch op latency, convergence errors, snapshot size.

docs.title: Stock trading (Robinhood)
docs.text:
Push prices to millions, and never lose or duplicate an order.

  • Deciding number: Thousands of updates/s across ~10k symbols; 20M users, so push not poll.
  • Staff call: Persist the order as pending before calling the exchange, reconcile on timeout; throttle prices per symbol. Accept coarser price updates in the app.
  • Raise before you're asked: Unknown outcome on exchange timeout; duplicate orders; market-open spike.
  • Senior stops at: Separate price and order paths. Staff goes on to: An order state machine, reconciliation against exchange reports, audit requirements, graceful degradation at open.
  • Run it: Watch order ack latency, reconciliation breaks, price fan-out lag.

docs.title: Online auction
docs.text:
One hot row, and bids must be strictly ordered.

  • Deciding number: ~1k bids/s on one auction in its final seconds.
  • Staff call: Conditional update on the auction row; a Kafka partition per auction for the hottest ones. Accept serialized throughput per auction.
  • Raise before you're asked: Deadline fairness (use server time); sniping; durability of an accepted bid.
  • Senior stops at: A lock. Staff goes on to: Anti-sniping as a product decision, serializing through a log for extreme auctions, an audit trail.
  • Run it: Watch bid acceptance latency, rejected-bid rate, partition lag.

docs.title: LLM chat (ChatGPT)
docs.text:
GPUs are scarce; every queueing choice is a cost choice.

  • Deciding number: ~12k generations/s, each holding a GPU for seconds.
  • Staff call: Priority queue with admission control in front of the GPU pool, streamed tokens. Accept 429s or waiting for the free tier.
  • Raise before you're asked: Client disconnecting mid-stream; GPU pool failures; runaway cost.
  • Senior stops at: Streaming. Staff goes on to: Capacity planned in GPU-seconds, fairness and priority policy, batching for throughput, cost per request.
  • Run it: Watch time-to-first-token, queue wait, GPU utilisation, cost per 1k tokens.

docs.title: Chat app (WhatsApp)
docs.text:
Route between servers, deliver to offline devices, keep order.

  • Deciding number: ~600k messages/s; hundreds of millions of open connections.
  • Staff call: WebSockets + user→server registry + per-user pub/sub; persist before ack; an inbox per device. Accept at-least-once delivery with client dedupe.
  • Raise before you're asked: Server crash holding connections; order within a chat; multi-device sync; what end-to-end encryption rules out.
  • Senior stops at: WebSockets + a database. Staff goes on to: Delivery semantics, draining connections during deploys, the limits end-to-end encryption puts on server features.
  • Run it: Watch delivery latency, undelivered inbox size, reconnect rate.

docs.title: Ticketmaster
docs.text:
No seat sold twice while 10M people arrive at once.

  • Deciding number: ~100k seats vs 10M users: bookings are capped, reads are not.
  • Staff call: Conditional-update holds; virtual waiting room; browse is AP, booking is CP. Accept fans waiting in a queue.
  • Raise before you're asked: Payment timing out while the hold expires; bots; the read storm hitting the booking database.
  • Senior stops at: Row locking. Staff goes on to: The waiting room as load control, bot mitigation and fairness, shielding the booking path.
  • Run it: Watch hold success rate, queue length, admit rate, booking p99.

docs.title: Payment system (Stripe)
docs.text:
Stay correct when a call to the bank has an unknown outcome.

  • Deciding number: ~10k TPS: moderate. Correctness is the problem.
  • Staff call: Pending record first, idempotency keys, outbox, double-entry ledger, daily reconciliation. Accept extra writes for auditability.
  • Raise before you're asked: Processor timeouts; duplicate webhooks; partial refunds; PCI scope creep.
  • Senior stops at: Idempotency keys. Staff goes on to: Ledger design, reconciliation, isolating card data to shrink compliance scope.
  • Run it: Watch reconciliation breaks, age of pending payments, webhook delivery success.

docs.title: Online judge (LeetCode)
docs.text:
Run untrusted code safely, through contest spikes.

  • Deciding number: ~100 submissions/s at peak; ~500 sandboxes running at once.
  • Staff call: Queue + microVM sandboxes + autoscaling workers. Accept a few seconds of latency.
  • Raise before you're asked: Sandbox escape; noisy neighbours; contest start spike (pre-warm capacity).
  • Senior stops at: Queue + containers. Staff goes on to: Defence in depth for isolation, pre-warming before contests, fairness between users.
  • Run it: Watch queue wait, sandbox start time, verdict latency.

docs.title: Job scheduler
docs.text:
10k jobs/s, each within 2 s of its time, never lost.

  • Deciding number: 864M executions/day.
  • Staff call: Time-bucketed store + poller + delay queue + leases. Accept at-least-once execution, so jobs must be idempotent.
  • Raise before you're asked: Poller leader failing; clock drift; duplicate execution; every cron job firing at :00.
  • Senior stops at: A jobs table and a queue. Staff goes on to: Reasons through the two-tier design, leader election with fencing, isolation between tenants.
  • Run it: Watch schedule-to-start lag p99, missed jobs, retries.

docs.title: Video platform (YouTube)
docs.text:
Reliable huge uploads and smooth playback anywhere.

  • Deciding number: ~1 PB/day raw uploads.
  • Staff call: Presigned multipart uploads, a segment-parallel transcoding DAG, CDN delivery. Accept encoding long-tail formats lazily.
  • Raise before you're asked: Transcode failures and retries; storage cost; popularity spikes.
  • Senior stops at: S3 + CDN. Staff goes on to: A cost model (storage tiers, lazy encoding), DAG retries, CDN strategy.
  • Run it: Watch upload success, time to playable, CDN hit ratio, rebuffer rate.

docs.title: File storage and sync (Dropbox)
docs.text:
Sync efficiently and handle conflicting edits.

  • Deciding number: A 50 GB file is ~10k chunks; a 1-byte edit changes one chunk.
  • Staff call: Content-defined chunking with dedupe, a change log with cursors. Accept "conflicted copy" files for offline edits.
  • Raise before you're asked: Conflicts; partial uploads; cross-user dedupe leaking whether a file exists.
  • Senior stops at: Chunking. Staff goes on to: Conflict UX, the privacy risk of cross-user dedupe, change-log retention.
  • Run it: Watch sync latency, bytes uploaded per change, conflict rate.

docs.title: Photo sharing (Instagram)
docs.text:
A feed plus a media pipeline.

  • Deciding number: ~115k feed reads/s; ~200 TB/day of media.
  • Staff call: Presigned uploads, async processing, CDN; hybrid fan-out. Accept a post appearing only after processing.
  • Raise before you're asked: Processing backlog; celebrity fan-out; storage cost.
  • Senior stops at: Feed + S3. Staff goes on to: Storage tiering and cost, processing SLOs, regional reads.
  • Run it: Watch time to visible, feed p99, CDN hit ratio.

docs.title: 29 problems
docs.text:
Every page follows the same template: requirements, numbers, a v1 design and where it breaks, the final design and why each part exists, deep dives, a minute-by-minute interview script, and common mistakes.

Interviewing for staff? Each page has a Staff-level lens section, and all 29 are collected in Staff-level answers.

New to this? Start with URL shortener, Rate limiter and Ticketmaster.

docs.title: Scaling reads
docs.text:
Pattern: Scaling reads

Problem Difficulty What makes it interesting URL shortener (Bitly) Easy It sounds like a toy, but it is the cleanest example of a read-heavy system: almost every request is a redirect. Rate limiter Medium Every public API needs one, and the obvious implementation has a race condition. Business discovery (Yelp) Medium The trap is over-engineering: the whole dataset fits on one database server. News feed (Facebook) Medium The canonical fan-out problem: build a personalised feed for billions of users in a few hundred milliseconds. News aggregator (Google News) Easy A feed problem where the feed is the same for everyone in a region, which changes everything. Local delivery (Gopuff) Easy It looks like an ordering system, but most of the load is people checking what is available near them. Dating app (Tinder) Medium Swipes are a firehose of writes, and two people swiping right at the same moment must never miss their match. Distributed cache Medium Design Redis itself: data structures inside one node, then distribution across many.

docs.title: Scaling writes
docs.text:
Pattern: Scaling writes

Problem Difficulty What makes it interesting Top-K videos (YouTube) Hard The design falls straight out of one number: hundreds of thousands of views per second. Ad click aggregator Hard Clicks are money, so the numbers must be fast for dashboards and exact for billing. Web crawler Hard Ten billion pages in five days is a pipeline problem, constrained by politeness and network bandwidth. Metrics monitoring (Datadog) Hard Millions of data points per second arrive, and alerts must fire within a minute. Fitness tracking (Strava) Medium The key insight is where the work happens: on the phone, not the server. Post search (Facebook) Medium Search over billions of posts, where like counts change constantly. Price tracker (CamelCamelCamel) Medium Five hundred million products can't all be crawled often, so decide what is worth checking.

docs.title: Real-time updates
docs.text:
Pattern: Real-time updates

Problem Difficulty What makes it interesting Ride sharing (Uber) Hard Four problems in one: a flood of location updates, matching, locking drivers, and a multi-step trip lifecycle. Live comments (Facebook Live) Medium One popular stream can mean a million viewers each expecting new comments within a fraction of a second. Collaborative editor (Google Docs) Hard The challenge is correctness, not scale: everyone must end up with the same document. Stock trading (Robinhood) Hard Two separate problems: pushing live prices to millions, and never losing or duplicating an order. Online auction Medium Many people bid on one row at the same time, and exactly one of them must win each race. LLM chat (ChatGPT) Hard GPUs are the scarce resource, so every queueing decision is really a cost decision. Chat app (WhatsApp) Medium Chat looks like CRUD until you notice the two users are on different servers and one of them is offline.

docs.title: Dealing with contention
docs.text:
Pattern: Dealing with contention

Problem Difficulty What makes it interesting Ticketmaster Hard Millions of people arrive for one on-sale, and no seat may ever be sold twice.

docs.title: Multi-step processes
docs.text:
Pattern: Multi-step processes

Problem Difficulty What makes it interesting Payment system (Stripe) Hard Throughput is moderate. The hard part is staying correct when a call to the bank has an unknown outcome. Online judge (LeetCode) Medium You are running strangers' code on your servers, so isolation comes first. Job scheduler Hard Ten thousand jobs per second, each within two seconds of its scheduled time.

docs.title: Handling large blobs
docs.text:
Pattern: Handling large blobs

Problem Difficulty What makes it interesting Video platform (YouTube) Hard Two hard problems: getting gigabyte uploads in reliably, and streaming smoothly on any connection. File storage and sync (Dropbox) Easy Syncing a 50 GB file after a one-byte edit should not mean uploading 50 GB again. Photo sharing (Instagram) Medium A news feed plus a media pipeline: two well-known problems combined.

docs.title: Ad click aggregator
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Scaling writes · DDIA: Ch 11 windows, exactly-once · Ch 12 Lambda · Ch 3 column stores

Clicks are money, so the numbers must be fast for dashboards and exact for billing.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: AD CLICK AGGREGATOR on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Redirect immediately and publish the click to Kafka; never aggregate raw rows at query time.
  • A stream processor counts clicks per ad per minute and writes them to a column store for fast queries.
  • Deduplicate by a signed impression ID, and recount from raw logs in a nightly batch job for billing accuracy.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Click on an ad redirects the user to the advertiser
  2. Advertisers query click metrics over time (minute granularity), with filters

Non-functional

  • 10k clicks/s peak, 100M/day
  • Never lose or double-count clicks (it is billing)
  • Metrics queries < 1s
  • Freshness ~1 minute

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 100M clicks × 100B ≈ 10GB/day raw. Aggregated rows: ads × minutes, which is small. A 10k/s peak is easy for Kafka.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
click(impression_id, ad_id, ts, user) → agg(ad_id, minute, count)

GET /click?ad_id&impression_id → 302 advertiser_url
GET /metrics?ad_id&from&to&granularity

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
When a user clicks an ad, the click service inserts a row (ad_id, ts, user) into Postgres and redirects the user to the advertiser. Advertisers' dashboards run SELECT ad_id, date_trunc('minute', ts), count(*) … GROUP BY … over the time range they ask for.

Where it breaks:

  • Queries: 100M clicks a day adds up to billions of rows within weeks. "Clicks per minute for my ads over the last 30 days" means scanning and grouping millions of rows on every dashboard load, nowhere near the 1-second target.
  • Contention: those heavy queries run on the same database that's absorbing up to 10k inserts a second, so each slows the other down.
  • Correctness: clicks are money, since advertisers pay per click. Double-clicks, retries and bots must not be counted twice or at all, and nothing can be lost.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: redirect immediately, aggregate in a stream
docs.text:
Why: the user should never wait for click accounting, and counting at query time is too slow. Counts should be precomputed as clicks arrive.

How: the click service publishes each click to Kafka (durable, handles 10k/s easily) and immediately returns the 302 redirect. A Flink job reads the stream and counts clicks per (ad_id, minute), using the click's event time so late-arriving clicks land in the right minute. Every minute it upserts the counts into an OLAP column store (such as ClickHouse or Druid). Dashboards now read a few thousand small pre-aggregated rows instead of scanning raw clicks.

docs.title: Step 2: deduplicate with a signed impression ID
docs.text:
Why: the same click can arrive more than once: a double-click, a browser retry, a replay after a Flink restart. Fraudsters may also forge clicks. Each duplicate or fake overcharges the advertiser.

How: when an ad is shown, the ad server generates a unique impression ID and signs it with a secret key, embedding it in the ad's click URL. The click service verifies the signature, which rejects forged clicks. Flink keeps the impression IDs it has seen (with an expiry) and counts each ID once, so repeats are ignored.

docs.title: Step 3: reconcile with a nightly batch job
docs.text:
Why: streaming systems are fast, but bugs, edge cases with very late events, or a misconfigured deploy can make counts drift. For billing, "probably right" isn't enough.

How: every raw click is also written to S3, partitioned by date and never modified. A nightly batch job recomputes exact counts from those raw files and corrects the aggregates. The streaming numbers serve live dashboards; the batch numbers are what invoices use. This is the Lambda pattern (DDIA Ch 12).

docs.title: Flink crashes?
docs.text:
Why it's a risk: Flink keeps its running counts in memory. A crash could lose counts, or, on restart, re-read clicks it already counted and count them again.

How: Flink checkpoints periodically, saving its state (counts and seen impression IDs) together with the Kafka offsets it had reached. After a crash it restores the last checkpoint and re-reads Kafka from those offsets, so nothing is lost. Some clicks are re-processed, so the sink must tolerate repeats. It upserts (ad_id, minute) → count, which overwrites the row with the correct total instead of adding to it. Replays become harmless.

docs.title: Hot ad (Super Bowl)?
docs.text:
Why it's a problem: partitioning by ad_id sends every click on one ad to one Flink task. A Super Bowl ad might get a huge share of all clicks within minutes, overloading that one task.

How: spread the hot ad across several partitions by keying on ad_id + random(0..N), so N tasks each count part of its clicks. Then add a second aggregation step that sums the N partial counts per (ad_id, minute). Only do this for ads you know are hot, because it adds a step.

docs.title: Why also batch?
docs.text:
Why have two paths? Streaming gives numbers within a minute but is complex, with late data, restarts and deduplication state, so small errors can creep in. Batch is slower but simple: it reads immutable raw data, computes once, and can be re-run any time.

How they work together: dashboards show the streaming numbers; billing uses the batch-corrected numbers. If the stream has a bug, fix it and re-run batch over the raw clicks. Nothing is lost, because the raw data was never modified.

docs.title: Why OLAP?
docs.text:
Why not Postgres for the aggregates? Advertisers slice the data many ways: by campaign, country or device, over days or months. Those queries scan and sum many rows.

How a column store helps: it stores each column separately and compresses it heavily, so a query reads only the columns it needs. Combined with pre-aggregated per-minute rows, queries over billions of underlying clicks return in under a second (see DDIA Ch 3 on column storage).

docs.title: 7. Interview script (45 minutes)
docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Click on an ad redirects the user to the advertiser; Advertisers query click metrics over time (minute granularity), with filters 5–8 Non-functional requirements 10k clicks/s peak, 100M/day; Never lose or double-count clicks (it is billing); Metrics queries < 1s; Freshness ~1 minute 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 100M clicks × 100B ≈ 10GB/day raw. Aggregated rows: ads × minutes, which is small. A 10k/s peak is easy for Kafka. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Kafka → Flink → OLAP → Advertiser → S3 raw → Spark nightly. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Flink crashes? · Hot ad (Super Bowl)? · Why also batch? · Why OLAP? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.text:
Question Staff answer The real problem Counts that are fast for dashboards and exact for billing. Deciding number 10k clicks/s at peak, 100M/day, ~10 GB/day raw. Staff call and trade-off Kafka → Flink (dedupe by signed impression ID) → OLAP store, plus a nightly batch recount. Accept running two paths to get money right. Raise before you're asked Click fraud; double counting on replay (idempotent upserts); events arriving after the window closed. Senior stops at Stream aggregation. Staff goes on to Adds batch reconciliation because it is money, signed impression IDs, and an audit trail for advertiser disputes. Run it Watch stream vs batch difference, consumer lag, dedupe rate.

All 29 problems through this lens: Staff-level answers.

docs.title: 8. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Aggregating raw rows at query time in the OLTP database.
  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.
  • Skipping failure handling: what happens on timeouts, retries and crashes.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why redirect immediately and publish the click to Kafka?

The user shouldn't wait for counting; Kafka durably buffers the click stream for the stream processor.

How do you avoid counting the same click twice?

Deduplicate by a signed impression ID, so replays and retries of the same click are ignored.

Why also run a nightly batch job if the stream is already counting?

Billing needs exact numbers; the batch recount from raw logs corrects any stream errors (the Lambda-style reconciliation).

docs.title: Business discovery (Yelp)
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Scaling reads · DDIA: Ch 3 geo indexes · Ch 7 atomic updates · Ch 5 read replicas

The trap is over-engineering: the whole dataset fits on one database server.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: BUSINESS DISCOVERY (YELP) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Ten million businesses at ~1 KB each is about 10 GB, small enough for one Postgres instance.
  • Two-dimensional "near me" queries need a geospatial index (PostGIS, geohash), not two B-tree indexes.
  • Keep the average rating correct under concurrent reviews by updating it atomically in the same transaction.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Search businesses by location + radius, category, text
  2. View business details and reviews
  3. Leave one review per user per business; see average rating

Non-functional

  • Search p99 < 500ms
  • 100M DAU, read-heavy
  • Ratings can lag slightly (eventual)
  • Reviews durable

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 10M businesses × 1KB = 10GB, which fits in memory. Search: 100M × 5 / 86,400 ≈ 6k/s, ~20k/s peak. Reviews ~12/s.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
businesses(id, name, location, category, avg_rating, num_ratings)
reviews(id, business_id, user_id, rating, text, UNIQUE(user_id, business_id))

GET /businesses?lat&lng&radius&category&q&cursor
GET /businesses/{id}
POST /businesses/{id}/reviews {rating, text}

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Store businesses in Postgres with lat and lng columns, and answer "near me" with a bounding box:

SELECT * FROM businesses
WHERE lat BETWEEN :lat1 AND :lat2
  AND lng BETWEEN :lng1 AND :lng2
  AND category = :cat;

with a normal B-tree index on lat and another on lng.

Where it breaks: a B-tree index sorts by one value. The lat index finds every business in a horizontal strip of the world: all businesses at that latitude, across every longitude. The lng index finds a vertical strip. The database must take one huge strip and filter it, or intersect two huge strips. Either way it reads far more rows than the few hundred businesses actually nearby. At ~20k searches a second at peak, that's too slow for the 500 ms p99.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: use a geospatial index, and keep it in Postgres
docs.text:
Why: "nearby" is a two-dimensional question, and it needs an index that narrows both dimensions at once.

How: add PostGIS with a spatial (GiST, R-tree style) index on a location column, and query with ST_DWithin(location, :point, :radius). The index groups nearby points together, so the query reads only rows close to the user. For searching by name, add a trigram index (pg_trgm). The whole dataset is about 10 GB, which fits in one Postgres instance's memory, so there's no need yet for a separate search cluster to operate and keep in sync.

docs.title: Step 2: spread the read load
docs.text:
Why: about 20k searches a second at peak is a lot of geospatial queries for one database primary, which also has to handle writes.

How: send searches to read replicas, since search can be a few seconds stale, and cache the most-viewed business pages in Redis. The primary handles only writes: new reviews and business edits, about a dozen a second.

docs.title: Step 3: keep ratings and reviews correct
docs.text:
Why: two features have rules that concurrency can break: each user may review a business only once, and the average rating must count every review.

How: a unique constraint on (user_id, business_id) enforces one review per user. Store a running sum and count on the business row, and update them in the same transaction as the review insert, using an atomic SET sum = sum + :rating, count = count + 1. The average is sum / count at read time. See the deep dives below for why the alternatives fail.

docs.title: Which geo index?
docs.text:
Why it matters: each option has different strengths, and interviewers like to hear the trade-offs.

How they work:

  • Geohash: divide the world into a grid and give each cell a string. Each extra character divides the cell further, so nearby places share a prefix (9q8yy…). It works with an ordinary B-tree index on a string column. The catch: two places can be close but sit either side of a cell edge, so query the user's cell plus its 8 neighbours.
  • Quadtree: recursively split any square that holds too many businesses into four. Dense cities get small cells, empty deserts large ones, so each cell holds a similar number of businesses. It's usually kept in memory.
  • R-tree (PostGIS GiST): groups nearby points into nested bounding rectangles. This is the production default in databases; you get it by adding a spatial index.

docs.title: Average rating with concurrent reviews?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: the naive way is "read the current average and count, compute the new average, write it back". Two reviews at the same moment both read the same old values, and one of them is lost (a lost update, DDIA Ch 7).

How: store rating_sum and rating_count, not the average, and update them with an atomic statement in the same transaction as the review insert:

UPDATE businesses SET rating_sum = rating_sum + :r, rating_count = rating_count + 1
WHERE id = :business_id;

The database applies these one at a time to the row, so nothing is lost. The average is computed at read time.

docs.title: One review per user?
docs.text:
Why the obvious way fails: "check if this user already reviewed, and if not, insert" is a check-then-act race. Two quick double-clicks both see "no review yet", and both insert.

How: let the database enforce it with a unique constraint on (user_id, business_id). The second insert fails with a constraint violation, and the API returns "you've already reviewed this place" (or turns it into an edit).

docs.title: When would you add Elasticsearch?
docs.text:
Why not at the start: it's a second system to run and keep in sync, and Postgres with PostGIS and trigram indexes already handles 10 GB and these query types well.

When it becomes worth it: when search needs relevance ranking, typo tolerance, synonyms and facets ("open now, $$, 4+ stars") beyond what Postgres does well, or when query volume outgrows the replicas. Then feed it from Postgres using CDC, so it follows the database's change log. Never write to both from the application (the dual-write problem, see DDIA Ch 11).

docs.title: 7. Interview script (45 minutes)
docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Search businesses by location + radius, category, text; View business details and reviews; Leave one review per user per business; see average rating 5–8 Non-functional requirements Search p99 < 500ms; 100M DAU, read-heavy; Ratings can lag slightly (eventual); Reviews durable 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 10M businesses × 1KB = 10GB, which fits in memory. Search: 100M × 5 / 86,400 ≈ 6k/s, ~20k/s peak. Reviews ~12/s. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: PostGIS GiST + pg_trgm → Read replicas → Review service. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Which geo index? · Average rating with concurrent reviews? · One review per user? · When would you add Elasticsearch? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.title: Staff-level lens
docs.text:
Question Staff answer The real problem 2-D "near me" search and correct ratings, without over-engineering. Deciding number 10M businesses × 1 KB ≈ 10 GB; ~20k searches/s at peak. Staff call and trade-off One Postgres + PostGIS + replicas + page cache. Accept simpler ranking for far less to operate; add Elasticsearch only when relevance needs it. Raise before you're asked Replica lag hiding a new review; hot cities skewing load; review spam. Senior stops at Adds a geo index. Staff goes on to Uses the 10 GB number to argue against a search cluster, and defines the trigger and CDC migration path for adding one later. Run it Watch search p99, replica lag, cache hit. Trigger for Elasticsearch: fuzzy relevance or QPS beyond replicas.

All 29 problems through this lens: Staff-level answers.

docs.title: 8. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A geo-sharded cluster for 10GB of data. One Postgres with PostGIS plus replicas is enough.
  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.
  • Skipping failure handling: what happens on timeouts, retries and crashes.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why is one Postgres instance enough for the business data?

Ten million businesses at about 1 KB each is about 10 GB, which fits comfortably on one server with replicas for reads.

Why not two B-tree indexes on latitude and longitude?

Each index narrows only one dimension, so a "near me" query still scans a long strip. A geospatial index (PostGIS, geohash) narrows both at once.

How do you keep the average rating correct with concurrent reviews?

Update the stored sum and count atomically in the same transaction as the review insert, rather than reading, computing and writing back.

docs.title: Chat app (WhatsApp)
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Real-time updates · DDIA: Ch 5 consistent prefix · Ch 11 at-least-once + idempotency

Chat looks like CRUD until you notice the two users are on different servers and one of them is offline.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: CHAT APP (WHATSAPP) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Keep a persistent WebSocket per device; route messages between chat servers with a registry and per-user pub/sub.
  • Persist each message and add it to the recipient's inbox before acknowledging the sender, so nothing is lost.
  • Partition by conversation and number messages within it so every device shows the same order.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. 1:1 and group chats (up to ~100 members)
  2. Send and receive messages in real time
  3. Offline users get messages when they reconnect
  4. Delivery and read receipts; media

Non-functional

  • Delivery < 500ms when online
  • Messages never lost
  • Ordered within a chat
  • 1B DAU

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 50B messages/day ≈ ~600k msgs/s. Hundreds of millions of concurrent connections, at ~1M connections per tuned server → hundreds of chat servers.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
messages(chat_id, seq, msg_id, sender, body, ts) partitioned by chat_id
inbox(device_id, msg_id) until acked
chat_members

WS connect → send {chat_id, client_msg_id, body}; receive {msg, seq}; ack {msg_id}
POST /media → presigned upload URL

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Each user's app keeps a WebSocket connection open to a chat server, so messages can flow both ways instantly without polling. Alice sends a message over her connection; the server looks up Bob's connection and writes it there.

Where it breaks:

  • Many servers: with 1 billion daily users there are hundreds of millions of open connections, about 1M per well-tuned server, so hundreds of chat servers. Alice is almost always connected to a different server from Bob. The server receiving Alice's message doesn't hold Bob's connection.
  • Offline users and crashes: if Bob's phone is off, or a server crashes after receiving the message but before delivering it, the message is lost. "Messages never lost" is the core requirement.
  • Ordering: in a group, messages from different people pass through different servers and could appear in different orders on different phones.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: route messages between chat servers
docs.text:
Why: the sender's server and the recipient's server are usually different machines. We need a way to get a message from one to the other.

How: keep a connection registry (in Redis) of which server holds each user's device connections, and give every user a pub/sub channel. When Bob connects to server 2, server 2 subscribes to Bob's channel. When Alice sends a message, server 1 publishes it to Bob's channel, and server 2 receives it and delivers it down Bob's WebSocket. Server 1 doesn't need to know where Bob is.

docs.title: Step 2: persist before acknowledging, and deliver from an inbox
docs.text:
Why: a message must survive server crashes and the recipient being offline for days.

How: when a message arrives, first write it to the messages table (partitioned by chat_id) and add an entry to each recipient device's inbox. Only then acknowledge to Alice (one tick ✓). Delivery is attempted immediately. When Bob's device receives the message, it acknowledges, and the inbox entry is removed (two ticks ✓✓). If Bob is offline, the entry stays, a push notification is sent, and when his app reconnects it syncs everything waiting in its inbox.

docs.title: Step 3: order messages per chat
docs.text:
Why: everyone in a chat must see messages in the same order, and "the reply appears before the question" is confusing.

How: give each message a sequence number within its chat, assigned by a single writer for that chat (the owner of the chat_id partition). Clients display messages in sequence order and notice gaps (missing sequence 41 → ask to resync).

docs.title: Never lose a message?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: a message passes through several machines (sender's server, storage, recipient's server, recipient's device), and any of them can fail at any moment.

How: persist before acknowledging. The sender gets its tick only after the message is durably stored with an inbox entry for each recipient. Delivery from the inbox is at-least-once: it is retried until the device acknowledges, so a message might arrive twice after a reconnect. The client deduplicates by msg_id, which the sender's app generates once and reuses on retries, so duplicates never show.

docs.title: Ordering?
docs.text:
Why it's tricky: two group members send messages at nearly the same time through different servers. Without a single authority, each phone might order them differently. Timestamps from different machines can't be trusted to agree (DDIA Ch 8).

How: all messages for one chat go to the same partition (chat_id is the partition key), where one writer assigns increasing sequence numbers. That gives one agreed order per chat, which is all users need. There is no global order across chats, and none is needed. This is the "consistent prefix" guarantee from DDIA Ch 5.

docs.title: Groups?
docs.text:
Why they're different: one message must reach up to ~100 members, each possibly on several devices and different servers.

How: fan out at send time. Store the message once, then add an inbox entry for each member's devices and publish to each member's channel. With groups capped around 100 members, that's at most a few hundred small writes per message, which is cheap. For much larger "channels" (thousands of members), switch to fan-out on read: members fetch from the channel's message log instead of getting an inbox entry each.

docs.title: Media?
docs.text:
Why not send it through the chat servers: photos and videos are megabytes. Pushing them through WebSocket servers built for tiny text messages would tie up their bandwidth and memory.

How: the sender's app asks for a presigned URL and uploads the file directly to object storage (S3). The chat message then carries only the object key (plus a small thumbnail). Recipients download the file directly, ideally through a CDN, when they open it. For end-to-end encrypted chat, the file is encrypted on the device before upload, and the key travels inside the encrypted message.

docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements 1:1 and group chats (up to ~100 members); Send and receive messages in real time; Offline users get messages when they reconnect; Delivery and read receipts; media 5–8 Non-functional requirements Delivery < 500ms when online; Messages never lost; Ordered within a chat; 1B DAU 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 50B messages/day ≈ ~600k msgs/s. Hundreds of millions of concurrent connections, at ~1M connections per tuned server → hundreds of chat servers. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Chat server 2 → Redis → Pub/sub → Cassandra → Inbox → APNs / FCM. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Never lose a message? · Ordering? · Groups? · Media? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.text:

  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

When do you acknowledge a message to the sender?

Only after it is persisted and added to the recipient's inbox, so nothing is lost if a server crashes.

How do chat servers route a message to the recipient's connection?

A registry of which server holds each user's connection, plus per-user pub/sub between chat servers.

How do all devices show the same message order?

docs.title: Collaborative editor (Google Docs)
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Real-time updates · DDIA: Ch 5 conflict resolution · Ch 9 total order · Ch 11 event log

The challenge is correctness, not scale: everyone must end up with the same document.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: COLLABORATIVE EDITOR (GOOGLE DOCS) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Send small operations, not whole documents; last-write-wins on documents loses people's work.
  • One server per document orders operations and transforms concurrent ones (OT); CRDTs are the serverless alternative.
  • Append every operation to a log before acknowledging it, and snapshot periodically for fast loading.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Create and open documents
  2. Many users edit concurrently and see each other's changes live
  3. See collaborators' cursors and presence

Non-functional

  • Remote edits visible < 100ms
  • All replicas converge to the same document
  • No lost edits (durable)
  • ~100 concurrent editors per doc; millions of docs

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: Each keystroke is an op (~100B). 100 editors × 5 ops/s = 500 ops/s per hot doc, which one server handles easily. The challenge is correctness, not scale.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
doc_ops(doc_id, version, op) append-only
doc_snapshots(doc_id, version, content)

WS /docs/{id}: send op {type, pos, char, base_version}; receive transformed ops
GET /docs/{id} (snapshot + version)

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Each user edits a local copy of the document, and the app saves the whole document to the server every few seconds. Other users periodically reload it.

Where it breaks: Alice and Bob both open the doc. Alice fixes a typo in paragraph 1; Bob adds a sentence to paragraph 5. Both save. The server keeps whichever save arrives last, so the other person's work disappears without warning (last write wins). With 100 people editing, almost everyone's changes get overwritten. And edits only appear after the next save and reload, nowhere near the 100 ms target for seeing others type.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: send operations, ordered and transformed by one server
docs.text:
Why: whole-document saves can't be merged. Small operations can, but concurrent operations interfere. If Alice inserts 3 characters at position 2 while Bob deletes the character at position 10, by the time Bob's delete arrives, the character he meant is now at position 13. Applying "delete at 10" blindly deletes the wrong character.

How: each keystroke becomes an operation like insert("x", pos 5), tagged with the document version it was based on, sent over a WebSocket. One server per document receives all operations, puts them in a single order, and transforms each one against any operations it hadn't seen. Bob's "delete at 10, based on version 41" is adjusted to "delete at 13", because Alice's insert (version 42) shifted the text. This is Operational Transformation (OT). The server broadcasts the transformed operation to everyone, and all copies end up identical.

docs.title: Step 2: make every operation durable before acknowledging it
docs.text:
Why: an acknowledged edit must never be lost, even if the server crashes. And loading a document by replaying millions of operations from the start would be slow.

How: append each operation to an op log (doc_ops(doc_id, version, op)) before acknowledging and broadcasting it. Periodically save a snapshot of the full document at a version. To open a document, load the latest snapshot and apply only the operations after it.

docs.title: Step 3: route every editor of a document to the same server
docs.text:
Why: OT needs one place deciding the order for each document. If two servers both accepted operations for the same doc, they'd order them differently and the copies would diverge.

How: route WebSocket connections by doc_id using consistent hashing, so all editors of a document reach the same server. Record which server owns which document in a coordination service (ZooKeeper or etcd), so after a server failure ownership moves cleanly to exactly one new server, which reloads the snapshot and op log.

docs.title: OT or CRDT?
docs.text:
Why there are two approaches: both solve "concurrent edits must converge", in different ways.

How they differ:

  • OT (Operational Transformation): a central server orders operations and transforms them against each other. Operations stay small and simple, but you need that coordinator per document. Google Docs works this way.
  • CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types): each character gets a unique, ordered identifier, so operations commute: they can be applied in any order and still converge. No central server is needed, which suits offline editing and peer-to-peer. The cost is extra metadata per character, and more complex data structures. Figma's multiplayer and libraries like Yjs and Automerge take this approach.

In an interview, OT with a server per document is the simpler story when there's always a server. Mention CRDTs for offline-first.

docs.title: Why one server per doc?
docs.text:
Why it's needed: OT's correctness depends on every operation being transformed against a single, agreed order of the operations before it. That's a total order, which requires one place making the decision (DDIA Ch 9).

Why it's fine: a hot document has ~100 editors doing a few operations a second each, about 500 operations a second, which one server handles easily. The many millions of documents are spread across many servers, so the system scales by documents, not by splitting one document.

docs.title: Offline edits?
docs.text:
Why it's tricky: a user edits on a plane for an hour. Meanwhile, others changed the same document hundreds of times.

How: the client buffers its operations locally, each tagged with the base version it last saw. On reconnect, it sends them. The server transforms them against every operation since that version, in order, then applies and broadcasts the results. The client also receives the missed operations and transforms its view similarly. Very long divergences may be shown as suggestions instead.

docs.title: Cursors?
docs.text:
Why they're different: showing where collaborators' cursors are, and who's present, is important for the experience but has no long-term value. Old cursor positions are worthless.

How: send cursor and presence updates over the same WebSocket, but treat them as ephemeral: broadcast to other editors, throttled to a few updates a second, and never written to the op log or database. If one is lost, the next update replaces it.

The challenge is correctness, not scale. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Document server → Op log → Snapshots → LB → ZooKeeper. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives OT or CRDT? · Why one server per doc? · Offline edits? · Cursors? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

Why send operations instead of whole documents?

Last-write-wins on whole documents loses concurrent edits; small operations can be merged.

Why one server per document?

When would you choose CRDTs over OT?

When you need offline or peer-to-peer editing without a central server ordering operations.

docs.title: Dating app (Tinder)
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Scaling reads · DDIA: Ch 7 write skew · Ch 3 Bloom filters, LSM

Swipes are a firehose of writes, and two people swiping right at the same moment must never miss their match.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DATING APP (TINDER) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Precompute each user's stack of nearby candidates and hide already-swiped profiles with a Bloom filter.
  • Swipes are write-heavy and append-only, a good fit for an LSM store like Cassandra.
  • Detect matches atomically on one key per pair of users, so simultaneous swipes can't both miss each other.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Profile with preferences (age, distance)
  2. Get a stack of nearby candidates
  3. Swipe left/right; get notified on a mutual match

Non-functional

  • Stack load p99 < 300ms
  • No missed matches (strong consistency on swipes)
  • Don't re-show swiped profiles
  • 20M DAU × 100 swipes

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 2B swipes/day ≈ 25k/s avg, ~100k/s peak, which is write-heavy. Stacks precomputed: 20M × 200 IDs × 8B ≈ 32GB.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
profiles
swipes(swiper_id, swipee_id, decision) partitioned by swiper
matches(a, b, ts)

GET /feed?lat&lng → [profiles]
POST /swipes {target_id, decision}
push: match notification

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Each time a user opens the app, query a search index such as Elasticsearch, which handles geo and filter queries well: "profiles within 30 km, aged 25–35, matching my preferences, that I haven't swiped on, sorted by some score". Swipes are inserted into a database, and after each right swipe the app checks whether the other person already swiped right on you.

Where it breaks:

  • Stack loads are slow and repetitive. Each open runs a heavy geo plus filter query, and must exclude everyone you've already swiped. For an active user that's thousands of IDs, making the query slower over time. Hard to keep under 300 ms at scale.
  • Swipes are a firehose. 20M users × 100 swipes is 2 billion a day: 25k a second on average, about 100k at peak. That's far more writes than a typical relational database primary handles.
  • Matches can be missed. Two people swiping right on each other at the same moment can both miss the match (see deep dive).

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: precompute stacks, and hide swiped profiles with a Bloom filter
docs.text:
Why: the candidate list for a user changes slowly, and it only needs to change when they move or new people join nearby. Rebuilding it on every app open wastes work and makes users wait.

How: a background job computes each active user's next ~200 candidates and stores the IDs in Redis (20M users × 200 IDs × 8 bytes ≈ 32 GB). Opening the app reads that list instantly, and a refill job tops it up as the user swipes through it. To avoid showing someone again, keep a Bloom filter per user of everyone they've swiped. It's a compact structure that answers "definitely not swiped" or "probably swiped", and candidates the filter flags are skipped. (Why a Bloom filter is fine here: see the deep dive.)

docs.title: Step 2: store swipes in a write-optimized database
docs.text:
Why: ~100k swipes a second at peak, and swipes are append-only: they're written once and rarely changed.

How: an LSM-tree store such as Cassandra, partitioned by swiper_id. It turns writes into sequential appends and spreads them across many nodes, so 100k writes a second is routine. Reading "who did I swipe" for one user is a single-partition read.

docs.title: Step 3: detect matches atomically
docs.text:
Why: the naive check, "save my right swipe, then look up whether they swiped right on me", has a race when both people swipe at the same moment (see the deep dive).

How: store each pair's decisions under one key, built from the two IDs in a fixed order: match:{min(a,b)}:{max(a,b)}. A Redis Lua script atomically records my decision and reads theirs. Because both swipes touch the same key and Redis runs one script at a time, exactly one of them sees "both said yes", creates the match and sends both notifications.

docs.title: Both swipe at once: why can a match be missed?
docs.text:
Why it happens: Alice and Bob swipe right on each other within the same millisecond. Alice's request saves "Alice → Bob: yes", then checks "has Bob said yes to Alice?". At that moment, Bob's save hasn't landed yet, so the answer is no. Meanwhile Bob's request saves his swipe and checks for Alice's, which also hasn't landed yet from his point of view. Both checks say no, and no match is created, even though both said yes. Each request read before the other's write was visible. That's write skew (DDIA Ch 7).

How: make "record my decision and read theirs" a single atomic operation on a single key for the pair. With a Lua script on match:{min}:{max} (or a conditional write in a database), the two operations are applied one after the other. The first sees only its own yes; the second sees both, and creates the match. Exactly one side wins, and no match is ever missed or created twice.

docs.title: Hide already-swiped profiles?
docs.text:
Why it's tricky: heavy users swipe on thousands of people. Storing and checking a full list on every candidate is memory- and time-hungry.

How: a Bloom filter per user: a fixed-size bit array where each swiped ID sets a few bits. Checking a candidate is a few bit lookups. It can give a false positive ("probably swiped" when they weren't), which means occasionally skipping a profile the user never saw. That's harmless. It never gives a false negative, so a swiped profile is never shown again. A few kilobytes per user cover thousands of swipes.

docs.title: Location changes?
docs.text:
Why it matters: the precomputed stack was built for where the user was. After a flight to another city, it's full of people hundreds of kilometres away.

How: when the app reports a location more than some distance (say 10–20 km) from where the stack was built, invalidate it and trigger a recompute. Serve a quick on-demand query for the first screen while the background job builds the new list.

docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Profile with preferences (age, distance); Get a stack of nearby candidates; Swipe left/right; get notified on a mutual match 5–8 Non-functional requirements Stack load p99 < 300ms; No missed matches (strong consistency on swipes); Don't re-show swiped profiles; 20M DAU × 100 swipes 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 2B swipes/day ≈ 25k/s avg, ~100k/s peak, which is write-heavy. Stacks precomputed: 20M × 200 IDs × 8B ≈ 32GB. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Redis → Swipe service → Cassandra → Redis Lua → Push (APNs/FCM). Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Both swipe at once: why can a match be missed? · Hide already-swiped profiles? · Location changes? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.text:
Question Staff answer The real problem Write-heavy swipes, and a mutual match must never be missed. Deciding number ~100k swipes/s at peak; precomputed stacks ≈ 32 GB. Staff call and trade-off Precomputed stacks + Bloom filter of swiped profiles; one atomic operation per pair of users for matches. Accept rare skipped profiles from Bloom false positives. Raise before you're asked Two right-swipes at the same instant (write skew); stacks stale after the user moves; bots. Senior stops at Stores swipes. Staff goes on to Names the race precisely, uses a pair-keyed atomic op, sizes precomputation, weighs recommendation quality against cost. Run it Watch match detection latency, stack freshness, swipe write lag.

All 29 problems through this lens: Staff-level answers.

docs.title: 8. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Separate "write swipe" and "check other swipe" calls without atomicity, so matches are lost.
  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.
  • Skipping failure handling: what happens on timeouts, retries and crashes.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

How do you avoid showing profiles a user already swiped?

Keep a Bloom filter of swiped IDs per user: compact, fast, and a rare false positive only hides one extra profile.

Why is Cassandra a good fit for swipes?

Swipes are write-heavy and append-only, which suits an LSM-tree store partitioned by user.

How can two simultaneous right-swipes miss the match, and how do you fix it?

Each checks for the other's swipe before either is saved. Store both directions on one key per pair and check-and-write atomically.
