docs.title: Distributed cache
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Scaling reads · Long-running tasks · DDIA: Ch 6 consistent hashing · Ch 5 async replication

Design Redis itself: data structures inside one node, then distribution across many.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: DISTRIBUTED CACHE on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• One node is a hash map plus a doubly linked list for O(1) least-recently-used eviction.
  • Spread keys with consistent hashing and virtual nodes, so adding a node moves only a small share of keys.
  • Replicate asynchronously for failover, and spread hot keys over several nodes.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. get(key), set(key, value, ttl), delete(key)
  2. LRU eviction when full

Non-functional

  • p99 ~1ms
  • ~1TB data, 100k+ ops/s
  • Survive node failure
  • Eventual consistency acceptable

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 1TB ÷ ~32GB usable per node ≈ 32+ nodes (+ replicas). Each node handles ≫ 100k ops/s, so memory, not CPU, sets the node count.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
per node: HashMap key → node in a doubly linked list (LRU order) + expiry

GET /cache/{key}
PUT /cache/{key} {value, ttl}
DELETE /cache/{key}

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Start with a cache on one machine. It needs two things: fast lookups, and a way to decide what to throw out when memory is full.

  • Lookup: a hash map from key to entry gives O(1) get and set.
  • Eviction (LRU): when memory is full, remove the least recently used entry, the one nobody has asked for in the longest time. To find it instantly, also keep all entries in a doubly linked list ordered by use. On every access, move that entry to the head. When space is needed, remove the entry at the tail. Each hash map value points straight to its list node, so both operations are O(1).
  • Expiry (TTL): check the expiry time when a key is read (lazy expiry), and run a background sweep that samples keys and deletes expired ones, so unread keys don't sit in memory forever.

Where it breaks: the requirement is about 1 TB of data. One machine has maybe 32–64 GB of usable memory. And if that one machine dies, the whole cache is gone at once, and every request falls through to the database. We need many nodes, and a way to know which node holds which key.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: shard keys across nodes with consistent hashing
docs.text:
Why: 1 TB ÷ about 32 GB per node is 32+ nodes. Every client must agree on which node owns a key, and adding or removing a node must not reshuffle everything.

How: place nodes on a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes, about 100–200 points per server, so load is even. A key belongs to the first node clockwise from its hash. The client library computes this itself and talks directly to the owning node, with no extra network hop through a router. Adding a node moves only about 1/N of keys (see Consistent hashing).

docs.title: Step 2: replicate each node for failover
docs.text:
Why: with 32 nodes, one failing is routine. Without copies, a node failure empties 1/32 of the cache instantly, and those requests all hit the database at once.

How: each primary node streams its writes asynchronously to a replica. If the primary dies, the replica is promoted and takes over its keys, still warm. Asynchronous replication means the last few writes may be lost in a failover. That's fine for a cache: a missing entry just causes a miss and a reload from the database.

docs.title: Step 3: track membership centrally, and protect hot keys
docs.text:
Why: clients need an up-to-date view of the ring as nodes join, leave or fail over. And one extremely popular key still lives on one node, however well the others are balanced.

How: keep the ring membership in a small coordination service such as etcd or ZooKeeper. Clients watch it and update their ring the moment it changes. For hot keys, see the deep dive below.

docs.title: LRU in O(1)?
docs.text:
Why it's asked: a naive LRU sorts entries by last access time, which is O(n log n), or scans for the oldest, which is O(n). That's far too slow for a cache answering in microseconds.

How: combine a hash map with a doubly linked list. The map gives O(1) lookup from key to list node. On get, unlink the node and move it to the head. Because the list is doubly linked, unlinking is O(1): you have pointers to both neighbours. On eviction, remove the tail node and delete its key from the map. Every operation touches a constant number of pointers.

docs.title: Add a node?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: a new node starts empty. Whatever keys move to it become misses until they're reloaded from the database.

How: consistent hashing limits the damage to about 1/N of keys, and virtual nodes spread that small share evenly across all existing nodes. To soften it further, warm the node gradually: give it a small weight on the ring at first, so it owns few keys, and raise the weight over a few minutes as its cache fills.

docs.title: Hot key?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: sharding spreads different keys. One key read 500k times a second, such as a homepage config or a celebrity profile, always lands on one node, which overloads while the others sit idle.

How: two common fixes.

  • Replicate the key under several names (profile:7#0 … profile:7#9). These hash to different nodes, and readers pick one at random, so the load is split 10 ways. Writes must update all the copies.
  • A local cache in each client (L1): keep the hottest keys in the application's own memory for a second or two. Most reads never leave the app server at all. The cost is a little staleness.

docs.title: Why not hash % N?
docs.text:
Why it fails: with node = hash(key) % N, changing N from 32 to 33 changes the answer for almost every key. Suddenly almost every lookup goes to the wrong node and misses.

What happens next: all those misses fall through to the database at the same moment, a cold-cache stampede that can take the database down exactly when you were trying to add capacity. Consistent hashing exists to prevent this.

docs.title: 7. Interview script (45 minutes)
docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements get(key), set(key, value, ttl), delete(key); LRU eviction when full 5–8 Non-functional requirements p99 ~1ms; ~1TB data, 100k+ ops/s; Survive node failure; Eventual consistency acceptable 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 1TB ÷ ~32GB usable per node ≈ 32+ nodes (+ replicas). Each node handles ≫ 100k ops/s, so memory, not CPU, sets the node count. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Cache node A → Cache node B → Cache node C → Replica A′ → Replica B′ → Replica C′ → Config / ZK. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives LRU in O(1)? · Add a node? · Hot key? · Why not hash % N? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.text:
Question Staff answer The real problem Build the cache itself: eviction, distribution, failover. Deciding number 1 TB ÷ ~32 GB per node ≈ 32+ nodes; each node ≫ 100k ops/s, so memory sets the count. Staff call and trade-off Consistent hashing with virtual nodes, async replica per primary. Accept losing a few writes on failover. Raise before you're asked Hot key overloading one node; scale-out causing cold misses and a DB stampede; split brain on promotion. Senior stops at LRU + consistent hashing. Staff goes on to Membership via a config service, gradual warm-up on scale-out, client routing vs proxy trade-off. Run it Watch hit ratio, evictions, per-node p99 and memory, rebalance traffic.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

How do you get O(1) LRU eviction?

A hash map for lookup plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency; move to front on access, evict from the tail.

Why consistent hashing instead of hash(key) % N?

With % N, adding a node remaps almost every key. Consistent hashing with virtual nodes moves only about 1/N of the keys.

How do you handle a hot key?

Replicate it to several nodes (or add suffixes to spread it) and read from any copy, or cache it locally in the clients.

docs.title: File storage and sync (Dropbox)
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Difficulty: Easy · Patterns: Handling large blobs · DDIA: Ch 5 conflicts · Ch 11 change log / cursor

Syncing a 50 GB file after a one-byte edit should not mean uploading 50 GB again.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: FILE STORAGE AND SYNC (DROPBOX) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Split files into chunks fingerprinted by hash, and upload only the chunks the server doesn't already have.
  • Upload and download directly to object storage with presigned URLs.
  • Other devices follow a per-user change log with a cursor and fetch only what changed.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Upload and download files (up to 50GB)
  2. Automatic sync across a user's devices
  3. Share files and folders

Non-functional

  • Resumable uploads
  • Changes visible on other devices within seconds
  • Durable (S3 11 nines)
  • Bandwidth-efficient sync

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: Large files chunked at ~5MB: a 50GB file = 10k chunks. Only changed chunks are re-uploaded, so a 1-byte edit sends 5MB, not 50GB.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
files(id, owner, path, version)
file_chunks(file_id, idx, sha256)
chunks(sha256, s3_key)
shares(file_id, user, perm)

POST /files {name, size, chunk_hashes[]} → missing chunks + presigned URLs
GET /changes?cursor → file metadata diffs
GET /files/{id} → chunk list + presigned download URLs

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
The client uploads each changed file whole through the API, which stores it. Other devices periodically ask "what changed?" and download changed files whole.

Where it breaks:

  • Large files: a 50 GB file uploading through your API takes hours. If the connection drops at 99%, it starts over.
  • Small edits: change one byte in a 50 GB file and the whole 50 GB is uploaded again, then downloaded again by every other device. Wasteful for users with limited bandwidth.
  • Slow sync: devices find out about changes only at their next check, not "within seconds".

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: split files into chunks, upload them directly to S3
docs.text:
Why: large uploads must be resumable and must not pass through the API servers.

How: the client splits each file into chunks of about 5 MB, so a 50 GB file is about 10,000 chunks. The API returns presigned URLs, and the client uploads chunks directly to S3, several in parallel. If the connection drops, only the unfinished chunks are retried. Metadata (file, version, list of chunks) lives in the database.

docs.title: Step 2: fingerprint chunks, and upload only what's missing
docs.text:
Why: after a small edit, most of the file is unchanged. Re-sending it wastes bandwidth. And many users store identical files.

How: the client computes a hash (SHA-256) of each chunk and sends the list of hashes first. The server replies with the hashes it doesn't already have, and only those chunks are uploaded. A small edit uploads just the one or two changed chunks. Identical chunks across files and users are stored once (deduplication).

One subtlety: with fixed 5 MB boundaries, inserting one byte near the start shifts every boundary after it, so every chunk looks new. Content-defined chunking places boundaries where the data matches a pattern (using a rolling hash), so an insert changes only the chunk around it and boundaries further on stay put.

docs.title: Step 3: sync other devices from a change log
docs.text:
Why: other devices must learn about changes within seconds, and download only what changed.

How: every change to a user's files appends an entry to a per-user change log. Each device keeps a cursor, its position in that log. A device holds a long-poll or WebSocket connection open so it's notified as soon as something new arrives, then calls GET /changes?cursor=… to get the metadata changes since its cursor. For each changed file, it compares chunk hashes with what it already has and downloads only the new chunks.

docs.title: Resume after failure?
docs.text:
Why it matters: uploads of big files over home or mobile connections fail regularly. Restarting from zero makes large files nearly impossible to sync.

How: chunking makes progress durable: every uploaded chunk is stored in S3 under its hash. When the client reconnects, it sends the file's chunk-hash list again. The server says which hashes it already has, and the client sends only the missing ones. A 50 GB upload interrupted at 99% resumes by sending the last 1%.

docs.title: How do devices learn about changes?
docs.text:
Why polling isn't great: frequent polling from millions of devices is wasteful; infrequent polling makes sync slow.

How: a change log with a cursor per device, plus a notification channel. The device keeps a long-poll request or WebSocket open to a notification service. When the user's log gets a new entry, the service wakes the device, which then fetches the changes since its cursor and advances it. If the device was offline for a week, it simply reads everything since its cursor when it returns, so nothing is missed.

docs.title: Edits on two offline devices?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: you edit report.docx on your laptop on a plane, and a colleague edits it on their computer. Both later sync, and both changes are based on the same old version. Neither can simply win without destroying the other's work. This is the multi-leader conflict from DDIA Ch 5.

How: each upload states the base version it was edited from. If the server's current version is newer than that base, there's a conflict. Instead of overwriting, save the second upload as a separate "conflicted copy" (report (Asha's conflicted copy).docx) and let the people involved merge them. It's simple, nothing is lost, and the user decides.

docs.title: Trust the client said "done"?
docs.text:
Why not: the client could crash after saying "upload complete", or be buggy, or be malicious, claiming chunks it never uploaded. Marking the file as committed would point other devices at data that doesn't exist.

How: verify with storage before committing the new version. Either react to S3 event notifications for each chunk, or check that every listed chunk exists and its ETag/checksum matches the expected hash. Only then mark the file version as committed and add it to the change log for other devices.

Only changed chunks are re-uploaded, so a 1-byte edit sends 5MB, not 50GB. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. docs.title: Fitness tracking (Strava)
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Scaling writes · DDIA: Ch 11 event time · Ch 12 idempotent upload

The key insight is where the work happens: on the phone, not the server.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: FITNESS TRACKING (STRAVA) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Record GPS on the device and upload the whole activity when it ends; no need to stream every point.
  • Store the track in object storage and the metadata in a database, with an idempotent, resumable upload.
  • Compute stats and leaderboards asynchronously from a queue; leaderboards are Redis sorted sets.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Start/pause/stop recording an activity (GPS track)
  2. View activity stats and maps
  3. Share with friends; see friends' activities; leaderboards

Non-functional

  • Works offline; never lose an activity
  • 10M DAU
  • Feed eventually consistent
  • Uploads resumable

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 10M activities/day; 1hr at 1 point/5s = 720 points ≈ 15–100KB per track → ~1TB/day of track blobs.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
activities(id, user_id, type, start, distance, duration, track_s3_key)
follows
leaderboard:{segment} ZSET

POST /activities (complete track, idempotency key)
GET /activities/{id}
GET /feed?cursor

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
While a user runs or rides, the app streams every GPS point to the server as it's recorded, and the server stores each point in a database. When the activity ends, the server computes distance, pace and the map from the stored points.

Where it breaks:

  • Load for nothing: with many users recording at once, every point is a write. Millions of devices sending a point every few seconds is hundreds of thousands to millions of writes a second, yet nobody looks at the activity until it's finished.
  • Lost activities: runners go through tunnels, hikers through valleys with no signal, and phones switch networks. Every gap in connectivity is a gap in the recorded route, and losing someone's marathon is the worst possible failure for this product.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: record on the device, upload when finished
docs.text:
Why: the activity is only needed after it ends, and the phone is the one thing guaranteed to be there for the whole activity, with or without a signal.

How: the app records GPS points locally: they're written to the phone's storage, so even a crash or a dead battery keeps what was recorded. When the user taps "finish", the app uploads the whole activity in one go. If there's no signal, it waits and retries later. The upload uses a client-generated activity ID as an idempotency key, so a retry after a lost response never creates a duplicate. Large tracks upload in resumable chunks, so a dropped connection resumes rather than restarting.

docs.title: Step 2: store the track as a file, the summary in a database
docs.text:
Why: a track is a blob, around 15–100 KB of points, adding up to about 1 TB a day, and it's read whole, when someone opens the activity. The summary fields (distance, duration, type) are what feeds and searches use.

How: store the track file in S3 (cheap, durable, served via CDN for map rendering), and a small row in Postgres: activities(id, user_id, type, start, distance, duration, track_s3_key).

docs.title: Step 3: process asynchronously, build leaderboards in Redis
docs.text:
Why: after upload there's real work to do: compute statistics, match the route against popular segments (a famous climb, a park loop), update leaderboards and feeds. Doing it inside the upload request would make the user wait and could fail the upload.

How: the upload returns as soon as the data is safely stored, then puts a job on a queue. Workers compute stats and segment matches. Segment leaderboards are Redis sorted sets, one per segment, with the effort time as the score, so "top 10" or "my rank" are single fast commands. Feeds of friends' activities update asynchronously; eventual consistency is fine.

docs.title: Why device-first?
docs.text:
Why not live streaming: signal is unreliable exactly where people exercise, so a server-first design loses data whenever coverage drops. It also generates enormous write load for data nobody reads until later.

How it works: the device is the source of truth during recording, and the server becomes the source of truth after upload. Live tracking, letting a family member follow your run, is an optional, best-effort extra: the app sends a point every 30 seconds or so when it can, and gaps are fine. The final recorded track always comes from the device upload.

docs.title: Upload reliability?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: mobile uploads fail mid-way, and responses get lost. The app doesn't know whether the server received the activity, so it must retry without creating duplicates.

How: the app creates the activity ID when recording starts and sends it as the idempotency key. The server's insert uses that ID, so a repeated upload finds the existing activity and returns success instead of creating a second one. The track uploads in chunks that can resume. The app keeps the local copy and keeps retrying until the server confirms, and only then may it delete local data.

docs.title: Leaderboards?
docs.text:
Why Redis: a leaderboard needs "insert a time", "top N" and "my rank" to be fast, for millions of segments.

How: one Redis sorted set per segment: ZADD segment:{id} <time_seconds> <user_id> (keeping only each user's best time). ZRANGE segment:{id} 0 9 gives the 10 fastest, and ZRANK gives a user's position, both in O(log n). Periodically snapshot the sets to the database, so they can be rebuilt if Redis is lost.

docs.title: Time correctness?
docs.text:
Why it matters: an activity recorded Saturday morning but uploaded Monday (no signal on the mountain) must show as Saturday's run, in the right order in feeds and weekly totals.

How: use the device's timestamps from recording (event time) for the activity's start and each point, not the server's upload time. Sanity-check them (the phone clock might be wrong; compare with GPS time if available), but never replace them with arrival time.

Then add, in order: Postgres → S3 → Queue → Stats / segment workers → Redis. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Why device-first? · Upload reliability? · Leaderboards? · Time correctness? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.text:

Why record GPS on the device and upload at the end?

Streaming every point is costly and fragile on poor connections; one upload per activity is simpler and works offline.

How do you make uploads reliable?

docs.title: Job scheduler
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Multi-step processes · Long-running tasks · DDIA: Ch 9 leader election · Ch 8 leases / fencing · Ch 6 time partitioning

Ten thousand jobs per second, each within two seconds of its scheduled time.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: JOB SCHEDULER on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Cron on one machine is a single point of failure that can't scale.
  • Store executions partitioned by time; a poller moves soon-due jobs into a delay queue that releases each on time.
  • Workers lease jobs with a visibility timeout, so crashed jobs are retried; jobs must be idempotent.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Schedule jobs: one-off at time T, or cron
  2. Execute jobs with a retry policy
  3. View job status and history

Non-functional

  • 10k job executions/s
  • Start within 2s of scheduled time
  • At-least-once; jobs idempotent
  • Never lose a job; billions of jobs stored

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 10k executions/s = 864M/day. A DB poll every second for "due now" across billions of rows will not hold, so use a two-layer design.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
jobs(id, user, schedule, payload)
executions(time_bucket, execution_id, job_id, scheduled_at, status, attempt) partitioned by time bucket

POST /jobs {schedule (cron | at), payload, retry_policy}
GET /jobs/{id}/executions

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Use cron on one server: each scheduled job is a line in the crontab, and the server runs it at the right time.

Where it breaks:

  • Single point of failure: if that server is down at 9:00, every 9:00 job silently doesn't run. If it's down for an hour, an hour of jobs are lost.
  • Scale: the requirement is 10k job executions a second (864 million a day) from billions of stored jobs. One machine can't run that many, and a crontab can't hold billions of entries.
  • No retries or history: if a job fails, nobody knows and nothing retries it, and users can't see what ran.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: store executions in a database, partitioned by time
docs.text:
Why: jobs must survive any server failure, and we need to quickly find "what's due soon" among billions of rows.

How: store each job's definition in jobs, and each upcoming run as a row in executions, partitioned by time bucket (say, one partition per hour). For recurring jobs, after a run completes, the next one is inserted. A poller periodically reads the current and next buckets to find executions due in the next few minutes. Partitioning by time means it reads only a tiny, relevant slice instead of scanning billions of rows.

docs.title: Step 2: add a delay queue for second-level precision
docs.text:
Why: jobs must start within 2 seconds of their scheduled time. Polling the database every second for exactly-due jobs at 10k a second would hammer it. Polling every few minutes is gentle, but far too coarse.

How: use two layers. The poller scans the database every few minutes for jobs due soon, and hands each to a delay queue that releases it at its exact time. Examples: a Redis sorted set scored by timestamp, polled every few hundred milliseconds with "give me everything with score ≤ now", or SQS with a per-message delay (up to 15 minutes). The database sees a gentle, batched read; the in-memory delay queue handles the precise timing.

docs.title: Step 3: run on workers with leases, and coordinate the pollers
docs.text:
Why: workers crash mid-job, and a crashed job must run again rather than vanish. And several pollers must not hand out the same execution twice.

How: workers take jobs from the queue with a visibility timeout (a lease). While a worker holds it, nobody else sees the job. If the worker dies, the lease expires and the job reappears for another worker. That makes execution at-least-once, so jobs must be idempotent. Pollers either each own separate time-bucket partitions, or one is elected leader through etcd or ZooKeeper, so each execution is enqueued by exactly one poller.

docs.title: How do you hit 2s precision?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: precision means checking often, and checking a huge database often is expensive. Those pull in opposite directions.

How: split them. Coarse, cheap database scans every few minutes find jobs due in the next window (for example the next 5 minutes) and load them into a precise, in-memory delay structure. A Redis sorted set keyed by run time is polled every ~100–500 ms for due items, which are pushed to the work queue. Timing precision comes from the in-memory layer; durability comes from the database. If the delay layer is lost, the next database scan reloads anything not yet run.

docs.title: Worker dies mid-job?
docs.text:
Why it matters: jobs run for seconds to hours, and workers will crash, be redeployed or lose network during them.

How: the lease (visibility timeout) expires and the job becomes available again, then is retried by another worker. For long jobs, the worker sends heartbeats that extend its lease, so healthy long jobs aren't stolen. Danger: a worker that was paused, not dead, might wake up and finish after another worker has taken over. So completion writes carry a fencing token, the lease's attempt number, and the database rejects a stale one (see fencing tokens).

docs.title: Duplicate enqueues?
docs.text:
Why they happen: a poller crashes after enqueuing but before marking the execution as enqueued, and the next scan enqueues it again. Or two pollers overlap during a failover.

How: give every execution a unique execution_id and deduplicate on it: the queue can drop repeats (SQS FIFO deduplication), or the worker checks "already started or done?" with a conditional update on the execution's status before running. Combined with idempotent jobs, an occasional duplicate is harmless.

docs.title: User history queries?
docs.text:
Why it's tricky: executions are partitioned by time for the scheduler's benefit, but users ask "show my job runs", across all time buckets.

How: add a secondary index on (user_id, scheduled_at), or keep a separate history table partitioned by user_id that each finished execution is written to. That way, "my last 50 runs" is a single-partition read instead of a scan across every time bucket.

docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Schedule jobs: one-off at time T, or cron; Execute jobs with a retry policy; View job status and history 5–8 Non-functional requirements 10k job executions/s; Start within 2s of scheduled time; At-least-once; jobs idempotent; Never lose a job; billions of jobs stored 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 10k executions/s = 864M/day. A DB poll every second for "due now" across billions of rows will not hold, so use a two-layer design. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Poller → Delay queue → Workers → etcd / ZK. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives How do you hit 2s precision? · Worker dies mid-job? · Duplicate enqueues? · User history queries? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

Raise before you're asked Poller leader failing; clock drift; duplicate execution; every cron job firing at :00. Senior stops at A jobs table and a queue. Staff goes on to Reasons through the two-tier design, leader election with fencing, isolation between tenants. Run it Watch schedule-to-start lag p99, missed jobs, retries.

docs.title: Live comments (Facebook Live)
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Real-time updates · DDIA: Ch 11 pub/sub · Ch 6 partition by video

One popular stream can mean a million viewers each expecting new comments within a fraction of a second.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: LIVE COMMENTS (FACEBOOK LIVE) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Polling at this scale is a self-inflicted denial of service; push with Server-Sent Events.
  • Write each comment once and publish it once; pub/sub fans it out to every server holding viewers of that video.
  • Route viewers of the same video to the same servers so each server subscribes to few channels.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Post a comment on a live video
  2. Viewers see new comments in near real time
  3. Late joiners can scroll back through earlier comments

Non-functional

  • Delivery p99 < 200ms
  • Millions of concurrent viewers; mega-streams with 1M+ viewers
  • Eventual consistency and ordering are acceptable

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: Hot stream: 1M viewers × 1k comments/s = 1B deliveries/s for one video. Polling every 2s = 500k req/s from that one stream.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
comments(video_id, comment_id, user_id, text, ts) partitioned by video_id, clustered by ts

POST /videos/{id}/comments
GET /videos/{id}/comments?cursor (history)
GET /videos/{id}/comments/stream (SSE)

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Posting a comment inserts a row into the database. Each viewer's app polls every couple of seconds: "any comments on this video newer than the last one I have?"

Where it breaks:

  • Latency: a comment appears only at the viewer's next poll, up to the full interval late. Shortening the interval makes the next problem worse.
  • Load: one popular stream with 1 million viewers polling every 2 seconds is 500k requests a second, for a single video. Most return nothing new. It's a denial-of-service attack you're running on yourself.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: push comments with Server-Sent Events
docs.text:
Why: viewers need new comments within 200 ms, and asking repeatedly is both slow and wasteful.

How: each viewer opens one long-lived SSE connection (GET /videos/{id}/comments/stream), and the server writes each new comment to it the moment it arrives. No more empty polls: data flows only when there's a new comment. Posting a comment stays a normal POST. SSE is plain HTTP, works through proxies and reconnects automatically.

docs.title: Step 2: write once, publish once, fan out through pub/sub
docs.text:
Why: viewers of one video are spread across many realtime servers, maybe 1,000 of them. A comment arrives at one server, but must reach viewers connected to all the others.

How: when a comment is posted, it is written once to Cassandra (partitioned by video_id, sorted by time) and published once to a pub/sub channel for that video (Redis Pub/Sub, or Kafka). Every realtime server subscribes to the channels of the videos its connected viewers are watching. When the message arrives, each server pushes it down its own local SSE connections. The poster's server doesn't need to know where any viewer is.

docs.title: Step 3: group viewers of the same video on the same servers
docs.text:
Why: if viewers are spread randomly, every server ends up with a few viewers of almost every live video, so every server subscribes to every channel, and each comment is delivered to all servers.

How: the L7 load balancer routes connections by video_id (consistent hashing), so viewers of the same video land on the same few servers. Each server subscribes to only a handful of channels, and each comment goes only to the servers that actually have viewers for it. Huge streams are spread over a group of servers (see the mega-streams deep dive).

docs.title: SSE or WebSocket?
docs.text:
Why it's a question: both keep a connection open so the server can push.

How to choose: look at the direction of the traffic. Here it is overwhelmingly server to client: millions receive, and a few send. SSE fits exactly. It's one-way, plain HTTP, has automatic reconnection with "last event ID" resume, and works through corporate proxies. Sending a comment is a rare, ordinary POST. WebSockets are worth their extra complexity when both sides send frequently, as in chat or multiplayer games.

docs.title: How does one comment reach 1,000 servers?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: the server that receives a comment holds only a tiny share of the viewers. It can't push to connections on other machines directly, and calling 1,000 servers one by one is slow and fragile.

How: pub/sub fan-out. The comment is published once to the video's channel. The pub/sub system delivers one copy to each subscribed server, perhaps 1,000 deliveries, and each server then fans it out locally to its thousands of viewers over their SSE connections. Two levels of fan-out turn one write into millions of deliveries, without any server needing to know where viewers are.

docs.title: Mega-streams?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: a stream with 1M viewers and 1,000 comments a second means 1 billion deliveries a second. And no human can read 1,000 comments a second anyway.

How: don't deliver everything to everyone. Sample the stream per viewer (show, say, 10–20 comments a second, chosen fairly), and prioritize comments that matter to that viewer: from friends, from the streamer, or highly reacted. That cuts delivery volume by 50–100× and makes the experience better, not worse. The viewers of a mega-stream are spread over a dedicated pool of servers, all subscribed to the same channel.

docs.title: Late join?
docs.text:
Why it matters: someone joining 20 minutes into a stream should see recent conversation, not an empty box.

How: on join, first fetch the last N comments from Cassandra with a cursor query, partitioned by video_id and sorted by time, so it's a fast single-partition read. Then attach to the live SSE stream. To avoid a gap or duplicates between the two, the client passes the ID of the newest comment it loaded, and the stream starts after it.

Polling every 2s = 500k req/s from that one stream. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Realtime servers → Pub/sub → L7 LB. docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why SSE instead of polling?

Millions of viewers polling every few seconds is a self-inflicted denial of service; one open push connection per viewer is far cheaper.

How does one comment reach viewers on 1,000 servers?

It is published once to a pub/sub channel for that video; every server with viewers of that video subscribes and forwards it.

Why route viewers of the same video to the same servers?

Each server then subscribes to few channels, cutting pub/sub fan-out.

docs.title: LLM chat (ChatGPT)
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Real-time updates · DDIA: Ch 11 logs and streams · Ch 1 tail latency

GPUs are the scarce resource, so every queueing decision is really a cost decision.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: LLM CHAT (CHATGPT) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Stream tokens to the client as they are generated so the first words appear in under a second.
  • Put a queue with priorities in front of the GPU pool for backpressure, fairness and batching.
  • Buffer tokens per message so a client that reconnects can resume where it left off.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Send a message in a conversation
  2. Stream the model's answer token by token
  3. View conversation history

Non-functional

  • Time to first token < 1s
  • GPU capacity is the scarce resource
  • Conversations durable
  • 100M DAU; bursty

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 100M DAU × 10 msgs = 1B/day ≈ 12k/s generations. Each holds a GPU for seconds, so GPUs are the bottleneck and every queueing decision is about them.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
conversations(id, user_id)
messages(conversation_id, id, role, content, status)

POST /conversations/{id}/messages → message_id
GET /messages/{id}/stream (SSE, Last-Event-ID resume)
GET /conversations/{id}

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
The client sends a message, the API server calls a GPU model server, waits for the complete answer, and returns it in the HTTP response.

Where it breaks:

  • Waiting: a long answer takes 20–30 seconds to generate. The user stares at a spinner, and the time-to-first-token target of under 1 second is impossible.
  • Timeouts: load balancers and mobile networks often drop requests open that long. The answer is generated, but the user never sees it, so they retry, and the GPU does the work twice.
  • No backpressure: about 12k generations a second on average, bursting much higher, sent straight to GPUs. GPUs are the scarce, expensive resource. When they're full, requests pile up or fail randomly, with no way to prioritize.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: stream tokens as they're generated
docs.text:
Why: the model produces text one token at a time. Making the user wait for the last token before showing the first wastes 20+ seconds of perceived latency.

How: the client opens an SSE stream for the message, and each token is sent the moment it's generated. The first words appear in well under a second, and the rest flows in as the model writes. SSE fits because the data flows server to client, it works over plain HTTP, and it supports resuming with Last-Event-ID.

docs.title: Step 2: put a queue in front of the GPUs
docs.text:
Why: GPU capacity is fixed in the short term and very expensive. Demand is bursty. Without a buffer, bursts overload GPUs, and there's no way to say "paid users first" or to group requests efficiently.

How: POST /messages saves the user's message, puts a generation job on a priority queue, and returns a message_id immediately. GPU workers pull jobs when they have capacity. The queue gives:

  • backpressure: jobs wait instead of overloading GPUs;
  • priority: paid tiers first;
  • fairness: limits per user;
  • batching: a worker can run several requests together, which uses a GPU far more efficiently;
  • admission control: when the queue is too long, new requests get a clear 429.

docs.title: Step 3: buffer tokens per message so clients can resume
docs.text:
Why: phones switch networks and tabs get closed. If tokens go straight from the GPU to one connection, a dropped connection loses the rest of the answer, even though the GPU keeps generating it.

How: workers write each token to a Redis Stream keyed by message_id. SSE servers read from that stream and forward to the client. If the client reconnects (to any server) with Last-Event-ID, the SSE server continues from that position. When generation finishes, the full text is saved to the messages table, and the Redis stream expires.

docs.title: Why a queue before GPUs?
docs.text:
Why it's needed: a GPU can serve only a limited number of generations at once, and each one holds it for seconds. Unlike stateless web servers, you can't spin up thousands more in a minute.

How it helps: the queue turns overload into waiting instead of failure, and gives you control over who waits: paid before free, short before long, a fair share per user. Workers can pull several jobs at once and batch them on the GPU. Generating for 8 users together costs much less than 8 separate runs. When the wait gets too long, return 429 with a retry hint rather than letting requests time out.

docs.title: Client disconnects?
docs.text:
Why it matters: generation is expensive. Throwing away a half-finished answer because the user's Wi-Fi blinked wastes GPU time and frustrates the user.

How: decouple generation from the connection. The worker keeps generating and appending tokens to the message's Redis Stream whether or not anyone is connected. The client reconnects with Last-Event-ID (the last token it received) and receives everything after it. If the user really leaves and nobody reads the stream for a while, the job can be cancelled to save GPU time.

docs.title: Long context?
docs.text:
Why it's a problem: the model can read only a limited amount of text (its context window), and the cost grows with the length of input. A conversation with hundreds of messages may not fit, and resending all of it on every turn is expensive.

How: load the most recent messages that fit, and replace older parts with a summary that is generated once and stored with the conversation. Keep hot conversations' recent messages cached so each turn doesn't hit the database. Some model servers can also cache the processed prefix of a conversation (KV or prompt caching), making repeat turns cheaper.

docs.title: Cost control?
docs.text:
Why it's needed: every generated token costs GPU time. One user or script sending thousands of long requests could consume a large share of capacity.

How: enforce per-user rate limits (requests per minute) and token quotas (tokens per day, by plan) at the API gateway, before anything reaches the queue. Cap the maximum output length per request. Track usage per user for billing and abuse detection.

docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Send a message in a conversation; Stream the model's answer token by token; View conversation history 5–8 Non-functional requirements Time to first token < 1s; GPU capacity is the scarce resource; Conversations durable; 100M DAU; bursty 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 100M DAU × 10 msgs = 1B/day ≈ 12k/s generations. Each holds a GPU for seconds, so GPUs are the bottleneck and every queueing decision is about them. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: SSE servers → Request queue → Inference workers → Redis Streams. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Why a queue before GPUs? · Client disconnects? · Long context? · Cost control? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

Run it Watch time-to-first-token, queue wait, GPU utilisation, cost per 1k tokens.

docs.title: Local delivery (Gopuff)
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Difficulty: Easy · Patterns: Scaling reads · DDIA: Ch 7 conditional updates · Ch 5 replica lag

It looks like an ordering system, but most of the load is people checking what is available near them.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: LOCAL DELIVERY (GOPUFF) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Browsing availability is far more frequent than ordering, so cache it and serve it from replicas.
  • Find nearby warehouses with an in-memory list and a cheap distance filter before calling any travel-time API.
  • Prevent overselling with conditional stock decrements for every item in one transaction.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Check availability of items deliverable to a location (DCs within 1 hour)
  2. Order multiple items; never sell stock you don't have

Non-functional

  • Availability p99 < 100ms
  • Orders strongly consistent (no overselling)
  • 10k distribution centres (DCs), ~100k SKUs
  • Browse load ≫ order load

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: Browse ~10M × 10 / 86,400 ≈ 1.2k/s, ~10k/s peak. Orders ~1M/day ≈ 12/s. The DC list (10k rows) fits in memory.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
dcs(id, lat, lng, region)
inventory(dc_id, item_id, qty) PK(dc_id, item_id)
orders, order_items

GET /availability?lat&lng&item_ids
POST /orders {items:[{id, qty}], lat, lng}

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
To show what a customer can order, find the distribution centres (DCs) that can deliver to them within an hour, then check those DCs' stock. The simplest version asks a travel-time API (like a maps service) for the drive time from every DC to the customer, keeps those under an hour, and queries inventory for them.

Where it breaks: there are 10,000 DCs. That's 10,000 travel-time API calls per page view. Even in parallel it takes seconds, costs a fortune in API fees, and at ~10k availability checks a second at peak it means 100 million external calls a second. The p99 target of 100 ms is impossible. Separately, ordering needs a guarantee that two customers can't buy the last unit of an item.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: filter DCs cheaply before asking for travel times
docs.text:
Why: almost all of the 10,000 DCs are obviously too far away. You don't need a maps API to know that a DC 500 km away can't deliver in an hour.

How: the DC list is tiny, 10,000 rows with coordinates, so keep it in memory in every app server. For each request, compute the straight-line distance to every DC (microseconds) and keep only those within, say, 30 km. Then call the travel-time API for just those few candidates, and cache the results by area, because nearby customers get the same answer.

docs.title: Step 2: serve browsing from caches and replicas
docs.text:
Why: browsing happens far more often than ordering (about 10k a second at peak vs about 12 orders a second). Browsing can tolerate data a few seconds old; ordering cannot.

How: answer availability from a short-TTL cache (a few seconds) and read replicas. If the page says "in stock" and the item sold out a second ago, the order step catches it. This path is deliberately AP: fast and available, slightly stale.

docs.title: Step 3: make ordering exact
docs.text:
Why: if two customers order the last can of a drink at the same moment, only one may get it. "Read quantity, check it, write quantity − 1" lets both through (a race).

How: the order runs on the primary database, in one transaction, with a conditional decrement for each item:

UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - :n
WHERE dc_id = :dc AND item_id = :item AND qty >= :n;

If any item's update affects 0 rows, that item doesn't have enough stock, so roll back the whole order and tell the customer. This path is deliberately CP: correct first.

docs.title: How do you prevent overselling?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: checking stock and then decrementing it are two steps. Between them, another order can take the last unit. Both orders see "1 left", both succeed, and you've sold stock you don't have.

How: put the check inside the write, with the conditional UPDATE … WHERE qty >= :n above. The database locks the row while it applies the update, so concurrent orders for the same item are applied one at a time. The second one sees the reduced quantity and matches 0 rows. Doing all items in one transaction means a multi-item order is all-or-nothing: you never charge for half a basket.

docs.title: Stale availability vs orders?
docs.text:
Why it matters: the browse page might say an item is available when it has just sold out. Is that a bug?

How to think about it: use different consistency for different paths. Browsing is cached and eventually consistent, because a few seconds of staleness costs little and keeps the page fast. Checkout reads and writes the primary and is strictly correct. The rare case where browse said "available" but checkout fails is handled with a clear message ("sorry, just sold out") and maybe a substitute suggestion.

docs.title: Scale orders?
docs.text:
Why it might be needed: if order volume grows far beyond today's ~12 a second, one primary's write capacity could become a limit.

How: partition inventory by region. An order is only ever fulfilled from DCs near the customer, so all its rows live on the same shard, and you never need a transaction across shards. Each region's database handles only its own orders.

docs.title: Hot item (flash sale)?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: during a flash sale, thousands of orders a second all try to decrement the same inventory row. Each update must wait for the row lock held by the one before it, so they queue up, latency soars and requests time out.

How: two options.

  • Queue orders per item: put orders for the hot item into a queue and process them one by one in a single worker. There's no lock contention, and the queue absorbs the burst.
  • Split the stock into buckets: spread the 1,000 units across 10 rows of 100. Each order picks a bucket at random and moves on to another if it's empty. That's 10× less contention per row, at the cost of slightly more complex "is it sold out?" logic.

Orders ~1M/day ≈ 12/s. The DC list (10k rows) fits in memory. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Nearby-DC service → Travel-time API → Redis → Read replicas → Order service → Postgres primary. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives How do you prevent overselling? · Stale availability vs orders? · Scale orders? · Hot item (flash sale)? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.text:

docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why serve availability from caches and replicas?

Browsing is far more frequent than ordering, and availability can be a little stale; the order path checks the real stock.

How do you prevent overselling?

Conditional stock decrements (WHERE stock >= qty) for every item in one transaction; if any fails, the whole order fails.

Why filter warehouses by straight-line distance before calling a travel-time API?

The API is slow and costly; a cheap distance filter on an in-memory list removes most candidates first.

docs.title: Metrics monitoring (Datadog)
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Scaling writes · DDIA: Ch 3 LSM, compression · Ch 11 stream alerting

Millions of data points per second arrive, and alerts must fire within a minute.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: METRICS MONITORING (DATADOG) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Buffer the write firehose through Kafka into a time-series database built for appends and compression.
  • Downsample old data and move it to cheap storage; dashboards read rollups.
  • Evaluate alert rules on the stream itself instead of polling the database.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Ingest metrics from 500k servers
  2. Query dashboards over time ranges
  3. Alert rules with notifications

Non-functional

  • 5M datapoints/s ingest
  • Recent-data queries < 1s
  • Alerts within ~1 minute
  • Late/out-of-order tolerant, durable

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 500k hosts × 100 metrics ÷ 10s = 5M points/s. Gorilla compression ≈ 1.4B/point → ~600GB/day; downsample after 7 days.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
series(metric, tags) → (ts, value) blocks
rollups 1m / 1h
alert_rules

POST /ingest (batched points from agents)
GET /query?metric&tags&from&to&step
POST /alerts {rule, threshold, channel}

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
An agent on each server sends its metrics (CPU, memory, request counts…) every 10 seconds. The ingest service inserts one row per data point, (metric, tags, ts, value), into Postgres with a B-tree index. Dashboards query a time range, and an alert job runs every rule as a query every minute.

Where it breaks:

  • Write volume: 500k servers × 100 metrics ÷ 10 s = 5 million data points a second. A relational database with B-tree indexes manages tens of thousands of inserts a second, about 100× too few.
  • Storage: each row with its index entries costs maybe 50–100 bytes, so 5M a second means tens of terabytes a day.
  • Alerting: thousands of alert rules each querying the database every minute adds a large read load on top of the write firehose.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: buffer through Kafka into a time-series database
docs.text:
Why: metrics data has a very particular shape. It's append-only (you never update a past CPU reading), always written in time order, and always read as "one series over a time range". A general-purpose database pays for flexibility this data doesn't need.

How: agents send batches to an ingest tier, which writes them to Kafka. Kafka absorbs spikes and lets the storage tier fall behind briefly without losing anything. Consumers write into a time-series database (TSDB), such as Prometheus-style storage, M3, VictoriaMetrics or InfluxDB:

  • Each series' points are grouped into blocks by time.
  • Writes are sequential appends (LSM-style), with no random index updates.
  • Values are heavily compressed. Timestamps arrive at regular intervals, so storing the difference of differences is mostly zeros. Consecutive values are similar, so XOR-ing them leaves mostly zero bits. That gets each point down to about 1.4 bytes instead of 16 or more, roughly 600 GB a day.

docs.title: Step 2: downsample and tier old data
docs.text:
Why: nobody needs 10-second resolution for last year's CPU graph, but keeping it all at full resolution would cost a fortune and make long-range queries slow.

How: keep raw data for about 7 days. Background jobs compute rollups: per-minute aggregates (min, max, average, count), then per-hour. Older raw blocks are deleted, and rollups move to cheap object storage (S3). A dashboard for "last 30 days" reads hourly rollups, a few hundred points per series, so it loads in well under a second.

docs.title: Step 3: evaluate alerts on the stream
docs.text:
Why: polling the TSDB with thousands of alert queries every minute adds heavy read load and latency, and an alert can only fire as fast as the polling interval.

How: a stream processor (such as Flink) reads the same Kafka stream and evaluates alert rules as data arrives, using time windows ("average CPU over 5 minutes > 90%"). When a rule triggers, it sends the event to an alert manager, which deduplicates, groups and routes notifications (pager, Slack, email). Alerts fire within about a minute of the problem, without touching the database.

docs.title: Why a TSDB?
docs.text:
Why not a normal database: relational databases are built for random reads and updates, transactions and flexible queries, none of which metrics need. And they pay for those features in write throughput and storage.

What a TSDB does instead: time-ordered appends suit LSM-style storage (sequential writes, very high throughput). Specialized compression gets about 10× smaller storage. Queries are range scans over one series' blocks, read in order. It's a database shaped exactly like the data.

docs.title: High cardinality?
docs.text:
Why it's dangerous: each unique combination of metric name and tag values is a separate series, with its own index entry and buffers. A tag like host (500k values) is fine. Add a tag like user_id (100M values), and one metric becomes 100 million series, exploding memory and index size. This is the most common way to break a metrics system.

How: limit cardinality: reject or drop labels with too many unique values, enforce per-customer series limits, and alert on fast-growing series counts. Per-user or per-request data belongs in logs or traces, not metrics.

docs.title: Late data?
docs.text:
Why it happens: an agent loses network for 5 minutes, then sends its buffered points. They arrive late, after the windows they belong to may already have been computed.

How: process by event time (the timestamp on the point), not arrival time. Windows use a watermark, the stream processor's estimate of "all data up to time T has arrived", plus an allowed lateness period during which late points still update the window. Points later than that are stored in the TSDB but don't re-trigger alerts.

docs.title: Alert flapping?
docs.text:
Why it happens: a metric hovering around its threshold (CPU at 89%, 91%, 88%…) fires and resolves an alert over and over, flooding the on-call engineer with pages.

How: require the condition to hold for N consecutive windows (or a set duration, such as "for 5 minutes") before firing. Use a lower threshold to resolve than to fire (hysteresis). And let the alert manager deduplicate and group related alerts, for example 50 servers in one cluster becoming one notification.

docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why a time-series database instead of Postgres?

It is built for append-heavy, time-ordered writes with heavy compression and fast range scans and rollups.

How do you keep long-term storage cheap?

Downsample old data into rollups and move it to cheaper storage; dashboards read rollups for long ranges.

Why evaluate alerts on the stream?

Alerts fire as data arrives without repeatedly querying the database for every rule.

docs.title: News aggregator (Google News)
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Difficulty: Easy · Patterns: Scaling reads · DDIA: Ch 1 load parameters · Ch 10 ingest pipelines

A feed problem where the feed is the same for everyone in a region, which changes everything.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: NEWS AGGREGATOR (GOOGLE NEWS) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Writes are tiny (new articles); reads spike hard when big news breaks.
  • Precompute one list per region and category at ingest time instead of querying on every request.
  • Because the feed is not per-user, a CDN can cache it for a minute and absorb almost all traffic.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Feed of recent articles from thousands of publishers, by region and category
  2. Click through to the publisher; infinite scroll

Non-functional

  • Feed p99 < 200ms
  • 100M DAU with breaking-news spikes
  • New articles visible within ~30 min
  • Availability over consistency

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 100M × 10 = 1B feed reads/day ≈ 12k/s, 50k+/s spikes. Writes: ~100k articles/day ≈ 1/s.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
articles(id, canonical_url UNIQUE, title, summary, thumbnail_url, publisher_id, region, category, published_at)

GET /feed?region&category&cursor → [{title, summary, thumbnail, url, publisher}]

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
A scheduler fetches each publisher's RSS feed or sitemap every few minutes and inserts new articles into Postgres. When a user opens the app, the API runs a query such as WHERE region = ? AND category = ? ORDER BY published_at DESC LIMIT 20.

Where it breaks: writes are tiny, about 100k articles a day, roughly 1 a second. Reads are not. There are about 12k feed requests a second normally, and 50k+ when big news breaks, exactly when everyone opens the app at once. Each request runs the same query against the database, recomputing the same answer thousands of times a second. The database becomes the bottleneck during the very spikes that matter most.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: precompute each feed at ingest time
docs.text:
Why: there are only a limited number of distinct feeds, one per (region, category) pair, and they change only when an article arrives, about once a second. Recomputing them on each of 12k+ requests a second wastes almost all that work.

How: when a new article is ingested, insert its ID into a Redis sorted set for each feed it belongs to (feed:US:tech), ordered by publish time and capped at a few thousand entries. Serving a feed becomes one list read, with no query planning, sorting or joins.

docs.title: Step 2: let a CDN absorb the spikes
docs.text:
Why: even a cheap Redis read is 50k requests a second during breaking news. But here's the key observation: everyone in the same region and category gets exactly the same response. The feed isn't personalized.

How: set cache headers so a CDN caches each feed response for about 60 seconds per region and category. In each 60-second window, each CDN location asks your servers once and serves everyone else from its cache. A 50k/s spike becomes a handful of requests a second at your origin. News that is up to a minute old meets the "visible within 30 minutes" requirement easily.

docs.title: Step 3: serve images from your own CDN, and get pushes instead of polling
docs.text:
Why: thumbnails hotlinked from publishers' sites are slow, unreliable, and can break. And polling thousands of publishers every few minutes is wasteful when most have nothing new.

How: at ingest, copy each thumbnail to S3 and serve it through the CDN. For publishers that support push (WebSub, webhooks), let them notify you of new articles instead of being polled.

docs.title: Why can a CDN cache the feed?
docs.text:
Why this matters: CDNs normally can't cache API responses, because each user gets different data (their own feed, their account).

How it works here: this feed is the same for everyone with the same region and category, so the URL (/feed?region=US&category=tech) fully determines the response. The CDN can safely give one cached copy to millions of users. The trade-off is up to 60 seconds of staleness. For news that's acceptable: availability and speed matter more than showing an article in the very same second (an AP choice). If a major story must appear instantly, purge that feed's cache entry.

docs.title: Polling cost vs freshness?
docs.text:
Why it's a trade-off: polling every publisher every minute is fresh but wasteful (most have nothing new) and can get you rate-limited. Polling hourly misses breaking news.

How: use adaptive polling. Track how often each publisher actually posts. Busy outlets get polled every few minutes; quiet blogs hourly or daily. Speed up when a publisher is active and back off when it isn't. Use conditional requests (If-Modified-Since, ETags) so an unchanged feed costs almost nothing, and use webhooks or WebSub where the publisher offers them.

docs.title: Duplicate stories?
docs.text:
Why it happens: the same article shows up through several feeds or URLs (tracking parameters, mobile versions), and many outlets publish near-identical wire stories.

How: first, normalize each URL (strip tracking parameters, follow the canonical link tag) and put a unique constraint on canonical_url, so exact duplicates are rejected at insert. For near-duplicates, compute a similarity fingerprint (SimHash or MinHash) of the title and text, and cluster articles with close fingerprints into one story with several sources, the way news aggregators show "and 12 more sources".

docs.title: Pagination?
docs.text:
Why offsets break: new articles constantly arrive at the top. With page numbers, a user scrolling to page 2 sees items they already saw on page 1.

How: a cursor: return items older than the (published_at, id) of the last item the user saw. The id breaks ties between articles published in the same second. New arrivals don't shift what comes next.

docs.text:
• Per-user fan-out like a social feed when the feed is per region and category: build it once per region and let the CDN cache it.
  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.
  • Skipping failure handling: what happens on timeouts, retries and crashes.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why can a CDN cache the feed here but not in a social network?

The feed is the same for everyone in a region and category, not personalised, so one cached copy serves millions of readers.

Why precompute lists at ingest time?

Writes (new articles) are rare and reads are huge and spiky, so doing the work once per article is far cheaper than once per request.

How fresh can the feed be with CDN caching?

About as fresh as the cache TTL, for example a minute, which is usually acceptable for news; breaking stories can purge the cache.

docs.title: News feed (Facebook)
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Scaling reads · DDIA: Ch 1 Twitter load · Ch 11 materialized views · Ch 6 hot keys

The canonical fan-out problem: build a personalised feed for billions of users in a few hundred milliseconds.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: NEWS FEED (FACEBOOK) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Computing the feed on every read means hundreds of queries per page view, so precompute it when people post.
  • Push new post IDs into each follower's feed list in Redis (fan-out on write); a feed read becomes one lookup.
  • Accounts with millions of followers break fan-out on write, so pull their posts at read time instead (hybrid).

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Create posts
  2. Follow users
  3. View feed of followed users' posts, newest first, paginated

Non-functional

  • Feed p99 < 500ms
  • 2B users; eventual consistency (post appears within ~1 min)
  • Handle accounts with millions of followers
  • Highly available

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 1B DAU × 10 feed loads = ~115k feed reads/s. ~500M posts/day ≈ 6k/s. With ~200 followers each, fan-out on write ≈ 1.2M feed inserts/s.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
posts(id, author_id, content, ts) partitioned by author
follows(follower_id, followee_id) + reverse index
feed:{user} = Redis ZSET(ts, post_id), capped at 500

POST /posts {content}
PUT /users/{id}/followers
GET /feed?cursor=(ts,post_id)

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
The simplest feed is computed when the user opens it (fan-out on read). Look up the ~200 people they follow, fetch each one's recent posts, merge them by time, and return the newest 20. Posting is just one insert into posts.

Where it breaks: reads. There are about 115k feed loads a second, and each needs the follow list plus recent posts from ~200 authors, spread across many database partitions. That's tens of millions of lookups a second, plus merging and sorting, on every page view. The p99 under 500 ms can't be met, and the database spends nearly all its time rebuilding the same feeds over and over.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: precompute feeds when people post (fan-out on write)
docs.text:
Why: feeds are read far more often than posts are written (115k reads a second vs about 6k posts a second). It's cheaper to do the work once per post than once per feed view.

How: when someone posts, save the post, then put a "new post" event on Kafka. Fan-out workers look up the author's followers and push the post ID into each follower's feed list in Redis: a sorted set ordered by timestamp, capped at about 500 entries. Opening the feed is now one Redis read (ZREVRANGE feed:{user} 0 19), which returns in a millisecond or two. The cost moved to write time: 6k posts a second × ~200 followers ≈ 1.2M feed inserts a second, done asynchronously by workers. A post appearing in feeds a few seconds later is fine (eventual consistency).

docs.title: Step 2: handle celebrities differently (hybrid)
docs.text:
Why: fan-out on write assumes ~200 followers. An account with 100 million followers would trigger 100M Redis writes for one post, taking minutes and swamping the workers, while everyone else's posts wait behind it.

How: don't fan out for accounts above a threshold (say 100k–1M followers). Their posts are stored normally. When a user opens their feed, read their precomputed list, plus the recent posts of the few celebrities they follow, and merge the two by time. Most users follow only a handful of celebrities, so the extra work per read is small.

docs.title: Step 3: turn IDs into posts, and paginate
docs.text:
Why: the feed list holds only post IDs (to keep memory small), but the app needs text, images and author names. And scrolling must work while new posts keep arriving.

How: hydrate the 20 IDs with one batch read from the posts store, with a post cache in front, because popular posts appear in millions of feeds. Paginate with a cursor, the (timestamp, post_id) of the last item shown, rather than page numbers.

docs.title: Celebrity with 100M followers?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: fan-out on write costs one write per follower. For a celebrity that's 100M writes per post: a huge delay before followers see it, and a backlog that delays everyone else's posts.

How: the hybrid model. Fan out on write for normal accounts; for accounts above a follower threshold, skip fan-out and pull their recent posts at read time, merging them into the precomputed feed. Tune the threshold (roughly 100k–1M followers) by measuring the cost of each path. Keep celebrities' recent posts heavily cached, since many readers fetch the same ones.

docs.title: How much memory for feeds?
docs.text:
Why it matters: storing a feed for 2 billion users in Redis could be enormous.

How to keep it small: store only post IDs (about 8 bytes each), cap each feed at about 500 entries, and keep feeds only for active users, say 300M. That's 300M × 500 × ~8 B ≈ 1.2 TB, which spreads comfortably over a Redis cluster. When an inactive user returns, rebuild their feed on demand with fan-out on read, once, then keep it updated.

docs.title: Pagination?
docs.text:
Why offsets fail: with ?page=2, if 5 new posts arrive while you're reading page 1, page 2 now starts 5 items earlier, and you see duplicates.

How: use a cursor: "give me 20 items older than (ts, post_id) of the last item I saw". The post ID breaks ties when two posts share a timestamp. New posts at the top don't affect it, and the sorted set supports it directly with a score range query.

docs.title: User follows someone new?
docs.text:
Why it matters: fan-out on write only pushes future posts. Right after following someone, their existing posts aren't in your feed, and it looks broken.

How: an asynchronous backfill: when a follow happens, a job fetches the new followee's recent posts (say the last 20) and inserts them into the follower's feed list. On unfollow, a similar job removes them, or the read path filters them out. It doesn't need to be instant, just within seconds.

docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Create posts; Follow users; View feed of followed users' posts, newest first, paginated 5–8 Non-functional requirements Feed p99 < 500ms; 2B users; eventual consistency (post appears within ~1 min); Handle accounts with millions of followers; Highly available 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 1B DAU × 10 feed loads = ~115k feed reads/s. ~500M posts/day ≈ 6k/s. With ~200 followers each, fan-out on write ≈ 1.2M feed inserts/s. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Kafka → Fan-out workers → Redis feeds → Celebrity posts. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Celebrity with 100M followers? · How much memory for feeds? · Pagination? · User follows someone new? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.text:
• Fan-out on write for everyone: one celebrity post means 100M writes and workers hours behind.
  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.
  • Skipping failure handling: what happens on timeouts, retries and crashes.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What is fan-out on write?

When someone posts, push the post ID into every follower's precomputed feed list, so reading a feed is one lookup.

Why does fan-out on write break for celebrities?

One post would mean millions of writes. Instead, their posts are pulled at read time and merged in (the hybrid approach).

Why store only post IDs in the feed lists?

IDs are small, so feeds for many users fit in Redis memory; post bodies are fetched and cached separately.
