docs.title: Online auction
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Real-time updates · Dealing with contention · DDIA: Ch 7 lost update · Ch 11 partitioned log · Ch 8 clocks

Many people bid on one row at the same time, and exactly one of them must win each race.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: ONLINE AUCTION on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Comparing bids in application code loses updates under concurrency.
  • Accept a bid with one conditional update: set the new maximum only if it beats the current one and the auction is open.
  • Push accepted bids to watchers in real time; for very hot auctions, serialize bids through a partitioned log.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Create an auction (item, starting price, end time)
  2. Place bids that must beat the current highest
  3. Watch the highest bid update live; winner decided at the end

Non-functional

  • Bids strongly consistent (never accept a stale "highest")
  • Live updates < 1s
  • No lost bids
  • Hot auctions spike in the final seconds

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 10M auctions, ~100 bids each over a week ≈ low average QPS, but a hot auction can see ~1k bids/s on one row near the end.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
auctions(id, max_bid, max_bidder, end_time, status)
bids(auction_id, bid_id, user_id, amount, ts) append-only

POST /auctions
POST /auctions/{id}/bids {amount} + Idempotency-Key
GET /auctions/{id}/stream (SSE)

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
To place a bid, the server reads the auction's current highest bid, checks in application code that the new bid is higher, and if so writes the new maximum and inserts the bid.

Where it breaks: the highest bid is $100. Two bidders send $110 and $120 at the same moment. Both requests read $100, both pass the check, and both write. If the $110 write lands second, the auction now says $110 is winning and the $120 bid is silently lost. Or both bidders are told they're the highest bidder. This is a lost update (DDIA Ch 7). It's rare on quiet auctions, but popular auctions get ~1k bids a second in the final seconds, all on the same row, so it happens constantly exactly when it matters most.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: make "is it higher?" and "save it" one atomic step
docs.text:
Why: the bug lives in the gap between reading the maximum and writing the new one. Close the gap and the race disappears.

How: let the database do the comparison inside the update:

UPDATE auctions SET max_bid = :amount, max_bidder = :user
WHERE id = :auction AND max_bid < :amount AND end_time > now();

The database applies updates to one row one at a time. 1 row updated means your bid is now the highest. 0 rows means someone outbid you first, or the auction has ended, so tell the bidder. Every bid is also appended to the bids table for history. The check includes end_time > now(), so late bids are rejected by the same rule.

docs.title: Step 2: push accepted bids to watchers
docs.text:
Why: watchers need to see the new highest bid within a second. Polling by thousands of watchers in the final seconds would add huge load at the worst moment.

How: after a bid is accepted, publish it to a pub/sub channel per auction. Realtime servers subscribed to that channel push it to every watcher over SSE.

docs.title: Step 3: serialize bids for very hot auctions, and close auctions on time
docs.text:
Why: at about 1k bids a second, every bid waits for the row lock held by the one before it. Latency climbs, connections pile up, and the database row becomes a bottleneck.

How: send bids for hot auctions through Kafka, partitioned by auction_id. All bids for one auction go to one partition, in order, and are durably stored as soon as Kafka acknowledges them. One consumer per partition applies them to the database one by one, with no lock contention, and returns the result to the bidder. A delayed job fires at each auction's end time to mark it closed and notify the winner.

docs.title: Two bids at the same instant?
docs.text:
Why it's the core problem: comparing in application code means each request decides based on a value that may already be stale by the time it writes. That's the classic lost update.

How: make the database the referee. Either use the conditional update above, where the comparison happens atomically on the row, or lock the row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE before comparing, so the second bid waits for the first to commit and then sees the new maximum. Both guarantee that exactly one bid at a time can raise the maximum.

docs.title: Clock fairness at the deadline?
docs.text:
Why it matters: if the server checking the end time uses its own clock, or worse, trusts the time the client sends, then two servers with slightly different clocks can disagree about whether a bid at 11:59:59.900 was on time. Clients can lie about their time.

How: use one clock: the database server's now(), evaluated inside the same conditional update that accepts the bid. Every bid is judged against the same clock at the moment it's applied. With the Kafka path, the single consumer per auction applies the same rule in order.

docs.title: Durability?
docs.text:
Why it matters: telling a bidder "you're winning" and then losing that bid after a crash is unacceptable, and could be a legal problem.

How: acknowledge only after the bid is durably stored: after the database transaction commits, or, on the Kafka path, after Kafka confirms the write to all in-sync replicas (acks=all). A crash before that means the bidder gets an error and can retry (with an idempotency key, so the retry isn't counted twice).

docs.title: Anti-sniping?
docs.text:
Why it's a problem: "snipers" bid in the final second so others have no time to respond. Many auction sites consider that unfair.

How: extend the end time when a bid arrives near the end: if a bid lands in the last 30 seconds, push end_time out by another 30 seconds. Do it inside the same conditional update that accepts the bid (SET end_time = GREATEST(end_time, now() + interval '30 seconds')), so the extension and the bid are atomic, and the close job checks the current end time before closing.

docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Create an auction (item, starting price, end time); Place bids that must beat the current highest; Watch the highest bid update live; winner decided at the end 5–8 Non-functional requirements Bids strongly consistent (never accept a stale "highest"); Live updates < 1s; No lost bids; Hot auctions spike in the final seconds 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 10M auctions, ~100 bids each over a week ≈ low average QPS, but a hot auction can see ~1k bids/s on one row near the end. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Pub/sub → SSE → Watchers → Kafka → Delayed job. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Two bids at the same instant? · Clock fairness at the deadline? · Durability? · Anti-sniping? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.title: 8. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Comparing bids in a Redis cache without atomicity.
  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.
  • Skipping failure handling: what happens on timeouts, retries and crashes.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why can't you compare bids in application code?

Two concurrent bids both read the old maximum and both "win" (lost update).

How is a bid accepted safely?

One conditional update: set the new maximum only if the bid beats the current one and the auction is still open.

How do you handle very hot auctions?

Serialize bids for that auction through a partitioned log, so one consumer processes them in order.

docs.title: Online judge (LeetCode)
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Multi-step processes · Long-running tasks · DDIA: Ch 11 queues · Ch 1 bursty load

You are running strangers' code on your servers, so isolation comes first.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: ONLINE JUDGE (LEETCODE) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Run every submission in a locked-down sandbox: no network, read-only filesystem, strict CPU, memory and time limits.
  • Queue submissions and return immediately; workers autoscale on queue depth and the client polls for results.
  • Keep contest leaderboards in a Redis sorted set.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Browse problems
  2. Submit code in several languages; get pass/fail per test
  3. Contest leaderboard

Non-functional

  • Untrusted code fully isolated
  • Result within ~5s
  • Contest spikes (100k users submitting)
  • Scalable

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: Contest: 100k users × ~5 submissions in 90 min ≈ ~100 submissions/s peak; each run takes 1–5s of sandbox CPU, so ~500 concurrent sandboxes.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
problems
test_cases (S3)
submissions(id, user, problem, status, results)
leaderboard:{contest} ZSET

POST /problems/{id}/submissions {lang, code} → submission_id
GET /submissions/{id} (poll status)
GET /contests/{id}/leaderboard

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
When a user submits code, the API server writes it to a file, compiles and runs it against the test cases, and returns the results in the HTTP response.

Where it breaks:

  • Security: you are running code written by strangers on your own servers. It can read your files and secrets, call your internal network, delete things, or mine cryptocurrency. This is the biggest problem.
  • Resource hogging: one infinite loop or memory bomb ties up the API server, slowing or crashing everyone else's requests.
  • Spikes: in a contest, 100k users submit around the same time, about 100 submissions a second, each needing 1–5 seconds of CPU. The API servers can't run ~500 programs at once and keep serving pages.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: run every submission in a locked-down sandbox
docs.text:
Why: untrusted code must not be able to affect anything outside its own run: not the host, not other submissions, not the network.

How: run each submission in a fresh, isolated sandbox: a lightweight virtual machine (Firecracker microVM) or a strongly isolated container runtime (gVisor). Inside it there's no network, a read-only filesystem except a small scratch directory, a seccomp filter allowing only the system calls a normal program needs, and strict CPU, memory and time limits. When the time limit is hit, the sandbox is killed. Each run starts clean and is thrown away afterwards.

docs.title: Step 2: queue submissions and run them on separate workers
docs.text:
Why: running code takes seconds and must not block the API. Contests create bursts far above normal load.

How: POST /submissions stores the submission as QUEUED, puts a job on a queue, and returns a submission_id immediately. A separate fleet of judge workers, autoscaled on queue depth, take jobs, run the sandbox against the test cases (stored in S3) and write results. The client polls GET /submissions/{id} about once a second until the status is final. This is the long-running tasks pattern.

docs.title: Step 3: keep the contest leaderboard in Redis
docs.text:
Why: during a contest, thousands of users refresh the leaderboard constantly, and it changes with every accepted submission. Computing it with a database query each time would be heavy.

How: one Redis sorted set per contest, leaderboard:{contest}, with each user's score. Updating a score and fetching the top 50 or a user's rank are single, fast commands. The score encodes both points and penalty time, so ties are broken correctly (see deep dive).

docs.title: Security layers?
docs.text:
Why one layer isn't enough: sandboxes have had escape bugs. If a single mechanism fails, the attacker is on your infrastructure.

How: defence in depth, several independent layers:

  • Isolation: a microVM (own kernel) or gVisor (a user-space kernel), stronger than a plain container.
  • No network at all inside the sandbox.
  • Read-only filesystem, with only a small temporary directory writable.
  • seccomp system-call filtering and dropped Linux capabilities.
  • Resource limits on CPU time, memory, process count and output size, with a hard kill on timeout.
  • Workers run on separate machines in a separate network, with no access to secrets or production databases.

An attacker would have to break several layers at once.

docs.title: Contest spike?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: when a contest starts, demand jumps from a trickle to ~100 submissions a second within minutes, and slow results make contestants furious.

How: the queue absorbs the burst, so nothing is dropped, and results just take a little longer. Autoscale workers on queue depth, and since contests are scheduled, pre-scale before the start. Pre-warm sandboxes for each language, because starting a JVM or compiler environment from scratch is slow. Optionally, give contest submissions their own higher-priority queue.

docs.title: Polling vs push?
docs.text:
Why it's a choice: the client needs to know when results are ready. Push (SSE or WebSocket) is faster; polling is simpler.

How to decide: results take a few seconds, and polling once a second at ~100 submissions a second means only a few hundred cheap status reads a second, which is trivial. Polling is perfectly fine here and avoids managing long-lived connections. Add SSE later if you want live per-test progress.

docs.title: Leaderboard ties?
docs.text:
Why it matters: contests rank first by points, then by time penalty (less is better). A sorted set sorts by one number only.

How: combine both into a single score: score = points × 1,000,000 − penalty_seconds. More points always wins, because one point is worth more than any possible penalty; among equal points, lower penalty gives a higher score. Sort descending, and ZREVRANGE gives the correct ranking.

Then add, in order: Sandbox → Postgres → Queue (SQS) → Workers → Redis ZSET. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Security layers? · Contest spike? · Polling vs push? · Leaderboard ties? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What sandbox limits does a submission run under?

No network, read-only filesystem, and strict CPU, memory and time limits, in an isolated container or VM.

Why queue submissions instead of running them in the request?

Runs are slow and spiky (contests); a queue lets workers autoscale on depth while the client polls for the result.

Where do contest leaderboards live?

In a Redis sorted set keyed by contest, with score and tie-break encoded.

docs.title: Payment system (Stripe)
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Multi-step processes · DDIA: Ch 8 unknown outcomes · Ch 12 end-to-end idempotency, integrity · Ch 11 outbox

Throughput is moderate. The hard part is staying correct when a call to the bank has an unknown outcome.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: PAYMENT SYSTEM (STRIPE) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Record the payment as pending before calling the processor, and pass your ID as the idempotency key.
  • On a timeout, query by that key or retry it; never create a second charge.
  • Publish status changes through an outbox, keep an append-only double-entry ledger, and reconcile daily.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Merchants create payment intents; customers pay by card
  2. Merchants receive status via webhooks
  3. Refunds

Non-functional

  • Never double-charge (exactly-once effect)
  • Durable and auditable; strongly consistent ledger
  • ~10k TPS
  • PCI: raw card data isolated

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 10k TPS is moderate for a well-indexed Postgres cluster. The hard part is correctness under unknown outcomes, not throughput.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
payment_intents(id, merchant, amount, status state machine)
ledger_entries(id, txn_id, account, debit, credit) append-only
outbox

POST /payment_intents {amount, currency} + Idempotency-Key
POST /payment_intents/{id}/confirm {payment_method_token}
webhook → merchant: payment.succeeded / failed

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
When a customer pays, the API calls the card processor ("charge this card $50"), waits for the result, and then writes a payments row with the outcome.

Where it breaks: look at what happens if anything fails between the processor call and the database write.

  • The server crashes after the processor charged the card but before the row was written. The customer has been charged, and we have no record of it.
  • The processor call times out. Did it charge or not? We don't know (see DDIA Ch 8). If we retry, we may charge twice. If we don't, we may lose a real payment.
  • The merchant's own server retries its request after a network blip, and we create a second payment.

Throughput (about 10k transactions a second) isn't the hard part. Correctness when outcomes are unknown is.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: record intent first, call the processor with our ID
docs.text:
Why: we need a record that exists before money can move, so after any crash or timeout we can find out what happened instead of guessing.

How: create the payment intent in our database with status PENDING first. Then call the processor, passing our intent ID as the processor's idempotency key. Then record the result (SUCCEEDED or FAILED). If we crash or time out, the PENDING row remains. A recovery job retries the call with the same idempotency key, which the processor treats as the same request and never charges twice, or queries the processor for that ID's status. We never create a fresh charge for an existing intent.

docs.title: Step 2: protect against client retries, and isolate card data
docs.text:
Why: merchants' servers retry too, and each retry mustn't become a new payment. And raw card numbers are dangerous to store: any system that touches them falls under strict PCI rules.

How: every mutating API call requires an Idempotency-Key from the merchant, stored with a unique index. A repeated key returns the original response instead of doing the work again. Card numbers go straight into an isolated, tightly controlled vault that returns a token. The rest of the system only ever sees tokens, which keeps most of it out of PCI scope.

docs.title: Step 3: reliable events, a ledger, and reconciliation
docs.text:
Why: merchants must be told reliably when a payment's status changes. The record of money must be correct and auditable forever. And bugs or processor errors must be caught.

How:

  • Every status change writes an outbox row in the same transaction. A relay publishes it, and webhooks go to the merchant, signed and retried with backoff (see Transactional outbox).
  • Money movements are recorded as append-only double-entry ledger rows (see deep dive).
  • A daily reconciliation job compares our ledger with the processor's settlement files and flags every difference.

docs.title: Processor times out?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: a timeout doesn't mean failure. The charge may have succeeded and only the reply was lost. Assuming failure and retrying with a new request double-charges. Assuming success loses money if it actually failed.

How: treat it as unknown. Keep the intent PENDING, and resolve it by either retrying with the same idempotency key (the processor returns the original result if it already charged) or querying the processor's status for our reference. The user sees "processing" until it's resolved. Reconciliation is the final safety net.

docs.title: Webhook delivery?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: we must notify the merchant of every status change, but their server may be down, slow or failing. And sending the webhook separately from the database update risks one without the other (the dual-write problem).

How: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the status change, so the event exists if and only if the change does. A relay delivers webhooks with exponential backoff for hours or days, signs each one (HMAC) so merchants can verify it came from us, and includes an event_id so merchants can deduplicate the inevitable repeats.

docs.title: Why double-entry?
docs.text:
Why not just a balance column: updating balance = balance - 50 overwrites history. If a bug or race corrupts it, you can't tell what happened or fix it reliably.

How: record every movement of money as entries that sum to zero: debit the customer $50, credit the merchant $48.50, credit fees $1.50. Entries are appended, never updated or deleted. A mistake is fixed by adding correcting entries. Any account's balance is the sum of its entries, and the books must always balance across all accounts. Any imbalance immediately reveals a bug, and you have a complete audit trail.

docs.title: Distributed transaction with the bank?
docs.text:
Why you can't have one: the processor and the banks are separate companies. They won't hold locks or take part in a two-phase commit with your database, and their operations can't be rolled back like a database transaction.

How: design the payment as a state machine (created → pending → succeeded / failed → refunded), where every transition is recorded durably and every external call is idempotent. When something must be undone, use a compensating action, a refund, rather than a rollback. Use reconciliation against the processor's records to catch anything that slipped through.

docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Merchants create payment intents; customers pay by card; Merchants receive status via webhooks; Refunds 5–8 Non-functional requirements Never double-charge (exactly-once effect); Durable and auditable; strongly consistent ledger; ~10k TPS; PCI: raw card data isolated 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 10k TPS is moderate for a well-indexed Postgres cluster. The hard part is correctness under unknown outcomes, not throughput. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Postgres → Card vault → Kafka (outbox relay) → Webhook service → Daily reconcile. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Processor times out? · Webhook delivery? · Why double-entry? · Distributed transaction with the bank? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

Staff call and trade-off Pending record first, idempotency keys, outbox, double-entry ledger, daily reconciliation. Accept extra writes for auditability. Raise before you're asked Processor timeouts; duplicate webhooks; partial refunds; PCI scope creep. Senior stops at Idempotency keys. Staff goes on to Ledger design, reconciliation, isolating card data to shrink compliance scope. Run it Watch reconciliation breaks, age of pending payments, webhook delivery success.

docs.title: 8. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using 2PC or assuming the processor call succeeds or fails cleanly.
  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.
  • Skipping failure handling: what happens on timeouts, retries and crashes.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why record the payment as pending before calling the processor?

If you crash or time out you still have a record and an ID to reconcile with; nothing exists only at the processor.

The processor call times out. What do you do?

Query by your idempotency key, or retry with the same key. Never create a second charge.

Why a double-entry ledger?

Every movement is two balancing entries, so money is never created or lost and errors show up when sums don't match.

docs.title: Photo sharing (Instagram)
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Handling large blobs · Scaling reads · DDIA: Ch 1 fan-out · Ch 11 async pipelines

A news feed plus a media pipeline: two well-known problems combined.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: PHOTO SHARING (INSTAGRAM) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Upload media straight to object storage; process thumbnails and sizes asynchronously; serve them from a CDN.
  • Build feeds with fan-out on write into Redis, and pull celebrity posts at read time.
  • Show a post only once its media has finished processing.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Post photos and videos with captions
  2. Follow users
  3. View a feed of followed users' posts

Non-functional

  • Feed p99 < 500ms
  • Media upload and delivery fast globally
  • 500M DAU
  • Eventual consistency for the feed

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 500M DAU × 20 feed loads ≈ ~115k feed reads/s. 100M posts/day; media ~2MB avg → 200TB/day to S3, served by CDN.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
posts(id, author, caption, media_keys, status)
follows
feed:{user} ZSET

POST /posts {caption} → {post_id, presigned upload URL}
GET /feed?cursor
POST /users/{id}/follow

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Users upload photos and videos through the API, which stores them and creates a post. The feed is built when a user opens it: find who they follow, fetch those users' recent posts, merge by time.

Where it breaks: both halves fail at this scale.

  • Media: 100M posts a day at ~2 MB average is about 200 TB a day passing through the API servers, plus all the downloads. The servers become expensive bandwidth pipes, and uploads on mobile connections fail and restart.
  • Feed: about 115k feed loads a second, each needing lookups across hundreds of followed accounts, means millions of queries a second. The 500 ms p99 isn't achievable (the same problem as News feed).

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: media goes straight to object storage, is processed asynchronously, and is served by a CDN
docs.text:
Why: media bytes are large and must be fast to upload and view anywhere in the world. App servers should handle only small requests.

How:

  • POST /posts creates the post with status PROCESSING and returns a presigned upload URL.
  • The app uploads the photo or video directly to S3.
  • An S3 event triggers workers that create thumbnails and several sizes (and video renditions). When they finish, the post's status becomes READY.
  • All media is served through a CDN, so viewers download from a nearby edge server, and your servers never touch the bytes.

docs.title: Step 2: precompute feeds, with a hybrid for celebrities
docs.text:
Why: feeds are read far more often than posts are created, so computing them on each read wastes work, exactly as in the news feed problem.

How: when a post becomes READY, put a "new post" event on Kafka. Fan-out workers push the post ID into each follower's feed list in Redis (a sorted set by time). Reading a feed is then one Redis read, plus a batch fetch of post details. Accounts with millions of followers are not fanned out; their posts are pulled at read time and merged in (the hybrid approach).

docs.title: Post visible before media is processed?
docs.text:
Why it's a problem: if a post appears in followers' feeds as soon as it's created, they may see a broken image or a video that won't play, because thumbnails and renditions aren't ready yet.

How: keep the post in PROCESSING status and only fan it out to followers when processing marks it READY. Meanwhile, the author can see it in their own profile with a "processing" indicator, using the original upload or a local copy on their phone.

docs.title: Celebrities?
docs.text:
Why they're a problem: pushing one post into 100M followers' feeds means 100M writes, delaying it by minutes and backing up everyone else's posts.

How: the same hybrid as News feed: skip fan-out for accounts above a follower threshold. When a user opens their feed, merge their precomputed list with the recent posts of the celebrities they follow, which are heavily cached because many users fetch the same ones.

docs.title: Like counts?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: a popular post can get thousands of likes a second. Running UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 for each one makes every like wait on the same row's lock.

How: count likes in Redis with atomic INCR (thousands a second per key is fine), or spread one post's count over several sharded counters (likes:post7:0 … :9) added up on read. Flush totals to the database periodically for durability. The displayed count can lag a little, and nobody minds. Who liked what is recorded separately (one row per like), so a user can't like twice.

docs.title: Global latency?
docs.text:
Why it matters: users are everywhere, and round trips to one data centre add hundreds of milliseconds for distant users.

How: media is served by the CDN from edge locations near users, which is the bulk of the bytes. For feeds and metadata, run read replicas or caches in several regions, so feed reads are served locally. Writes go to the home region, and a few seconds of replication lag is fine for a feed.

docs.title: Post search (Facebook)
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Scaling writes · Scaling reads · DDIA: Ch 3 inverted index · Ch 6 term-partitioned index · Ch 11 stream indexing

Search over billions of posts, where like counts change constantly.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: POST SEARCH (FACEBOOK) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Build an inverted index (term → post IDs) from the stream of new posts, sharded by term.
  • Keep two orderings per term, recency and likes, and update like-based ranking only at thresholds or in batches.
  • Keep hot postings in memory, move old ones to cheaper storage, and cache popular queries.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Search posts by keyword
  2. Sort results by recency or by likes
  3. (Inputs: create posts, like posts)

Non-functional

  • Search < 500ms
  • New posts searchable within ~1 minute
  • Huge write volume (posts and likes)
  • Read volume ~10k searches/s

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: ~1B posts/day ≈ 12k/s and ~10× that in likes. Indexing every like individually is far too much write load, so batch it.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
inverted index: term → post IDs (recency list) and term → ZSET(post_id, like_bucket)

GET /search?q&sort=recency|likes&cursor

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Search the posts table directly: SELECT … FROM posts WHERE content LIKE '%term%' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20.

Where it breaks: a LIKE '%term%' with a leading wildcard can't use a normal index, because the database doesn't know where in the text the word starts. So every search reads every post. With about a billion new posts a day, the table holds hundreds of billions of rows. One search would take hours, and we need 10k searches a second under 500 ms. Sorting by likes makes it worse: like counts change constantly, about 10× more often than posts are created.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: build an inverted index
docs.text:
Why: we need to go from a word to the posts containing it without reading every post.

How: an inverted index maps each term to its list of post IDs (its posting list): "marathon" → [post 981, post 4410, …], like the index at the back of a book. New posts flow from an event stream (Kafka). An indexer splits each post into terms and appends its ID to each term's posting list. New posts become searchable within seconds. The index is sharded by term, so all of one term's postings live on one shard, and a single-word search reads one list from one shard.

docs.title: Step 2: keep two orderings, and don't re-index on every like
docs.text:
Why: users sort by recency or by likes. Recency is easy: posts arrive in time order, so appending keeps each list sorted. Likes are hard. There are about 10× more likes than posts, and re-sorting a posting list on every like is far too much write load.

How: for each term, keep a recency list (append-only) and a separate likes-sorted set (term → sorted set of (post_id, like_score)). Don't update the like score on every like. Update it only when a post's count crosses a threshold (1, 2, 4, 8… likes, powers of two), or in per-minute batches. Ranking only needs to be roughly right, and exact like counts live in the posts store.

docs.title: Step 3: tier storage, cache popular queries, handle multiple words
docs.text:
Why: posting lists for common terms grow huge, and most searches are for recent content. Some queries ("world cup") are repeated by millions of people.

How: keep the recent, hot part of each posting list in memory and move older parts to cheaper storage (blob storage), fetched only when someone scrolls far back. Cache results for popular queries for a short time. For multi-word queries, fetch each term's list and intersect them (see deep dive).

docs.title: Why not just Elasticsearch?
docs.text:
The honest answer: in a real system, Elasticsearch (or OpenSearch) is a perfectly good choice, and it's built on exactly this inverted index. Know how it scales: it partitions by document, so each shard indexes its own subset of posts, and a search asks every shard and merges (scatter-gather). New documents become searchable after a refresh interval (about 1 second by default).

Why the interviewer asks: this problem tests whether you understand what's underneath: posting lists, partitioning by term vs by document, and how to handle a ranking signal that changes constantly. Say you'd use Elasticsearch, then show you could reason about its internals.

docs.title: Likes change constantly?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: a viral post can get thousands of likes a second, and each would move it in the likes-sorted set of every term it contains: dozens of index writes per like.

How: decouple ranking from exact counts. The index stores a coarse like score that changes only when the count crosses a threshold (powers of two means a post with a million likes has changed score only about 20 times), or that is refreshed in batches every minute. Exact counts live in a separate counter store. Search ranking doesn't need to know whether it's 10,341 or 10,342 likes.

docs.title: Multi-keyword?
docs.text:
Why it's tricky: "marathon training plan" needs posts containing all three words. Each posting list may have millions of entries.

How: intersect the posting lists, starting with the shortest one ("marathon" is rarer than "plan"). Walk through the short list and check membership in the longer ones, which is fast if the lists are sorted by post ID or have skip pointers. For common phrases, a bigram index (pairs of adjacent words, such as "training plan") gives a short list directly.

docs.title: Hot term?
docs.text:
Why it's a problem: with a term-partitioned index, all searches for one term go to one shard. During a big event, millions of people search the same word, and that shard is overwhelmed while others are idle.

How: replicate hot terms across several shards and spread reads among the copies. Combine that with query result caching: when millions search "world cup", most get a cached result a few seconds old, and the index barely notices.

docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Search posts by keyword; Sort results by recency or by likes; (Inputs: create posts, like posts) 5–8 Non-functional requirements Search < 500ms; New posts searchable within ~1 minute; Huge write volume (posts and likes); Read volume ~10k searches/s 8–10 Numbers that drive the design ~1B posts/day ≈ 12k/s and ~10× that in likes. Indexing every like individually is far too much write load, so batch it. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Kafka → Indexing workers → Inverted index → Query service → Like batcher → Cold postings → S3 → Query cache. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Why not just Elasticsearch? · Likes change constantly? · Multi-keyword? · Hot term? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.title: Price tracker (CamelCamelCamel)
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Scaling writes · Scaling reads · DDIA: Ch 11 event-driven · Ch 3 time-series storage

Five hundred million products can't all be crawled often, so decide what is worth checking.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: PRICE TRACKER (CAMELCAMELCAMEL) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Prioritise crawling by how many people track a product and how often its price changes.
  • Add crowd-sourced prices from a browser extension, validated before they trigger alerts.
  • Make alerts event-driven: when a price drops, look up subscriptions for that product only.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Track price history for products
  2. Users subscribe to alerts at a target price
  3. View price charts

Non-functional

  • 500M products
  • Alert within ~1 hour of a drop
  • Respect site rate limits (crawl budget)
  • Charts load fast

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 500M products crawled daily = ~6k pages/s, which runs into rate limits. Subscriptions are concentrated on a small fraction of products, so prioritize those.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
price_history(product_id, ts, price) time-series
subscriptions(product_id, user_id, target_price) indexed (product_id, target_price)

POST /subscriptions {product_id, target_price}
GET /products/{id}/history?range

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Crawl every one of the 500 million tracked product pages once a day, store each price, and once a day run a job that compares every subscription's target price with the latest price.

Where it breaks:

  • Crawl budget: 500M pages a day is about 6k page fetches a second, all against a handful of retailer sites. Retailers rate-limit and block crawlers long before that. Even if allowed, once a day is too slow: the requirement is an alert within an hour of a price drop.
  • Wasted effort: most of those 500M products have no subscribers, and their prices rarely change. Meanwhile, products people actually care about are checked only once a day.
  • Alert matching: scanning all subscriptions every day to find matches is slow and mostly finds nothing.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: prioritize what to crawl
docs.text:
Why: the crawl budget is limited by retailers' rate limits, so spend it where it matters. Subscriptions are concentrated on a small fraction of products.

How: a scheduler gives each product a crawl frequency based on how many people track it and how often its price changes. A popular, volatile product (a TV during sales season) is checked every hour or so; a product with no subscribers and a stable price might be checked weekly. The scheduler puts due products into the crawl queue, and crawlers respect each retailer's robots rules and rate limits.

docs.title: Step 2: add crowd-sourced prices from a browser extension
docs.text:
Why: even prioritized crawling can't check everything often. But users already visit these product pages constantly.

How: a browser extension reports the price a user sees when they view a product page. That's extra coverage, for free, exactly on the products people are looking at. This data can be wrong (a regional price, a logged-in discount, a malicious report), so validate it: require several agreeing reports, or trigger a crawler re-check before trusting a price drop enough to send alerts.

docs.title: Step 3: record price changes, alert on events
docs.text:
Why: checking every subscription every day is wasteful when most prices didn't change.

How: whenever a crawl or validated report shows a different price, emit a price-change event and append it to the price history, a time-series table. Each event triggers the alert check for that product only: SELECT … FROM subscriptions WHERE product_id = ? AND target_price >= :new_price, served by an index on (product_id, target_price). Matching users are notified, deduplicated so a user isn't alerted twice for the same drop.

docs.title: Crawl budget?
docs.text:
Why it's the core constraint: retailers limit how fast you can fetch, and ignoring that gets you blocked entirely. You can't check 500M products often, so the design is really about choosing which to check when.

How: score each product by subscriber count and observed price volatility, and turn the score into a check interval. Adapt continuously: if a product's price just changed, check it again sooner; if it hasn't changed in weeks, back off. Respect robots.txt and per-retailer rate limits with a per-domain token bucket, and use retailers' official product APIs where they exist.

docs.title: Bad extension data?
docs.text:
Why it's a risk: extension reports come from users' browsers. They might show a member-only price, a different country's price, a temporary cart discount, or be deliberately faked. A false "price dropped!" alert sends thousands of users to a deal that doesn't exist.

How: treat extension data as a hint, not the truth. Trigger alerts only when N independent reports agree (from different users and IPs), or when a crawler re-check confirms the new price. Track each reporter's reliability over time and down-weight or ignore those who are often wrong.

docs.title: Matching efficiently?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: there can be hundreds of millions of subscriptions. Comparing all of them against all prices on a schedule is a massive, mostly pointless job.

How: invert the direction: react to price changes instead of scanning subscriptions. A price change for product P runs one query, "subscriptions for P with a target at or above the new price", which an index on (product_id, target_price) answers by reading only the matching rows. Work is proportional to actual price drops, not to the number of subscriptions.

docs.title: Charts?
docs.text:
Why they need care: a product's full history can be thousands of price points, and popular products' charts are viewed constantly.

How: precompute daily aggregates (minimum, maximum, closing price per day) from the price history, and render charts from those. A year is just 365 points. Cache the chart data per product and refresh it when a new price change arrives.

Subscriptions are concentrated on a small fraction of products, so prioritize those. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Browser extension → Kafka → Time-series DB → Alert matcher → Subscriptions DB → Email / push. docs.title: Rate limiter
docs.text:
Intermediate

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Scaling reads · Dealing with contention · DDIA: Ch 7 lost update · Ch 6 shard by key

Every public API needs one, and the obvious implementation has a race condition.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: RATE LIMITER on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Counting per server gives each client N times its limit; the counter must be shared, usually in Redis.
  • Read-then-write on a shared counter races. Do the refill, check and decrement atomically in one Lua script.
  • Decide what happens when Redis is down: allow traffic (fail-open) or block it (fail-closed), per endpoint.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Limit requests per client (user, IP, API key) by configurable rules
  2. Return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers

Non-functional

  • Adds < 10ms latency
  • Accurate across many API servers
  • Highly available (choose fail-open vs fail-closed)
  • 1M requests/sec total

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 1M req/s = 1M Redis ops/s; one Redis node does ~100k ops/s, so a ~10–20 shard Redis Cluster keyed by client. 10M active keys × 100B ≈ 1GB of memory.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
rules(endpoint, limit, window)
bucket:{client}:{rule} → {tokens, last_refill}

isAllowed(client_key, rule) → {allowed, remaining, reset_at}
Response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit / Remaining / Reset

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
The simplest rate limiter lives inside each API server: an in-memory map from client to a request counter. When a request arrives, increment the client's counter. If it's over the limit (say 100 a minute), return 429 Too Many Requests.

Where it breaks: the API runs on many servers behind a load balancer, and each server counts only the requests it sees. With 50 servers, a client spreading requests across them can make 100 per minute on each one, which is 50× the limit. Adding servers to handle traffic makes the limit even weaker. The count has to be shared.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: move the counters to a shared store
docs.text:
Why: every server must see the same count for a client, or the limit is multiplied by the number of servers.

How: keep the counters in Redis, keyed by client and rule (bucket:{api_key}:{rule}). Every API server reads and updates the same key. Redis answers in well under a millisecond on the same network, which fits the "adds under 10 ms" requirement. At 1M requests a second, use a Redis Cluster of about 10–20 shards. Keys are spread by client, so each shard handles its share.

docs.title: Step 2: make the check-and-update atomic
docs.text:
Why: the obvious code is "GET the count, check it, SET count + 1". Two servers handling the same client at the same moment both GET 99, both decide 99 < 100, and both allow the request. That's a lost update race, and under load it lets clients exceed their limits.

How: do the whole check inside Redis in one step. Redis runs commands one at a time, so a Lua script that refills the client's tokens, checks and decrements runs atomically, and no other command can sneak in between. It's also one network round trip instead of two. For a simple fixed window, INCR followed by EXPIRE is atomic enough, because INCR returns the new value.

docs.title: Step 3: load rules from config, and decide what happens when Redis fails
docs.text:
Why: limits change (a customer upgrades their plan), and you can't redeploy every server to change a number. And Redis is now on the path of every request: if it's unreachable, every request must still get an answer, allow or block.

How: store rules (endpoint, limit, window) in a config store and cache them in each gateway, refreshing every few seconds. For Redis outages, decide per endpoint: fail-open (allow traffic) for normal APIs, because blocking everyone is worse than briefly allowing too much; fail-closed (block) for sensitive endpoints such as login or payments, where abuse is the bigger risk.

docs.title: Which algorithm?
docs.text:
Why it matters: different algorithms let through different bursts and cost different amounts of memory.

How they compare:

  • Token bucket (the industry default): each client has a bucket holding up to capacity tokens, refilled at a steady rate. Each request spends one, and an empty bucket means 429. It allows short bursts up to the capacity while enforcing the average rate, and it stores just two numbers per client.
  • Fixed window: count requests per calendar minute. It's simple, but a client can send 100 at 10:00:59 and another 100 at 10:01:00, which is 200 in two seconds.
  • Sliding-window log: store every request timestamp and count those in the last 60 seconds. It's exact, but stores one entry per request.
  • Sliding-window counter: blend the current and previous fixed windows by how far into the current window you are. It's a close approximation with fixed-window cost.

docs.title: Race between servers?
docs.text:
Why it happens: read-modify-write from several servers on the same counter is the classic lost update (DDIA Ch 7). Both servers read the old value before either writes.

How: never split the read and the write across round trips. Use a Lua script that does refill, check and decrement in one atomic step, or atomic commands like INCR. Redis is single-threaded per shard, so these are applied one after another.

docs.title: Redis is down?
docs.text:
Why it matters: every request now depends on Redis, so its outage must not become your outage.

How: fall back to local limiting in each server, using the limit divided by the number of servers. It's imprecise, but it still stops floods. Whether to fail open or closed is a product decision per endpoint: open for browsing APIs, closed for login, signup and payments. Put a short timeout on the Redis call (a few milliseconds) so a slow Redis can't slow every request.

docs.title: Very hot client?
docs.text:
Why it's a problem: one client's key always maps to one Redis shard. A client sending 100k requests a second sends all of that load to a single shard.

How: give each API server a local allowance, a share of that client's limit that it can spend without asking Redis, and sync the counts every few hundred milliseconds. Redis sees one update per server per interval instead of one per request. The trade-off is accuracy: the client might slightly exceed the limit between syncs. That's usually acceptable for very high limits.

Then add, in order: Redis Cluster → Lua script → Rules config. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Which algorithm? · Race between servers? · Redis is down? · Very hot client? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

Staff goes on to Plan tiers, global vs regional limits, rules as versioned config with shadow mode, and protecting the limiter itself. Run it Watch rejection rate per rule, limiter p99, Redis CPU. Roll out new rules in shadow (log-only) first.

docs.text:
• Counters in Postgres: 1M writes/sec of throwaway data.
  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.
  • Skipping failure handling: what happens on timeouts, retries and crashes.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why can't each API server count requests on its own?

With N servers behind a load balancer each client effectively gets N times its limit. The counter must be shared, typically in Redis.

How do you avoid races between servers updating the same counter?

Do the refill, check and decrement atomically in one Redis Lua script (or an atomic INCR with expiry), not read-then-write.

What happens when Redis is down?

You choose per endpoint: fail-open (allow traffic, risk abuse) for most APIs, fail-closed (block) for sensitive ones such as login or payments.

docs.title: Ride sharing (Uber)
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Real-time updates · DDIA: Ch 8 leases · Ch 3 geo index · Ch 6 partition by region

Four problems in one: a flood of location updates, matching, locking drivers, and a multi-step trip lifecycle.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: RIDE SHARING (UBER) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Driver locations are ephemeral and frequent, so keep them in Redis's geospatial index, not a database.
  • Offer a ride to one driver at a time and lock that driver with a short TTL so they can't get two offers.
  • Run ride requests through a durable, per-region queue so a crashed matcher loses nothing.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Rider requests a ride (pickup, destination) and sees a fare estimate
  2. Match to a nearby available driver; driver accepts or declines
  3. Live location of driver during the trip

Non-functional

  • Match within ~1 minute
  • A driver is never assigned two rides (consistency)
  • High availability for location updates
  • Handle surge peaks per city

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 1M active drivers × 1 update/4s = 250k location writes/s, ephemeral (only the latest matters). Ride requests ~100/s avg.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
rides(id, rider, driver, status, pickup, dest, fare)
driver_location in Redis GEO (TTL)

POST /rides/estimate
POST /rides {estimate_id}
POST /drivers/location {lat, lng}
PATCH /rides/{id} {accept|decline}

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Every driver's app sends its GPS position every few seconds, and the server updates a driver_locations row in Postgres. When a rider requests a ride, the matcher queries the nearest available drivers and assigns the closest one.

Where it breaks:

  • Location writes: 1M active drivers, each updating every 4 seconds, is 250k writes a second, each one an update that creates a new row version and touches indexes. That's far beyond one Postgres primary. And all that data is throwaway: only each driver's latest position matters, and it's stale within seconds.
  • Double assignment: two riders requesting at the same moment can both be matched with the same nearby driver.
  • Lost requests: if the matcher process crashes mid-match, the rider's request may simply vanish.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: keep driver locations in memory, in Redis GEO
docs.text:
Why: location data is high-volume, short-lived and only the latest value matters. That's the opposite of what a durable, transactional database is built for.

How: store locations in Redis's geospatial index. GEOADD drivers <lng> <lat> <driver_id> overwrites the driver's position in memory in microseconds, and GEOSEARCH finds drivers within a radius of a pickup point. Give each driver a TTL key refreshed on every update, so drivers whose app goes silent drop out of matching automatically. At 250k updates a second, shard by city or region across Redis nodes.

docs.title: Step 2: offer to one driver at a time, and lock them while you wait
docs.text:
Why: a driver must never get two rides. Without coordination, two matchers can pick the same closest driver for two different riders.

How: the matcher picks the best candidate and takes a lock on that driver before offering: SET driver_lock:{id} {ride_id} NX PX 10000. NX means only one matcher can set it; the 10-second expiry matches the accept window. Then it sends the offer. If the driver declines or doesn't answer in 10 seconds, the lock expires and the matcher tries the next driver. When the driver accepts, the ride is assigned in Postgres with a conditional update (UPDATE rides SET driver_id = :d WHERE id = :r AND driver_id IS NULL), so even a stray duplicate can't assign twice.

docs.title: Step 3: run requests through a durable, regional queue
docs.text:
Why: matching can take a minute (several offers and declines). If the matcher crashes in the middle, the request must not be lost. And demand spikes city by city (concert ends, rain starts).

How: ride requests go onto a durable queue partitioned by region. Matchers for each region consume their partition, so a surge in one city is handled by scaling that city's matchers. A request is acknowledged only once the ride is assigned or cancelled. If a matcher dies, the request is redelivered to another, which carries on safely because each step is keyed by ride_id.

docs.title: Driver double-assigned?
docs.text:
Why it happens: matching is "find nearest free driver, then assign". Two matchers handling two riders near each other both find the same driver free and both assign them, a check-then-act race.

How: two layers. A per-driver lock with a TTL (Redis SET NX PX) means only one offer at a time per driver; the TTL equals the accept window, so an ignored offer automatically becomes a decline. Then the durable assignment in Postgres is a conditional update that only succeeds if the ride, and the driver's current status, are still unassigned. The lock prevents wasted offers; the database guarantees correctness.

docs.title: Reduce location load?
docs.text:
Why it matters: 250k updates a second costs bandwidth, battery and server capacity, and much of it is redundant.

How: make updates adaptive. A driver who is parked or waiting at a light sends updates less often (every 15–30 seconds); a moving driver on a trip sends more. The app can also batch a few points per request. Only send when the position has changed meaningfully, say 20+ metres.

docs.title: Why not query Postgres + PostGIS?
docs.text:
Why it's tempting: PostGIS answers "drivers within 2 km" perfectly well, and keeping everything in one database is simpler.

Why not here: the problem isn't the query, it's the writes. 250k updates a second of data that is obsolete within seconds would swamp a disk-based, transactional database: each update writes a new row version, a WAL record and index changes, for data you never need to keep. It belongs in memory. Postgres keeps what must be durable: rides, payments, ratings.

docs.title: Matcher crash mid-match?
docs.text:
Why it's a risk: a matcher might have locked a driver and sent an offer when it crashes. Without care, the rider waits forever, or a retry offers the same ride twice.

How: the request stays on the durable queue until matching completes, so a crash means redelivery to another matcher. Every step is idempotent, keyed by ride_id. The lock value is the ride ID, so a retry recognises its own lock, and the final assignment is conditional. A workflow engine (Temporal, Step Functions) can also track each ride's progress explicitly.

docs.title: 7. Interview script (45 minutes)
docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Rider requests a ride (pickup, destination) and sees a fare estimate; Match to a nearby available driver; driver accepts or declines; Live location of driver during the trip 5–8 Non-functional requirements Match within ~1 minute; A driver is never assigned two rides (consistency); High availability for location updates; Handle surge peaks per city 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 1M active drivers × 1 update/4s = 250k location writes/s, ephemeral (only the latest matters). Ride requests ~100/s avg. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Redis GEO → Matching service → Redis lock → Request queue. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Driver double-assigned? · Reduce location load? · Why not query Postgres + PostGIS? · Matcher crash mid-match? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

docs.text:

Staff call and trade-off Redis GEO for locations; offer to one driver at a time with a driver lock and conditional assignment; durable per-region queue. Accept slightly slower matching. docs.title: 8. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Offering a ride to many drivers at once without locks, so two drivers accept the same ride.
  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.
  • Skipping failure handling: what happens on timeouts, retries and crashes.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why keep driver locations in Redis rather than a database?

Locations are ephemeral and updated every few seconds by every driver; an in-memory geospatial index handles the write rate and nearby queries.

How do you stop a driver getting two ride offers at once?

Offer to one driver at a time and lock that driver with a short-TTL key while the offer is pending.

What if the matcher crashes mid-match?

Ride requests sit in a durable per-region queue, so another matcher picks the request up again.

docs.title: Stock trading (Robinhood)
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Real-time updates · DDIA: Ch 8 unknown outcomes · Ch 12 idempotency · Ch 11 pub/sub

Two separate problems: pushing live prices to millions, and never losing or duplicating an order.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: STOCK TRADING (ROBINHOOD) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Prices: one consumer of the exchange feed publishes per symbol; push servers subscribe and stream to clients.
  • Orders: persist the order as pending with your own ID before sending it to the exchange.
  • Treat exchange calls as having unknown outcomes; reconcile by your order ID instead of resubmitting.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. See live stock prices for watched symbols
  2. Place market and limit orders; cancel orders
  3. See order status and fills

Non-functional

  • Price updates < 200ms
  • Orders never lost or duplicated
  • Strong consistency on order state
  • 20M users; market-open spikes

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: Exchange feed ~ thousands of updates/s for ~10k symbols. 20M users polling = millions of req/s, so push instead. Orders ~ thousands/s at peak.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
orders(id, user_id, symbol, status PENDING|SUBMITTED|FILLED|CANCELLED, exchange_order_id) partitioned by user

GET /prices/stream?symbols (SSE)
POST /orders {symbol, side, qty, type, limit?} + Idempotency-Key
DELETE /orders/{id}

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
There are really two separate problems here, with opposite needs, so it helps to look at the naive version of each.

  • Prices: the app polls GET /prices?symbols=… every second. With 20M users, that's millions of requests a second, mostly returning prices that barely changed, and still up to a second late.
  • Orders: the app calls our API, which forwards the order to the exchange and saves the result in our database after the exchange replies.

Where it breaks: polling can't meet the 200 ms price target at a sane cost. The order flow has a dangerous gap. If our server crashes, or the exchange call times out, after the order reached the exchange but before we saved anything, there is now a live order at the exchange that we don't know about. The user may retry and buy twice. For money, "orders never lost or duplicated" is the most important requirement.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: push prices, fanned out per symbol
docs.text:
Why: prices change continuously, and millions of users watch overlapping sets of symbols. Pushing each change once per symbol is far cheaper than millions of polls.

How: one consumer reads the exchange's market data feed and publishes each update to a channel per symbol (pub/sub). Realtime servers hold users' SSE connections and subscribe to the symbols their connected users are watching, then forward updates. Humans can't read hundreds of updates a second, so throttle to about one update a second per symbol for the app. That cuts load hugely without users noticing.

docs.title: Step 2: record the order before sending it
docs.text:
Why: the exchange call can fail in the worst way: we don't know whether it went through. We need a record that exists before the order could exist at the exchange, so we can always find out what happened.

How: when the user submits, first insert the order into our database with status PENDING and our own order ID. Then send it to the exchange, passing our ID as the clientOrderId. If we crash or time out at any point, the PENDING row tells us there might be an order out there, and we can ask the exchange "what's the status of clientOrderId X?" to reconcile rather than guess.

docs.title: Step 3: update from exchange events, and reconcile daily
docs.text:
Why: orders don't complete in the request. They're acknowledged, partially filled, filled or cancelled over seconds to days.

How: the exchange sends execution reports asynchronously, and a consumer updates each order's status from them (SUBMITTED → PARTIALLY_FILLED → FILLED), applying each report idempotently. A daily reconciliation job compares our orders and positions with the exchange's official reports and flags any difference for investigation.

docs.title: Write DB before or after the exchange call?
docs.text:
Why it matters: this single choice decides whether a crash can leave an order we don't know about.

How to think about it: after fails dangerously. If we crash between sending and saving, a real order sits at the exchange with no record on our side: the user's money is committed and we can't show it, cancel it or reconcile it. A timeout is the same: the exchange may have accepted it (see DDIA Ch 8). Before fails safely. The worst case is a PENDING row for an order that never reached the exchange, which reconciliation finds and marks as failed. Always record intent first.

docs.title: Duplicate submits?
docs.text:
Why it happens: a user double-taps "Buy", or the app retries after a timeout, and without protection that's two orders.

How: the app generates an Idempotency-Key per order attempt, and our orders table has a unique index on it, so a duplicate request returns the existing order instead of creating a new one. And because we pass our order ID as clientOrderId, the exchange also rejects a duplicate with the same ID. That's two independent layers.

docs.title: Cancel races with a fill?
docs.text:
Why it's tricky: the user taps "Cancel" just as the order executes at the exchange. Which wins?

How: treat cancel as a request, not a state change. Mark the order "cancel requested", send the cancel to the exchange, and update the status only from the exchange's reply: "cancelled", or "too late, filled". If it was partially filled, the filled part stands and only the rest is cancelled. The UI must show exactly what the exchange confirms.

docs.title: Market-open spike?
docs.text:
Why it happens: at 9:30 a.m., millions of users open the app at once, and order volume jumps many times over.

How: autoscale the realtime (SSE) servers ahead of the known daily spike, since it's predictable. Put per-user rate limits on order placement, queue order submissions so the exchange gateway isn't overwhelmed, and keep the price fan-out throttled. Prices can lag slightly under load, but orders must stay correct.

docs.title: 7. Interview script (45 minutes)
docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements See live stock prices for watched symbols; Place market and limit orders; cancel orders; See order status and fills 5–8 Non-functional requirements Price updates < 200ms; Orders never lost or duplicated; Strong consistency on order state; 20M users; market-open spikes 8–10 Numbers that drive the design Exchange feed ~ thousands of updates/s for ~10k symbols. 20M users polling = millions of req/s, so push instead. Orders ~ thousands/s at peak. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Price processor → Pub/sub → SSE servers → Order service → Postgres → Exchange gateway → Fill processor. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Write DB before or after the exchange call? · Duplicate submits? · Cancel races with a fill? · Market-open spike? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

Accept coarser price updates in the app. Raise before you're asked Unknown outcome on exchange timeout; duplicate orders; market-open spike. Senior stops at Separate price and order paths. Staff goes on to An order state machine, reconciliation against exchange reports, audit requirements, graceful degradation at open. Run it Watch order ack latency, reconciliation breaks, price fan-out lag.

docs.title: 8. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating the exchange call as a local function call, so timeouts create ghost or duplicate orders.
  • Adding components before showing which number makes them necessary.
  • Skipping failure handling: what happens on timeouts, retries and crashes.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why persist the order before sending it to the exchange?

If you crash after sending, you still have a record with your own ID to reconcile against; otherwise the order could exist only at the exchange.

The exchange call times out. Do you resubmit?

No. The outcome is unknown; query or reconcile by your order ID instead of resubmitting, which could double-trade.

How are live prices fanned out?

One consumer of the exchange feed publishes per symbol; push servers subscribe and stream to clients.

docs.title: Ticketmaster: selling seats without selling any seat twice
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Medium · Patterns: Dealing with contention · Scaling reads · Core concept: Caching · DDIA: Ch 5 Replication, Ch 7 Transactions

Tip

One-page sketchnote: TICKETMASTER on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Two very different paths share one system. Browsing events is enormous, read-only traffic that can be slightly stale, so cache it hard. Booking is small but must be exactly right.
  • The core bug is check, then book: two people both see seat 12A as free and both buy it. Fix it by making the check and the write one atomic statement in the database.
  • For a huge on-sale, don't let 10 million people hit the booking path at once. A virtual waiting room admits them at the rate the system can actually handle.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional (what users can do)

  1. View an event and its seat map.
  2. Search for events by name, date and location.
  3. Book tickets: pick seats, hold them while paying, then confirm.

Out of scope for this page: resale, dynamic pricing, recommendations.

Non-functional (how well it must work; these drive the design)

NFR Target Why it matters here Consistency (booking) A seat is never sold twice This is the whole product. Choose consistency over availability on this path. Availability (browse) Event pages and search stay up during spikes Choose availability; a seat map that's a few seconds stale is fine. Latency Event page p99 < 300 ms, search p99 < 500 ms Fans refresh constantly during an on-sale. Scale ~10M users arrive for one popular on-sale Traffic is extremely spiky, not steady. Hold time A held seat is reserved ~10 minutes during checkout Long enough to pay, short enough not to block others.

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text:
• A stadium has roughly 50k–100k seats. That is the ceiling on successful bookings for one event, however many people show up.
  • 10M fans refreshing every few seconds is millions of reads/sec, but nearly all of them are identical page views. That makes them ideal for a CDN or cache.
  • So the read path needs to absorb millions of requests/sec, while the write path handles at most ~100k bookings spread over minutes.

Tip

Say this in the interview: "Reads and writes differ by orders of magnitude here, so I'll design two paths: a cached, eventually consistent browse path and a small, strongly consistent booking path."

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
Entity Key fields Event id, venue_id, name, date Ticket id, event_id, seat, price, status (AVAILABLE / HELD / BOOKED), hold_until, user_id Booking id, user_id, ticket_ids, payment_status 
GET  /events/{id}                       → event details + seat map
GET  /search?q=&date=&location=         → events
POST /bookings/hold    {ticket_ids}     → booking_id, hold_until
POST /bookings/{id}/confirm             → called after payment succeeds

Every POST carries an Idempotency-Key header so a retry never creates a second booking. The user id comes from the auth token, never from the request body.

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
One API server and one Postgres database. To book, the API reads the seat, sees AVAILABLE, then inserts a booking.

What breaks: the read and the write are two separate steps. Two requests that arrive within milliseconds both read "free" before either has written, and both succeed. Adding more servers makes this more likely, not less.

This is a write skew: each transaction is fine on its own, but together they break the rule "one seat, one buyer". Most databases don't prevent it at their default isolation level. Postgres defaults to Read Committed.

docs.title: 5. Final design
docs.text: Component Why it exists CDN Serves event pages and a seat-map snapshot from the edge, so millions of identical reads never reach your servers. Event service + Elasticsearch Search by text, date and location. Elasticsearch is a derived copy, kept in sync from Postgres by change data capture (CDC), never written to directly. Waiting room Only switched on for hot on-sales. Users join a queue and are admitted in batches, so the booking path sees steady, survivable load. Booking service Holds seats with one atomic conditional UPDATE (see the deep dive), then confirms after payment. Postgres The single source of truth for tickets and bookings. One primary is enough, because booking volume is capped by seat count. Payment provider Called with an idempotency key. Its webhook flips the booking from HELD to BOOKED.

docs.title: 6.1 How exactly do we stop double booking?
docs.text:
Put the check inside the write:

UPDATE tickets
SET    status = 'HELD', user_id = :user, hold_until = now() + interval '10 minutes'
WHERE  id = :ticket
  AND (status = 'AVAILABLE' OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_until < now()));

The database locks the row while it applies the update, so concurrent requests are serialized. 1 row updated means you hold the seat. 0 rows means someone else got there first.

Notice what we didn't need:

  • No background job to release abandoned holds. An expired hold simply satisfies the WHERE clause again.
  • No long transaction while the user pays. The hold is a row state, not an open lock, so the database never waits on a human.

Alternatives, and when they fit:

Option Good when Watch out for Conditional UPDATE (above) Default. Single database. None for this problem. SELECT … FOR UPDATE Multi-step logic on a few rows Holding locks too long; deadlocks across several seats. Lock seats in a fixed order. Redis SET seat:12A user NX EX 600 Holds shared across services; very hot seats Redis is not the source of truth, so still write the final booking to Postgres. Locks need fencing if a process can pause.

docs.title: 6.2 Ten million people at 10:00:00
docs.text:
Without protection, everyone hits Book in the same second. Even a correct database melts, and users see errors instead of "sold out".

Virtual waiting room:

  1. Users who arrive before the on-sale get a queue position (Redis sorted set, score = arrival time).
  2. Every few seconds, admit the next N users. N is chosen from what the booking path can sustain.
  3. Push "it's your turn" over SSE. Admitted users get a short-lived token that the booking service checks.

The booking service only ever sees the load you planned for, and users get a fair, honest wait instead of errors.

docs.title: 6.3 The seat map is stale. Is that a bug?
docs.text: No, as long as you're deliberate about it. The seat map is a snapshot served from cache or CDN and refreshed every few seconds. A user might click a seat that was taken a second ago, and the conditional update simply tells them so. The browse path is allowed to be wrong; the booking path never is.

docs.title: 6.4 What if payment times out?
docs.text: The outcome is unknown: the card may or may not have been charged. Keep the booking HELD and retry with the same idempotency key, or ask the provider for the status of that key. Never start a second charge. The webhook is the source of truth for the final state, and it must be idempotent too, because providers deliver webhooks more than once.

docs.title: 7. Interview script (45 minutes)
docs.text: Time What you do What you say 0–5 Functional requirements "Users can view events, search, and book seats with a short hold during checkout." 5–8 NFRs "No seat sold twice: that path is CP. Browsing must survive huge spikes: that path is AP." 8–10 Numbers "Bookings are capped by seat count (~100k); reads are millions per second and identical." 10–13 Entities + API Ticket with status and hold_until; hold and confirm endpoints with idempotency keys. 13–22 v1 and its bug Draw v1, then show the check-then-book race with two users. 22–30 Fix Conditional UPDATE; why no cleanup job is needed; why no long transaction. 30–40 Scale CDN + cache for browse; Elasticsearch via CDC for search; waiting room for on-sales. 40–45 Wrap-up Payment timeouts and idempotency; what you'd monitor (hold success rate, queue length, p99).

docs.title: Staff-level lens
docs.text:
Question Staff answer The real problem No seat sold twice while 10M people arrive at once. Deciding number ~100k seats vs 10M users: bookings are capped, reads are not. Staff call and trade-off Conditional-update holds; virtual waiting room; browse is AP, booking is CP. Accept fans waiting in a queue. Raise before you're asked Payment timing out while the hold expires; bots; the read storm hitting the booking database. Senior stops at Row locking. Staff goes on to The waiting room as load control, bot mitigation and fairness, shielding the booking path. Run it Watch hold success rate, queue length, admit rate, booking p99.

All 29 problems through this lens: Staff-level answers.

docs.title: 8. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Check, then insert in application code. Correct-looking, wrong under concurrency.
  • Holding a database transaction open while the user pays. Locks pile up and throughput collapses.
  • Using Redis as the only record of a booking. Redis is a fine place for holds, but the booking must land in the durable database.
  • Treating browse and book the same. Making browsing strongly consistent wastes money; making booking eventually consistent sells seats twice.
  • Sharding the bookings database "for scale". Booking volume is capped by seat count; one primary handles it.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

What is the core double-booking bug?

Check, then book: two people both see the seat as free, then both buy it.

How do you fix it?

Make check and write one atomic statement, for example a conditional update on the seat (WHERE status = available), or a short reservation with a TTL.

How do you survive ten million people at on-sale time?

A virtual waiting room admits users at the rate the booking path can handle; browsing is cached separately.
