docs.title: Top-K videos (YouTube)
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Scaling writes · DDIA: Ch 11 windows, partitioned streams · Ch 6 partition by key

The design falls straight out of one number: hundreds of thousands of views per second.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: TOP-K VIDEOS (YOUTUBE) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• A counter row per video in a database can't take ~800k updates per second.
  • Stream views through Kafka partitioned by video ID; each consumer counts its videos in memory and keeps a local top-K.
  • Merge the per-partition top-K lists; the result is exact because each video lives in exactly one partition.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Top K most-viewed videos for the last hour, day, month, and all time

Non-functional

  • Query latency < 100ms
  • Freshness ~1 minute
  • Accurate counts (billing-grade not required, but no big drift)
  • Massive view volume

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 70B views/day ≈ ~800k views/s. 4B videos × 8B counters ≈ 32GB of state, spread over partitions.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
view events (video_id, ts) → per-minute counts per video → per-window top-K heap

GET /topk?window=hour|day|month|all&k=100

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Keep a views counter column on each video row. Every view runs UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1 WHERE id = ?. The top-K query is SELECT … ORDER BY views DESC LIMIT 100.

Where it breaks:

  • Writes: about 70 billion views a day is ~800k updates a second. Popular videos get thousands of updates a second on the same row, and each update must wait for the row lock held by the previous one. No single database can do this.
  • Reads: ORDER BY views over 4 billion videos is a huge sort, and an index on a constantly changing column would be updated 800k times a second.
  • Time windows: a single all-time counter can't answer "top videos in the last hour".

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: stream views through Kafka, partitioned by video
docs.text:
Why: 800k writes a second needs to be spread over many machines, and each video's views must be counted in one place, or you'd need to combine partial counts for every video.

How: each view becomes an event on Kafka, keyed by video_id. Kafka hashes the key, so every view of a given video goes to the same partition, and so to the same consumer. With, say, 100 partitions, each consumer handles about 8k views a second, which is easy to count in memory.

docs.title: Step 2: count in memory and keep a local top-K
docs.text:
Why: writing every single view to a database is exactly the problem we're escaping. And we only care about the top few, not the exact count of every one of 4 billion videos at every moment.

How: each consumer keeps per-video counts in memory, in per-minute buckets, and maintains a min-heap of its top K videos (K = 100). A min-heap keeps the smallest of the top K at the root, so checking whether a video now belongs takes O(1), and replacing takes O(log K). An aggregator collects each partition's top K, 100 partitions × 100 candidates = 10,000 videos, and picks the overall top 100. That merge is exact, not approximate (see the first deep dive).

docs.title: Step 3: support time windows, cache results, keep a safety net
docs.text:
Why: users want the top videos for the last hour, day and month, not just all time. And in-memory counts need a backup if consumers lose state.

How: with per-minute buckets, the last hour is the sum of the last 60 buckets. Each minute, add the new bucket and subtract the one that just fell out, so you never rescan. Longer windows use hourly or daily buckets. The finished top-K lists are written to a cache and served from there in well under 100 ms. Raw view events also land in S3, so a batch job can recompute exact counts if a stream bug is ever found.

docs.title: Why is the merge exact?
docs.text:
Why you might doubt it: merging "top 100 from each partition" sounds like it could miss a video that's 101st in two partitions but large overall.

Why it's exact: that can only happen if a video's views are split across partitions. Here they never are: Kafka sends all views of a video to the same partition, so each partition holds the complete count for its videos. If a video is in the global top 100, it must beat everything in its own partition except at most 99 others, so it is in that partition's local top 100. The global top K is therefore always inside the union of the local top Ks.

docs.title: Sliding windows?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: "the last hour" changes every minute. Recounting 60 minutes of events each time would mean rescanning millions of events.

How: keep a ring buffer of per-minute counts for each active video (60 slots for an hour). Every minute, the window total is updated as total += newest minute − minute that just expired. That's constant work per video, not a rescan. For a month, use hourly buckets (720 slots), because minute precision isn't needed at that range.

docs.title: Very hot video?
docs.text:
Why it's a problem: partitioning by video means a viral video sends all its views to one partition. Millions of views a second on one video can overload that consumer.

How: pre-aggregate before Kafka. Each server producing view events counts views per video locally for a second, then sends one event, "video 7: +3,412 views", instead of 3,412 events. The hot video's partition receives a few hundred messages a second instead of millions, and the total is identical.

docs.title: Approximate is OK?
docs.text:
Why consider it: exact counting needs memory for every active video, and careful partitioning.

How: a Count-Min Sketch estimates counts for any number of items in fixed memory. It may overestimate slightly, but never underestimates. Pair it with a heap of the current top candidates. That's ideal for "trending now", where small errors don't matter. Anything that pays people, like creator revenue, uses the exact partitioned counts.

docs.title: 7. Interview script (45 minutes)
docs.text: Time What you do Content 0–5 Functional requirements Top K most-viewed videos for the last hour, day, month, and all time 5–8 Non-functional requirements Query latency < 100ms; Freshness ~1 minute; Accurate counts (billing-grade not required, but no big drift); Massive view volume 8–10 Numbers that drive the design 70B views/day ≈ ~800k views/s. 4B videos × 8B counters ≈ 32GB of state, spread over partitions. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: Kafka → Counter P0 → Counter P1 … Pn → Aggregator → Redis / cache → S3 raw → batch. docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why not keep a counter row per video in a database?

About 800k updates a second on hot rows is far beyond what a database can take with row-level contention.

Why is merging per-partition top-K lists exact?

Partitioning by video ID means each video's full count lives in exactly one partition, so its true count is in that partition's list.

How would you handle one extremely hot video?

Pre-aggregate before Kafka (count locally for a second, then send one update) so one partition isn't overwhelmed.

docs.title: URL shortener (Bitly)
docs.text:
Beginner-friendly

Difficulty: Easy · Patterns: Scaling reads · DDIA: Ch 5 replicas · Ch 6 hash sharding

It sounds like a toy, but it is the cleanest example of a read-heavy system: almost every request is a redirect.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: URL SHORTENER (BITLY) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Redirects outnumber new links about 100 to 1, so the design is mostly about serving reads fast.
  • Generate short codes from a counter encoded in base62: unique by construction, no collision checks.
  • Put a cache in front of the database; a small share of links gets most clicks, so the hit rate is high.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Create a short URL for a long URL (optional custom alias, expiry)
  2. Redirect short URL → original URL

Non-functional

  • Redirect p99 < 100ms
  • 99.99% available for redirects
  • Short codes globally unique
  • Read:write ≈ 100:1

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 100M DAU × 10 clicks = 1B redirects/day ≈ 12k/s avg, ~100k/s peak. Writes ~1M/day ≈ 12/s. 1B URLs × 500B = 500GB, which fits one Postgres.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
urls(code PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at)

POST /urls {long_url, alias?, expires_at?} → short_url
GET /{code} → 302 Location: long_url

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Start with the smallest thing that meets the functional requirements: one service and one Postgres table.

  • Create: POST /urls generates a short code, inserts (code, long_url, …) into urls, and returns https://sho.rt/<code>.
  • Redirect: GET /{code} looks up the code by primary key and replies 302 with the long URL in the Location header.

Where it breaks: not on writes. About 12 new links a second is nothing for Postgres. It breaks on reads. Redirects run at about 12k a second on average and ~100k a second at peak, and every one is a database query. One Postgres primary serving 100k primary-key lookups a second is at or past its limit, and the redirect p99 target of 100 ms suffers first during spikes. Code generation also needs a decision: how do we make codes unique without checking the database for collisions every time?

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: put a cache in front of the database
docs.text:
Why: redirects outnumber writes 100 to 1, and the database can't serve 100k lookups a second by itself. But clicks are very uneven. A small share of links (a viral tweet, a campaign) gets most of the traffic. That pattern is perfect for a cache.

How: use cache-aside with Redis. On a redirect, look up code → long_url in Redis. On a hit (80%+ of the time, often far more), redirect in under a millisecond without touching Postgres. On a miss, read Postgres, store the result in Redis with a TTL, then redirect. Links almost never change, so stale data isn't a concern. If Postgres still sees too many misses, add read replicas.

docs.title: Step 2: generate codes from a counter, not a hash or random string
docs.text:
Why: random or hashed codes can collide, and each create would need "check if the code exists, retry if it does". That's an extra query, and a race if two creates pick the same code at once.

How: keep a global counter (Redis INCR, or a database sequence) and encode each number in base62 (0–9a–zA–Z). Every number is different, so every code is different: unique by construction, with no checks needed. Seven base62 characters give 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes. To avoid a counter call per create, each app server reserves a batch of 1,000 numbers at once and hands them out locally.

docs.title: How do you guarantee unique codes?
docs.text:
Why it's hard: with many app servers creating links at once, two of them could pick the same code. With random or hashed codes, collisions become more likely as the table fills up.

How: the counter-plus-base62 approach makes collisions impossible, because each number is issued once. If you prefer hashing (say, the first 7 characters of an MD5 of the URL), put a unique constraint on code and retry with a salt on conflict. One catch with counters: consecutive codes are guessable, so anyone can walk through all links. If that matters, pass the number through a reversible shuffle (a small block cipher or a multiplicative permutation) before encoding. It stays unique but looks random.

docs.title: 301 or 302?
docs.text:
Why it matters: the status code decides whether browsers come back to you on the next click.

How to choose: a 301 (permanent) redirect is cached by the browser, so later clicks go straight to the long URL without reaching you. That's less load, but you lose click analytics and can't change or expire the link. A 302 (temporary) redirect isn't cached, so every click reaches your service and can be counted, expired or edited. Most shorteners use 302 because analytics is part of the product. The cache in step 1 keeps the extra load cheap.

docs.title: What if the counter node dies?
docs.text:
Why it matters: if the counter is a single Redis instance and it is lost, a new one might start again from an old value and reissue codes that already exist.

How: make the counter durable: Redis with append-only persistence plus a replica, or use a Postgres sequence, which is durable by design. Combined with batching, servers lease ranges ("give me the next 1,000"), so the counter is touched rarely. If a server crashes holding an unused range, those numbers are simply skipped. Gaps are harmless; duplicates are the only real danger.

docs.title: Custom aliases?
docs.text:
Why it's tricky: users want readable codes like sho.rt/summer-sale, which must not clash with generated codes or with each other.

How: store aliases in the same table, protected by the same unique constraint on code. If the insert fails, the alias is taken, so tell the user. To make sure an alias can never collide with a future generated code, separate the namespaces: for example, generated codes are exactly 7 characters and aliases must be 8 or more, or contain a character the generator never uses.

docs.text:

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Try to answer before you open each one.

Why use a counter encoded in base62 instead of hashing the long URL?

A counter is unique by construction, so there are no collisions to check. Hashing needs a collision check and retry on every insert.

Should the redirect be 301 or 302, and why?

302 (temporary) if you need click analytics, because browsers don't cache it and every click reaches you. 301 is cached by browsers and saves load but hides repeat clicks.

Why does a cache work so well here?

Redirects outnumber writes about 100:1 and a small share of links get most clicks, so the hit rate is high and links rarely change.

docs.title: Video platform (YouTube)
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Handling large blobs · Scaling reads · DDIA: Ch 10 batch DAGs · Ch 1 bandwidth math

Two hard problems: getting gigabyte uploads in reliably, and streaming smoothly on any connection.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: VIDEO PLATFORM (YOUTUBE) on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Upload directly to object storage with presigned, multipart, resumable URLs; bytes never touch your servers.
  • Split videos into segments and transcode them in parallel into several resolutions.
  • Serve segments from a CDN and let the player switch quality per segment (adaptive bitrate).

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Upload videos (up to many GB)
  2. Watch videos with smooth playback on any network

Non-functional

  • Resumable uploads
  • Fast start, adaptive quality
  • ~1M uploads/day; billions of views
  • Metadata availability over consistency

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 1M uploads/day × 1GB raw ≈ 1PB/day raw, plus several renditions. Views are mostly served from the CDN, not origin.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
videos(id, uploader, title, status UPLOADING|PROCESSING|READY, manifest_url)
S3 raw/ + processed/{rendition}/{segment}

POST /videos → {video_id, presigned multipart URLs}
GET /videos/{id} → manifest URL
PUT parts directly to S3

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Users upload a video file through the API, which saves it to storage. Viewers download the same file through the API and play it.

Where it breaks:

  • Uploads: a 1 GB+ file through the API servers ties up a connection, memory and bandwidth for minutes. A dropped connection at 90% means starting over. About 1M uploads a day is roughly 1 PB a day flowing through your servers.
  • Playback: one big file at one quality is a terrible experience. On a slow phone connection it buffers constantly; on a fast one, a low-quality file looks bad. The player has to download a large chunk before playing.
  • Views: billions of views a day served from your origin servers would need enormous bandwidth.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: upload directly to object storage, in parts
docs.text:
Why: your API servers should never carry video bytes, and uploads must survive bad connections.

How: POST /videos creates a videos row with status UPLOADING and returns presigned multipart upload URLs. The client splits the file into parts (say 10 MB each) and uploads them in parallel, directly to S3. If a part fails, only that part is retried. If the app is closed, the upload resumes later from the missing parts. Your servers handle only small metadata calls (see Handling large blobs).

docs.title: Step 2: transcode in parallel into segments and renditions
docs.text:
Why: viewers need many versions: different resolutions (240p to 4K) for different devices and network speeds, and short segments, so playback can start quickly and quality can change mid-video. Transcoding a 2-hour 4K video in one piece takes hours.

How: when the upload completes, an S3 event starts a processing pipeline, a DAG of tasks:

  1. Split the video into short segments (a few seconds each).
  2. Transcode every segment into every resolution, in parallel across many workers.
  3. Write HLS/DASH manifests: index files listing each rendition and its segments.
  4. Mark the video READY.

Hundreds of workers each handling a small segment turn hours of transcoding into minutes.

docs.title: Step 3: serve from a CDN with adaptive bitrate
docs.text:
Why: billions of views need to be served from close to viewers, and each viewer's bandwidth changes from moment to moment.

How: the player fetches the manifest and then the segments from a CDN, so your origin rarely serves a byte. The player measures how fast segments arrive and picks the quality for each next segment. On a fast connection it moves up to 1080p; if the train enters a tunnel, it drops to 360p rather than stalling. This is adaptive bitrate streaming.

docs.title: Why presigned URLs?
docs.text:
Why not proxy through the API: every byte through your servers costs bandwidth, memory and time, and multi-GB uploads make servers fragile and expensive to scale.

How it works: a presigned URL is an S3 URL with a signature that grants permission to upload one specific object for a short time, without giving the client credentials. The client talks directly to S3, which is built for massive parallel uploads. Multipart upload adds parallel parts and resumability. Your API only issues URLs and records metadata.

docs.title: Fast transcoding?
docs.text:
Why it's slow by default: transcoding is CPU-heavy, and a long video processed start-to-finish on one machine takes far longer than the video itself.

How: parallelize at the segment level. Split the video into segments of a few seconds, and transcode each segment into each rendition as an independent task on a large worker pool. A 2-hour video might become thousands of small tasks running at once. An orchestrator tracks the DAG, so it knows when every task for a rendition is done, retries failures, and writes the manifest when everything's ready.

docs.title: Adaptive bitrate?
docs.text:
Why it's needed: network speed varies between viewers and over time for the same viewer. A fixed quality either buffers or looks unnecessarily bad.

How: the manifest lists the available renditions (240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p…), each split into the same time-aligned segments. Because segments line up, the player can switch rendition at any segment boundary. It measures download throughput and buffer level, and chooses the highest quality it can fetch faster than it plays.

docs.title: Cost?
docs.text:
Why it matters: transcoding every upload into every format and storing all of it is expensive, and most videos get very few views.

How: transcode eagerly only the common renditions that nearly every video needs. Generate rarer ones (4K, extra codecs) lazily, only when a video becomes popular enough to justify them. Move rarely-watched videos' files to cheaper storage tiers over time. The CDN already keeps popular content close to viewers, so origin bandwidth stays low.

Views are mostly served from the CDN, not origin. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: S3 raw → Transcode DAG → S3 processed → CDN → Viewer. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Why presigned URLs? · Fast transcoding? · Adaptive bitrate? · Cost? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

Raise before you're asked Transcode failures and retries; storage cost; popularity spikes. Senior stops at S3 + CDN. Staff goes on to A cost model (storage tiers, lazy encoding), DAG retries, CDN strategy. Run it Watch upload success, time to playable, CDN hit ratio, rebuffer rate.

docs.title: Web crawler
docs.text:
Advanced

Difficulty: Hard · Patterns: Scaling writes · DDIA: Ch 10 batch pipelines · Ch 3 Bloom filters · Ch 11 queues

Ten billion pages in five days is a pipeline problem, constrained by politeness and network bandwidth.

Tip

One-page sketchnote: WEB CRAWLER on a single page, for revision or printing.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• About 23k pages per second; size the fleet by network bandwidth, not CPU.
  • Split fetching and parsing into separate stages with queues and stored raw pages, so each scales and retries on its own.
  • Respect per-domain rate limits and robots.txt, and skip already-seen URLs and duplicate content.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional

  1. Crawl from seed URLs, fetch pages, extract text, follow links
  2. Store text for LLM training: 10B pages in 5 days

Non-functional

  • Politeness: robots.txt, per-domain rate limits
  • Fault tolerant: resume without losing progress
  • No duplicate URLs or content
  • Efficient (network-bound)

docs.title: 2. Back-of-envelope numbers
docs.text: 10B ÷ 5 days ≈ 23k pages/s. × ~2MB ≈ 46GB/s, so size the fleet by network bandwidth, not CPU. Raw storage ~20PB → S3.

docs.title: 3. Core entities and API
docs.text:
urls(url_hash PK, url, status, last_crawled)
domains(domain, robots, crawl_delay, next_allowed_at)

internal: frontier queue messages {url, depth}
S3: raw/{url_hash}, text/{url_hash}

docs.title: 4. v1: the simplest design, and where it breaks
docs.text:
Put the seed URLs in a frontier queue. A pool of workers loops: take a URL, download the page, extract the text and the links, save the text, and add the new links back onto the queue.

Where it breaks: the target is 10 billion pages in 5 days, about 23k pages a second, or roughly 46 GB/s of downloads. One kind of worker doing everything hits several problems at once:

  • Mixed bottlenecks: downloading waits on the network, while parsing HTML burns CPU. Each worker spends time idle on one while the other waits, so you can't size the fleet well for either.
  • Fragility: if parsing crashes on a weird page, the download is wasted. If you improve the parser later, you'd have to re-download billions of pages.
  • Impoliteness: nothing stops 500 workers hitting the same site at once, which gets you blocked and can take small sites down.
  • Duplicates: the same URL is discovered thousands of times, and without dedup it is crawled thousands of times.

docs.title: 5. Evolving to the final design
docs.text: Each step fixes one specific problem with the step before it.

docs.title: Step 1: split fetching from parsing
docs.text:
Why: fetching is network-bound and parsing is CPU-bound. They need different machines in different numbers, and they fail for different reasons.

How: fetchers take URLs from the frontier, download the raw HTML, save it to S3 keyed by the URL's hash, and put a message on a second queue. Parsers read from that queue, load the HTML from S3, and extract the text and links. Each stage scales on its own, and a parser crash just retries the parse. Because the raw pages are stored, you can re-parse everything with an improved parser without crawling again.

docs.title: Step 2: be polite, per domain
docs.text:
Why: websites have limits and rules. robots.txt says what you may crawl and how fast. Ignoring it gets your crawler blocked and can overload small sites.

How: for each domain, fetch and cache robots.txt in Redis, and keep a per-domain rate limit, such as a token bucket or a "next allowed fetch time". Before fetching, a worker checks the domain's limit. If it isn't allowed yet, the URL is re-queued with a delay (for example by setting the queue message's visibility timeout), and the worker moves on to a URL from another domain. Total throughput stays high while each site sees only a gentle trickle.

docs.title: Step 3: deduplicate URLs and content
docs.text:
Why: popular pages are linked from millions of places, and many sites serve the same content under different URLs. Crawling duplicates wastes bandwidth and fills the dataset with repeats.

How: normalize each extracted URL (lowercase the host, remove fragments and tracking parameters, sort query parameters), hash it, and check whether it has been seen before adding it to the frontier. Use the urls table, or a Bloom filter for a fast first check. After fetching, hash the content too: identical content under a different URL (mirrors, http vs https) is stored once.

docs.title: Why separate stages?
docs.text:
Why it's worth the complexity: the two halves have different bottlenecks (network vs CPU), different failure modes (timeouts and slow servers vs malformed HTML) and different change rates (the parser changes often, while fetching is stable).

What you get: each stage scales and retries independently, and stored raw pages make the expensive part, the crawl, a one-time cost. When you improve text extraction, you re-run only the parsers over 20 PB in S3, which is far cheaper and faster than re-crawling 10 billion pages.

docs.title: Crash mid-crawl?
docs.text:
Why it matters: over 5 days and thousands of machines, workers will crash. You must not lose progress or corrupt anything.

How: a fetcher acknowledges a URL's queue message only after the raw page is safely in S3. If it crashes before that, the message becomes visible again and another worker fetches it. That's at-least-once processing. A page might occasionally be fetched twice, so make it harmless: it's stored under its URL hash, so a second fetch simply overwrites the same object (idempotent). Crawl status in the urls table lets you resume after a full restart.

docs.title: Crawler traps?
docs.text:
Why they exist: some sites generate infinite URLs, like calendars with a "next month" link forever, or session IDs in every link, so a naive crawler never leaves them.

How: cap the depth and the number of pages per domain, normalize URLs so session-ID variants collapse into one, and use content hashes to notice when "new" pages are the same content again. Domains that hit the caps are flagged for review.

docs.title: DNS bottleneck?
docs.text:
Why it happens: each fetch needs the domain's IP address. At 23k fetches a second, querying DNS each time overwhelms public resolvers and adds latency to every request.

How: cache DNS answers in each worker (respecting their TTLs). Most fetches go to domains already crawled recently, so the hit rate is very high. Run your own resolvers, or several, so DNS isn't a single point of failure or a rate-limited shared service.

Raw storage ~20PB → S3. 10–13 Entities and API Keep it short: the endpoints in §3, idempotency keys on writes. 13–25 v1, then evolve it Draw v1 and show where it breaks. Then add, in order: S3 raw HTML → Parse queue → Parser workers → S3 text → Redis → URL dedupe. Justify each addition with a number. 25–40 Deep dives Why separate stages? · Crash mid-crawl? · Crawler traps? · DNS bottleneck? 40–45 Wrap-up Remaining bottlenecks, failure modes, what you would monitor.

One hand-drawn page per topic, with as much as fits on a single sheet: the TL;DR, requirements, numbers, the final architecture, the naive version and why it breaks, deep dives, and what to say or avoid. Use them for revision, print them, or pin one above your desk.

Each page links to the full write-up. All 59 pages are also in one printable file: sketchnotes PDF.

docs.title: Slide decks
docs.text:
Three interactive decks with the same content as the handbook, for quick review and out-loud practice. Diagrams build up one step at a time. Use → or Space to step, ↓ to skip a slide, A to show all steps, O for an overview of all slides. They work on phones too: swipe, or tap a diagram.

Deck Slides Use it to DDIA in diagrams 96 Review all 12 chapters of Designing Data-Intensive Applications, each ending with its interview angle Learn deck 81 See the 7 patterns, 9 concepts and 29 problems built step by step Staff atlas 29 See every problem at staff level at once: deciding number, staff call, failures to raise, how to run it Interview deck 96 Rehearse: requirements and numbers, architecture, then deep-dive questions with hidden answers

Each deck is a single HTML file, so you can download it and use it offline.
